Oṃ, homage to you, the one who takes away [evil] with your pure luster; homage to you, the radiant flame!
May your other weapons burn others than us; O Purifier, be auspicious toward us. (8)

Oṃ, vāc for the one seated among men, vāc for the one seated in the waters, vāc for the one seated on the sacrificial grass, vāc for the one seated in the forest, vāc for the one who finds the light! 9.

Oṃ! Those gods who among the gods are worthy of sacrifice, who among those worthy of sacrifice sit for their share of the year-long [offering], they, unswerving at this sacrifice of the oblation, let them themselves drink of the honey and the ghee. 10.
Oṃ! Those gods who have attained divinity among the gods, who are the precursors of this Brahman; without whom no abode whatsoever is purified, neither from heaven nor from earth—Oṃ!
Giver of out-breath, giver of in-breath, giver of diffused breath, giver of splendor, giver of wide space!
Let your other weapons scorch them; O Purifier, be auspicious toward us. 12.
Then, one should perform the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).

Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ haṃ saḥ sohaṃ | The vital breaths (prāṇas) of this image of the venerable Durgā are here; they are here. Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ haṃ saḥ sohaṃ | Of this venerable... [image].
Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ haṃ saḥ sohaṃ. O Soul of this image of Śrī Durgā, remain here!
[May] all the senses of this image of Śrī Durgā—speech, mind, skin, eyes, ears, tongue, nose, hands, and feet—[be present].
May the anus and the generative organ come here and remain happily for a long time, svāhā! Oṃ!
May the inspiration of the mind enjoy the clarified butter; may Bṛhaspati further this sacrifice;
may he establish the sacrifice as unimpaired; may all the gods rejoice here, oṃ 3.

Pratiṣṭhā. "Oṃ, this indeed is the sacrifice named Pratiṣṭhā; where they perform this sacrifice, everything becomes firmly established. Having thus performed the Pratiṣṭhā, then follows the opening of the eyes: "Oṃ, you are the pupil of Vṛtra; you are the giver of sight; bestow sight upon me. [Offer] perfumes and other articles.
Having offered the five types of worship (pañcopacāra), one should perform the repetition of the sixteen Praṇavas for the sake of perfecting the consecration.

"By this, I perform for this image of Śrī Durgā the sixteen sacraments, beginning with *garbhādhāna*," thus one should recite. Then, having placed the image of Śrī Durgā upon the principal water-jar (*pradhānakalaśa*), one should worship it with either the sixteen or the five articles of offering (*upacāra*).
Oṃ! [I bow to her] who is endowed with a mass of matted hair marked by the crescent moon, who is possessed of three eyes, and whose face resembles a lotus or the moon. (1)
Having the luster of the color of an Atasī flower, well-established, with beautiful eyes, endowed with fresh youth, and adorned with all ornaments. || 2 ||
Likewise, she has a most beautiful face and full, elevated breasts;
she stands in the triple-bend posture (tribhaṅga) as the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
One should place a trident in the right hand, and below it, a sword and a discus in succession; likewise, understand that a sharp arrow and a spear are to be placed from the left as well.
One should present a shield, a full bow, a noose, a goad, and a raised banner,
or else a bell or an axe, on the left side.
Likewise, one should depict below it a buffalo with two heads,
and similarly a Dānava arising from the severing of its head, holding a sword in his hand.
His heart was pierced by a spear, he was adorned with ornaments,
his limbs were stained crimson with blood, and for a moment his eyes were wide open with blood.
His face was terrifying with a frown, and he was encircled by the serpent-noose;
Durgā held him by the hair with her left hand, which still grasped the noose.
One should visualize the lion of the Goddess as having a face dripping with blood;
the Goddess’s right foot is placed evenly upon the lion.
One should likewise place the left thumb slightly raised above a buffalo,
that form being praised by the immortals.
Ugracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā, Caṇḍanāyikā, Caṇḍā, Caṇḍavatī, Caṇḍarūpā, and Aticaṇḍikā. || 11 ||
One should constantly meditate upon the Goddess, who bestows dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as she is perpetually surrounded by these eight powers.
36) Having thus meditated upon the Goddess and raised Kuṇḍalinī from the Mūlādhāra together with Śiva—

Having joined [the breath] with the seed-syllable of Vāyu, one should invoke the Goddess into the nostril with a handful of flowers, saying: "Come, O Durgā, O Great Goddess! For the sake of my protection at all times, I invoke you, O Goddess, for the attainment of all desires."

Having thus offered a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) into the flask or the yantra, one should meditate upon oneself in the form of the Goddess and perform worship. The mantras for that are as follows:
Now follows the procedure for the Vedic worship of Durgā;
next is the invocation (āvāhana) [as stated by Vācaspati on that very point].
One should always perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) for an image made of clay; however, for a [metal] idol, water, or fire, there is neither invocation nor dismissal (*visarjana*).
Oṃ, golden-hued, tawny, adorned with garlands of gold and silver!
O Jātavedas, bring to me the golden Lakṣmī who is as radiant as the moon.
Oṃ. The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.
Having pervaded the earth on all sides, he stood beyond it by ten fingers' breadth. || 1 ||
Oṃ, come here, O Great Goddess! O bestower of all prosperity! Remain present until this vow is completed. Thus is the invocation.
Oṃ! O Jātavedas, bring to me that ever-present Lakṣmī, through whom I may find gold, cattle, horses, and men. (1)
Oṃ. The Person alone is all this—that which has been and that which is to be;
moreover, he is the lord of immortality, which transcends through food. 2.
"Please accept this divine throne, composed of refined gold, joined with many jewels and endowed with various collections of gems. Thus [is the offering of] the seat.
Water for washing the feet.
Oṃ! I invoke the goddess Śrī, who is borne upon a chariot filled with horses, who rejoices in the trumpeting of elephants; may the goddess Śrī be pleased with me.
Oṃ. Such is His greatness, yet the Puruṣa is even greater than this.
All beings constitute one quarter of Him; His three quarters are the immortal in heaven. 3.

"This water, pleasing to the touch, brought by me from all the sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā at your request—please accept it for the purpose of washing the feet. Thus [is offered] the water for the feet (pādya).
Arghya:
Om! Her whose smile is like bell-metal, who has a golden rampart, who is moist, blazing, satisfied, and satisfying;
who dwells upon a lotus, who is lotus-colored—her, Śrī, I invoke here.
Oṃ. With three quarters the Puruṣa rose upward; one quarter of him came into being here again.
Thence he spread out over everything, over that which eats and that which does not eat.
O Goddess seated upon a lion! You indeed possess priceless qualities among all treasures and jewels; accept this water of honor (arghya); salutations unto you. (4) Thus ends the offering of arghya.

Now, regarding the *madhuparka* [Pārāśara states: "Clarified butter is said to have one quality; purified honey has two qualities. In the ritual for the *madhuparka*, curd is said to be equal to the clarified butter"].
*Oṃ madhuvvātā ṛtāyate madhukṣarantisindhavaḥ*.
May the plants be honey-sweet for us.
Accept this madhuparka, consisting of curd, honey, and clarified butter, presented together with a pair of vessels; O auspicious one, be the bestower of welfare.
Now, the ritual sipping of water (ācamana):
Oṃ. I take refuge in that lotus-faced one, the moon-like, radiant, and glorious Śrī, who blazes with fame and is cherished by the gods in the world; may misfortune perish through you.
I choose.
Oṃ. From that, Virāj was born; from Virāj, Puruṣa was born as the overlord.
Once born, he extended beyond the earth, both behind and before.
"O Goddess! May you accept this water for the purpose of sipping (ācamana), fragrant with camphor, sweet-smelling, pure, delicious, and cool. Thus ends the ācamana.
(p. 38) Now, the bath:
Oṃ, born from the heat of asceticism, with the color of the sun, the tree of you [the deity] is the *bilva* tree.
May its fruits dispel internal delusions through austerity, as well as external obstacles and misfortune.
Oṃ. From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) was gathered.
He made those animals dependent on the wild and the non-domestic, such as those belonging to Vāyu.
Scented with golden lotuses brought from the Mandākinī river.
"Perform your bath, O Goddess of gods, with fragrant waters! Thus ends the bath (snāna). 7.
Once again, this water for sipping:
for him by whose mere remembrance even one who is defiled by food remnants or impure attains purity— to you, this water for sipping.
It is likewise prescribed at the conclusion of bathing, changing one's clothes, and putting on the sacred thread.
For the fragrant oil bath:
*Oṃ aguṃ śunāte 'aguṃśuḥ pṛcyatāṃ paruṣāparuḥ | gandhaste somamavatu madāya raso 'cyutaḥ || Oṃ, accept this unguent with unguent.*
O Queen of the World! O Great Sinless One! O Pure-Souled One in all worlds! I bestow upon you supreme affection.
The bath with the five nectars: Oṃ, may there be milk on the earth, milk in the plants, milk in the divine atmosphere, and milk below; may the quarters of space be full of milk for me.
Produced from the wish-fulfilling cow, it is the supreme sustenance for all.
The water offered for the purpose of bathing is purifying and a cause for sacrifice. || 1 ||
The curd-bath:
*Oṃ dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣaṃ jiṣṇor aśvasya vājinaḥ | surabhi no mukhā karat pra ṇa āyūṃṣi tāriṣat*. [This] has arisen from milk; it is sweet and sour.
"O Goddess! Please accept this moon-like radiance brought by me for the purpose of your bath. (11)
The ghee-bath:
*oṃ* ghṛtaṃ ghṛtapāvānaḥ pibata vasāṃ vasāpāvānaḥ pibatāntarikṣasya.

Havir asi svāhā! To the quarters, the intermediate quarters, the primary quarters, the subsidiary quarters, and the upward quarters—svāhā to the quarters! I shall offer this sacred clarified butter, produced from fresh butter and causing the satisfaction of all;
please accept it for the purpose of bathing. 12.
Honey-bath:
*Oṃ madhunaktaṃ madhuṣasaḥ madhumatpārthivaṃ rajaḥ | madhu dyaurastu naḥ pitā ||* Honey produced from trees and flowers, delicious, sweet honey, which bestows vigor and nourishment.
Please accept this divine [garment] for the purpose of bathing. || 13 ||
The sugar-bath:
*Oṃ apāṃ guṃ rasam udvayasa guṃ sūrye santaṃ guṃ samāhitam | apāṃ guṃ rasasya yo rasas taṃ vo gṛhṇāmy uttamam upayāmagṛhīto 'sīndrāya tvā juṣṭam*.

I take this, O Lord, as your most beloved womb for Indra. This divine sugar, produced from the essence of sugarcane, which bestows nourishment and removes impurities, is accepted for the purpose of bathing.

The Bath with the Five Nectars (*pañcāmṛta-snāna*) [from the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "Milk is ten times [more effective than water]; curd is ten times more than that; ghee is ten times more than that; honey is ten times more than that; and sugar is even greater than that. Oṃ! The five rivers flow into the Sarasvatī with their currents; the Sarasvatī, however, flows in five ways.
In that region, there are rivers, as well as milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar.
"The five nectars have been brought by me for the purpose of bathing; please accept them. (15)
For the sandalwood bath: Oṃ, we invoke here that Śrī, who is the gate of fragrance, invincible, eternally nourishing, bountiful,
and the sovereign of all beings.
Produced on the Malaya mountain, it originates from sandalwood and agallochum.
"O Goddess! O Queen of Gods! Please accept this sandalwood for the purpose of bathing. || 16 ||
p.
40) Fragrant unguent for bathing:
*oṃ aguṃ śunāte 'guṃ śuḥ pṛcyatāṃ paruṣāparuḥ | gandhaste soma*.
May this unshakable essence not lead to intoxication.
Various fragrant substances, sandalwood, and turmeric—this unguent has been offered by me; please accept it for the purpose of bathing. (17)
Now, the ritual bath with pure water:
*Oṃ śuddhavālaḥ sarva-śuddhavālo maṇivālasta āśvināḥ śyetaḥ śyetākṣoruṇaste rudrāya paśupataye karṇāyāmā-avaliptā raudrāḥ*.
Those belonging to Parjanya have the form of the sky.
Again, I offer water for sipping; obeisance.
Two [deities], the friend of the gods and Kīrti, together with Maṇi, have approached this garment;
having manifested here in Surāṣṭra, may they grant me fame and prosperity.
From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the Ṛg-verses and Sāman-chants were born;
from it the meters were born, and from it the Yajus-formula was produced.
O Goddess! O Durgā, destroyer of misfortune! Out of compassion, please put on this pair of silken garments along with the bodice.
Thus ends the pair of garments. Again, the water for sipping.
Now, the sacred thread (upavīta).
Oṃ! I destroy hunger, thirst, impurity, and the elder goddess of misfortune;
drive away from my home all ill-fortune and lack of prosperity.
Oṃ, from that [the waters] were born horses, and whatever other [beasts] there were that fear this.
From him cows were born; from him goats and sheep were born.
"O Supreme Goddess, accept this divine sacred thread made of golden thread, fashioned by Brahmā in ancient times, which has been offered by me."
Now, for the sandalwood bath:
Oṃ, I invoke here Śrī, who is the gate of fragrance, invincible, eternally nourishing,
and the mistress of all beings.
Om. They sprinkled that sacrifice upon the sacrificial grass—the Puruṣa born in the beginning.
By means of him, the gods and the ṛṣis who were perfected performed the sacrifice.
O Queen of Gods! Please accept this divine sandalwood paste from Śrīkhaṇḍa, rich in fragrance and most enchanting, as an unguent.
Thus ends the section on sandalwood. Now follows the gift of the auspicious thread (*saubhāgyasūtra*).
Oṃ! O Bestower of Boons, O Goddess of Gods! I bind this auspicious thread, joined with gold and jewels, around my neck; grant me perpetual good fortune.
I offer this sacred thread; salutations.
Unharmed—Om! They have eaten and they have rejoiced; the beloved ones have shaken themselves; they have praised, O self-radiant ones, with their most excellent hymn.
You have yoked your two bay steeds for the sake of the sacrifice.
"O Great Goddess! Accept these unbroken, stainless, pure, and pearl-encrusted grains;
grant me a stainless intellect. Thus, [the offering of] the unbroken grains (akṣata).
O Goddess, you who bestow happiness and good fortune, you are dyed with the powder of turmeric;
therefore, I worship you here— grant me happiness and peace.
I offer turmeric powder; obeisance.
Gulāla is saffron, divine and bestowing beauty, born from the desire of amorous women;
O Goddess, Supreme Sovereign, be gracious to me who have worshipped you with saffron!
Thus, I offer saffron; homage!
Sindūra is vermilion, possessing a reddish luster like that of a hibiscus flower.
O Goddess! This has been offered by me to you; be gracious, O Supreme Sovereign!
I offer vermilion; salutations.
O fortunate one! O Supreme Goddess! Accept this beautiful collyrium, produced from the light of camphor, which brings peace and is pleasing to the eyes.
Thus, I offer collyrium to the eyes; obeisance!
O Jātavedas, bring hither the Durvā sprout, Oṃ Dārdrā, Puṣkariṇī, Puṣṭi, Piṅgalā, Padmamālinī, Candrā, Hiraṇmayī, and Lakṣmī.
Oṃ! From joint to joint you sprout, from knot to knot you grow.
Even so, O dūrvā grass, spread yourself forth with a thousand and a hundred shoots.
O Goddess who are as pure as a blade of dūrvā grass, O Earth-form beloved of Hari!
Therefore, O Śivā, I worship you always with dūrvā blades.
Thus, I offer blades of dūrvā grass; obeisance!
The Offering of Bilva Leaves:
Oṃ, bring here to me, O Jātavedas, the golden Lakṣmī, who is radiant, who holds a beautiful golden staff, who wears a garland of gold, and who is like the sun.
Oṃ, homage to the one who is armored and to the one who wears a breastplate; homage to the one who is clad in mail and to the one who possesses a chariot-fender;
homage to the one who is renowned and to Śrutasena; homage to the one who is the drum and to the one who is the drumstick.
The sacred tree born from nectar is always dear to Mahādeva.
O Goddess of the gods, I offer you this sacred bilva leaf!
Thus, I offer bilva leaves; salutations.
The offering of the sacrificial fee (pallārpaṇa):
Oṃ, O Jātavedas, bring here for me Lakṣmī, who does not depart;
through her, may I obtain gold, abundance, cows, female slaves, horses, and male servants.
Oṃ! Your seat is on the aśvattha tree; your dwelling is made upon the parṇa leaves.
O you who share in the cattle, you have indeed protected the man who strives for you.
And at the door of the house, O fierce destroyer of even the most wicked asuras!
O lady of beautiful limbs! I perform worship with sprouts born from the Nandana grove.
Thus I offer these sprouts; obeisance!
The Offering of the Garland of Fruits:
*Oṃ mahādevīṃ ca vidmahe viṣṇupatnīṃ ca dhīmahi | tanno devīḥ pracodayāt*. *Oṃ yāḥ phalinīryā aphalā apuṣpā yāśca puṣpiṇīḥ | bṛhaspati...*
May those who have brought forth release us from the *agu* and the *hasa*.
O Goddess, crusher of the demon Niśumbha! O you who are worshipped by the gods! Accept this excellent garland of fruits produced in the autumn season.
Thus, I offer this garland of fruits; obeisance!

Wearing a Garland of Jewels: "Pearl, ruby, lapis lazuli, agate, diamond, coral, topaz, emerald, *garuḍodgāra* (sapphire), and cat's-eye—strung together with gold by means of these, it is called a 'garland of jewels' (*ratnamālā*). —From the *Śāradā*.

Oṃ, Agni, the lord of wandering mendicants and the seer, has stepped forth toward the sacrificial offerings, bestowing jewels upon the donor. Oṃ, through the primordial mud (*kardama*) all beings were born; O *Kardama*, bestow your attention upon me! Dwell in my house (or lineage), O Mother adorned with a garland of lotuses, wearing a necklace of pearls. [Bestow] the garland joined with pearls.
O Giver of Boons, salutations to you! Please accept this [garland] of radiant jewels and lapis lazuli, strung with rubies and gold.
Thus, I offer this garland of jewels; homage!
Oṃ! May the waters produce a garland; may they make my house smooth and pleasant. O Goddess Śrī, the Mother, dwell within my family.
Oṃ! Śrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives; day and night are your two sides; the stars are your form; the Aśvins are your gaping mouth.
Bestowing, bestow upon us; bestow upon all the world; bestow [upon me].
The variety [of the lake] is created by lotuses, conch-born flowers, and other blossoms such as the hundred-petaled lotus.
I offer this garland of flowers; please accept it, O Sovereign of the Gods!
Thus, I offer this garland of flowers; homage!
O Flower!
May we obtain the desire of the mind and the intention of speech;
may the form of cattle and the essence of food, prosperity, and glory rest within me.
Oṃ. When they divided the Puruṣa, into how many parts did they arrange him? What was his mouth, what were his arms, and what are said to have been his thighs and feet?
O Goddess, worship is performed for you with various divine flowers, such as water-lilies and campaka blossoms;
please accept these flowers.
He worshipped with mandāra, pārijāta, and other flowers, as well as pāṭalī and ketakī.
"O beautiful one, take these jasmine and campaka flowers!"
Thus I offer flowers; obeisance!
The flowers to be offered to Durgā are:
kunda, mandāra, punnāga, pāṭalī, nāga, keśara, āragvadha, karṇikāra, jayantī, and the fresh mallikā. || 1 ||
Saugandhika, kaṅkola, punnāga, aśoka, mallikā, and other fragrant flowers and leaves [are to be used] as prescribed by the experts. (2)
Thus, in the Śaktipallava.
The Ornament.
May you accept these ornaments— necklaces, bracelets, armlets, girdles, earrings, and so forth—
rich with jewels and endowed with precious earrings.
In the absence of ornaments, I offer unbroken grains; homage!

Fragrant with its garland, Oṃ! Like a serpent with its coils, it encircles the arm; warding off the blow with its bowstring, the hand-guard, possessing all knowledge, may that man-like hero protect us from every side.
One should smear sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, as well as gorocana, musk, and other fragrant substances upon all the limbs.
Thus, I offer this fragrant substance; salutations!
For the limb-worship: Oṃ, salutation to Durgā; I worship the feet, salutation. Oṃ, salutation to Mahākālī; I worship the ankles, salutation.
Oṃ, salutations to Maṅgalā; I worship the two knees, salutations. Salutations to Kātyāyanī; I worship the two thighs, salutations. Oṃ, salutations to Bhadrakālī; I worship the waist.

Salutation! Oṃ, salutation to Kamalavāsinī; I worship the navel, salutation! Oṃ, salutation to Śivā; I worship the abdomen, salutation! Oṃ, salutation to Kṣamā; I worship the heart, salutation! Oṃ, salutation to Kaumāryā; I worship the breasts, salutation! Oṃ, salutation to Umā...
I worship the two hands; obeisance. Oṃ, obeisance to Mahāgaurī; I worship the right arm; obeisance. Oṃ, obeisance to Vaiṣṇavī; I worship the left arm; obeisance. Oṃ, obeisance to Ramā;
I worship the two shoulders; obeisance. Oṃ, obeisance to Skandamātṛ; [I worship] the throat.
I worship; obeisance. Oṃ, obeisance to Mahiṣamardinī; I worship the eyes; obeisance. Oṃ, obeisance to Siṃhavāhinī; I worship the face; obeisance. Oṃ, obeisance to Māheśvarī;
I worship the head; obeisance. Oṃ, obeisance to Kātyāyanī; I worship all the limbs; obeisance.
Thus, dear one, is the worship of the limbs.
The offering of incense:
Oṃ! He who, having become pure and self-restrained, should offer clarified butter daily;
and he who desires prosperity should constantly recite the hymn consisting of fifteen verses.
Oṃ! You are the remover; remove [evil]. Remove him who harms us;

may we remove him who harms us. You are the best bearer of the gods, the most refreshing, the most satisfying, the most beloved, and the best invoker of the gods. [I offer] incense of ten-ingredient guggulu.
O Great Goddess! Please accept this sandalwood and agallochum, combined together and offered by me with devotion.
The incense vessel and the deity are on the left; thus, I offer the incense for you to smell: *namaḥ*.
Now, for the lamps and unbroken grains (akṣata):
Oṃ! O Goddess whose abode is the lotus, who holds a lotus in your hand, who are adorned with most brilliant garments, perfumes, and garlands;
O Blessed One, beloved of Hari, charming one, bestower of prosperity upon the three worlds, be gracious unto me! Oṃ.
Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā! Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā!
Agni is splendor, light is splendor; Svāhā! Sūrya is splendor, light is splendor; Svāhā! Light is Sūrya, Sūrya is light; Svāhā!
O Queen of Gods! I shall offer this lamp, filled with a ghee-wick and blazing with great splendor; may you be forever well-pleased.
(As stated on p. 46:
One should display a lamp—specifically a ghee lamp with a white wick—on the right side of the deity;
[and] an oil lamp with a red wick on the left side of the deity.
Now, the food offering (naivedya).
I offer the food offering; obeisance. Having sprinkled with water.

Having covered [the vessel] with fragrant flowers, having rendered it nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā*, and having displayed the *yonimudrā*, one should ring the bell while reciting: "I sprinkle you with truth" (*satyantvartena paripiñcāmi*) in the morning; "I sprinkle you with truth through Ṛta" (*ṛtaṃtvāsatyena paripiñcāmi*) in the evening.

Having displayed the *grāsa-mudrā*: *Oṃ prāṇāya svāhā*, with the thumb, ring finger, and little finger. *Oṃ apānāya svāhā*, with the thumb, index finger, and middle finger. *Oṃ udānāya svāhā*, with the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger. *Oṃ vyānāya svāhā*.
With the thumb, index finger, and middle finger: *Oṃ samānāya svāhā*. With all the fingers:
*Oṃ ādrāṃ puṣkariṇīṃ puṣṭiṃ suvarṇāṃ hemamālinīm | sūryāṃ hiraṇmayīṃ lakṣmīṃ jātavedo ma āvaha*. *Oṃ from the navel arose the intermediate space; from the head, the sky.*
He evolved. From his feet the earth [arose], from his ears the directions; thus they fashioned the worlds.
O Goddess, please accept this fourfold food, sweet and endowed with the six flavors; grant me unwavering devotion.
I offer this food offering; obeisance!
I offer water for sipping at intervals; obeisance. For the purpose of refreshing the mouth, I repeatedly offer food offerings; obeisance. Again, I offer water for sipping; obeisance.
[This is] the sipping of water (ācamana).
O Jātavedas, bring to me that Lakṣmī who is tender, who holds a golden staff, who is tawny-hued, adorned with a garland of lotuses, moon-like, and made of gold.
Oṃ. With the Puruṣa as the oblation, the gods performed the sacrifice.
Spring was its clarified butter, summer its fuel, and autumn its oblation.
"O Goddess, please rinse your mouth; indeed, make my devotion unwavering."
Grant me my desired boon, and in the hereafter, grant me the supreme goal.
I offer the ceremonial sipping of water; salutations.
O Goddess! This hand-rotation rite performed with fragrant, scented substances—
grant me my desired boon and, in the hereafter, the supreme state.
I offer fragrance for the purpose of massaging the hands; homage!
This water for washing the hands has been brought as fragrant water contained within a golden vessel;
I offer this water to you for the purpose of washing your hands.
The fruit of the seasons.

Oṃ! Those plants which bear fruit and those which are unfruitful, those which blossom and those which are flowerless—impelled by Bṛhaspati, may they release us from the consumption of poison. [May there be] grapes, dates, plantains, jackfruit, mango, and wood-apple.
Please accept these fruits such as coconut, sugarcane, and jambu; I offer seasonal fruits, obeisance!
Tāmbūla is the betel nut (pūgīphala).

Oṃ! O Jātavedas, bring to me that Lakṣmī who never departs, through whom I may obtain gold, abundance, cows, female slaves, horses, and men. Oṃ! Seven were her enclosing sticks, and thrice seven were the fuel-sticks prepared when the gods were performing the sacrifice.
O Goddess of the Suras, I offer this betel-roll for the purpose of perfuming the mouth!
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consists of material goods.
Oṃ. In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists. He supported this earth and this heaven. To what god shall we offer our worship with oblation?
O Īśvarī! For the sake of the full fruition of the merit of this worship, gold has been placed before you;
therefore, being pleased with me, fulfill my heart's desires.
O Durgā! When remembered, you remove the fear of all living beings; when remembered by those established in well-being, you grant them supreme intelligence.

"You grant auspiciousness. O remover of the fear of poverty and suffering! Who else but you has a heart always tender toward performing every kind of assistance? Having thus bowed, one should mark a span on the ground with the mantra: "Oṃ! May the gods come; may the sorcerers depart. O Goddess Durgā! Protect the sacrifice."
One should prostrate.
The worship of the nine Durgās. First, the worship of Śailaputrī.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O Śailaputrī, come here! Stay here! Homage to Śailaputrī! I invoke Śailaputrī; I establish her, homage! Having performed the worship with water for the feet and other offerings:

Oṃ! O you who are worshipful to the world, worthy of veneration by the world, whose very nature is all-pervading power! O Kaumārī, accept this worship; O Mother of the World, salutations to you! || 1 ||
The worship of the celibate student (brahmacārin).

Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ! O Brahmācāriṇī! Come here, stay here; salutation to Brahmācāriṇī. I invoke Brahmācāriṇī, I establish her; salutation. Having performed the worship with water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings: Oṃ, to Tripurā, the support of the three qualities (guṇas), whose nature is the knowledge of the path.
I worship the Goddess, the triple-formed one, who is saluted by the three worlds. || 1 ||
The worship of Candraghaṇṭā.

Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ, O Candraghaṇṭā, come here, stay here; obeisance to Candraghaṇṭā. I invoke Candraghaṇṭā, I establish her; obeisance. Having performed the worship with water for the feet and other offerings: Oṃ, [I bow to] Kālikā, who transcends all parts, whose heart is auspicious, and who is Śivā.
I constantly worship the auspicious one, the mother of all that is good. || 3 ||
The worship of the Kūṣmāṇḍas.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, O Kūṣmāṇḍa, come here, stay here; obeisance to Kūṣmāṇḍā.
I invoke Kūṣmāṇḍā; I establish her; obeisance! Having performed the worship with water for the feet and other offerings:
"Oṃ, I worship that Kāmākṣī, who is exalted by qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and others, whose eyes are shaped like a sea-monster (makara), and who possesses infinite varieties of power. (4)
The worship of Skandamātā.

Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O Mother of Skanda! Come here; stay here, O Mother of Skanda, obeisance! I invoke the Mother of Skanda; I establish her, obeisance! Having performed the worship with water for the feet and other offerings: [I worship] Caṇḍavīrā, Caṇḍamāyā, and Caṇḍamuṇḍaprabhañjinī.
I bow to that Goddess of gods, Caṇḍikā, and I worship her. || 5 ||
The worship of Kātyāyanī.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O Kātyāyanī! Come here, stay here; obeisance to Kātyāyanī.
I invoke Kātyāyanī; I establish her; obeisance! Having performed the worship with water for the feet and other offerings.
Oṃ, she who bestows bliss and joy, the peaceful one, who is saluted by all the gods.
I worship the goddess Śāmbhavī, who is the self of all beings. || 6 ||
The worship of Kālarātrī.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O Kālarātri! Come here! Stay here! Salutation to Kālarātri!
"I invoke Kālarātri; I establish her; obeisance. Having performed the worship with water for the feet and other offerings.
I bow to that Goddess Caṇḍavīrā, Caṇḍamāyā, Raktabījaprabhañjinī; I worship Gāyatrī, the Mistress of the Gods. || 7 ||
The worship of Mahāgaurī.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O Mahāgaurī! Come here! Stay here! Homage to Mahāgaurī!
I invoke Mahāgaurī; I establish her; obeisance! Having performed the worship with water for the feet and other offerings:
Oṃ, I worship Subhadrā, the goddess who is beautiful, whose limbs are the color of gold, who bestows happiness and good fortune, and who generates contentment. (8)
Worship bestows success.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, O Siddhide! Come here, stay here; obeisance to Siddhidāyā.
"I invoke and establish you, the bestower of success; obeisance! Having performed the worship with water for the feet and other offerings.
Oṃ! O you who are difficult to reach, who are difficult to overcome in any task, and who destroy the fortress of fear! I always worship with devotion Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune. || 9 ||
Thus concludes the worship of the nine Durgās.
The worship of light.

Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O you who arise from the primordial essence, the sun, and the vital energy, whose nature is splendor, salutations to Śrī Durgā. Oṃ! We offer the Soma to Jātavedas; may he, who knows, burn away those who act as enemies. May he carry us across all difficulties, even as Agni carries us across the ocean, like a boat, beyond all misfortunes. [Offer] water for the feet and other articles [of worship].
Having performed the worship.
Meditative concentration.

May that supreme light of Māyā, which is the common essence of the three worlds due to the existence of the nature of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and its various manifestations, protect the universes eternally— even though she is manifest here through knowledge (*vidyā*). (From the *Yoginītantra*)

Having proclaimed the place and time during the great festival of the Nine Durgās: "For the pacification of all obstacles, for the attainment of my desired goal, and for the completion of this undertaking without impediment, through the grace of Śrī Durgā and by means of spiritual success (siddhi), I shall perform the worship of Kumārī accompanied by Vaṭuka, Gaṇeśa, and the others."

The Worship of Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, and the Nine Kumārīs. Now, regarding the worship of the Kumārīs and its procedure, it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa: Brahmā said: "O Śakra! The Goddess is not so pleased here by burnt offerings, gifts, or recitations as She is gratified by the feeding of a Kumārī. Here, during Navarātra—having washed..."

O Vāsava, all the young maidens should have their feet washed upon a beautiful, well-smeared ground; there they should be seated upon thrones. One should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and delightful garlands. Having worshipped them according to the prescribed rite, one should cause food to be given to them, consisting of sugar-candy, sweetmeat balls, molasses, clarified butter, curd, and milk.
[The offering] should include honey. To those maidens, one should give [the gift] and feed them with excellent food.

Water should be given when requested, or auspicious food when requested. When they are all satisfied, then one should offer water for sipping (ācamana). Having sipped water and offered unbroken rice grains (akṣata), one should say, "May you forgive me," while placing it upon the head of the donor.
Then unbroken grains (akṣatāḥ) should be offered by the young girls; he, in turn, should perform a prostration with devotion.

O Śakra! By this method, the Goddess quickly becomes propitious; O Lord of the Gods, she grants various desires cherished by the mind. Having ruled a kingdom, one subsequently goes to the world of the Goddess. It is also stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "One should worship each maiden with an increase of one [offering] at a time."

And likewise: two, three, or even nine [years] for each is excellent. By nine [years], one obtains the earth; by double that, sovereignty. By increasing by one [year at a time], one obtains security; by each [additional year], one obtains prosperity. A girl who is one year old should be used for the purpose of worship.

One should avoid [such a woman], for she finds no pleasure in perfumes, flowers, fruits, and the like. However, if the prescribed [gifts] are unavailable, even a married woman who is menstruating should be worshipped; until that time, she retains her status as a maiden, even though her marriage has already been consummated.

"A maiden is worshipped only so long as a flower is not seen [by her]"—thus, from the statement in the *Devīpurāṇa* made by the Lord Bhāskara. A specific rule regarding their worship in sequence according to their respective desires has been stated.

In that very [text]: "A person should worship the Kumārīs for the destruction of suffering and poverty, for the destruction of enemies, for the sake of longevity and the increase of strength; one desiring long life should worship Trimūrti, and for the attainment of the fruits of the three goals of life (trivarga), as well as for the removal of untimely death, the affliction of disease, and suffering, [one should worship] Saubhāgya."

For the increase of grain, wealth, health, sons, grandsons, and so forth, the wise man should daily worship Kalyāṇī for the sake of the growth of auspiciousness. A man desiring health and happiness, as well as one desiring wealth, and one constantly desiring fame, should worship Rohiṇī. Furthermore, one seeking knowledge, one seeking victory, and especially one seeking a kingdom [should do the same].

A man desiring the destruction of his enemies should worship Kālikā; one desiring victory in battle should fully worship Caṇḍikā; and [one should worship her] for the destruction of suffering and poverty, as well as for the enchantment of kings.

For the destruction of great sins, one should worship Śāmbhavī. In all worlds, for the performance of fierce rites against enemies, the wise man should diligently worship Durgā for the destruction of difficult distress. For the attainment of the fruits of desired objects, such as good fortune, wealth, grain, and the like, a mortal should worship Subhadrā.
For the increase of male and female servants, the method of worship is described in that very same place: specifically at the time of dawn, one who has especially performed an oil massage.
Then the girl to be avoided said:

One should avoid a girl who has missing or extra limbs, or who suffers from diseases such as leprosy; one who has a foul odor, or whose entire body is covered in knots and open sores marked by blood and pus; one who is born blind, squint-eyed, one-eyed, ugly, or excessively hairy; and one who is diseased or born of a slave’s womb.

Now, regarding the different desires according to the distinction of kinsmen, he states the manner in which she is to be worshipped: "A man with wealth should worship Brahmāṇī in all undertakings; for the sake of victory, one born of a royal lineage; for the sake of gain, one born of a Vaiśya lineage; for the sake of a son, one born of a Śūdra lineage; and in a terrible situation, one of the lowest caste."

There is a distinction in worship according to the difference in purpose and color: for the complete accomplishment of all desired objects, one should worship Gaurī; for victory and fame, the yellow-limbed goddess; for the sake of gain, the one with limbs of the ruddy class; and for rites such as subjugation (māraṇa), the dark-complexioned one—so it is stated in some places. One should properly worship a maiden born of a single lineage, according to the *Kaulāvalī Tantra*.
p. 51) Worship of Gaṇeśa.
Oṃ Gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. Having performed the worship with water for the feet and other offerings.
Meditative absorption.

Oṃ, [I bow to] the elephant-faced one, who possesses the luster of the rising sun and holds in his lotus-like hands the noose, the goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons.
One should meditate upon Gaṇeśa, who wears red garments, who removes all suffering, who is gracious, and who is beautiful with every ornament. (1)
Oṃ! To the dwarf with a stout body, the face of a lordly elephant, the pot-bellied and handsome one,
whose broad cheeks are swarming with bees greedy for the scent of flowing ichor,
who creates the splendor of vermilion with the blood of enemies torn apart by his tusks.
I bow to the son of the Daughter of the Mountain, Gaṇapati, the bestower of supernatural powers and the fulfiller of desires. || 2 ||
The worship of Vaṭuka.
Oṃ vaṃ, obeisance to Vaṭuka. Having performed the worship with water for the feet and other offerings.
Meditative concentration (dhyāna).

Oṃ! Victorious is Vaṭukanātha, the bestower of accomplishments upon practitioners; he who holds a skull and a staff, wears earrings, and has a dark-blue serpent as his sacred thread—like youthful darkness; he who is the cause for severing obstacles during the performance of sacrifices and ritual worship.
The procedure for that is as follows.

The patron (yajamāna) should worship a group of nine auspicious girls; he should fully honor the maidens from two years of age up to ten years of age. By implication, those younger than one year should be excluded. Having seated them upon their seats, he should invoke them with the mantra. Now...

The invocation mantra: Oṃ, I invoke the maiden who is composed of the syllables of the mantra, who assumes the forms of the Mothers, and who is the manifest embodiment of the nine Durgās. With this very mantra, one should invoke all nine. If one is unable, one may worship even a single one according to one's capacity. [Then follows] the water for the feet (pādya) and so forth.
Having performed the worship.
A two-year-old girl is designated as a *kumārī*.
O you whose very nature is all things! O Sovereign of all! O you whose form is every power!
O Kaumārī, Mother of the World, accept this worship; salutations be unto you! || 1 ||
The three-year-old cow is known by the name Trimūrti.
I worship the Goddess Tripurā, the support of the three cities, whose form is the knowledge of the three aims of life, who is adored by the three worlds, and who is the triple embodiment. || 2 ||
A maiden of four years is auspicious.

I worship the auspicious Goddess, the mother of all well-being, who consists of the creative powers (kalās) yet transcends them, whose heart is compassion, and who is the source of all prosperity. || 3 ||
Rohiṇī is five years old.
I worship Lakṣmī, who is Rohiṇī, the infinite power whose essence consists of the letters beginning with 'A', and who is the substratum of qualities such as *aṇimā*.
Kālikā is six years old.
I worship Kālikā, who acts according to her will, who is auspicious and beloved, whose very form is the Wheel of Time (Kālacakra), who grants all desires, and who is noble in her compassion. || 5 ||
Caṇḍikā is seven years of age.
I always worship the goddess Caṇḍikā, who possesses fierce valor, who is fierce in her heroism, fierce in her illusory power, and the one who shatters the fierce Muṇḍa.
A Śāmbhavī [union] lasts for eight years.
I worship Lakṣmī, the consort of Śambhu, who bestows eternal bliss, who is peaceful, who is honored by all the gods, and who is the self of all beings. 7.
Durgā is nine years old.
I always worship with devotion Durgā, the destroyer of the suffering of worldly existence, who is difficult to reach and difficult to overcome in action, and who destroys the afflictions of distress.
Subhadrā was ten years old.
I worship the goddess Subhadrā, who is beautiful, whose complexion has the luster of gold, who bestows happiness and good fortune, and who is the mother of Subhadra.
p.

54) At the conclusion of the daily *ārati* and the worship of the virgin (*kumārī*), having placed the unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and other offerings from her hand upon one's own head with devotion.

She should follow the newly married woman, afterwards feed the Brāhmaṇas, and then eat herself together with her beloved friends, kinsmen, and others; she should spend the remainder of the time with singing, instrumental music, and other such activities.
Thus concludes the worship of the maiden.
There is no fault in this during an eight-night festival, nor when there is a loss of a lunar day during a nine-night festival;
even during a period of ritual impurity (sūtaka), worship is prescribed, and recitation and giving are especially so.

If [the ritual] is performed with the Goddess in mind, no fault is found therein; likewise, one should worship a Brahmin woman even when she is menstruating or in a state of impurity. For women who have husbands, the use of perfumes and the like during Navarātra does not constitute a fault. This has been stated in the Hemādri: "Perfumes, ornaments, betel..."
With flower garlands and ointments.
Regarding the specific procedure for the worship of the Kumārī, the Kaulāvalī Tantra states:
"In this manner, one should worship the Consciousness (Caitanya) along with the Praṇava;
then Vāṇī, Māyā, Lakṣmī, Māyā, and the two Kūrca-mantras."
These *praṇavas* are to be known for the worship of the Virgin (*kumārī*).
[The first is] enriched with the fourteenth vowel and joined with *bhṛgu*, *vindu*, and *indu*.
Consciousness is said to be the seed that bestows prosperity upon practitioners;
thus, it is [manifested] in two ways, three ways, seven ways, and again nine ways.
One should worship regularly and invariably according to the prescribed ritual.
Water should be offered with the Vāgbhava mantra, and water for washing the feet with the Māyā mantra.
One should offer sandalwood with the *lakṣmī* mantra and the *kūrca* seed-syllable;
one should offer flowers with the *śakti* seed-syllable, and incense with the sixth [mantra].
Through Vāgbhava there is the agitation of the city; through Māyā, the eightfold qualities;
through the Śrī-bīja, the attainment of prosperity; and through Māyā, the destruction of enemies.
By means of the Bhairava seed-syllable, one attains the state of a neuter;
one should first perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and other rites according to one's own tradition.
Thereafter, one should perform the supreme special placement (viśeṣanyāsa) upon the limbs of the maiden.
Then follows the offering of the unbroken lamp; the investigation of lamps and so forth is found in the Ḍāmara Tantra.
It may be made of gold, silver, bell-metal, iron, or clay,
and likewise fashioned from the flour of wheat, black gram, and mung bean.
(55) Success in one's undertakings shall occur with gold; with silver, the world becomes submissive.
In the absence of those two, copper may be used; with bell-metal, there shall be the subjugation of the gods.
Killing occurs in an iron vessel, and likewise, expulsion in one made of clay;
in a vessel fashioned from wheat flour, there shall be victory in dispute.
From *māṣaja* comes the paralyzing of enemies; from *maudga*, the highest peace;
for the purpose of making a treaty, [the clay] originating from the soil of both riverbanks is used.
In the absence of all [other] bowls, one may use one made of copper or clay.
In a lamp made of gold and other materials, the measurement of the gold and so forth is to be applied right there.
In a calculation of one thousand palas, the vessel is prescribed at one hundred palas;
for a measure of fifty palas, the excellent vessel consists of thirty palas.
A vessel weighing ninety-six [palas] is called a *ṣaṣṭika*;
this is half of a *śatamāna*, increased by one *pala*.
O Ambikā, it is declared that for a thousand [lamps], one *digpala* is prescribed;
indeed, the measure for a perpetual lamp (*nityadīpa*) is seven *palas*.
Now, the essential nature of the lamp.
The base is said to be six finger-breadths in width and six finger-breadths in height;
with a length of sixteen finger-breadths, this beautiful vessel is considered supreme.
In all ritual acts, the measure for the perpetual lamp should be half of that [half]. (The word *budhna* means "root. Now, the distinction between ghee and oil is stated in that very same place:
A lamp should be prepared with cow's ghee for the accomplishment of all aims;
for the rite of killing, that of a buffalo is prescribed, while for causing enmity, that of a camel would be used.
A lamp made from sheep's fat is prescribed for rites of pacification (śāntika), while one made from goat's fat should be used for rites of eradication (uccāṭana);
or rather, a lamp should be prepared with sesame oil for the accomplishment of all aims.
O Maheśānī! In the absence of ghee, one should use mustard oil for the rite of killing.
Now, the wick.
An odd number of wicks should be taken, up to one hundred and one; it is said that more are prescribed for important tasks, while fewer are considered appropriate for minor ones, O beloved!
One should employ white, yellow, madder-red, saffron-colored, black, and variegated thread for the six types of ritual actions.
In the absence of all [other materials], one should prepare the wicks individually using white thread alone.
Furthermore, for the purpose of moving [the pieces], the counting-stick (śalākā) is also placed in that very same spot.
The probe (śalākikā) should measure sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and be made of gold, silver, or udumbara wood; it should be well-proportioned and pleasing to the wise.
Likewise, [the line] in the middle is sharp, fierce, and straight, marked with a trident.
Then, the Dīpamukha [rite] is performed right there.
Facing east, however, there is the attainment of all goals; likewise for paralyzing and eradication.
For protection and inciting enmity, the lamp should be placed facing west.
For the attainment of prosperity, one faces north; for the rite of killing, one faces south.
Now follows the vow regarding the offering of lamps.
In that regard, first, regarding the type of *ghaṭārgala* machine at the front of the jar [as described in the *Śāradā-tilaka*, chapter 9, verse 95]:

having drawn either a *ghaṭārgala* machine or a hexagonal (*ṣaṭkoṇa*) machine, and having uttered the lunar day (*tithi*), the weekday (*vāra*), and so forth, [one should recite]: "Today here, for a duration of as many thousands of years as there are particles of this lamp-flame..."

Having made this vow: "Desiring the pleasure of the Blessed Lady—who moves through difficult terrains as defined by the sacred observance—I shall, from today until the ninth day, day and night, light this lamp, free from defects such as wind and the like, dedicated to the deity Śrī Durgā, before Śrī Durgā. Thus it is said.
Having recited the respective prayers for each desire regarding sensual objects and offered a lamp according to the prescribed rite,
one should worship it with perfumes, unbroken grains of rice, and other offerings.
Regarding the omens, obstacles, and so forth in the installation of a lamp, it is stated in the *Ḍāmara-tantra* as follows:
O Goddess, listen as I explain the omens of the lamp in their proper order;
by the mere knowledge of them, success or failure arises.
O Sureśānī! At the commencement of the lamp, nine auspicious verses [should be recited];
for whatever is spoken at that time shall certainly come to pass exactly so.
At that time, especially, one should avoid inauspicious speech;
the twice-born man should wear red garments, be free from physical defects, and be adorned with red garlands and unguents.
At the commencement of the lamp-offering, he arrives; his success is certain, without a doubt.
When one of the Śūdra caste arrives, it is declared that middling success is attained.
In the case of seeing a barbarian (mleccha), bondage is declared for the giver of the lamp;
seeing a cat, a mouse, or similar creatures is considered a middling sight.
O Goddess! when the excellent lamp has been lit, both the auspicious and the inauspicious are observed. O beautiful one! if the flame of the lamp becomes perfectly smooth, [it portends good].
Within eight days, his success will certainly be achieved;
however, O Goddess of Gods, if the flame of the lamp should become crooked, then—
O Goddess of the gods! If there should be a blaze of light resembling that of a donkey or a heron, it is declared to bring destruction to him, to his kinsmen, and to destroy all wealth.
For the maker of the lamp, death accompanied by obstacles will certainly occur;
O Mother! O Goddess worshipped by the gods! the lamp’s radiance becomes dark.
O Ambika! When a lamp is offered, the enemy's undertaking becomes fruitless;
for as soon as the lamp is lit, their destruction occurs at that very moment.
The accomplishment of the task will occur with delay; there is no doubt.
The lamp that was lit will be extinguished within three *praharas*.
O beautiful one, it is declared that success in one's undertaking occurs within a month or a year;
however, if the excellent lamp should ever be extinguished during the night, [the result will fail].
In his house, wealth and property will certainly be lost;
however, if a lamp is offered, it will surely be restored with a "caṭa-caṭa" sound.
At that time, one should predict that his work will be ruined;
if the best of lamps vomits [flame], it brings fear from thieves.
O Goddess, O beautiful one! If the lamp-vessel should leak again, there is no doubt that an ox-killer will be born to that maker of the lamp.
If the vessel of the preeminent lamp is indeed seen to be broken,
then within eighteen days the sacrificer, along with his kinsmen, [shall perish].
O beloved, O passionate one! He goes to the abode of Śrāddhadeva;
like a fool who, when his lamp is extinguished, seeks to light another lamp.
A donor of lamps will always have dim vision;
however, if a person, after a lamp has been offered, causes it to be maintained again, [he shall not suffer this].

If an impure person should touch the most excellent lamp, disease indeed arises in the bodies of men who made that lamp. O Umā! Dogs, cats, mice, and other such creatures [may also touch] the wooden wick of the lamp.
"O auspicious one! If they touch [the lamp], one should inflict a beating from the king.
For in this manner, many obstacles indeed arise regarding the excellent lamp."
Therefore, O Queen of the Gods! a lamp should indeed be observed at every step.
(p. 58) Now follows the pacification of obstacles to the lamp.

In that regard, others say one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sugar, ghee, sesame seeds, rice, and lotuses, using the *jayaṃtī* mantra in ten parts (*daśāṃśa*). Still others say it should be done with the nine-syllable mantra (*navārṇa*). [The mantra is: "O Goddess!
O remover of the pain of those who prostrate! Be gracious! O Goddess! Be gracious; may You grant us auspiciousness."
The traditional teaching is that the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with any one of the mantras using the aforementioned substances.
The Ritual for the Dismissal of the Kalaśa Vessel.

That sacrificer, having performed the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) preceded by the recitation for well-being (*svastivācana*), and having proclaimed the place and time, makes this vow: "On the first lunar day, I shall perform the concluding worship (*uttarapūjana*) of the deities, beginning with Gaṇapati, who were installed [previously], together with an offering of coconuts. Having thus made the vow, he proceeds with the ritual services (*upacāra*) as prescribed.

Having worshipped Gaṇapati and the other deities, one should then take a pure coconut or a pumpkin, worship it, and perform the ritual placement of the life-force (*jīva-nyāsa*) and so forth within it. Then: *Oṃ Mahāmāye!
O Mother of the World, O Bestower of all desires, I offer this coconut (or pumpkin).*
O Bali, be gracious; become the bestower of boons. Having placed half the portion before the Goddess, [one should offer] again:
*oṃ prāṇāya svāhā* || *oṃ apānāya svāhā* || *oṃ udānāya svāhā* || *oṃ vyānāya svāhā* || *oṃ samānāya svāhā* || with these, *svāhā*. *oṃ vyānāya svāhā* || *oṃ*...

"Samānāya svāhā! With these mantras ending in "svāhā," one should offer five oblations into the Jyotis fire. Therein, according to family custom, on the eighth, ninth, or tenth day, at the conclusion of the Goddess's worship, having prostrated before her and taken flowers with palms joined in reverence (añjali):
Oṃ! Arise, O Brahmaṇaspati; we, seeking the gods, entreat you. May the Maruts, the bounteous givers, come forward; O Indra, be swift and be with us. 1.
Oṃ, O Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati), you are the controller of this hymn; awaken it and cause its lineage to live.
Now, the offering of the sacrificial oblation (balidāna). || 1 ||
In this regard, one view is that one should offer the bali-oblation every day for three fortnights.
O Śakra! When the sun is situated in Virgo, having worshipped on the eighth day of the bright fortnight with *droṇa* flowers, as well as *bilva*, mango, *jātī*, *punnāga*, and *campaka* flowers;
Having recited "Kālī, Kālī" according to the rite for five days, one should strike with a sword [the victim] who is endowed with the five marks and provided with perfumes and flowers.
The second [view] is that it occurs on both the eighth and ninth days, according to the words of the Devīpurāṇa.
p.
59) "O gods, may all that you protect be auspicious; may we, possessing brave sons, proclaim this great [truth] in the assembly.
On the ninth day, the offering of the bali-oblation must indeed be performed according to the prescribed rule. And on the ninth day...
The third position is that it should be performed on the ninth day itself, both because of the scriptural injunction and because of the practice of the learned.

In this matter, one of the three alternatives—whether according to local custom or family tradition—should be adopted. Here too, there are three alternatives: in the first alternative, one should perform worship every day from the first lunar day (*pratipad*) until the ninth, starting from the first day of the bright fortnight (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
[Note: According to the *Niruttara-tantra*, "Through worship one obtains worship; through recitation (*japa*), one attains perfection; of this there is no doubt."]

"Through *homa* all success shall be attained; therefore, one should worship these three. [The *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* states: "If the worship, recitation, *homa*, and *bali* offerings are omitted, there will be famine; if the fragrance is omitted, misfortune; likewise, if the incense is omitted, anxiety; and if the cloth is omitted, the loss of wealth. Regarding the performance of the *bali* offering and so forth, this constitutes one [method].

The second [method] is: from the first day until the eighth, one performs only the practice of worship, recitation (*japa*), offering of oblations (*bali-dāna*), and so forth; on the ninth day, it is performed with *homa*. The third [method] is: from the first day until the eighth, one performs daily only the practice of recitation, offering of oblations, and so forth; on the ninth day, it is performed with *homa*. Here, the former...

Having adopted one of the two positions, the priority of the offering to Bali is accepted; however, if one adopts the remaining position, the learned authorities state that it should be performed wherever appropriate.
Now, the method for the offering of the sacrificial animal (*balidāna*):

Having performed the recitation for well-being (*svastivācana*) there, one should bring forward the animal, join the palms in reverence (*añjali*), and say: "O best of animals, for the benefit of living beings, you have now been sprinkled by me for the pleasure of Caṇḍikā, for my sake and for my own self."
One should recite "tārayet. Then, having bound [the victim] in the animal sacrifice within a pillar shaped like a cloud.
Having turned facing north, [he should offer] the *bali* facing east; thus it is said.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
One should bathe the sacrificial animal, facing eastward, with water from a conch shell, [reciting]:
"Vārāhī, Yamunā, Gaṅgā, Karatoyā, Sarasvatī."

"O Maheśānī! By this mantra, may the Kāverī, Candrabhāgā, Sindhu, Bharavā, and Sāgara rivers provide their presence here during the goat-bath (chāga-snāna). Then, one should sprinkle [the goat] with water mixed with kuśa grass: 'May the gods, the Vasus, the Rudras, those who travel in the most excellent celestial chariots (vimāna), the planets, and the lords of the worlds [protect] you.'"
May Sādhyas, the Aśvins, and the two excellent physicians—these and other sages—sprinkle you with water infused with *kuśa* grass.
Having thus sprinkled [him].
The Goddess consists of all forms, and the entire world consists of the Goddess;
therefore, I bow to you, the Supreme Sovereign, who are the universal form.
O Maheśvarī! By your grace, may all that has been offered—whether deficient in ritual procedure, deficient in action, or deficient in devotion—become complete.
Having said, "O Mother, forgive me," one should perform the dismissal by offering a single flower in the northeast with the mantra: *oṃ durgāyai namaḥ*.
Then, the victorious consecration (*jayamānābhiṣeka*) is performed with the water from the unestablished jar (*kalaśa*).
Thereafter, one should cause the image made of clay or other materials to rise so that it may be carried away in the current of the river.
Oṃ! Arise, O Goddess Caṇḍeśī! Having accepted this auspicious worship, bring about my well-being together with your eight Śaktis. (3)
Go, go to the supreme abode, your own place, O Goddess Caṇḍikā!
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the limbs of the sacrificial animal as follows:
I purify your speech; I purify your breath; I purify your eye; I purify your ear;
I purify your navel; I purify your penis; I purify your anus; I purify your limbs; I purify your womb. May those cruel things of yours be sprinkled away along with your great powers—svāhā!

May the deities of the sacrificial animal quickly release the head, forehead, heart, ears, navel, neck, anus, penis, chest, feet, and likewise all other limbs. You have been born from an animal womb for the sake of increasing the efficacy of the offering; having shed the hair-follicles, depart quickly.

"Deities! [Thus saying], having bid farewell to the deities residing there, one should perform the worship of the goat with the five offerings (pañcopacāra). Having smeared vermilion (sindūra) on its two horns and bound garlands upon them, one should then contemplate the animal as the deity Agni, the source of pleasure for Durgā. Then, having purified its limbs by reciting: "Omnipresent Devourer of Flesh, obeisance to you," over all its limbs.

"The animal has been produced by the gods according to the injunctions for the purposes of sacrifice. O animal! For the sake of dharma, artha, and the fulfillment of kama, I shall slaughter you. Having thus addressed him, the performer, facing north, should hold the animal's right ear and recite: "O animal! You have appeared before me through my good fortune in the form of a sacrificial offering (bali)."
I bow, therefore, to Him who possesses all forms, who through the granting of joy to Caṇḍikā brings about the destruction of the donor's calamities.

"O Cāmuṇḍā! O Bali! Salutations to you in the form of the sacrificial offering (bali)! Animals were created by the Self-born One himself for the sake of sacrifice; therefore, I shall cause you to be slain. Thus, in a sacrifice, killing is not truly killing. Having meditated upon his own form with the mantra "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ," he should place a flower upon the victim's head.

Having consecrated Bhairava and taken hold of his right hand, [one should say]: "O Goat! O mighty-armed one, you are the vehicle of the god Agni! O animal! By the offering of your sacrifice, may the beloved of Hara be pleased. Abandoning this form, attain the state of a Gandharva. Salutations again and again to Chāgalāya, the bestower of all desires!"
(61) "Stay here in this water so that the stream of the cow-pen may increase its flow."
Oṃ! O Durgā, O Goddess, Mother of the World, you who have been worshipped, go to your own abode, so that you may indeed return once the year has passed. || 5 ||

"O Goddess! This worship has been performed by me according to my ability"—thus he should recite. Then, taking the right ear [of the vessel], [he says]: "Oṃ! Today, for this sacrificer of such-and-such lineage, may there be the pacification of all afflictions and the abundance of wealth and grain."

Desiring the attainment of a beautiful body, health, and immovable prosperity, and desiring the continuous attainment of happiness in the world of the Goddess for as many years as there are hairs on the animal’s body, [I offer] this goat (or pumpkin, or coconut), well-bathed and purified with fire, to the Blessed One, the Great Form, Śrī Durgā, of the Kātyāyanīya lineage.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "I shall slay the deity," one should recite the *Paśugāyatrī*: "Oṃ, may we know the King of Beasts; may we meditate upon Mahādeva; may Durgā impel us toward that. Regarding the goat: "Oṃ, may we know the Goat, whose deity is Agni; may we meditate upon the Severing of the Head; may the Goat impel us toward that. Thus [it is said].
Having recited: "O you who dwell in heaven, accept this goat (this offering) for the sake of Śakti."
"For the destruction of the pride of enemies and for the accomplishment of all desired aims"—having thus addressed the Goddess.
Then, taking up the horn, one should recite: "O goat's horn, you have been taken up; may your state as an animal be cast off."
Then follows the worship of the sword (khaḍgapūjā).
There, having made the formal proposition as before: "O Nandaka, you who are of supreme form, the destroyer of my enemies!"

O destroyer of all evil dreams, dark-hued like the petal of a blue lotus! You are the sword, the slayer, the blade, sharp-edged and difficult to approach; you are the womb of prosperity, victory itself, and likewise the support of Dharma.

Thus, these eight names of yours were spoken by the Creator himself: your asterism is Kṛttikā; Maheśvara is the divine preceptor of your lineage; the Rohiṇīs are your body; and Janārdana is your deity. May the great god, your grandfather, protect you and me forever—he by whom this earth was supported and [the demon] was slain.

O Lakṣmī! By your wisdom you have been constantly worshipped, and by your command remain steadfast in this house of mine, bringing about progeny (and sovereignty). 10.
The thousand-rayed suns resounded with the cries of hosts of calamities, while the wish-fulfilling cows [bestowed] desired objects.
May the dust from the lotus feet of Caṇḍī, which serve as bridges across the ocean of this endless saṃsāra, protect me.
Having recited this, one should offer three handfuls of flowers with the root mantra.
Now, the hymn for seeking forgiveness for offenses against the Goddess.

Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. I know neither mantra nor yantra, nor do I know hymns of praise, invocation, or meditation; I know not the ritual gestures (mudrās), nor do I know the supreme lamentations. O Mother, I know only this: following after you is the remover of all suffering.

O Mother! O Śivā, the savior of all! Through ignorance of the prescribed rules, lack of wealth, laziness, or the impossibility of performing what was enjoined, I have fallen away from Your feet; this must be forgiven. For even a wicked son may occasionally be born.
He does not have a young mother. || 2 ||
O Mother! There are many upright sons upon this earth, but among them, I, your son, am exceedingly fickle.
This abandonment of me is not at all fitting for you, O Śivā; for even a wicked son may occasionally be born somewhere.
He does not have a young mother. || 3 ||
O Mother of the World! O Mother! I have not rendered service at Your feet, nor, O Goddess, have I offered You abundant wealth.
Yet, You bestow upon me an incomparable affection; for even a bad son is born somewhere.
He does not have a young mother. || 4 ||

Having abandoned the gods due to being preoccupied with various kinds of service, and having reached an age exceeding eighty-five years— if even now, O Mother, you show no compassion, then I shall be left without support, O Mother of Lambodara!
To whom shall I go for refuge? || 5 ||
A dog-cooker becomes a chatterer with speech like that of a honey-drinker; free from fear, even a pauper dwells for a long time amidst ten million pieces of gold.
O Aparṇā, when this mantra enters your ear, O Mother, what person knows this fruit to be obtained from reciting that which is to be chanted during the rite of *japa*? (6)
O Bhavānī! Paśupati— smearing himself with funeral pyre ashes, consuming poison, wearing a garment of directions, bearing matted locks, with the lord of serpents as his necklace,
a bearer of skulls, and the master of spirits— attains the singular status of the Lord of the Universe through the grasping of your hand.
This is the fruit of the sequence. || 7 ||
I have no longing for liberation, nor do I desire worldly power, nor have I any need for higher knowledge, O moon-faced one; nor even do I desire pleasure.
Therefore, O Mother! O Mṛḍānī, O Rudrāṇī, O Śivā! I entreat you: let there truly be birth for me once again.
"O Śiva! O Bhavānī!"—thus they muttered. || 8 ||
Have you not been propitiated by me with various ritual services according to the prescribed rites? Have words not been offered by me that were more than merely dry reflections?
O Śyāmā! If it is only you who bestow even a fraction of compassion upon me, a helpless one, then, O Mother, that alone is sufficient. It is indeed fitting.
It belongs to you alone. || 9 ||
Immersed in calamities, O Durgā, O Śivā, ocean of compassion, I remember you;
do not consider this to be deceit on my part, for those tormented by hunger and thirst remember their mother.
O Mother of the World, if there is even a trace of wondrous compassion for me, is it not fully present?
For a mother never neglects her son, however great his transgression or how much he has turned away from her.
"There is no sinner equal to me, and indeed there is no destroyer of sin equal to you.
Knowing this, O Great Goddess, act as is appropriate."
Thus ends the *Devī-aparādha-kṣamāpana-stotra*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrīmac-Śaṅkarācārya.
(p. 72) Now, the *Aṣṭaka* on Durgā as the Deliverer from Distress (*Āpaduddhārāṣṭaka*).
Salutations to you, O refuge, O auspicious one, O compassionate one; salutations to you, O Ke! who pervades the universe, O you whose form is the cosmos!
Salutations to you, O goddess whose lotus-feet are worshipped by the world; salutations to you, O savior of the world! Protect me, O Durgā! || 1 ||
Salutations to you whose very nature is contemplated by the world; salutations to you, O great yoginī, whose form is pure consciousness.
Salutations to you, salutations to you, whose form is eternal bliss; salutations to you, O savior of the world, protect me, O Durgā! 2.

For the helpless, the wretched, the one afflicted by thirst, the one tormented by fear, the terrified, and the bound creature—O Goddess, you alone are the refuge and the savior; salutations to you, O Deliverer of the World! Protect me, O Durgā! || 3 ||

In the forest, in a fierce battle, amidst enemies, in the water, in a crisis, or in the royal palace during a storm—O Goddess, you alone are my refuge! You are the cause of deliverance; salutations to you, O Savior of the World! Protect me, O Durgā! || 4 ||

O Goddess, you are the sole refuge for embodied beings sinking in the ocean of calamity—boundless, exceedingly difficult to cross, and most terrible; you are the boat for crossing over. Salutations to you, O Durgā, who delivers the world! Protect us! || 5 ||

Salutations, O Caṇḍikā! You are the sole refuge for him whose entire host of enemies has been utterly shattered by the playful sport of your fierce, staff-like arms; you are the destroyer of the multitude of obstacles. Salutations to you, O Savior of the World! Protect me, O Durgā! 6.
You alone are worshipped by the virtuous, you are the speaker of truth, the manifold, the all-encompassing, the wrathful, and the one whose essence is fire;
you are the *iḍā*, the *piṅgalā*, and the *suṣumṇā* among the channels—salutations to you, O deliverer of the world! Protect me, O Durgā! 7.
(p. 73) Now, the hymn for the destruction of distress (*saṅkaṭanāśanastotra*).
Oṃ! I bow to you, Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune, who are the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, who contain the Vedas within, and who pervade the entire universe; O refuge, I worship you. (1)

I bow to you, O Goddess Durgā, the sovereign lady who destroys all misfortune; you who are known as Kāmākhyā, the bestower of desires, dark-hued, capable of assuming any form at will, and enchanting to the mind.
I salute you, Vijayā, the three-eyed Durgā adorned with all ornaments, who is endowed with a smile and who destroys the state of misery. || 3 ||
I bow to you, Bhavānī, who are praised by Brahmā and the other gods, served by Siddhas and Gandharvas, and who are Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune.
I bow to Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune, who possesses a divine form, who is the crusher of Niśumbha and Śumbha, and the slayer of the demon Mahiṣa.
I bow to the goddess Durgā, who destroys misfortune, who possesses twenty-five arms, who resembles pure gold, and who has the form of Gaurī.
I bow to you, Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune, who holds a trident, a sword, a discus, an arrow, a spear, and a battle-axe.
I bow with my whole being to the Great Wisdom (Mahāvidyā) who pervades the universe, who effects creation and dissolution, and who is Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune. 8.
This divine armor, a great mantra of great fruit,
which any man who recites daily while endowed with devotion to us [shall obtain].
I bestow wealth and grain by means of the Sakṛdāvartana rite.
The hymn for the destruction of distress addressed to Durgā, as spoken in the Matsya Sūkta, is complete.
O Sovereign of the Gods! O Goddess, Supreme Sovereign! May all that which was deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, and deficient in devotion be forgiven; be gracious!
Whatever has been done by me, whether deficient or excessive, out of delusion— may all that become complete through your grace, O Maheśvarī!
I do not know how to invoke you, nor do I know how to dismiss you;
I do not even know how to perform your worship—forgive me, O Supreme Goddess!
Oṃ! May the Rudras, Ādityas, and Vasus kindle you again; may the Brahmins [kindle you] again with sacrifices for the sake of the guidance of the Vasus.
May you cause your body to grow with clarified butter; may the desires of the sacrificer come true. || 1 ||

"May there be strength for you! May there be vigor for you! O Vāyus, may the divine Savitṛ impel you toward the most excellent work."—may the Brahman priest grant you well-being, and likewise the twice-born;
and those who are the best among the reptiles, may they grant you well-being at all times.
Yayāti, Nahuṣa, Dhundhumāra, and Bhagīratha—
all these royal sages constantly bestow blessings upon you.
May there be well-being for you from those with two feet and indeed from those with four feet;
may Svāhā, Svadhā, and Śacī likewise always grant you well-being.
May Lakṣmī and Arundhatī both grant you well-being, O sinless one;
and may Asita, Devala, Viśvāmitra, and likewise Aṅgiras do the same.
May Kārttikeya, the six-faced one, bestow well-being upon you today;
may the divine Vivasvat grant you auspiciousness in every way.
The four elephants of the quarters, the earth, the sky, and the planets—
He who always supports the earth from below with His arms.
And Śeṣa, the best of serpents, grants you well-being;
may the purposes of the mantras be fruitful, and may your desires be fulfilled.
May there be the destruction of the intellect of enemies, and likewise the prosperity of friends;
may those without sons have sons, and may those with sons have grandsons.
May those without wealth become wealthy; may all accomplish their goals;
and likewise, may there be the desire for long life, fame, sons, and grandsons.
May health, wealth, desire, and all your wishes be fulfilled for you (or: may they be fulfilled for me).

Thus [composed] by Paṇḍita Śrī Bulākhīrāma, son of Gosvāmī, a resident of Argalapura, born of the Gauḍa caste and the lineage of Bhāradvāja, the preeminent scholar and former teacher of the Karmakāṇḍa and Yajurveda at the Śrī Vidyādharmavardhinī Pāṭhaśālā.

The procedure for the installation of the ritual pitcher (*kalaśasthāpanavidhi*) as declared in the Vedas, compiled by Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Gosvāmin, adorned with the title *Vidyābhūṣaṇa Karmakāṇḍamaṇi*, is complete.
77) Incidentally, [there follows] the rule for reciting hymns:
"Neither a hymn composed by oneself nor one composed by another [should be recited]."
For in the Kali age, they praise that which has been spoken by the sages.
The Hymn to Sarasvatī.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim this most rare hymn,
which contains the essence of the mantra of Vāgīśī and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Oṃ. Of this mantra of the Śrī Vāgvādinī Śāradā Stotra, Mārkaṇḍeya and Aśvalāyana are the seers (ṛṣis); Sragdharā and Anuṣṭubh are the meters (chandas); Śrī Sarasvatī is the deity (devatā); Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Oṃ is the power (śakti); Aiṃ is the pin (kīlaka); its application (viniyoga) is in recitation for the swift increase of eloquence.
Meditative concentration.
She is white, the supreme essence of the investigation of Brahman, primordial, pervading the universe,
holding a lute and a book, bestowing fearlessness, and dispelling the darkness of ignorance.
I bow to that Supreme Goddess, the Blessed Śāradā, who bestows wisdom, seated upon the lotus posture with a crystal rosary held in her hand. (1)
Brahmā said:
Hrīṃ hrīṃ! O you whose single heart-seed syllable is Hrīṃ; O you who possess the luster of the moon and a beauty as radiant as a lotus;
O Padmā, seated upon a lotus; O bestower of joy upon the minds of those who bow before you!
O Goddess, essence of the cycle of existence, whose own beloved Lord has utterly consumed the mass of ignorance! || 2 ||
Aiṃ Aiṃ Aiṃ! O You who are the form of the lotus-face of the Creator (Brahmā) and other deities; O You whose true nature is the desired mantra;
O You who are unknown even by the gross or the subtle, and whose essential reality is not fully realized;
O Supreme among Gods, saluted by the best of deities; O Partless One, eternally pure, existing within the universe and in the space between all worlds. || 3 ||
Hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ! O you who are pleased by the recitation, who wear a crown of moonlight, and hold a lute in your busy hands;
O Mother, Mother, salutations to you! Burn away my dullness and grant me excellent wisdom.

O Śāradā, wearer of white garlands, grant me your blessing—you who are the embodiment of knowledge, sung in the Vedānta, recited in the Śrutis, the path to liberation that bestows emancipation, and whose power transcends all paths. || 4 ||
Dhīṃ dhīṃ dhīṃ! To her who is called Dhāraṇā; who is to be celebrated by the names Dhṛti, Mati, and Nūti;
who is eternal and non-eternal, both with and without cause; who is saluted by the hosts of sages; who is both new and ancient; and who possesses the power of merit upon merit.

O you whose intellect is fixed on the mantra Hari Hara, which is eternally pure and golden; O you whose intellect is fixed on the reality that is the meaning of the mantra! O you who possess the wisdom of the Mother of Intellect! O you who delight in the sound of Mādhava! || 5 ||
Hrāṃ kṣrīṃ dhrīṃ hrīṃ! O you whose hand is occupied with a book, burn, burn away all misfortune in your own form!

O you whose mind has the form of contentment, O smiling-faced one, O auspicious one, O Jṛmbhiṇī, O Vidya of paralyzing power! O Delusion, O Bewildering One, O you of radiant power, O praised one who destroys the darkness of ignorance, grant me a lack of evil intent! You are Speech, the speech of the gods, O Bhāratī; you are the tongue of the bull among poets, the bestower of perfection, the perfected Vidyā. 6.
I praise you; I bow to you; take refuge in my tongue—never forsake it!

O Goddess, may my intellect never become perverse, nor may my mind ever turn toward sin. May no suffering come to me, and even in times of calamity, may there be no agitation within me. May [my mind] flow forth in sacred scriptures, in debate, and in poetry.
May my resolve never be blunted at any time. || 8 ||

Thus, with these principal verses, the devotee who is humble and whose speech is eloquent, possessing a power favored even by Bṛhaspati and having cleansed his impurities, praises Vāṇī every day at dawn.

There is the attainment of desired objects such as crops; that goddess constantly protects him like a son. His good fortune spreads throughout the world, his poetry flourishes, and all obstacles go to their end.

A man who observes celibacy, keeps vows, maintains silence, and abstains from meat on the thirteenth lunar day becomes a master of eloquence; through recitation, he attains his desired goals, such as the growth of crops and other blessings. || 17 ||
On both fortnights, the wise man, having meditated upon the goddess Sarasvatī, should recite [this] twenty-one times on the thirteenth day without interruption, out of devotion.
The goddess is clad in white garments and adorned with white ornaments.
One obtains the desired fruit along with the world; of this there is no doubt.
