Thus Brahmā himself spoke this auspicious hymn of praise to Sarasvatī; whoever recites it daily with diligence attains immortality.
Recite the mantra according to one's capacity.
Oṃ śrīṃ sauṃ hrīṃ klīṃ dhīṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī and Mahāsarasvatī.
Thus says Manu. Thus ends the Sarasvatī Stotra within the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, in the section on the secret doctrine of the ten Vidyās.
p.
79) The Ritual Procedure for the Worship of the Sūta.
In the Viśvasāra: "O Dear One, having taken up the Mahāvidyā, one should recite it until the end of life;
in the event of the death of a great guru or similar occurrences, there is no restriction regarding worship."
If the practitioner does not perform worship due to delusion or perhaps by fate, his everything shall be destroyed; Sadāśiva will surely slay him.
Whether in an impure place or a pure one, at all times and always, one should worship with supreme devotion; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
In the Rudrayāmala.
One should perform worship even during a death-impurity, at a birth, or even when one is afflicted by disease.
This procedure is declared to be universally applicable, bestowing the fruits of all desires.
Now I shall describe the worship for one who is in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka), as enjoined by the Āgamas.
One should perform the external worship according to the sequence by means of the yoga of meditation.
The external worship of the Goddess should be performed in the sacred precinct, according to the specific injunctions.
And so it is said in the Vārāhī Tantra:
And of Tārā, Kālī, and Tripurā, O lady of excellent vows!
During both birth-impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka), one should not abandon the recitation of mantras and the worship of deities.
In the Yāmala:
Whether impure or pure, whether walking, standing, or even sleeping;
There is no fault in reciting [the mantra] mentally at all times and in all places.
In the Viśvasāra:
Whether waking, sleeping, rising, eating, or even walking;
There shall be no fault in the case of one who has mastered mantras, even regarding the rules of ritual impurity.
Neither at night from the beginning of the kalpanā, nor at the conclusion of the twilight.
In the Śruti.
Immediately following that, even impurity (aśauca) does not constitute an obstacle.
In the observance of vows, sacrifices, marriages, ancestral rites, fire offerings, worship, and recitation;
If the rite has commenced, there is no impurity; but if it has not commenced, there is impurity.
In a sacrifice, the commencement is the obstacle; in a vow and the recitation of mantras, it is the formal resolve.
The *nāndī-śrāddha* occurs at the beginning of a marriage and other ceremonies; it is the ritual preparation of the food for the *śrāddha*.
For the Śruti declares that the invitation itself constitutes the commencement of the Śrāddha.
In the Rudrayāmala:

"Birth-impurity (sūtaka) occurs for as many months as [the child] has been born; death-impurity (mṛtasūtaka) occurs at the time of death. A mantra conjoined with both types of impurity does not bestow success."

The meaning is that there is a period of impurity (*sūtaka*) for both the beginning and the end of the recitation (*japa*). O Supreme Goddess! Having bestowed the seed-syllable of Brahman upon the mantra, one should recite the mantra seven times; thus, one is liberated from the two types of impurity.
Thus, from the words of Viṣṇu composed by Rāghava Bhaṭṭa; [now] he states the meaning of the word *dīkṣā* in the Yāmala:

Because it bestows divine knowledge and because it effects the destruction of sins, that which is the meaning of the word *dīkṣā* is celebrated as "initiation" (*dīkṣā*) in this world by those who have reached the further shore of the Tantras.
In the Kulārṇava, chapter 15, there is a distinction regarding the recitation of mantras and their study.
O Goddess, he who merely remembers the hymn in his mind or mutters the mantra with his speech—both are fruitless, like water in a broken vessel. [This is the meaning of the word "guru."]
The syllable *gu* signifies darkness, while the syllable *ru* signifies its obstruction.
Because he has brought about the cessation of darkness, he is designated as "the Guru."

The letter *ga* bestows the perfection of knowledge; the letter *ra* is the burner of sin; and from the letter *u*, one receives identity with Śiva—thus is the Guru remembered. (From the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*).
For one who is indifferent toward the indifferent, dwelling in the forest among forest-dwellers,
a renunciant among renunciants, and a householder among householders is declared a true guru.

In the Vaiṣṇava [tradition], a Vaiṣṇava should be accepted; likewise, in the Śaiva, a Śaiva; and in the Śākta, one should know that all three are [acceptable]; such is the master of initiation, without a doubt. Furthermore, in the *Kulārṇava*, it is stated that even a householder may be a guru.
One who knows the meaning of all the scriptures and is a householder is called a *guru*.
The etymological meaning of the word *guru* is given in the *Yāmala*: [p. 81]
The letter *ga* is said to bestow accomplishment; the letter *ra* is the burner of sin;
the letter *u* is called power (*śakti*); the Guru is remembered as the essence of these three.
He states the etymological derivation of the word *mantra*:
Because it brings about the complete realization of all things and protection from the bonds of saṃsāra, that which is perfected is therefore called "mantra. (From the *Piṅgalāmata*)
"O Dear One, because it protects through contemplation and because it brings about the awakening to my own form,
it is correctly called 'mantra' due to my presiding over it— thus it is said in the Rudrayāmala."
The secret instruction is for the minister, because of both contemplation and protection; as stated in another tantra:
The procedure for the infusion of consciousness (caitanya) into the mantras as taught in the Toḍala Tantra.
O Pārvatī, listen with reverence to the consciousness of all mantras:
it is the supreme Śiva in the form of a drop within the great thousand-petaled lotus.
O Supreme Goddess, having raised Kuṇḍalinī by means of the Haṃsa mantra, the wise practitioner attains that steady gaze which is fixed on the tip of the nose.
At that very moment, the consciousness of the mantra becomes situated within the wheel of Kuṇḍalinī;
one should contemplate the Guru together with Kuṇḍalinī in the great thousand-petaled lotus.
One should meditate [on this], O Dear One, and the consciousness of all mantras arises;
one should then recite that very mantra, which bestows accomplishment—of this there is no doubt.
The specific procedure for the installation of an image of a goddess.
Durgā facing south bestows auspiciousness; facing east, she increases victory; however, she should never be installed facing west or north.
The Goddess [is described] in the *Bhaktitaraṅgiṇī*, in the *Devīpurāṇa*, and in the *Toḍalatantra*.
The illustrious Śiva said:
O Dear One! Kāmarūpa is at the Mūlādhāra, Jālandhara is in the heart, Pūrṇagiri is in the lower part, and Uḍḍiyāna is above that.
Vārāṇasī blazes between the eyebrows within the three eyes;
Māyāvatī is in the circle of the face; O Maheśānī! Aṣṭapurī is likewise in the throat and at the root of the navel.
Ayodhyāpurī is situated [there]. Kāñcī-pīṭha is in the Kaṭī region, and the Śrīcakra is in the Pṛṣṭha region. From Mūladhāra, Atala is proclaimed to extend for one hundred years;
Sutala extends for one hundred years, O beloved, and Talātala extends for one hundred years. It is established up to the end of the period of seven hundred and fifty years (ṛṣi-vāṇa-indu).
Mahātala is two hundred [yojanas] deep; Pātāla is two hundred, and Rasātala is indeed two hundred.

O Goddess of gods! Two finger-breadths from the mūlādhāra and situated nearby, in the space between those two, O Supreme Goddess, lies Pātāla. Thus, O Beloved, the essence of yoga has been told to you in brief.
One must never speak what should not be said in the presence of a beast, even at the cost of one's life.
In the *Toḍalatantra*, chapter 10.
Tārādevī is blue in form; Kamalā, Kūrma, and Caṇḍikā;
Dhūmāvatī, Varāha, Chinnamastā, and Nṛsiṃhikā.
Bhuvaneśvarī is Vāmana, Mātaṅgī is the form of Rāma,
Tripurā is Jāmadagnya, and Bhairavī is Balabhadra.
Mahālakṣmī shall be the Buddha, and Durgā shall take the form of Kalki;
the Goddess Kālī herself is born from the form of Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, O Goddess, the tenth incarnation has been described to you;
by worshipping these [deities], O Goddess, one becomes equal to Mahādeva.
In the Gandharva Tantra.
O Maheśvarī, one should not offer arghya to Bhāskara with water from a conch shell;
O Maheśvarī, [this applies] as long as arghya is not yet offered to Bhāskara.
One should not worship Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, or the Queen of the Gods until [the time for the five elements has passed]:
namely, the Sun, the Moon, Yama, Time, and the five great elements.
These nine, all the gods residing within the body, are the witnesses here to my auspicious and inauspicious actions; they are the witnesses to my mantra.
Bestow upon my hands the knowledge acquired in my previous birth.
The fruit of recitation is described in the Kulārṇava.
One should know that [the merit] in one's home is a hundredfold; in a cow-pen it becomes a hundred-thousandfold;
in a temple the merit is ten-millionfold; and in the presence of Śiva it is infinite.
The meaning of the word "upacāra" (metaphorical designation) is found in the *Jñānamālā*.
O Lord, because these offerings are made with devotion to the God and cause His presence to manifest for the practitioner, they are therefore called *upacāras* (services).
Or, because they are performed in proximity [to the deity], those fruits are likewise declared:
thirty-eight, sixteen, twelve, ten, and five types of ritual services (upacāras).
I shall explain them by dividing them: who they are, what was done by each of them, and what [result] arose from those deeds.
First among these is the seat, then the invocation, and then the attendance.
Bathing, the lustration rite (nīrājana), clothing, sipping water (ācamana), and the sacred thread; then again sipping water for the king, and thereafter the beholding of the mirror.
Then, in sequence: perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings;
thereafter, water for drinking, water for rinsing the mouth, and finally water for washing the hands.
Betel, ointment, and the repeated offering of flowers;
likewise, song, instrumental music, dance, praise, and circumambulation.
The offering of a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and prostrations (*namaskāra*), when performed thirty-eight times,
result in these offerings of flowers and prostrations becoming a source of supreme pleasure for Viṣṇu.
The ritual services mentioned in the Tantras.
I shall now describe the ritual services; listen with respect, O Pārvatī!
Without these services, worship does not bring about divine favor.
O Beloved! The eighteen modes of service (upacāra) are indeed the most excellent for all.
The sixteenth is the primary [syllable], and it is remembered as tenfold;
it is proclaimed as fivefold, and it should be practiced by one desiring spiritual power.
In the Phetkāriṇī Tantra: The eighteen modes of service (aṣṭādaśopacārāḥ).
A seat, a vehicle, water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana),
as well as a bath, garments, a sacred thread, and all kinds of ornaments;
Incense, flowers, as well as lamps, incense-sticks, food, and libations;
garlands, ointments, prostration, and the ritual dismissal.
The practitioner of mantras should perform the worship with the eighteen ritual offerings.
The sixteen modes of service are described in the Tantra.
A seat, a welcome, water for the feet, the arghya offering,
water for sipping, the honey-mixture, water for a second sipping, a bath, clothing, and ornaments.
One should employ perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and likewise prostrations; these are the sixteen services (upacāras) used in worship.
The ten offerings.

The water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), the water for sipping (ācamanīya), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and again the water for sipping, as well as the services beginning with fragrance (gandha) and ending with the food offering (naivedya), constitute the ten-fold ritual services (upacāra).
The five types of offerings.
O Supreme Goddess! One should offer perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offerings; this is the five-fold worship (pañcopacāra-pūjā).
Substances to be avoided during worship.
All stale leaves, flowers, fruits, and water are to be avoided;
however, the water of the Ganges is not to be avoided, nor is a leaf of the tulasī.
The bilva leaf should not be avoided, nor likewise the water-born lotus;
O Goddess, one should not worship with flowers that have been stale, even if they are made of gold.
The bilva leaf, arghya water, the leaves of tāla and āmalakī,
the kalhāra lotus, the tulasī leaf, the lotus, and the maṇipuṣpa flower.
This [juice] does not become stale, nor does any other [juice] that is of the nature of a bud;
likewise, the lotus and the āmalaka fruit remain pure for three days.
O one whose wealth is austerity, those who for even a single day offer karavīra flowers,
and others such as white and red lotuses, and blue water-lilies;
85) One should entertain the suspicion that these have been kept overnight if they have been struck [by lightning] after five days.
The Praise of Gaṇeśa in the Saddharmacintāmaṇi.

At dawn, I remember the Lord of the Gaṇas, the protector and kinsman, whose pair of cheeks is resplendent with a full application of vermilion; who wields a fierce staff capable of crushing arrogant obstacles,
and who is worshipped by the hosts of celestial leaders such as Indra.

At dawn, I bow to the son of Śiva and Pārvatī, who is worshipped by the four-faced Brahmā, who grants every boon according to one's desire, whose belly is stout, who wears the sacred thread, and who is clever in his playful charms. O Lord of the twice-born! O Sacrifice! I bow to you.
For Śiva. || 2 ||
In the morning, O devotee, I indeed worship the Lord of the Gaṇas, the giver of fearlessness, whose face is like that of a noble elephant;
I worship him who is the fire that destroys the forest of ignorance and who increases one's enthusiasm.
It has been heard from the Lord. || 3 ||
This meritorious triad of verses always bestows imperial sovereignty upon that man who, having risen at dawn, recites it constantly with a disciplined mind.
The Hymn to the Goddess from the *Saddharmacintāmaṇi*.
At dawn, I remember you, whose luster is like the flames of the rays of the autumnal moon, adorned with earrings and necklaces set with excellent jewels,
possessing a thousand hands powerful with divine weapons, and whose feet have the hue of red lotuses.
Of others. || 1 ||

At dawn, I bow to Caṇḍī, who is manifold and embodies the forms of all the gods; she is skilled in destroying the Daityas headed by the Asuras Mahiṣa, Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and Śumbha, and she is passionately devoted to the conduct that enchants Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, and the sages.
Form || 2 ||

At dawn, having attained supreme meditative absorption, I worship Māyā— the bestower of desires upon those who worship her, the nurse of all worlds, the destroyer of the heat of misfortune, and the cause of liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra.
Of the supreme Viṣṇu. || 3 ||
A person who recites these three verses of the goddess Caṇḍikā attains all desires and is glorified in the world of the Goddess.
And likewise, in the Śāradā-tantra, there are the words of Śiva addressed to Bhuvaneśvarī:
"Even now you possess the fresh youth of all the worlds; though you are the daughter of the King of Mountains, you remain exceedingly tender."
In the *Samayātantra*:
Sometimes there may be liberation for someone, and sometimes there is only worldly enjoyment;
but for this practitioner, both enjoyment and liberation are held in the palm of the hand.
In the Rudrayāmala.
Where there is worldly enjoyment, there is no liberation; where there is liberation, there is no worldly enjoyment.
For those who worship the pair of Śiva’s lotus feet, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are held in the palm of their hand.
He who desires both worldly enjoyment and liberation from other philosophical systems [should follow this].

O Pārvatī, if one were to become wealthy merely by killing someone encountered in a dream, or if a delusion regarding silver were to arise from mother-of-pearl, then likewise one might seek enjoyment and liberation from other philosophical systems.
In the sixth chapter of the Śāktānandatarangiṇī.
Abandoning the deity residing within themselves, they search for a god outside;
like one who, casting aside the Kaustubha gem held in their own hand, wanders about in thirst for mere glass.
Having visualized [the deity] within one's heart, one should worship Śivā who stands outside;
likewise, for whichever deity it may be, as well as their ornaments and vehicle.
O Supreme Goddess, one should contemplate that very [deity] during its worship;
now I shall describe the internal sacrifice (antaryajana) by which one becomes identical with the Divine.
Seated comfortably on a pleasant seat, facing either east or north,
one should meditate upon the supreme ocean of nectar within one's own heart.
In the midst of those five jewel islands is one consisting of golden sand,
adorned with well-flowered *kalpa* trees such as the *mandāra* and *pārijāta*.
Adorned on all sides with divine trees that perpetually bear flowers and fruit,
the fragrance of various sweet-smelling blossoms pervades every direction.
It was crowded with bees delighted by the fragrance of blossoming flowers,
and the quarters of the sky were made resonant by the association of warbling cuckoos.
It was a divine lotus made of shimmering gold, adorned on all sides with pearls,
flowers, garlands, silken garments, and golden javelins.
In the midst of that, one should visualize the enchanting wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) of the Goddess,
which has four branches representing the four Vedas and is endowed with the three qualities (guṇas).
O beautiful one, there were yellow, black, white, and red flowers;
they were green, variegated, and adorned with many kinds of blossoms.
O Goddess, having thus meditated upon the Kalpa tree, which is adorned with many birds such as cuckoos and bees, and its base consisting of a jeweled pedestal;
There, one should contemplate a red mandala pervading the upper region,
resembling the rising sun and adorned with jeweled stairways.
It was strewn with rows of banners, provided with four gates,
enriched with the splendor of various jewels and the like, and adorned with a wall of gems.
It was presided over by the world-protectors stationed in their respective abodes,
and by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Mahoragas.
It was filled on all sides with kinnaras and apsarases sporting about,
and joined by throngs of celestial women devoted to dancing and instrumental music.
It was adorned with banners bound with networks of small bells,
and embellished with great rubies, lapis lazuli, jewels, and yak-tail whisks.
It was adorned with large, dangling pearls of great brilliance,
and anointed with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and camphor.
In the center of that, one should visualize the goddess upon a pedestal of great rubies,
adorned with four corners and the radiance of the rising sun and moon.
There, one should meditate upon the lion-throne consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
O Maheśānī, one should place a cushion of flowers upon that lion-throne.
Then, having performed the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭha-pūjā) according to the sequence prescribed in the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa),
one should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess there upon the corpse-lotus seat (pretapadmāsana).
The meditation upon one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) is described here:
having offered the venerable jeweled sandals and brought [the deity] to the bathing chamber.
Once she is seated upon the lion-throne,
one should perform the ritual anointing with camphor, agallochum, musk, and likewise with deer-musk.
Having performed the rubbing of the Goddess with yellow pigment mixed with saffron and endowed with various fragrances,
one should anoint her with scented oil.
Having brought water from hundreds of thousands of divine sources and from thousands of golden jars, one should meditate upon the Supreme Deity who has been bathed with that water.
One should wipe the body with *dukūla* cloths, and likewise wrap it in *dukūla* garments;
one should groom the hair with a comb and bind it according to the prescribed rite.
One should apply a forehead mark (tilaka) adorned with various jewels upon the forehead using a cluster of silk cloth from the mass of hair,
and vermilion (sindūra) in the middle of the hair.
One should offer a beautiful conch fashioned from the tusks of the king of elephants,
as well as armlets for the hands, along with bracelets and bangles.
One should give a toe-ring adorned with various jewels;
one should place anklets on the feet and an elephant-pearl on the tip of the nose.
One should offer flowers, garlands, and ornaments according to one's ability;
one should apply an ointment of sandalwood and sihlaka to all parts of the body.
One should meditate upon the Goddess above the heart, adorned with a golden bodice; one should then perform the purification of the elements and other rites.
Having performed the web of ritual placements (nyāsa), one should always worship within meditative absorption;
with the sixteen types of offerings, one should worship Śivā residing in the heart.
One should offer a jeweled lion-throne and speak words of welcome and well-being;
O Goddess, one should present water for the feet at the feet and the respectful offering (arghya) upon the head.
One should offer the supreme nectar for sipping into the lotus of the mouth;
one should place the honey-mixture (madhuparka) in the mouth, and offer water for sipping three times into the mouth.
Divine, supreme rice-pudding, served on golden leaves and strewn about,
combined with the ghee of a tawny cow and accompanied by various side dishes.
An ocean of nectar, mountains of meat, heaps of fish, and fruits;
likewise, food to be eaten, chewed, licked, and sucked.
One should mentally offer betel leaf with camphor;
thereafter, the worship of the Goddess's enclosures should indeed be performed by the mind alone.
Thus, having propitiated [the deity] within by means of mental recitation alone,
and having performed a thousand or more repetitions of the mantra, one should offer water to the Goddess.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—
these alone are declared to be the couch of the Great Goddess.
One should prepare a bed resembling the foam of milk, adorned with various flowers—
a flower-bed— thereupon which one should place the Goddess, the Sovereign of the Gods.
The practitioner-yogi should meditate upon her who delights in manifold pleasures;
he should gratify the Supreme Goddess with dances, songs, and musical instruments.
Then one should perform the fire offering (homa) for the sake of making the worship meaningful.
The sixteen services for Durgā in mental worship.
It was bathed by streams of water reddened with saffron and fragrant sandalwood paste.
O Ambikā! Accept this [mirror] set with various priceless jewels and corals,
which has been offered and is being rubbed on all sides with lotus-like hands by celestial beauties out of devotion.
O Mother, O beautiful one! O wish-fulfilling creeper for devotees! [I worship] the venerable sandals with reverence. || 1 ||
The hosts of gods, led by the Lord of Devas, took up the lion throne,
which was fashioned from a mass of shimmering gold and was radiant with beautiful luster.
O Ambikā, please accept with reverence this exceedingly pure oil, fragrant with the scent of campaka and ketakī flowers, along with scented unguents offered by young maidens. || 2 ||
Afterwards, O Goddess! O Consort of Śambhu! O Śrīsundarī! take, as is generally the case, this stainless *dhātrī* fruit, which is filled with a multitude of fragrant substances.
Having cleansed your hair with a comb in the current of the Mandākinī and bathed there, O illustrious Sundarī, may radiant fragrance reside upon your face! (3)
She holds the lotus-stalk-like hands of the Goddess of Wine,
which are resplendent with sandalwood, fine saffron, and abundant aloe-wood paste.
O Bestower of Boons! O Tripurasundarī! Accept this fresh and pure musk, radiant with a great fragrance, at your auspicious feet. 4.
O Mother, [I bow to] the most excellent one, held in the lotus-palms of the offspring of the Gandharvas, gods, and Kinnaras, who are dear to them;
who is tawny like saffron,
radiant with the splendor of the shining orb of the sun, and brilliant with the light of her gift.
And may this stainless garment spread [its luster] for your delight, O Śrīsundarī! || 5 ||
Upon her two ears are earrings fashioned of gold; upon her lotus-hands are rings;
at the waist is a girdle; and upon her two feet, which possess the fullness of hips, are anklets.
A necklace upon the chest, the jingling of bracelets on the pair of hands, and a crown placed daily upon the head—let that which bestows intoxication be praised. (6)
Upon her neck she wears a beautiful necklace of radiant gems that holds a mass of lovely luster;
upon the surface of her forehead shines vermilion, bearing the seal of beauty.

O Śrī Śāmbhavī, may Your two eyes— whose beauty is like that of shimmering collyrium and the petals of a radiant blue lotus— bestow [this] upon my glorious feet, fashioned as it were from divine medicine. (7)
O Tripurasundarī! At your feet, which resemble the rays of the moon and arise from the ocean of milk churned by Mount Mandara, [I offer salutations].
O mirror, take hold of this face—which rests upon my lotus-like hand—to behold its reflection, fashioned from coral and covered with a silver casing. || 8 ||
It was drenched with streams of musk, liquid sandalwood, agallochum, and nectar,
and rendered fragrant by substances as sweet-smelling as blooming campaka and pāṭalā flowers.

O Goddess Ambika! Accept this pure water offered with great reverence by Ambhā, using a multitude of jars filled with great jewels and other precious substances, which rest upon the heads of the divine Śrīgaṇas. || 9 ||
A garland made of *kalhāra*, *utpala*, *nāgakeśara*, *saroja*, *mālatī*, *ballī*,
*kairava*, *ketaka*, and other flowers such as the red *aśvamāra*.
Indeed, with flowers, with an abundance of fragrant garlands, and with streams of various essences.
I worship the Blessed One, the illustrious Caṇḍikā, who dwells within the copper-colored lotus.
With the powders of māṃsī, guggulu, candana, aguru, karpūra, and śaileya;
Together with honey, well-prepared saffron, and mixed with clarified butter.
Its placement in a temple or within a vessel made of jewels shall lead to delight.
O beloved of the gods, O illustrious Caṇḍikā! This incense has been prepared for your mouth. 11.
It is joined with a beautiful jeweled staff that glistens and flows with clarified butter.
The destroyer of great darkness, created by the celestial damsels.
It is situated in a golden cup and provided with a wick made of solid essence.
O Tripurasundarī! O Goddess! Your lamp shines for the sake of joy. || 12 ||
The jasmine is fragrant, and the pure rice-gruel is pleasing to the taste.
It is indeed proper [to serve] side dishes prepared with asafoetida, black pepper, cumin, and fragrant ingredients.
Mixed with cooked rice, milk-rice (pāyasa), honey, curd, and clarified butter.
O Śrī Caṇḍikā! May this food offering, prepared by celestial nymphs, enter your mouth. 13.
A leaf of the *nāgavallī* plant, radiant with cloves and flower buds.
Tender nutmeg fruit together with camphor and betel nut.
It was filled with the sweetness of nectar and placed within a beautiful vessel of jewels.
Take this fragrant betel-leaf, shimmering with scent, in your lotus-like mouth.
It is as beautiful as the shimmering moonlight of both the autumn and spring moons.
The river of the Dalat-surat [song] possesses a charming abundance of pearls.
Take this staff, radiant with fragments of ninefold golden luster.
O Mahātripurasundarī! [This is] the great, manifest parasol. 15.
O Mother, may your joy increase, O fortunate one, ever swayed by women.
The white fly-whisk, resembling the moon and the jasmine flower, removes the suffering of perspiration.
Let the sound of the Veda bring blessings, even while it is being performed within one's own mind.
In the courtyard of heaven, he is being celebrated with songs accompanied by the sounds of flutes, clay drums, conchs, and kettledrums.
Thus the Vidyādharī remained, agitated by clamors for the sake of the pleasure of the art of dance.
O Goddess, may she whose conduct is permeated by the sentiment of devotion find pleasure in it, should she obtain it from anywhere.
In that regard, even a single birth that bears fruit is not obtained by hundreds of millions of efforts. || 17 ||
Whoever praises the Supreme Deity with these sixteen words arranged as ritual offerings shall obtain the fruit of those [offerings].
Invocation of Auspiciousness.

Having meditated upon the moon-crested Lord, who holds the *heramba* (trunk) and whose heart-delighting, beautiful state belongs to his own Guru, and having remembered the Supreme Maheśa, by whom the dense ocean of the birth of obstacles has been swallowed;
Lakṣmyagranārāyaṇa, the path for the mental delight of the multitude of the learned.
I shall explain this graceful procedure for the worship of Durgā for the sake of awakening the ignorant. || 1 ||
Homage to the gurus.
To you, Māyā, Bhavānī, the Sovereign of the World.
O Mother, whose heart is always moist with compassion, I bow to you.
Indeed, [he sees] the lamp of worship that is self-luminous.
I create a difficult path for the welfare of the world. || 2 ||
Having reverently bowed to the pair of lotus-feet of Caṇḍikā, (p. 91).
A certain wise man has composed this compendium of the ritual for worship. || 3 ||
Now I shall describe the procedure for worship that bestows all prosperity:
having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and meditated upon the Guru on one's own crown.

There, the practitioner, having risen at dawn, remains on his very bed in the bound lotus posture (*baddhapadmāsana*). [The *Kula* trees are: the *aśoka*, the *keśara*, the *bilva*, the *karṇikāra*, the *cyuta*, as well as the *nameru*, the *priyāla*, the *sinduvāra*, the two *kadambas*, the *maruvaka*, the *campaka*, and the *bilva*.

Twelve [types are] recorded: the *nameru* is the *rudrākṣa*; the *priyāla* is a specific kind of tree. In the fifteenth chapter (*ullāsa*) of the *Śāktānandatarangiṇī*: "Having bowed to the tree, one should meditate upon one's own guru, who resides within the lunar disc situated in the center of the pericarp of a white thousand-petalled lotus on the crown of one's head."

White in complexion, adorned with white unguents, garlands, and garments, he is embraced by his beloved who holds a red lotus in her left hand; with a serene countenance, he bestows the gestures of fearlessness and boons with his two hands— this is the supreme form of Śambhu, in which the wine intoxicates the pair of his lotus-eyes.
"One should meditate on the Guru situated upon the head. Having thus meditated.
Having worshipped with mental offerings.
Oṃ Laṃ; I offer fragrance, consisting of the element of earth, to the Guru; homage!
With the thumb and little finger: *Oṃ haṃ*, I offer flowers to the Guru, who is of the nature of space;
*namaḥ*. With the thumb and ring finger: *Oṃ yaṃ*, I cause the incense, which is of the nature of air, to be smelled by the Guru; *namaḥ*. With the thumb and middle finger: *Oṃ raṃ*...
I offer this lamp, consisting of fire, to the Guru; homage! (With the thumb and forefinger.)

Oṃ vaṃ, I offer this food (naivedya) consisting of nectar to the Guru; obeisance. [With the thumb and ring finger. Oṃ saṃ, I offer this betel (tāmbūla) consisting of the essence of the moon to the Guru; obeisance. [With all the fingers. I worship the Śrīpādukā of Amukānandanātha; obeisance. Thus.
Having fully worshipped.
Oṃ aiṃ hīṃ śrīṃ hasakhaphreṃ hsauḥ hasakṣamalavarayūṃ sahasakhaphreṃ sahausahakṣamalavāyūṃ hsauḥ [Name]ānandanātha.

"Amukīdevyām vā śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi namaḥ. Having thus recited the Guru-pādukā mantra ten or seven times, [one should place] the recitation upon the right hand of the Guru: "Oṃ, you are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by us. O Lord, may success be mine!"
"By your grace, O Great Guru! Having thus offered [the mantra].
Salutations to that venerable Guru who has revealed that state which is of the form of an unbroken circle and by which the moving and the unmoving are pervaded. || 2 ||
Salutations to that Guru, who is the very embodiment of the chosen deity.
The nectar of whose speech destroys the poison known as saṃsāra.
Having thus prostrated, one should offer praise.
Salutations, O Lord! O Blessed One! To Śiva in the form of the Guru.
He has assumed various forms for the sake of successfully bringing about the descent of knowledge.
Salutation to the one whose nature is Nārāyaṇa, who is the singular form of ultimate reality,
who is like the sun that dispels the darkness of all ignorance, and who consists of pure consciousness.

To the one who is independent, whose form is fashioned by compassion, and whose nature is auspiciousness; to the one who is dependent upon his devotees, appearing in auspicious forms for those who are destined for liberation.
Salutations to the one who is the discernment for the discerning, the reflection for those who reflect,
the illumination for those who illuminate, and the embodiment of knowledge for the wise.
In front, on both sides, behind, above, and below, I shall always pay homage; O Lord, please provide Your seat in the form of my very consciousness.
O Lord! By Your grace, I have accomplished all my goals in every respect;
I am liberated from the great snare of illusory death, and I am Śiva.
Having thus offered praise.
"O Lord of the World! Whatever I do from morning until evening, and from evening until morning thereafter—let that be an offering unto You. Having thus offered everything to the Guru.
Having received his command, one should contemplate oneself as purified, washed by the stream of nectar flowing from his feet.
Then, within the triangle situated in the pericarp of the four-petalled lotus located at the *mūlādhāra* [Note: ...].

In another Tantra: "Listen to the supreme secret wonder regarding the three triangles: the left line is Brahmā, the right line is Viṣṇu, and the lower line is Rudra; the Mātrā is Sarasvatī herself. She encircles the self-arisen Liṅga situated in the center with its face turned downward."
Having the form of a sleeping serpent,
with three folds in the shape of a conch-spiral, and possessing the brilliance of ten million flashes of lightning— (p. 93).
One should contemplate Kuṇḍalī, who is subtler than a lotus fiber, who is the primordial nature and the Root-Vidyā;

she who is like a crooked hook and possesses the form of ten million streaks of lightning. Kuṇḍalī is shaped like a hook, while Sadāśiva is the eternal void in the center. O fair-faced one, the left line resembles the hibiscus flower and fire, while the right line is like the autumn moon.

Having made [the deity] conscious by means of the *kūrca* seed-syllable and the triangular fire, which is the form of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) and possesses a right-lined appearance, one should lead it through the path of the *suṣumṇā* to the end of the twelve [fingers],
and unite it with the Supreme Sadāśiva residing in the thousand-petaled lotus at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
There, having satiated [the deities] with a stream of nectar flowing from the lunar disc,
one should meditate upon the Family Preceptor (kulaguru) right there within that radiance— [the preceptor] whose heart is surging with the essence of the family nectar,
whose eyes are rolling, and whose every austerity has been dissolved and pulverized by the embrace of the Kula [consort], together with the family disciples.

Having meditated thus: "They are surrounded [by attendants], their inner faculties are fully aroused, all of them bestow boons and fearlessness, and they are knowers of the meaning of the Durgā-tantras."
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Prahlādānandanātha.

Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Sakalānandanātha. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Kumārānandanātha. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Vasiṣṭhānandanātha. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Krodhānandanātha. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Asurānandanātha.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Dhyānānandanātha. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Bodhānandanātha. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Śukānandanātha. Having thus meditated:

Then, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *ṛṣi* and so forth, as well as the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) placement, one should bring Kuṇḍalinī into the twelve-petaled heart-lotus, meditate upon her in the form of Durgā according to the method to be described, and worship her with mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*).

"Oṃ, may we know the Great Goddess; may we meditate upon Durgā; may that Goddess inspire us. Having thus recited this Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times, twenty-eight times, or ten times, and having recited the root (nine-syllable) mantra one hundred times: "O You, the protector of the most secret of secrets..."

"Accept this recitation performed by me. May success be mine, O Goddess! By your grace, O Great Sovereign! Having thus offered the recitation into the left hand of the Goddess, and having praised and bowed to her, one should request the Goddess's permission: "O you who consist of the consciousness of the three worlds, O Triśakti!"
"O Mother of the Universe, by your very command, having risen in the morning for your sake, I shall follow the course of worldly life. Having thus prayed:
Then, having brought Kuṇḍalinī back to the Mūlādhāra by that very same path, one should contemplate the Self as follows: "O Goddess, I am not another;
I am Brahman alone, not subject to sorrow. I am the Self, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss."

O Goddess, O Bhavānī, O Durgā! By Your command alone, I shall—having risen at dawn for Your pleasure—follow the course of worldly life, while maintaining the identity of my Guru, the Deity, and myself as one, consisting of the consciousness of the three worlds. I know what is dharma, yet I have no inclination toward it; I know what is adharma, yet I have no aversion toward it.
Whatever I am commanded by the deity residing in my heart, that I shall do. || 2 ||
The characteristic of the goad (aṅkuśa) mudrā is as follows: the middle finger is straight, its middle joint is pressed down by the index finger, which is turned downward.
This is to be known as the Aṅkuśa (Goad) Mudrā:
having grasped the left fist with the right fist, one should extend the middle finger of the left hand and bend the index finger; this is the Aṅkuśa Mudrikā.
Meditating thus and realizing "I am indeed Brahman," one should pray to the Earth.
Oṃ! O Goddess whose girdle is the ocean, whose breasts are the mountain ranges, O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutations to you; forgive my touch of your feet.

Thus, following his breath, having placed his foot on the ground and gone outside, he should perform the necessary duties; then, having returned to the pure divine abode, removed the *nirmālya*, prostrated, and received permission, he should go to a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) for the purpose of bathing. Now, regarding the bath: having gone to a river or similar location...
Having smeared one's limbs with clay using the nine-syllable mantra and reciting the root mantra, one should perform the removal of impurities (*malāpakarṣaṇa*).

Having sipped water (*ācamya*), one should place a copper vessel filled with water, along with sesame seeds, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and hibiscus flowers (*javāpuṣpa*). With that, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Oṃ, today [and so forth], for the destruction of all sins that obstruct this mantra..."
Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the pleasure of the venerable Caṇḍikā, I shall perform the mantra-bath (*mantra-snāna*) as previously prescribed."

Having drawn a triangle with its apex downward in the water, one should invoke the sacred waters from the solar orb using the *aṅkuśa-mudrā* (the hook-gesture) with this mantra: "O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Kāverī, Narmadā, and Sindhu, please be present in these waters! Then, one should seal the seven openings [of the body] with the fingers.
Having restrained [the breath] and having immersed it three times with the root-mantra (mūlavidyā).
p.

95) *Mūlānta ātmatattvāya svāhā* || *Vidyātattvāya svāhā* || *Śivatattvāya svāhā* || Having thus sipped water three times, one should sprinkle water upon the head three times with the *mūla-mantra* using the *kumbha-mudrā*; this is the ritual bath (*snāna*).

Now, the procedure for the twilight rites (*sandhyā-vidhi*): Then, having put on two white garments and tied the topknot (*śikhā*) with the mantra: "Oṃ maṇidharani vajriṇi mahāpratisare rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā."
Having applied a tilaka with sindūra and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) while reciting the root mantra.

Having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) beginning with the *ṛṣi* and so forth, take water in the left hand and cover it with the right hand. Consecrate it by reciting the five elemental seed-syllables (*bīja*), namely *laṃ haṃ yaṃ raṃ vaṃ*. Then, while reciting the root mantra seven times, sprinkle drops of that water from between the fingers onto the head with the mantra.
Having performed the sprinkling with the *mudrā* upon the head and having drawn a line of water on the right, one should lead it toward the nostril;

drawing [the breath] through the left nostril, one should imagine that all the sins residing within the body are washed away by it, and that this water, black in color, enters the hand through the left nostril and is placed before oneself.

Having cast [the water] three times upon the imagined vajra-stone with the mantra "Astrāya Phaṭ," and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while exhaling with the root mantra, one should offer three handfuls of water to the Sun. Then, reciting the Gāyatrī: "Oṃ mahādevyai vidmahe durgāyai dhīmahi tanno devī pracodayāt," one should repeat it one hundred and eight times or twenty-eight times.
Or one may recite it eight times; this is the rule for the twilight devotion (saṃdhyā).
Now follows the libation.
Having visualized the *yantra* in the water, having requested the deities to be propitiated here and invoked them: Oṃ, may Brahmā-Bhairava be satisfied.
Oṃ, may Viṣṇu-Bhairava be satisfied. Oṃ, may Rudra-Bhairava be satisfied. Oṃ ha sa kṣa ma la va ra yūṃ svadhā, vauṣaṭ to the Goddess.

O Ānanda Bhairavī, may you be satisfied. This, O Lord, is the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Now, the libation for the sages (*ṛṣi-tarpaṇa*): Oṃ, may the Great Goddess Kālī be satisfied. Oṃ, may the Great Goddess Lakṣmī be satisfied. Oṃ, may the Great Goddess Sarasvatī be satisfied. Oṃ, may the Great Lord Ānandanātha be satisfied. Oṃ.

May Tripurāmbā be satisfied. Oṃ, may Bhairavānandanātha be satisfied. Oṃ, may Brahmānandanātha be satisfied. Oṃ, may Pūrṇānandanātha be satisfied. Oṃ, may Vandināthānandanātha be satisfied. Oṃ, may Calaccidānandanātha be satisfied.
Oṃ, may Cañcalānandanātha be satisfied. Oṃ, may Kumārānandanātha be satisfied.
Oṃ, may Krodhānandanātha be satiated. Oṃ, may Varadānandanātha be satiated. Oṃ, may Smaradīpānandanātha be satiated. Oṃ, may Māyāmbā be satiated.

May Mother Māyāvatī be satisfied. Oṃ, may Nātha Vimalānanda be satisfied. Oṃ, may Nātha Kuśalānanda be satisfied. Oṃ, may Nātha Gorakṣānanda be satisfied. Oṃ, may Nātha Bhojadevānanda be satisfied. Oṃ, may Nātha Prajāpatyānanda be satisfied.
Oṃ, may Mūladevānandanātha be satisfied. Oṃ, may Vighnadevānandanātha be satisfied. Oṃ, may Hutāśanānandanātha be satisfied.
Oṃ, may Samayānandanātha be satisfied. Oṃ, may Saṃtoṣānandanātha be satisfied.

Now, the libation to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa). One should offer libations with one's own name, preceded by the names of the Gurus: "Oṃ, [Name] Nātha, Guru, Paramaguru, Parāparaguru, Parameṣṭhiguru. Having worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings.

At the end of the root mantra, one should offer libations with: "I satisfy Śrī Caṇḍikā, together with her limbs, her retinue, her weapons, and her powers, accompanied by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; obeisance! One should perform this libation ten times or three times.

Thus, even when one is unable to perform the *tarpaṇa* at the twilight hours, one should meditate upon the Goddess of the three times and recite the root mantra or the *gāyatrī* according to one's capacity. Then, having offered the *arghya* to the Sun three times with the mantra: "Oṃ Hrīṃ Haṃsaḥ, to Mārtaṇḍa Bhairava together with the Śakti Prakāśā, this *arghya*, Svāhā," [one should offer it] into the solar orb.

Having visualized the Goddess and recited the root mantra, one should offer this *arghya* with the mantra: "To Caṇḍikā, who resides within the orb of the rising sun, who consists of consciousness, and who is accompanied by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra— *idam arghyaṃ svāhā*," using a vessel filled with red sandalwood paste, hibiscus flowers, *kuśa* grass, water, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).

Having offered *arghya* with a copper vessel to the Goddess residing in the solar orb, having recited the *Gāyatrī* as much as possible, and having made the offering with the mantra "O Guhye," one should dismiss the Goddess from the solar orb; such is the procedure for the *saṃdhyā*.
Now follows the procedure for worship.

Having put on a pair of garments as desired and having applied a tilaka with sandalwood paste and other unguents, one approaches the vicinity of the house of worship: "The Sun, the Moon, Yama, Time, and the five great elements—
these nine are the witnesses here of one's auspicious and inauspicious actions."
"O Goddess! My mind was previously vulgar and overcome by sin. Drive that sin out from my mind—phaṭ phaṭ! Homage to you! With this mantra, one performs the eradication of sin (*pāpotsādana*).

Having performed [the preliminary rites], one should bring water with the mantra: *vajrodake hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Having sprinkled the seat with this water and sat down, one should wash both hands and feet with the mantra: *oṃ viśuddhe sarvapāpāni śamayāśeṣavikalpānayanāpahaṃ*. Then, *oṃ hṛ*...

Saying "svāhā," one should sip water (ācamana). Having tied the topknot with this same mantra, one should prepare the general arghya vessel. For instance, having drawn a mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a square on one's left, one should worship the base (ādhāra) with: "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti. Thus, one should worship the base.
Having established [the deity], recite: *oṃ kraḥ astrāya phaṭ*. Thus, having washed the vessel and placed it upon the support (*ādhāra*), [proceed].

Saying "Oṃ krāṃ, obeisance to the heart," fill [the vessel] with water and invoke the sacred waters (tīrthas) with this mantra: "O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Kāverī, Narmadā, Sindhu—be present in this water! Having invoked the sacred waters from the solar orb using the *aṅkuśa-mudrā* with this mantra, [proceed]. Oṃ...
Having cast [the substances] such as fragrance with the syllable *mit*, one should display the *dhenu-mudrā* with the syllable *vam*; this is the general *arghya*.
Then, having sprinkled the house door with that water for worship, one should worship the deities of the door.
Above the door: *Gaṃ* to Gaṇapati, obeisance. To the left: *Kṣaṃ* to Kṣetrapāla, obeisance. To the right:
*Vāṃ* to Vaṭuka, obeisance. Below: *Yāṃ* to the Yoginīs, obeisance. In this same sequence:
above, *Gaṃ* to Gaṅgā, obeisance; to the left, *Yaṃ* to Yamunā, obeisance; to the right, *Śrī*.

"Obeisance to Lakṣmī" [at the bottom]; "Obeisance to Sarasvatī" [at the top]. In this manner, one should worship the doors starting from the east. "O Door-Goddess Śrī, I offer this arghya. Then: "Having observed the guardians of the door, may they protect the entrance with effort, warding off the multitude of obstacles"—such is the command of the Supreme Lord. Thus.

Having caused the command of the deity to be heard, contracting his left limb, and crossing the threshold with his right foot leading the way, he enters within, reciting: "Oṃ! Let the beings depart, the Piśācas, Pretas, and Guhyakas; and whatever other deities dwell upon the earth, let them go away. "Let them move away!"
May those beings who exist on earth, and those beings who create obstacles, perish by the command of Śiva.
Oṃ, drive away, drive away all obstacles, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! With these mantras,
by striking with the left heel, by raising three claps of the hands one after another, and with a gaze free from blinking—
Having dispelled terrestrial, atmospheric, and celestial obstacles, and having sprinkled that house with *arghya* water, one should worship as follows:
"Obeisance to Vāstupuruṣa in the southwest corner; obeisance to Dīpanātha in the northeast corner.
Having thus worshipped, [one recites]: "Oṃ! O sharp-fanged one, of massive body, resembling the fire at the end of an aeon!"

"Salutations to you, O Bhairava; you should grant me permission. Having thus received the command of Bhairava, he sprinkles the ground with the mantra: "Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa huṃ phaṭ svāhā. He consecrates the ground with the mantra: "Oṃ pavitra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. [Then he draws] the line for the Asuras: "Oṃ āsurekhe..."

Having drawn a triangular maṇḍala on the ground with "Vajrarekhe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," [one should offer obeisance as follows]: Oṃ [Oṃ kūrmāsanāya namaḥ || Oṃ hrīṃ ādhāraśaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ || Oṃ pṛthivyai namaḥ || Oṃ anantāsanāya namaḥ || Oṃ vimalāsanāya namaḥ || Oṃ]...
Salutation to Padmāsana. Hrīṃ, salutation to Ādhāraśakti Kamalāsana. Having thus worshipped [it].

There, having arranged a seat such as a *kaṃvala* (woolen blanket) and so forth, and having worshipped the seat by saying "Salutation to Gaṇeśa" in the south-eastern corner, "Salutation to Sarasvatī" in the south-western corner, "Salutation to Durgā" in the north-western corner, and "Salutation to Kṣetrapāla" in the north-eastern corner— proceeding clockwise— and then placing one's hand [upon the seat], [one recites] the *merupṛṣṭha* [verse] of the seat-mantra.

The seer is Sutala, the meter is Kūrma, the deity is Kūrma; the application is for sitting upon the seat. Oṃ! O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu. Therefore, O Goddess, support me. [Note: Regarding the purification of the place, the *Gandharva Tantra* says: "Inspection is Dharma..."]

One should perform the sprinkling of the sacrificial ground with the seed-mantra (bīja), and the sprinkling of the site of sacrifice with the Astra-mantra. Whatever may be unknown, defiled, or otherwise flawed regarding the place, such as the sweeping and other rites—O Dear One, all such things are removed by the recitation of that mantra. [The ground is purified] by the masses of fat from Madhu and Kaiṭabha.

"Having attained firmness, the earth is always pure for all worship of the gods; for the liberation from that defect, one should write the seed-syllable of Kāma (Klīm) upon the ground. Make the seat sacred.
Having recited this, having placed a grass mat (viṣṭara) on the lower part [of the ground], one should sit facing north in the Vīrāsana or another such posture.

Then, having accepted the materials for worship: [one should bow] with "guṃ, obeisance to the Gurus" on the right; "gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati" on the left; and "caṃ, obeisance to the goddess Caṇḍikā" in the center. Having thus bowed, [one places] the *arghya* on the left.
Having set [the vessel] down and having placed a little water in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel,

one should sprinkle oneself and the materials for worship with that water. One should place flowers and other items on one's right side, a vessel for washing the hands behind oneself, and the articles of worship behind the Goddess.

Having established [the deity], perform the purification of the flowers with the mantra: *oṃ puṣpaketurājārhataḥ śatāya samyaksambuddhāya | oṃ puṣpe puṣpe mahāpuṣpe supuṣpe puṣpasambhave | puṣpaṃ ca yāvakīrṇa huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Then, [recite] *oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
With the mantra [and the characteristics of the Nārāca-mudrā:

"The snapping of the tips of the thumb and forefinger is the Nārāca-mudrā"], having performed the purification of all the ritual requisites such as the perfumes by means of the Nārāca-mudrā and a steady gaze, one should touch the flame of the lamp with the syllable *ram*.

Having performed the purification of body, speech, and mind with the mantra *oṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*, and having performed self-protection by placing the hand upon the heart while reciting *rakṣa rakṣa huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Having rubbed sandalwood-smeared flowers with both hands and taken them in the left hand, one should smell them and say: "May all those who harm me and all harmful beings go to destruction."

Having cast [the offering] far toward the northeast with the mantra: "May death, disease, fear, and afflictions fall upon the head of the enemy," and having performed the triple *tāla* and the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with the nine-syllable mantra, [one should recite] the five-syllable mantra of the Supreme Goddess: *Kālī-kūrca-vadhū-māyā-phaṭ*.

Regarding Caṇḍikā’s Kullukā [in the Rudrayāmala]: "O Goddess, if one recites a great mantra without knowing the Kullukā, his four—life-span, knowledge, fame, and strength—are destroyed. [In the Vārāhī Tantra: "The practitioner of mantra should begin the recitation according to the rule, starting with the Kullukā. [The meditation on Earth: five colors.

The ground is variegated, endowed with various fragrances, strewn with heaps of flowers, and adorned with bells and chowries; it is as beautiful as the rising sun and brings delight to the mind. Having taken recourse to such ground, one should worship the Supreme Goddess. Thus it is proclaimed in the Viśuddheśvara [Tantra].
In the Tantra.
Having thus meditated on the *kullukā* at the crown of the head, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) with the root mantra: *ātmatattvāya svāhā*.
1. Mūlaṃ vidyā-tattvāya svāhā. 2. Mūlaṃ śiva-tattvāya svāhā. 3. Mūlaṃ śiva-tattvāya svāhā.

Having thus sipped water, wiping the two lips twice with the *mūla-mantra*, and washing the hands with the *mūla-mantra*, one should touch the seven apertures with water: "Oṃ, obeisance to Mahākālī" at the mouth; "Oṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī"; "Oṃ, obeisance to Mahāsarasvatī" at the nostrils; "Oṃ, obeisance to Nandajā."

Oṃ, salutation to Rakta-dantikā; [place] at the eyes. Oṃ, salutation to Śākambharī. Oṃ, salutation to Durgā; [place] at the ears. Oṃ, salutation to Bhīmā; [place] at the navel. Oṃ, salutation to Bhrāmī; [place] at the chest. Oṃ, salutation to Aṣṭādaśa-bhujā; [place] at the head. Oṃ, salutation to Aṣṭa-bhujā.
Homage! Oṃ, homage to the ten-armed one on the two arms. Having thus touched the limbs:

*Huṃ haṃ hīṃ astrāya phaṭ.* Having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with this, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). To do so: having fixed the mind on the *mūlādhāra* and holding the right nostril with the right thumb while reciting either the *praṇava* or the root seed-syllable (*mūlādyabīja*) sixteen times.
Having filled the air through the left nostril and holding the left nostril with the little and ring fingers, one should arrest the breath while reciting [the mantra] sixty-four times.

The first method is: recite [the mantra] thirty-two times while exhaling through the right nostril. The second method is: having filled the right nostril with air by means of that same [mantra] and retained it [in kumbhaka], exhale through the left. The third method is again as in the first; if performed with the root-mantra, there is one inhalation and four [recitations].
Having thus performed the breath control (prāṇāyāma) consisting of two [parts] for retention (kumbhaka) and one for exhalation (recaka).

In the *Nīlatantra*: "If a person recites the great mantra (*mahāmantra*) without knowing the *kullukā*, he will meet his death or become insane. By holding the *kullukā* upon one's head, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices."

One should wear the *kullukā* on the head, having written it upon birch bark; one will certainly be victorious at the royal gate and in the assembly hall. There is no other consideration: this is the view of Virūpākṣa everywhere. For men devoid of the *kullukā*, ignorance arises; my worship is always in vain for them.

Likewise, one should know the supreme mantra of Durgā, which consists of the true syllables of the sacrifice. That fool who does not know the *kullukā* yet recites the *Caṇḍikā* mantra must recite it for as long as he lives, yet it will never attain perfection.

p. 101) [In the Purification of the Elements (Bhūtaśuddhi): "In all external forms of worship, internal worship is prescribed. O Great Goddess! One obtains the fruit of ten million external worships through internal worship. || 1 ||
If one should worship without performing the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and the ritual placement of syllables (*lipinyāsa*),
it would yield contrary results, just as worship performed without devotion does.
[2] One should perform the purification of the elements.
Just as by means of the syllable *hūṃ*, one should raise the *kuṇḍalinī* from the *mūlādhāra*, unite it with the individual self (*jīvātman*),

and dissolve it into the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) by means of the mantra *haṃsa*; then, having dissolved the earth situated from the feet up to the knees into water, and that water situated from the knees up to the navel.

One should dissolve that [fire] into Prakṛti, which resides from the navel up to the heart; and one should dissolve that Prakṛti into Brahman, which resides from the heart up to the space between the eyebrows. Then, one should contemplate the sin accumulated through beginningless existence as resembling a man, with the murder of a Brahmin for its head, the theft of gold for its two arms, and so forth.
The drinking of liquor is joined to the heart; violating the Guru’s bed is the two thighs. Association with such persons is the pair of feet;
minor sins (upapātaka) are the limbs and sub-limbs. The hair of the body is the minor offenses; the blood is the beard and eyes. Wielding a sword and shield is sin; the big toe is the [great] sin.

One should visualize the *parimāṇaka* [the personification of sin] as being face-down and black in color within the left side of the belly. Having thus visualized the *pāpapuruṣa*, one should fill the breath through the left nostril with the seed-syllable *yaṃ* repeated sixteen times,
join it at the navel, and having meditated on *yaṃ* there, dry up the body along with its sins.

Having joined [the breath] at the *mūlādhāra* by means of the application of *kumbhaka* (retention) with the seed-syllable *Raṃ* recited sixty-four times, and having visualized *Raṃ*, one should burn the body along with its sins until it reaches the state of ashes; then,
with the seed-syllable *Yaṃ* recited thirty-two times, one should [expel] the ash of the personified sin through the right nostril.

One should recite [the mantra]. Then, by the recitation of the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, having caused a rain of nectar consisting of the letters of the Mātṛkā to fall from the moon on the forehead, one should drench the ashes, produce the limbs [of the body] according to the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*), and strengthen them by the recitation of *laṃ*. [This constitutes] the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of the Supreme Self, and from that, the principle of the Great One (*mahattattva*).

Then, having withdrawn the ego (ahaṃkāra), from that the ether (ākāśa), from that the air (vāyu), from that the fire (tejas), from that the water (jala), and from that the earth (pṛthivī), and having established each in its own respective place, [one should bring forth] the individual soul (jīvātman) from the presence of the Supreme Self (paramātman) residing in the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) by means of the mantra "So'ham" (I am He), like a lamp.

Having brought Kuṇḍalinī, who has the form of a coiled serpent, to the door of the heart-lotus and having established Kuṇḍalinī back in the Mūlādhāra, one should contemplate one's own body as being cleansed of all impurities and fit for the worship of the Deity; this is Bhūtaśuddhi (the purification of the elements). Having thus performed the Bhūtaśuddhi within one's own body...
One should establish the vital breaths of Caṇḍikā.
[Now begins the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) as taught in the Yamala.]
Oṃ! The Sun, the Moon, Yama, Time, Twilight, and the five elements—these nine are the witnesses here to my actions, both auspicious and inauspicious. (1)
O Lord! My mind has become base and overcome by sin;
drive that sin out from my heart. Homage, homage be to You! || 2 ||

Having thus prayed, one should bow down—saying "Oṃ Guṃ, salutation to the Gurus" on one's right side; "Oṃ Gaṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati" on one's left side; and "Oṃ Kṣaṃ, salutation to Kṣetrapāla" at the back—and then perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). Furthermore, during the retention of breath (kumbhaka) of prāṇāyāma, [one should contemplate] Kuṇḍalinī rising from the Mūlādhāra.
Having raised up the Supreme Deity, who resembles a strand of spider’s web and has reached the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),

and having perceived the individual soul (jīva) residing in the heart in the form of a flame of a lamp, one should take it through the path of the Suṣumṇā to the aperture of Brahmā and unite the soul with Brahman by means of the mantra "Haṃsaḥ So'haṃ."
Then, one should visualize the earth-maṇḍala, extending from the feet to the knees, as square, marked with vajras, golden in color, and enriched by the seed-syllable of earth, "Oṃ Laṃ. || 1 ||

One should meditate upon the lunar mandala, the locus of water, which extends from the knees to the navel, is shaped like a half-moon, marked with two lotuses, white in color, and enriched with the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, "Oṃ Vaṃ. || 2 ||
One should meditate on the fire-maṇḍala, which is triangular, marked with svastikas, red in color, extending from the navel to the heart, and enriched with the seed-syllable of fire, *oṃ raṃ*. 3.

One should meditate upon the wind-maṇḍala, which extends from the heart to the center of the brows, is circular, marked with six dots, smoke-colored, and enriched with the seed-syllable of wind, *oṃ yaṃ*.

Beginning from the midpoint between the eyebrows and extending to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one should visualize a circular, clear, and beautiful sphere of space (ākāśamaṇḍala) enriched with the seed-syllable of space, "Oṃ Haṃ. || 5 ||

Having thus recollected the host of elemental beings (*bhūtagaṇa*), one should then contemplate the eight steps in the center of the previously mentioned [mandala]: 1. the organ of the feet, 2. space, 3. the nose, 4. odor, 5. Brahmā, 6. Nivṛtti-kalā, 7. Samāna-vāyu, and 8. the destination to be reached. || 1 ||
In the midst of the water (the maṇḍala), the hand-faculty (1), grasping (2), the graspable (3), the tongue (4), taste (5), Viṣṇu (6), Pratiṣṭhā (7), and Dāna (8) are to be meditated upon. || 2 ||
In the center of the *tejas* (fire) mandala are: 1. *vāyu*, 2. *visarga*, 3. *visarjanīya*, 4. *cakṣu*.
Now follows the method for the self-consecration (*svaprāṇapratiṣṭhā*).

Oṃ. Of this mantra for the installation of one's own vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the ṛṣis; the Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī are the meters; the vital breaths (prāṇas) are the deity; Hrīṃ is the power (śakti); Kroṃ is the pin (kīlaka); and its application (viniyoga) is for the installation of the vital breaths within one’s own body in the goddess Caṇḍikā.
Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Ṛṣi and others.

Oṃ, salutation to the sages Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; [place this] on the head. Oṃ, salutation to the meters Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman; [place this] on the mouth. Oṃ, salutation to the power of breath (prāṇaśakti); [place this] on the heart.

Oṃ ĀṂ, salutation to the seed-syllable at the secret place. Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the power (śakti) at the feet. Oṃ Kra, salutation to the pin (kīlaka) on all limbs. Thus is the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seer and other elements.
In the wind-maṇḍala, one should meditate upon: 1. Upasthā, 2. Nanda, 3. Strī, 4. Sparśana, 5. Sparśa, 6. Īśāna, 7. Śāntyu, and 8. Pānā. || 5 ||

In the circle of space, one should contemplate these eight: speech (1), that which is to be spoken (2), the mouth (3), the ear (4), sound (5), Sadāśiva (6), Śāntyatītā (7), and the vital breaths (8). || 5 ||

Having thus reflected upon the elements, one should dissolve each preceding effect into its subsequent cause, until all effects are dissolved into Brahman. Accordingly: with the mantra "Oṃ Laṃ Phaṭ," one should dissolve the earth, which possesses five qualities, into water, thinking, "I dissolve the earth into water. (1)
Oṃ aṃ huṃ phaṭ. Having thus repeated this four times, one should dissolve the water into the fire, saying: "I withdraw [it] into the fire."
With the mantra *raṃ huṃ phaṭ*, [thinking] "I dissolve the threefold fire into air," one should cause the fire to melt away into the air. || 2 ||
Reciting "Oṃ yaṃ huṃ phaṭ" twice, one should dissolve the wind into space, thinking, "I am dissolving the wind into space. || 4 ||
Oṃ haṃ huṃ phaṭ! With this, I withdraw the single-fold space and the ego-sense.
Thus, one should dissolve the ether into the ego-sense.
Oṃ Oṃ, I dissolve the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) into the principle of the Great One (mahattattva). Thus, one should dissolve the ego-principle into the principle of the Great One. 6.
Oṃ, I dissolve the principle of the Great (mahattattva) into primordial nature (prakṛti). Thus, one should cause the principle of the Great to dissolve into primordial nature.
"I withdraw Prakṛti into myself"—by this [formula], one should dissolve Māyā into the Self. || 8 ||

Having thus become composed of pure consciousness and reality, one should contemplate the personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*). As it is said: "Consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), situated in the left side of the abdomen, black in color and the size of a thumb; having the murder of a Brahmin for its head, the theft of gold for its arms, the drinking of liquor for its heart, and sexual misconduct with the teacher’s wife for its hips; [and] associated with those [other sins]..."

Having thus meditated upon the personification of sin— a wicked being with two feet, a head shaped like a minor offense (*upapātaka*), bearing a sword and shield, and facing downwards, most difficult to endure— one should perform the *pūraka* breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) by reciting the seed-syllable of air, *Oṃ Yaṃ*, thirty-two times or sixteen times.
One should wither the personification of evil. || 1 ||

Then, one should burn the sin together with one's own body by means of the fire arising from the repetition forty-six (64) or thirty-two (32) times of the seed-syllable of fire, *oṃ raṃ*, during the *kuṃbhaka* [retention] of breath. || 2 ||
104) Now, the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*): *Oṃ ṅaṃ kaṃ khaṃ ghaṃ gaṃ*, salutation to the thumbs, which are the self of wind, fire, water, and earth; salutation to the heart.

Amaḥ) Oṃ ñaṃ caṃ chaṃ jhaṃ jaṃ, salutation to the two index fingers (*tarjanī*) who are the essence of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. (Salutation to the head, *svāhā*. Oṃ ṇaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍhaṃ ḍaṃ, salutation to the two middle fingers (*madhyamā*) who are the essence of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose.

*Namaḥ* (to the *śikhā*, *vaṣaṭ*). *Oṃ naṃ taṃ thaṃ dhaṃ daṃ*—to the self of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals; *namaḥ* to the two ring fingers (*anāmikābhyām*). *Kavacāya hūṃ*. *Oṃ maṃ paṃ phaṃ bhaṃ vaṃ*—to speech, grasping, movement...
Salutation with the two little fingers to the one whose nature is the bliss of emission (*visarga*). (*Vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes).

*Oṃ śaṃ yaṃ raṃ vaṃ laṃ haṃ ṣaṃ kṣaṃ saṃ laṃ*; salutation with both palms and backs of the hands to the one whose nature is speech and so forth, as well as intellect (*buddhi*), mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*).

Having performed the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) with the mantra "(astrāya phaṭ)," and having likewise performed the six-limbed assignments for the hands and the heart and so forth; one should contemplate the seed-syllable of the noose (*pāśa-bīja*), "a*?," starting from the navel down to the feet, and the seed-syllable of power (*śakti-bīja*), "hrīṃ," starting from the heart up to the navel.
One should place [them]. || 2 ||

Then, during the exhalation (recaka) of breath control (prāṇāyāma), having recited the seed-syllable of air, *oṃ yaṃ*, sixteen or eight times, one should expel that ash from one's own body through the right channel (nāḍī). || 3 ||
Then, having sprinkled the ash arising from the body with the nectar produced from that [ash] by reciting the nectar-seed syllable *oṃ vaṃ*,
one should subsequently solidify that ash into a mass using the earth-seed syllable *oṃ laṃ*,
and contemplate it as being like a golden pillar. || 4 ||
Then, reciting the seed-syllable of space, *oṃ haṃ*, one should meditate upon that mass as having the form of a mirror, and mentally fashion its limbs, from the head down to the nails. || 5 ||

Then, once again, by way of emanation, one should produce the elements beginning with space from Brahman. And thus: from Brahman comes primordial nature (prakṛti) [1]; from primordial nature, the Great One (mahat) [2];
from the Great One, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) [3]; from the ego-sense, space (ākāśa) [4]; from space, air (vāyu) [5]; from air, fire (agni) [6].
From fire comes water; from water, the earth; from the earth, plants;

from plants, food; from food, semen; from semen, the person—thus is he produced. Having established the one living soul (*jīva*) within his own heart-lotus as identical with Brahman by means of the mantra *Oṃ haṃsaḥ so’haṃ*, [one should meditate upon] Kuṇḍalinī.
One should meditate upon her as residing in the mūlādhāra.
Now, meditation.
Oṃ! May the Goddess, who is seated upon a lotus as red and radiant as the sun rising over the ocean of blood, who holds in her lotus-like hands a noose, a bow, a goad, and five arrows;
who carries a skull at her corner of the mouth, who is adorned with three eyes and full, swelling breasts; and who possesses the hue of the rising sun—may she be the bestower of happiness.
The vital energy (prāṇa-śakti) is the supreme bliss. Thus ends the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
From the head down to the heart, one should contemplate the seed-syllable *kroṃ*, which is the goad (*sṛṇi*). || 3 ||

Oṃ yaṃ, salutation to the self of the skin. Oṃ raṃ, salutation to the self of the blood. Oṃ laṃ, salutation to the self of the flesh. Oṃ vaṃ, salutation to the self of the fat. Oṃ śaṃ, salutation to the self of the bone. Oṃ paṃ, salutation to the self of the marrow. Oṃ saṃ, salutation to the self of the semen. Oṃ hoṃ.
"Oṃ, salutation to the self of fire (ojātman). Oṃ haṃ, salutation to the self of vital breath (prāṇātman). Oṃ saṃ, salutation to the individual self (jīvātman).

Having thus visualized, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) in the heart. Then, with "Oṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ kṣaṃ," one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa) from the head down to the feet. 4.
Then: Oṃ, salutation to the deities of the sacred seats (pīṭhadevatās), beginning with Maṇḍūka and ending with Paratattva. || 1 ||
Oṃ, salutation to the powers beginning with Jayā. || 2 ||
Having thus bowed, one should meditate upon the goddess Prāṇaśakti on the pedestal with the mantra: *oṃ ā& hī& kroṃ pīṭhāya namaḥ*.
Meditative absorption.

"Oṃ! I meditate upon the Goddess Prāṇaśakti, who is red in color, three-eyed, and holds in her hands a noose, a bow, a sword, a skull-bowl, a sickle, and a trident; she is seated upon a red lotus in a boat floating on a red ocean. Having thus meditated and placed his hand upon his heart:
Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hauṃ haṃsaḥ | Oṃ, may the vital breaths (prāṇas) of the deity Caṇḍikā abide here within my body. 2.

Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hauṃ haṃ saḥ || Oṃ, may the life-force (*jīva*) of the deity Caṇḍikā abide here in my body. Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hauṃ haṃ saḥ || Oṃ mama...
May all the sense organs of the goddess Caṇḍikā—speech, mind, eye, ear, tongue, nose, feet, anus, and genitals—come here to this very body and dwell happily for a long time; svāhā! || 3 ||

Having thus established the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the deity Caṇḍikā within one’s own body three times, one should then recite the syllable *oṃ* (the *praṇava*) fifteen times. By means of this, one should think: "I perform the fifteen sacraments (*saṃskāra*), beginning with conception (*garbhādāna*), for Caṇḍikā residing within my body. Thus.

Having established the vital breaths (prāṇas), having become a goddess, one should conquer the goddess; one should meditate upon oneself in the form of Caṇḍikā—this is the ritual for the establishment of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).
106) Now follows the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Intermediate Mātṛkās. [Ṭippaṇī on the *Bhaviṣya*: "A man should not proclaim the Goddess; he should worship her.
Having become identical with her through the placement (*nyāsa*), and having himself become the Goddess, he should sacrifice to her. 1. [In the *Āgneya-purāṇa*:]
"Power and so forth [are attained] through the worship of Power. [This means: from the worship of Power—that is, from the worship of Power and the rest.

Now, for the mantra of the *Antaramātṛkā-nyāsa*: Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī is the deity (*devatā*), the consonants are the seeds (*bījas*), the vowels are the powers (*śaktis*), and *kṣam* is the peg (*kīlakam*).

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of attaining everything through the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Having thus cast water upon the ground, one should perform *prāṇāyāma*. Specifically, one should fill [the breath] through the *iḍā* [nāḍī] with these vowels: *a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ, e, ai, o, au, aṃ, aḥ*. Then, one should retain [the breath] (*kuṃbhaka*) with the five groups of consonants: *ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa*. Again, [one should exhale] with *ya-ra-la-va-śa-ṣa-sa-ha*.
One should exhale with these eight syllables. Having thus performed the breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seer and other elements.
And so it is said: Oṃ Aṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the seer; Āṃ on the head. Oṃ Iṃ, salutation to Gāyatrī, the metre; Īṃ on the face. Oṃ Uṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī, the deity; Ūṃ...

In the heart: *Oṃ eṃ* to the seed-syllables of the consonants (*hal*), *namaḥ*; *eṃ* in the secret place (*guhya*). *Oṃ oṃ* to the powers (*śakti*) of the vowels (*svara*), *namaḥ*; *auṃ* in the two feet. *Oṃ aṃ kṣaṃ* to the pin (*kīlaka*), *namaḥ*; *aḥ* on all limbs. Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the rest. *Oṃ aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ*.
To the two thumbs (for the heart): *namaḥ*.
*Oṃ iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ* to the two index fingers: *namaḥ* (for the head: *svāhā*). *Oṃ uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ ūṃ* to the two middle fingers: *namaḥ* (for the crest-lock: *vaṣaṭ*).
Vaṣaṭ. Oṃ eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ; salutations to the two ring fingers (for the armor, *huṃ*). Oṃ aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ aḥ;
salutations to the palms and backs of the hands (for the weapon, *phaṭ*). Thus.

The Kara-nyāsa: Having thus performed the six-limbed nyāsa (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa) on the heart and other parts, one should then place the sixteen vowels upon the sixteen-petaled lotus situated at the throat—namely: *oṃ aṃ namaḥ*, and so on in sequence for all:
*oṃ āṃ, iṃ, īṃ, uṃ, ṛṃ, ḷṃ, eṃ, aiṃ, oṃ, auṃ, aṃ, aḥ*. Thus one should perform the nyāsa of the sixteen vowels.

Again, on the twelve-petalled lotus situated in the heart, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the twelve syllables as follows: *oṃ kaṃ namaḥ*, and likewise *khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ namaḥ*. Thus one should place the twelve letters.
Then, at the navel on the ten-petalled lotus, one should assign the ten syllables: *oṃ ḍaṃ namaḥ*, and likewise *ḍhaṃ*, *ṇaṃ*, *taṃ*, *thaṃ*, *daṃ*, *dhaṃ*, *naṃ*, *paṃ*, *phaṃ namaḥ*.

In the six-petaled *liṅga* below that, one should perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the six syllables: *oṃ vaṃ namaḥ*, and likewise *oṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ*. In the four-petaled *ādhāra* (the anus), one should place the four syllables: *oṃ vaṃ namaḥ*, and likewise *śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ*. Again, in the two-petaled [center] of the forehead, *oṃ haṃ*.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by placing the two syllables "Namaḥ" and "Oṃ Kṣaṃ Namaḥ," one should meditate.

In the Foundation (ādhāra), at the navel of the Liṅga, manifested in the Heart, at the root of the palate, in the forehead, in the two-petalled, sixteen-petalled, twenty-two-petalled, ten-petalled, twelve-petalled, and four-petalled [lotuses]; in the midst of the residence and the disciples, accompanied by the letters ḍa, pha, ka, tha, and sa; in the region of the throat, endowed with the meaning of the principles beginning with the vowels and ending with *haṃ* and *kṣaṃ*—[this is] the Sakala [form].
I bow to the color-form residing within the petals. Thus ends the internal Mātṛkā-nyāsa.
Now follows the external placement of the Mātṛkās.

For the sake of victory over all the gods, one should know that any ritual performed without the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the script (*lipi*) is fruitless; therefore, one should first place the script. *Oṃ*. Of this venerable *Vahirmātṛkānyāsa-mantra*, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chanda*), and the goddess Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī is the deity (*devatā*).

The vowels are the seed-syllables (*halabīja*), the powers (*śakti*), and *kṣam* is the peg (*kīlaka*); the application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of attaining everything through this ritual placement (*nyāsa*).

One should perform *prāṇāyāma*. Thus, one should fill [the breath] through the *iḍā* [channel] with these vowels: a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ, e, ai, o, au, aṃ, aḥ. Again, one should retain [the breath] (*kumbhaka*) with this group of five consonants: ku, cu, ṭu, tu, pu. Again, with eight [consonants] beginning with ya, ra, la, va, śa, ṣa, sa, ha, one should exhale (*recaka*). Having thus performed the *prāṇāyāma*.

One should perform the Nyāsa of the Seers and so forth. Thus: *Oṃ aṃ*, salutation to Brahmā, the Seer; *āṃ* on the head. *Oṃ iṃ*, salutation to Gāyatrī, the Metre; *īṃ* on the face. *Oṃ*, salutation to Sarasvatī, the Deity; *ūṃ* on the heart. *Oṃ eṃ*, salutation to the Consonants, the Seeds; *aiṃ* on the private parts. *Oṃ oṃ*, salutation to the Vowels...
