That which is impure, touched by the base, smelled, or opened by oneself; that brought from an impure vessel, brought by one who has bathed [for ritual purposes], or obtained through begging; || 42 ||
One should not offer flowers that are withered, stale, black, or fallen to the ground;
nor should one present flowers, leaves, or fruit to the deity with their faces turned downward.
There is no such fault regarding a handful of flowers, nor regarding those that have been kept overnight.
Having thus performed the flower worship, one should perform the worship of the protective deities (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
Then one should perform the rites beginning with the limbs (aṅga) and ending with the weapons (astra), followed by incense and other offerings.
Then, taking a handful of flowers, [one should pray]: "O Supreme Goddess, whose nature is consciousness! O Beloved of the essence of supreme nectar!
O Caṇḍikā, grant me permission to worship your retinue. Having prayed with this, offered the handful of flowers, and received the permission, the Goddess stands before me in the form of her retinue.

Having meditated [upon them], one should worship the surrounding deities. Here, in all cases, the east is defined as the direction between the object of worship and the worshipper. Having determined the directions such as the east accordingly, one should first worship the lineage of gurus, starting from the northwest (vāyavya) and ending with the northeast (īśa). Therein: they [are adorned] with red garlands and garments...

Having meditated thus: "Adorned with perfumes, beautifully decorated, and seated upon lotus-thrones," [one recites]: Oṃ, I worship the sandals of Mahādevyambā Śrī; obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance! Oṃ, I worship the sandals of Mahādevānandanātha Śrī; obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance! Oṃ...
I worship the venerable sandals of Tripurāmbā; salutations, I satiate you, salutations! Oṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Bhairavānandanātha; salutations, I satiate you, salutations!
These are the divine lineages (*divyaugha*). Oṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Brahmānandanātha;
salutations, I satiate you, salutations! Oṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Pūrṇadevānandanātha;
salutations, I satiate you, salutations! Oṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Calacittānandanātha.
Salutations, I satiate; salutations. Oṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Smaradīpānandanātha; salutations, I satiate; salutations. Oṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Māyāmbānanda;
salutations, I satiate; salutations. Oṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Māyāvatyambānātha.

Salutations, I satiate; salutations! These are the hosts of Siddhas. Oṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Vimalānandanātha; salutations, I satiate; salutations! Oṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Kuśalānandanātha; salutations, I satiate; salutations! Oṃ, [I worship the venerable sandals of] Bhīmasenānandanātha...
I worship the venerable sandals; salutations, I satiate you; salutations! Oṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Sudhākarānandanātha; salutations, I satiate you; salutations!

Oṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Mīnānandanātha; salutations, I satiate you, salutations! Oṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Gorakṣakānandanātha; salutations, I satiate you, salutations! Oṃ.

I worship the venerable sandals of Bhojadevānandanātha; salutations, I offer libations, salutations! Oṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Prajāpatyānandanātha; salutations, I offer libations, salutations! Oṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Mūladevānandanātha; salutations, I offer libations, salutations! Oṃ.

Oṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Rati-devānandanātha; salutations, I satiate you, salutations! Oṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Vighna-devānandanātha; salutations, I satiate you, salutations! Oṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Hutāśanānandanātha; salutations, I satiate you, salutations! Oṃ...

I worship the venerable sandals of Samayānandanātha; salutations, I satiate you, salutations! Oṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Santoṣānandanātha; salutations, I satiate you, salutations! These are the Mānavaugha [lineages]. Having gratified them with flowers and other offerings, [one should offer] the nectar from the Guru-vessel.

Having satisfied [the deities] three times or once with the *tantramudrā*, near the *mānavaugha*: OṂ AIṂ HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ HASAKHAPHREṂ HASAKṢAMALAVARAYŪṂ HASAKHAPREṂ | I worship the venerable sandals (*śrīpādukā*) of the venerable Amukānandanātha and the venerable goddess Amukī.

*Namaḥ tarpayāmi namaḥ.* Thus, by means of the name of the *saṃketa*: "I worship the *śrīpādukā* of my own Guru-Nātha; *namaḥ tarpayāmi namaḥ*. *Oṃ*, I worship the *śrīpādukā* of the Parāpara-Guru-Nātha; *namaḥ tarpayāmi namaḥ*. *Oṃ*, [the *śrīpādukā*] of the Parameṣṭhi-Guru-Nātha..."
"I worship, salutations; I satisfy, salutations. Thus, one should worship and satisfy the four gurus as before. Then, taking a handful of flowers, one should perform the hymn of praise to the gurus.
The Guru is reality.
With a radiance like the autumnal moon, eyes like autumn lotuses,
a slight smile, and a face resembling the full autumnal moon.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, and anointed with divine perfumes.
Joined with a deep red spear, it is enchanting on its left side.
His lotus-like hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and he is marked with all the auspicious characteristics.
I contemplate the Guru upon my head, within a great thousand-petaled lotus.
In the *Guptasādhanatantra*, chapter 1.
Oṃ, [I bow to Him] seated upon a cool-rayed lunar throne within the center of the lotus of the Brahma-abode.
Possessing the radiance of the shimmering sun, with hands granting boons and fearlessness, blazing like camphor and jasmine.
White, joined by his beloved who possesses the luster of lightning and is adorned with garments and unguents.
I reverently salute the Guru, whose body is joined in half and whose face is serene. || 1 ||
And opening the eyes of those seized by the great darkness of delusion, as if they were possessed by a planetary spirit.
He who, out of compassion, fashioned those beautiful [eyes] by anointing them with the collyrium of knowledge.
This triple world is pervaded by that splendor which arises from the awakening to reality.
I bow to that Guru of mine, who is the very form of Śiva and the bestower of the accomplishment of all goals.
Mātaṅgī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bagalā, Dhūmāvatī, and Bhairavī.
Tārā, Chinnaśirodharā, Bhagavatī, Śyāmā, Ramā, and Sundarī.
They are not able to grant us our desired fruit without his grace.
I bow to that very form of Śiva, my own Guru, who bestows the accomplishment of all goals. || 3 ||
Kāśī, Dvāravatī, Prayāga, Mathurā, Ayodhyā, Gayā, and Avantikā.
Māyā (Haridvāra), Puṣkara, Kāñcī, Utkala, Giri, Śrīśaila, Vindhya, and so forth—
none of these are capable of delivering one who lacks His grace.
I bow to that Guru of mine, who is the very form of Śiva and the bestower of the accomplishment of all goals. || 4 ||
The Revā, Sindhu, Sarasvatī, Tripathagā, Sūryātmajā, and Kauśikī.
The confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, the daughter of the mountain (the Yamunā), the Lohitya, the Śoṇa, and others.
Without whose grace one is not capable of bestowing the aforementioned fruits at the time [of their ripening].
I bow to that very form of Śiva, my own Guru, who bestows the accomplishment of all goals. || 5 ||
Pure fame, renown, skill in poetry, scholarship, and health—these are the fruits of merit.
In debate, eloquence; in family, cleverness; in depth, imperturbability.
Through whose grace there arises boldness, mastery, and skill in virtue.
I bow to that very one, my own Guru, who possesses the form of Śiva and bestows the accomplishment of all goals.
Lokeshvara, Hari, Ambika, Smara, Hara, Mother, Father, and Abhyagata.
The teacher, one honored by the family, the best of ascetics, the elderly, and likewise the mendicant.
These do not approach even a fraction of the likeness of that ocean of compassion.
I bow to that Guru of mine, who is the very form of Śiva and the bestower of the accomplishment of all goals.
Meditation, worship of the deities, [service to] the guru, austerity, charity, the fire-sacrifice (agnihotra), and so forth.
The recitation of sacred texts, the performance of fire-oblations, the service of ancestors, sacrifices, the honoring of guests, and the offering of oblations;
These inevitably become fruitless without his grace.
I bow to that my own Guru, who is the very form of Śiva and the bestower of the accomplishment of all goals.
Whoever, facing the eastern direction with palms joined in reverence, should recite this octet of verses;
Even without the ritual procedures for preliminary service (puraścaraṇa), one attains the supreme accomplishment of the mantra.
One is not overcome by obstacles and daily attains the fruit of worship.
At the end of the body, he indeed enters the supreme state, which is difficult even for yogis to attain. || 9 ||
In the Vāmakeśvara Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara, the King of Hymns to the Guru is complete.

O Blessed One! O Durgā! O Goddess! O You who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge, grant me the root-attainment of my desired goal! With devotion, I offer to You the worship of the lineage of Gurus. With this, one should scatter the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali). Then, as before:
The worship of the yantra.
Outside the triangle, the worship of the limbs (*aṅga-pūjana*) is performed in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center: *Oṃ aiṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ;
hṛc-chakti-śrī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi namas tarpayāmi namaḥ* in the southeast (*āgneya*). *Oṃ hrīṃ śirase svāhā; śiraḥ-śakti-śrī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.
Salutations, I satiate you; salutations to Īśānī.

Oṃ klīṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock; I worship the *śrīpādukā* of the Crest-Lock Power (*śikhāśakti*), I bow to it, I gratify it with libations, I bow to it, in the southwest (*nair-ṛtyām*). Oṃ, hūṃ to Cāmuṇḍā, the armor (*kavaca*).

I worship the Śrīpādukā of the Kavaca-Śakti; obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance! [To the northwest]. Oṃ Vicce, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes; I worship the Śrīpādukā of the Netra-Śakti; obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance! [To the east]. Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Cāmuṇḍāyai Vicce, phaṭ to the weapon; [the Astra-Śakti].

"I worship the venerable sandals; salutations, I satiate [them], salutations in all directions. With these words and so forth, in due order, one should worship and satiate the deities of the limbs (*aṅgadevatā*). Then, one should satiate [the deity] three times or once with the nectar from the venerable vessel (*śrīpātra*) using the *tatvamudrā*. Then, taking a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), [one says]: "O Blessed One! O Caṇḍikā! O Goddess!"

mū0: "O You who are affectionate toward those who have sought refuge, grant me the fulfillment of my desired goal! I offer this worship of the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa) to You with devotion. Having thus offered [the worship], then, at the triangular yantra (trikoṇayantra):
oṃ *sarasvatī-brahmabhyāṃ* namaḥ; I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Sarasvatī and Brahmā.

Salutations, I offer libations; salutations in the east. Oṃ, salutations to Lakṣmī and Hṛṣīkeśa; I worship the sandals of Lakṣmī and Hṛṣīkeśa; salutations, I offer libations; salutations in the southwest.
Oṃ, salutation to Gaurī and Rudra; I worship the venerable sandals of Gaurī and Rudra, salutation, I satiate them, salutation, in the northwest. Oṃ siṃ, salutation to Siṃha;
I worship the venerable sandals of Siṃha, salutation, I satiate him, salutation, to the south of the Goddess. Oṃ maṃ...

Salutation to Mahiṣa; I worship the venerable sandals of Mahiṣa, salutation, I satiate you, salutation—[this is] to the north of the Goddess. Oṃ Kāṃ, salutation to Kāla; I worship the venerable sandals of Kāla, salutation, I satiate you, salutation—[this is] to the south. Oṃ Mṛṃ, salutation to Mṛtyu; [I worship] Mṛtyu...
"I worship the Śrīpādukā; salutations, I satiate [it]; salutations" [recited] in the north. Then, one should satiate it three times or once with the nectar from the Śrīpātra using the *tattvamudrā*.

Taking up a handful of flowers: O Blessed One! O Caṇḍikā! O Goddess! [O Mother! Grant me the attainment of my desired goal, O You who are affectionate toward those who seek refuge! With devotion, I offer to You this worship of the second enclosure.
Then, one should worship the powers (śaktis) beginning with Nandajā in the six corners: "Oṃ Naṃ, obeisance to Nandajā;
I worship the śrī-pādukā of the power Nandajā; obeisance, I satiate her, obeisance" in the east.
Oṃ raṃ, obeisance to Raktadantikā. I worship the śrī-pādukā of the power (śakti) Raktadantikā;
obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance in the southeast. Oṃ śāṃ, obeisance to Śākambharī.

I worship the Śrī-pādukā of the power (śakti) Śākambharī; salutations, I satiate you, salutations! [In the] north-east—salutations, I satiate you, salutations! [In the] west—Oṃ Bhīṃ, salutations to Bhīmā; I worship the Śrī-pādukā of the power Bhīmā; salutations, I satiate you, salutations! [In the] northwest—Oṃ Bhrāṃ...

Salutation to Bhrāmarī; I worship the Śrī-pādukā of the power (śakti) Bhrāmarī; salutation, I offer libation, salutation in the northeast. Taking a handful of flowers in both hands: O Blessed One, Caṇḍikā! [Recite] the Mūla-mantra:
"O You who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge, grant me the attainment of my desired goal. I offer this with devotion unto You."
The worship of the third enclosure. Thus one should cast [the offerings] into the yantra. Then, upon the eight petals, one should perform the meditation on the powers (śaktis) beginning with Brāhmī.
Oṃ, [I meditate upon] Brāhmī, mounted upon a swan, golden-colored, and four-armed.
[He saw her] with four faces and three eyes, holding the Brahmakūrca vessel and a lotus.
She holds a staff, a lotus, and a rosary, and possesses a beautiful smile.
The best of practitioners should meditate upon the Goddess who wears a mass of matted hair. || 1 ||
Oṃ Āṃ, I worship the sandals of Brāhmī; salutations, I satiate her; salutations in the east. Oṃ, [I worship] Nārāyaṇī, the greatly radiant, dark-complexioned one, who rides upon Garuḍa.
Adorned with various ornaments, she has beautiful hair and four arms.
Holding a bell, a conch, a skull-cup, and a discus, she is supreme.
Her eyes were rolling with the intoxication of honey-wine, and she was beautiful in every limb.
Oṃ īṃ, I worship the sandals of Nārāyaṇī Śrī; salutations, I satiate you, salutations in the northeast.
Oṃ, [I salute] Māheśvarī, who is mounted upon a bull, white in color, and endowed with three eyes.
A skull-cup, a hand-drum, and likewise the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a trident.
And the goddess, holding a chisel and adorned with various ornaments. || 3 ||
Oṃ ūṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Māheśvarī; salutations, I satisfy [her] with libations; salutations in the north.
Oṃ, [homage to] Cāmuṇḍā, who possesses a fierce, loud laugh, whose teeth are bared, whose face is terrifying,
and who has three eyes.
She possesses the luster of a blue lotus and, with a joyful body, wears a garland of human heads and severed necks.
She holds a sword, a trident, a skull-cup fashioned from a human head, and a shield.
One should meditate upon her as mounted on a corpse, intoxicated and delighted by the intoxication of honey, possessing a fierce form. || 4 ||
Oṃ Ṛṃ! I worship the venerable sandals of Cāmuṇḍā; salutations, I satiate you, salutations! [In the northwest.]
Oṃ, [I salute] Kaumārī, who has the luster of saffron, possesses three eyes, and is seated upon a peacock.
Four-armed, she holds a spear, a noose, a goad, and displays the gesture of fearlessness.
I shall contemplate her as being adorned with various ornaments and intoxicated with passion. || 5 ||
Oṃ ḶṂ, I worship the venerable sandals of Kaumārī; salutations, I satiate you, salutations! In the west:
Oṃ, and [I worship] Aparājitā, who is yellow in luster, holding a rosary and granting boons.
I should meditate upon her as holding a lotus and a citron. || 6 ||

Oṃ Aiṃ, I worship the sandals of Aparājitā; salutations, I satiate you, salutations. [To the south-west]—Oṃ, I worship Vārāhī, who has the luster of smoke-colored hue, whose face is that of a boar, and who is auspicious.
She holds a shield, a sword, a mace, and a plough with her four arms. || 7 ||
Oṃ auṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Vārāhī; salutations, I satiate you with offerings, salutations! [To the] right.
Oṃ! Nārasiṃhī, possessing a body identical to that of Nṛsiṃha. || 8 ||
Oṃ Aḥ, I worship the venerable sandals of Nārasiṃhī; salutations, I satiate you, salutations! [In the southeast.]
Thus, having performed the worship.

As before, one should satisfy [the deity] three times or once with the nectar from the Yoginī-vessel (or with the water of the special *arghya*). Then, taking a handful of flowers, [one should pray]: "O Blessed Caṇḍikā!
O Goddess! O Mother! Grant me the fulfillment of my desires, O You who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge! [Recite this] with devotion.
"I offer to you the worship of the fourth enclosure. Having thus offered it, one should then meditate upon the eight Bhairavas.
They bear the tridents and staffs of the Ruru-demons and Vetālas, which are dark blue in color like a heap of collyrium.

149) He is joined with a small drum, has three eyes, and is heavy, having the form of an elephant fashioned from the trunks, tusks, and fragments of staffs of elephants; his forehead is marked by the knitting of his brows.
[He saw] those whose inner hearts were delighted, who were rich in the bloom of youth, and whose ears were adorned with earrings possessing the luster of swarms of playful bees.
Having meditated thus.

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Asitāṅga Bhairava; I worship the venerable sandals of Asitāṅga Bhairava, I offer libations with obeisance, obeisance in the east. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Ruru Bhairava; I worship the venerable sandals of Ruru Bhairava, I offer libations with obeisance, obeisance in the northeast. Oṃ...

Hrīṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍabhairava; I worship the venerable sandals of Caṇḍabhairava, obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance in the north. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Krodhabhairava; I worship the venerable sandals of Krodhabhairava, obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance in the northwest. Oṃ hrīṃ...

Salutation to Unmattabhairava; I worship the venerable sandals of Unmattabhairava, salutation, I offer libation, salutation in the west. Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to Kapālabhairava; I worship the venerable sandals of Kapālabhairava, salutation, I offer libation, salutation in the southwest. Oṃ...
*Hrīṃ*, obeisance to Bhīṣaṇa Bhairava; I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Bhīṣaṇa Bhairava, obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance—[in the] south. *Oṃ hrīṃ*, obeisance to Saṃhāra Bhairava;
I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Saṃhāra Bhairava, obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance—[in the] southeast. Thus.
Having performed worship.

As before, one should satisfy [the deity] three times or once with the nectar from the Yoginī-vessel. Then, taking a handful of flowers: "O Blessed Caṇḍikā! O Goddess! O Mother! Grant me the attainment of my desired goal, O You who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge! With devotion, I offer to You the worship of the fifth enclosure."
Having thus offered [it].
Then, on the twenty-four petals, starting from the eastern petal and ending with the southeast petal: Oṃ Viṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇumāyā.
I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Viṣṇumāyā; obeisance, I satiate her, obeisance. Oṃ Ceṃ, obeisance to Cetanā. I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Cetanā; obeisance, I satiate her, obeisance. Oṃ...
Oṃ ceṃ, salutation to Cetanā; I worship the venerable sandals of Cetanā, salutation, I offer libations, salutation.
Oṃ buṃ, salutation to Buddhi; I worship the venerable sandals of Buddhi, salutation, I offer libations, salutation. Oṃ niṃ, salutation to Nidrā; I worship the venerable sandals of Nidrā.
Salutations, I offer libations, salutations! Oṃ kṣuṃ, salutations to Kṣudhā; I worship the śrī-pādukā of Kṣudhā, salutations, I offer libations, salutations!
Oṃ chāṃ, obeisance to Chāyā; I worship the venerable sandals of Chāyā, obeisance, I offer libations, obeisance. Oṃ śaṃ, obeisance to Śakti; I worship the venerable sandals of Śakti.

Salutations, I satisfy you; salutations! Oṃ Tṛṃ, salutations to Tṛṣṇā (Thirst); I worship the venerable sandals of Tṛṣṇā; salutations, I satisfy you; salutations! Oṃ Kṣāṃ, salutations to Kṣānti (Forbearance);
I worship the venerable sandals of Kṣānti; salutations, I satisfy you; salutations! Oṃ Jāṃ, salutations to Jāti (Birth).

Salutation! I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Jāti; salutation! I satisfy [her] with libations; salutation! Oṃ Laṃ! Salutation to Lajjā! I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Lajjā; salutation! I satisfy [her] with libations; salutation! Oṃ Śāṃ! Salutation to Śānti! I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Śānti; salutation! I satisfy [her] with libations; salutation! Oṃ...

Śraṃ, salutation to Śraddhā; I worship the venerable sandals of Śraddhā, salutation, I satiate her, salutation. Oṃ Kāṃ, salutation to Kānti; I worship the venerable sandals of Kānti, salutation, I satiate her, salutation. Oṃ Laṃ, salutation to Lakṣmī; [I worship] the venerable sandals of Lakṣmī.

I worship, salutations, I satiate, salutations. Oṃ dhṛṃ, salutations to Dhṛti; I worship the venerable sandals of Dhṛti, salutations, I satiate, salutations. Oṃ vṛṃ, salutations to Vṛtti; I worship the venerable sandals of Vṛtti, salutations, I satiate, salutations. Oṃ śruṃ, salutations to Śruti...
Salutation! I worship the auspicious sandals of Śruti; salutation, I satiate them; salutation! Oṃ smṛṃ, salutation to Smṛti;
I worship the auspicious sandals of Smṛti; salutation, I satiate them; salutation!
Oṃ tuṃ, obeisance to Tuṣṭi; I worship the venerable sandals of Tuṣṭi, obeisance, I gratify her, obeisance.
Oṃ puṃ, obeisance to Puṣṭi; I worship the venerable sandals of Puṣṭi, obeisance, I gratify her, obeisance. Oṃ daṃ, obeisance to Dayā; I worship the venerable sandals of Dayā.

Salutations, I offer libations; salutations! Oṃ, Māṃ, salutations to Mātṛ. I worship the Śrī-pādukā of Mātṛ; salutations, I offer libations; salutations! Oṃ, Bhrāṃ, salutations to Bhrānti. I worship the Śrī-pādukā of Bhrānti; salutations, I offer libations; salutations! Having thus worshipped completely:

As before, one should satisfy [the goddess] three times or once with the nectar from the Yoginī’s vessel. Then, taking a handful of flowers, one should offer them with devotion, saying: "O Blessed Caṇḍikā! O Goddess! O Mother! Grant me the attainment of my desired goal, O you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge! This sixth round of worship is offered unto you."

Having thus offered [the oblation], then, starting from the well-known eastern direction and so forth within the perimeter of the *bhūpura*, [one recites]: *Oṃ laṃ indrāya surādhipataye sāṅgāya sāyudhāya savāhanāya saparivārāya*.

Salutation to the Goddess’s retinue together with their powers (śakti). || 1 || Oṃ raṃ, salutation to Agni, the lord of fire. || 2 || Oṃ maṃ, salutation to Yama, the lord of the departed spirits (preta). || 3 || Oṃ kṣaṃ, salutation to Nirṛti, the lord of the Rākṣasas. || 4 || Oṃ vaṃ, salutation to Varuṇa, the lord of the waters. || 5 || Oṃ saṃ, salutation to Soma, the lord of the constellations (nakṣatra). || 6 || Oṃ...
To Vāyu, the lord of the vital breaths... || 7 || Oṃ Haṃ, to Īśāna, the lord of beings...

|| 8 || Oṃ Hrīṃ, to Ananta, the lord of the Nāgas... || 9 || Oṃ Aṃ, to Brahmā, the lord of the worlds... || 10 || I invoke the world-protectors with their mudrās. With the fingers well-joined at the base of the palms, all the branches [of the fingers] are extended.

This is the mudrā of the Lords of the World; one should display it during their worship. *Laṃ*, obeisance to Indra; I worship the venerable sandals of Indra, obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance in the east. *Oṃ raṃ*, obeisance to Agni;
I worship the venerable sandals of Agni, obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance in the southeast. *Oṃ*...

Oṃ, salutation to Yama; I worship the venerable sandals of Yama, salutation, I offer libation, salutation to the South. Oṃ kṣaṃ, salutation to Nirṛti; I worship the venerable sandals of Nirṛti, salutation, I offer libation, salutation to the Southwest. Oṃ vaṃ, salutation to Varuṇa.

Oṃ, to Varuṇa, obeisance; I worship the venerable sandals of Varuṇa, obeisance, I offer libations, obeisance in the west. Oṃ, yaṃ, obeisance to Vāyu; I worship the venerable sandals of Vāyu, obeisance, I offer libations, obeisance in the northwest (vāyavya).
Oṃ, saṃ, obeisance to Soma; I worship the venerable sandals of Soma, obeisance, I offer libations.

Homage to the North. Oṃ haṃ, homage to Īśāna; I worship the venerable sandals of Īśāna, I offer libations with homage, homage to the Northeast (Īśānyā). Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Ananta; I worship the venerable sandals of Ananta, I offer libations with homage, homage to the Southwest (Nirṛti).

Between Varuṇa and [the western direction]: "Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to Brahmā; I worship the śrī-pādukā of Brahmā, obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance. Between the eastern and northeastern directions: having thus worshipped.
As before, one should satisfy [the deities] with the nectar from the yoginī-vessel. Then, taking a handful of flowers:
O Blessed Caṇḍikā! O Goddess! O Mother! Grant me the fulfillment of my desires, O You who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge!
"With devotion, I offer to you the worship of the seventh enclosure. Having thus offered it.

"Yellow, white, sky-colored, lightning-like, red, white, and black; the colors of the *kokanada* and *pāṭala* flowers are proclaimed for the Vajra and the others. Having thus meditated outside the *bhūpura*, [one recites]: *Oṃ vaṃ vajrāya vajralāñchita*.

Salutation to the Mother, together with her limbs, weapons, vehicles, retinues, and Śakti, and to the divine attendants (pārṣadas). Oṃ Śaṃ, salutation to the Śakti, marked by the Śakti; Oṃ Daṃ, salutation to the Daṇḍa, marked by the Daṇḍa; Oṃ Khaḍgāya, salutation to the Khaḍga, marked by the Khaḍga; Pāṃ, salutation to the Pāśa.
[Marked with a noose... Oṃ Aṃ, obeisance to the goad (Aṅkuśa), [marking] the goad with the syllable Laṃ. Oṃ Gaṃ, obeisance to the mace (Gadā), [marking] the mace with the syllable Laṃ.

Oṃ Śūṃ, obeisance to the trident (Śūla), [marking] the trident with the syllable Laṃ. Oṃ Caṃ, obeisance to the discus (Cakra), [marking] the discus with the syllable Laṃ. Oṃ Paṃ, obeisance to the lotus (Padma), [marking] the lotus with the syllable Laṃ. Oṃ Vaṃ, obeisance to the thunderbolt (Vajra); I worship the Vajra Śrīpādukā.

*Namaḥ tarpayāmi namaḥ pūrve* (Salutation, I satiate; salutation in the East). *Oṃ śaṃ śaktaye namaḥ śakti-śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi namaḥ tarpayāmi namaḥ āgneye* (Oṃ śaṃ, salutation to Śakti; I worship the venerable sandals of Śakti; salutation, I satiate; salutation in the South-East). *Oṃ daṃ daṇḍāya namaḥ daṇḍa-śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi namaḥ tarpayāmi namaḥ dakṣiṇe* (Oṃ daṃ, salutation to Daṇḍa; I worship the venerable sandals of Daṇḍa; salutation, I satiate; salutation in the South). *Oṃ khaṃ...* (Oṃ khaṃ...)

Oṃ, salutation to the sword; I worship the venerable sandals of the sword, salutation, I offer libation, salutation in the southwest. Oṃ pāṃ, salutation to the noose; I worship the venerable sandals of the noose, salutation, I offer libation, salutation in the west. Oṃ aṃ, salutation to the goad; [I worship] the goad...
(Dhvajā) I worship the venerable sandals; salutations, I satiate them; salutations to Vāyu.

Oṃ Gaṃ, obeisance to the mace; I worship the venerable sandals of the mace, obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance, in the northeast. Oṃ Caṃ, obeisance to the discus; I worship the venerable sandals of the discus, obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance, below (between Nirṛti and Varuṇa). Oṃ...

*Paṃ*, obeisance to Padmā; I worship the lotus-feet of Śrī, obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance. [Above] (between the East and the Northeast). Having worshipped thus, one should satiate her with the nectar from the Yoginī-vessel as before. Then, taking a handful of flowers, [one says]: "O Blessed Caṇḍikā! O Goddess!"
O You who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge, grant me the accomplishment of my desired goal!

"May this worship of the eighth enclosure be offered to you with devotion. Having thus offered it, [one proceeds] to the southern side of the Goddess: Oṃ Braṃ, salutation to Brahmā; I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Brahmā, I offer libations, salutation! Oṃ Viṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu; [I worship] the *śrīpādukā* of Viṣṇu...
I worship you, salutations; I satiate you, salutations.
Oṃ ruṃ, salutation to Rudra; I worship the venerable sandals of Rudra, salutation, I satiate you, salutation. Then one should worship the weapons of the goddess Mahālakṣmī, as follows: Oṃ aṃ...

Oṃ Akṣamālā, obeisance! I worship the venerable sandals of Akṣamālā; obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance! || 1 || Oṃ Paṃ, obeisance to Padma! I worship the venerable sandals of Padma; obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance! || 2 || Oṃ Sāṃ, obeisance to Sāyaka! [I worship] the venerable sandals of Sāyaka...

I worship, salutations; I satiate, salutations. || 3 || Oṃ Khaṃ, salutations to the sword; I worship the venerable sandals of the sword, salutations; I satiate, salutations. || 4 || Oṃ Vaṃ, salutations to the thunderbolt; I worship the venerable sandals of the thunderbolt, salutations; I satiate, salutations. || 5 || Oṃ Gaṃ, salutations to the mace.
Salutation! I worship the venerable sandals of Gadā; salutation! I satisfy [them]; salutation! || 6 || Oṃ Caṃ!
Salutation to the Discus (Cakra)! I worship the venerable sandals of Cakra; salutation! I satisfy [them]; salutation! || 7 ||

Oṃ suṃ, obeisance to Surābhājana; I worship the glorious sandals (śrīpādukā) of Surābhājana, obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance. || 8 || Oṃ śaṃ, obeisance to Śaṅkha; I worship the glorious sandals of Śaṅkha, obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance. || 9 || Oṃ śaṃ, obeisance to Śakti.

Oṃ, salutations; I worship the venerable sandals of Śakti; salutations, I satiate them; salutations. (10) Oṃ, paṃ, salutations to the axe; I worship the venerable sandals of the axe; salutations, I satiate them; salutations.
(11) Oṃ, dhaṃ, salutations to the bow; I worship the venerable sandals of the bow; salutations, I satiate them.

Namaḥ || 12 || Oṃ Caṃ, salutation to the shield (carman); I worship the venerable sandal of the shield; salutation, I satiate it; salutation. || 13 || Oṃ Daṃ, salutation to the staff (daṇḍa); I worship the venerable sandal of the staff; salutation, I satiate it; salutation. || 14 || Oṃ Kuṃ, salutation to the water-pot (kuṇḍikā); [I worship] the water-pot...

I worship the venerable sandals; salutations, I satiate you, salutations! || 15 || Oṃ Ghaṃ, salutations to the Bell; I worship the venerable sandals of the Bell; salutations, I satiate you, salutations! || 16 || Oṃ Pāṃ, salutations to the Noose; I worship the venerable sandals of the Noose; salutations, I satiate you, salutations!

17 || Oṃ śūṃ, salutation to the trident; I worship the trident’s venerable sandals, salutation, I satiate you, salutation. || 18 || On the outer corners of the wheel, in the northwest: Oṃ vaṃ, salutation to Vaṭuka;
I worship Vaṭuka’s venerable sandals, salutation, I satiate you, salutation.
In the northeast: *Oṃ yāṃ yoginībhyo namaḥ*. I worship the sandals of the Yoginīs; salutations, I satiate them; salutations. In the southwest: *Oṃ kṣaṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ*.

I worship the venerable sandals of Kṣetrapāla; salutations, I satiate you, salutations! In the southeast: Oṃ Gaṃ, salutations to Gaṇeśa; I worship the venerable sandals of Gaṇeśa; salutations, I satiate you, salutations!

In the center: Oṃ duṃ, obeisance to Durgā; I worship the venerable sandals of Durgā, obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance! In the northeast: Viṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu; I worship the venerable sandals of Viṣṇu, obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance! In the southeast: Oṃ śiṃ, obeisance to Śiva; [obeisance] to Śiva.

I worship the venerable sandals, salutations; I satiate [you], salutations. In the northwest: Oṃ sūṃ, salutations to Sūrya; I worship the venerable sandals of Sūrya, salutations; I satiate [you], salutations.
In the southwest: *Oṃ gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇeśa. I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Gaṇeśa;
obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance.* Having thus worshipped, one should satiate him with the nectar from the Yoginī vessel as before.
Then, taking a handful of flowers, [one should pray]: "O Blessed One, Caṇḍikā! O Goddess! [Mūla-mantra] grant me the attainment of my desired goal."
"O you who are affectionate toward those who have sought refuge! I offer this worship of the ninth enclosure to you with devotion. Having thus offered it:

Immediately following [these] are: the rosary (*akṣamālā*), axe (*paraśu*), mace (*gadā*), arrow (*iṣu*), thunderbolt (*kuliśa*), lotus (*padma*), bow (*dhanus*), water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*), staff (*daṇḍa*), spear (*śakti*), sword (*asi*), shield (*carman*), bell (*ghaṇṭā*), wine-vessel (*surābhājana*), trident (*triśūla*), noose (*pāśa*), the Sudarśana discus, plow (*hala*), conch (*śaṅkha*), club (*musala*), discus (*cakra*), iron bar (*parigha*), *bhuśuṇḍī* weapon, and head (*śiras*).
The treatise explains the etymological derivation of the term *mudrāpada* as follows:
Because it gladdens all the gods and because it dissolves the succession of sins.
Therefore, she is celebrated as "Mudrā" by the sages who are knowers of the tantras.
Now I shall explain the mudrās devised in all the tantras.
And by means of these [mantras] when they are properly composed, the deities of the mantras rejoice.
The rosary mudrā. || 1 ||
Having interlaced three fingers at the tips of the thumb and forefinger, one should extend them; this is proclaimed as the akṣamālā mudrā.
The parasu mudrā. || 2 ||
Placing one hand upon the other and joining the fingers of both hands crosswise, one should keep them pressed together and extended; this is considered the mudrā of the axe (paraśu).

165) The *Yāmalatantra* states the *mālā-japa* of the Yoginīs:

Recitation (*japa*) is ten times superior to a sacrifice performed according to ritual injunctions (*vidhi-yajña*). A whispered recitation (*upāṃśu*) is said to be a hundred times more effective, while a mental recitation (*mānasa*) is a thousand times more so. [One should use beads] made of pearls, pure gems, large lapis lazuli, *putrajīvaka*, lotus seeds, *rudrākṣa* seeds, crystal, or coral.
Having fashioned a rosary from rubies and other gems, red sandalwood, and having adorned it with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and musk, he assumed the form of Caṇḍikā.

Now, a rosary made of pearls bestows the fruit of sovereignty; as it is with pearls, so it is with one fashioned from crystal. A rosary of rudrākṣa beads grants all prosperity for the sake of liberation. A rosary of coral effects subjugation and accomplishes the purpose of all undertakings. A pure rosary of rubies [grants] sovereignty.

The rosary of *putrajīvaka* beads bestows fortune and grants the knowledge-mantras (*vidyā*). Through a rosary of lotus seeds (*padmākṣa*), fortune arises as well as great renown. A rosary of red sandalwood, moreover, bestows enjoyment and brings about subjugation (*vaśya*). By the term "rosary of beads" (*akṣamālā*), the *mātṛkā* (alphabet) from the letter 'a' to the letter 'kṣa' is intended.
"Having taken recourse to the rosary, which consists of the letters in the form of the Mātṛkās."
Now, the *Jñānārṇava* describes the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consisting of nine hundred thousand recitations.
O Goddess, by reciting it one hundred thousand times, one is liberated from great sins;
by two hundred thousand times, even the sins committed over seven lifetimes are destroyed. (1)

If one recites this vidyā four hundred thousand times, it will swiftly destroy even the sins of a thousand births, and one shall become a great Lord of Speech.

by reciting six hundred thousand of this great vidyā, one becomes a lord of wealth.
By reciting this mantra seven hundred thousand times, one will attain union with the Khecarīs;
and by reciting it eight hundred thousand times, O Maheśvarī, one masters the Vidyā.

O Gaurī, he is himself the creator and the destroyer, possessing unimpeded power in the world. (7)

The meaning of the word *durgā* is as follows.
O Goddess who removes all suffering for those who bow to you, you have crossed over the ocean of existence.
Having fallen into the difficult-to-traverse waters of existence, I am sinking with all my being.
O Mother, you are obstructed in the waters of existence; who is Kāla and who are the eyes?
O Mother, in the waters of worldly existence, you perform the sport of the tiger.
Durgā is present in the demon, in great obstacles, in the bondage of worldly existence, and in evil deeds.
In grief, in suffering, in hell, in the rod of Yama, and in rebirth. || 1 ||
And in the face of great fear and disease, this word [“haṃ”] denotes the slayer. || 2 ||
The goddess who slays these very ones is proclaimed as Sādurgā. Moreover:
The letter *da* is proclaimed to be the word for the destruction of the Daityas;
the letter *u*, according to the Veda, is the designator of the destruction of obstacles. || 2 ||
The letter *ra* is proclaimed to signify the destroyer of disease; *ga* signifies the destroyer of sin; and the letter *a* is celebrated as signifying the destroyer of fear and enemies.
And because by hearing her name and so forth, even memory and speech certainly perish,
she is therefore proclaimed by Hari as Durgā, the power of Hari.
The word *durgā* signifies the destroyer of the Daityas, while the syllable *ā* denotes destruction.
She who constantly destroys difficulties (durga) is celebrated as Durgā. || 5 ||
The letter 'A' signifies misfortune, difficulty, and destruction.
Because she destroyed him in the past, she is proclaimed as Durgā by the wise.
Her true nature is described in these words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa to Nanda:
The primordial Śakti Nārāyaṇī is the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution.
And by that [power] I create the world, as well as the deities beginning with Brahmā.
By whom the universe is conquered and by whom creation is produced—that Śivā, without whom the world does not exist, has been given away by me. (8)
Compassion, sleep, hunger, satiety, thirst, faith, forbearance, fortitude,
contentment, nourishment, as well as peace and modesty— she is indeed the presiding deity over these.
In Vaikuṇṭha she is the great virtuous lady, and in Goloka she is the chaste Rādhikā.
The goddess Lakṣmī in the mortal world, and Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, who resides in the Ocean of Milk; || 10 ||
That maiden Durgā Menakā is the destroyer of the miserable state of wretchedness.
She is Lakṣmī in heaven and Durgā in every house of Indra and the other gods.
She is Vāṇī, she is Sāvitrī, and she is the presiding deity of the Brahmins.
That burning power resides in fire, and the power of radiance resides in the sun.
Beauty resides in the full moon, and cooling power resides in water.
That power, beginning with the grain, and its maintenance reside in the earths.
The power of Brahmanhood resides in the Brahmins, and that same divine power resides in the gods.
For ascetics, that is their austerity; for householders, it is the knowledge of the home.
She is the power of liberation for those who are liberated, and she is the illusion (māyā) for one who is subject to worldly existence.
The power of devotion of my devotees always bestows devotion upon me.
The royal fortune of kings and the attainable form of wealth for merchants.
She is the triad that carries one across the oceans of saṃsāra, which are otherwise difficult to cross.
And the power of intelligence (medhā-śakti), whose nature consists of the cognition of the existent as existent, is her very form.
The power of exposition resides in the scripture, and the power of bestowing resides in the givers. || 17 ||
Devotion to Brahmins among Kshatriyas and others, and devotion to their husbands among virtuous wives.
And such was the power of illusion (māyā) that was bestowed upon Śiva. || 18 ||
Moreover, there is this speech of Pārvatī addressed to Śaṅkara:
I am Mahālakṣmī in Vaikuṇṭha, and I am Rādhikā herself in Goloka.
I am Śivā in the world of Śiva, and Sarasvatī in the world of Brahmā.
In ancient times, after I had slain the Daityas, Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, [departed].
"Through the reviling of you, she and I, the daughter of the mountain, have abandoned our bodies. (20)
And in the battle against Raktabīja, Kālī appeared through a differentiation of her forms.
I am Sāvitrī, the mother of the gods; I am Sītā, the daughter of Janaka.
And Rukmiṇī, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka, was in Dvāravatī in the land of Bhārata.
Now, by fate and due to the curse of Sudāmā, she has become the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu.

The five tender leaves (*pañcapallava*) are declared by the sages who know the tantras to be: the *añcapallava*, the heartwood of the jackfruit (*panasāra*), as well as the *aśvattha*, the *vaṭa*, and the *bakula*. Thus it is stated in the *Tantrasāra*.
And the lawful wife of Kṛṣṇa, in the holy forest of Vṛndāvana,
[spoke] these words to Kṛṣṇa, as Pārvatī did.
And I, most perfectly complete, abide upon the region of your chest.
"By your command, O Vaikuṇṭha-dweller, I am Mahālakṣmī. (23)
And Sarasvatī is also right there on the left side of Hari.
Born from your mind, I am the daughter of the Sindhu river by your command.
I am Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, present here by a portion of myself in the presence of Brahmā.
In the past, by your command, [they were placed] within the splendors of all the gods in the True Realm (Satyaloka).
There, a blessing was bestowed and a divine body was sustained.
And the Daityas, beginning with Śumbha, were likewise slain effortlessly.
Having slain Durga, she is Durgāhā; having slain Tripura, she is Tripurā;
and having slain Raktabīja, she is the destroyer of Raktabīja.
By your command, O Satī, daughter of Dakṣa, you whose nature is truth—
And by means of yoga, O Daughter of the Mountain, I shall cast off this body at your command.
[She] was given by you to Śaṅkara in Goloka, within the circle of the Rāsa dance.
By that [means], there is devotion to Viṣṇu, as well as the illusory power of Viṣṇu (Viṣṇumāyā) and the Vaiṣṇavī [power].
I am the Māyā of Nārāyaṇa; therefore, I am remembered as Nārāyaṇī.
By your command, I shall become fivefold, consisting of the five forms of primordial nature.
And I, as a mere fraction of a fraction, am in the house of every house of the wives of the gods.
And she was first worshipped by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul.
Fearing Madhu and Kaiṭabha, Brahmā [entrusted] her to him as a second [charge]. || 31 ||
By the Enemy of Tripura himself, who had been dispatched by Tripura, in the third [birth].
In ancient times, Mahendra was deprived of his splendor due to a curse from Durvāsas.
In the fourth [chapter], the divine lady Satī, the Blessed One, was worshipped with devotion.
Then [he was honored] by the lords of sages, the lords of perfected beings, the gods, the Manus, and human beings.
She was always worshipped everywhere throughout the entire universe.
O Sage, she appeared of old within the splendors of all the gods.
All the gods gave her weapons and ornaments;
and Durga and the other Daityas were slain by me through Durga.
His own kingdom was granted to the gods, as well as whatever boon he desired;
in the course of time, she was worshipped by the high-souled Suratha.
And by the disciple of King Medhasa, on the bank of a river, [an image] was made of clay.
And with rams, buffaloes, black antelopes, and gaṇḍakas. || 43 ||
O Sage, she was worshipped with goats, fish, kūṣmāṇḍa gourds, and bhakti offerings.
And having thus offered these sixteen services prescribed in the Vedas, || 44 ||
Having donned the armor and meditated upon it, one should worship it according to this ritual procedure.
Having granted an exemption, the king obtained the boon as he desired.
Having attained liberation, the Vaiśya, after performing worship on the riverbank, [departed].
Having performed difficult penance at Puṣkara, by the grace of Durgā, [he attained his goal]. || 46 ||
The Vaiśya, encouraged by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, went to Goloka.

The king also, having returned to his own kingdom, enjoyed various pleasures for sixty thousand years without any thorns in his side; thereafter, having entrusted [the kingdom] to his wife and son, he performed austerities at Puṣkara and became the Manu named Sāvarṇi. Thus it is said in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.

In the autumn season, the annual Durgā-pūjā is performed; it is renowned as being of three types: Sāttvikī, Rājasī, and Tāmasī. The Sāttvikī [worship] consists of offerings free from meat, along with recitations, sacrifices, and the like. The majesty of the Bhagavatī is proclaimed in the Purāṇas and other scriptures; the recitation thereof is declared to be *japa*.
One should likewise recite the Devī-mantra with a focused mind; the recitation of the Devī-sūkta, as well as sacrifice in the fires and libations, [constitute the ritual].
And the rājasī [worship] is performed with offerings of oblations and food-offerings containing meat.
But that which is performed without the consumption of liquor, meat, and the like, without recitations and sacrifices, and without mantras, is tāmasī;
it is the practice approved by the Kirātas.
The order of recitation is as follows: having first recited the *argala* and the *kīlaka*, one should then recite the *kavaca*.
Thereafter, one should recite the Saptashati; this is the sequence declared by Shiva.
The *argala* destroys misfortune, and likewise, the *kīlaka* bestows fruit.
One should always protect the armor as well as the triad of Caṇḍikās.
Having first recited the *praṇava*, one should then recite the hymn or the *saṃhitā*.
"And one should place the Praṇava at the beginning," so said the Primeval Being.

That which is written by one's own hand by a person other than a Brahmin who lacks the proper form yields little fruit; therefore, one should not recite it. One should not recite while attached to worldly actions; rather, one should recite with self-restraint. One should recite after placing the book upon a support, and not by holding it in the palm of the hand, for there would be no fruit [from the latter].
In the future.
Rites such as the Agnihotra, Vedic sacrifices accompanied by sacrificial fees—
none of these are equal even to a hundred-thousandth part of the worship of Caṇḍikā.

He is a giver, he is a perfected sage, he is an ascetic, and he is one who has reached the sacred ford— he who always worships Durgā with various flowers and unguents. He who always worships the Goddess or bows down to her with devotion is a yogi.

For one who possesses faith, liberation stands within the palm of his hand. Whatever fruit is obtained by giving a hundred gold pieces to a Brahmin devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice and proficient in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; [that fruit is attained here]. || 3-4 ||

O King, by worshipping Caṇḍikā on the ninth lunar day with a garland of bilva leaves and guggulu resin, one obtains that fruit. O lord of men, by worshipping the goddess Durgā with two garlands of bilva tree leaves,
one obtains the merit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
The sequence of recitation in the *Yogaratnāvalī*.
The armor is taught as the seed-syllable (bīja), and the bolt is said to be the power (śakti).
They say that for the great-minded [practitioner], each individual *kīlaka* (nail) of the *Saptaśatī* is a *kīlaka*. || 1 ||
As stated in the Yāmala:

In all mantras, the first mantra to be recited is that of the seed-syllable (bīja), the power (śakti), and the pin (kīlaka). Likewise, in the recitation of the *Saptaśatī*, the recitation of the armor (*kavaca*), the bolt (*argala*), and the pin (*kīlaka*) must be performed first; thereafter, the recitation of the *Rātrisūkta* is to be performed. This is stated in the *Marīcikakalpa*: "One should recite the *Rātrisūkta* at the beginning and in the middle..."
The Saptashati, however, should be recited at the end; O Goddess, the Devīsūkta is to be recited after that—this is the sequence.

After reciting the *Rātrisūkta*, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the nine-syllable mantra (*navārṇa-mantra*) one hundred and eight or one thousand times, preceded by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other elements. As it has been stated: "Then one should recite the *Caṇḍīstava* enclosed within the nine-syllable mantra. Thus, after the recitation of the nine-syllable mantra, the *Rātrisūkta* [is to be recited].
Someone states that the recitation [of the mantra] should be sandwiched [by the root mantra], but that is incorrect;
for according to the statement "it is sandwiched by the root mantra," it is contradictory to insert another mantra in the middle.
One should recite the nine-syllable mantra a hundred times at the beginning and a hundred times at the end of the *Caṇḍīsaptaśatī*.
"This is declared to be the 'Middle Saṃpuṭa'. Furthermore, because it contradicts the *Ḍāmara Tantra*, the recitation should be performed in this sequence:
first the recitation of the *Saptaśatī*, then the recitation of the nine-syllable mantra, then the recitation of the *Devīsūkta*, and finally the recitation of the three secrets (*rahasyatraya*).

171) At the commencement of the recitation of the *Saptaśatī*, the removal of curses and other rites must be performed; the method for this has been stated by the Keralas as follows: [The syllables of the mantra are] 13, 1, 12, 2, 11, 3, 10, 4, and 9.
Having recited the chapters in the order prescribed by Manu for the removal of curses from the *Sargas*— namely, "ṣvi" (13), "bha" (12), "rtavaḥ" (11), "aśvaḥ" (10), and "śva" (9)—
wherein the first [chapter] is the thirteenth, the second the twelfth, the third the eleventh, the fourth the tenth, and the fifth the ninth, and the sixth the eighth; having thus read them...

One should recite the seventh chapter twice; this is the method for the removal of curses. Just as a person whose limbs are deficient is incapable of performing all ritual acts, so too is the seven-hundred-verse hymn when deprived of its six constituent parts.

Therefore, one should recite the supreme *Saptaśatī* only after having read this [introduction]. Otherwise, one incurs a curse and suffers loss at every step; thus it is stated in the *Kātyāyanītantra*. Reciting the *Saptaśatī* alone, devoid of the *kavaca* and the other six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*), is itself the curse. Performing it with the inclusion of the *kavaca* and the rest is [the correct way].

They say it bestows liberation. However, in the *Gurukīlaka-paṭala* of the *Rahasyatantra*, having made the firm resolve, "I shall perform the recitation (*japa*) of the mantra known as the *Saptaśatī* for as long as I live, and therefore I shall not fall into negligence," one should indeed begin and continue it; for one who does not do so...

"Because it is said that [the merit] perishes, I shall not, for as long as I live, abandon the recitation of the *Saptaśatī*—whether by mistake or whether it be right or wrong. With this firm resolve, its commencement is a means of deliverance (*uddhāra*); in the absence of such resolve, its commencement is a curse (*śāpa*). This is established.
The unbolting.

Regarding the "unbolting" (utkīlana) of the chapters, the sequence is from the middle to the beginning and end; this is according to the statement of Kerala found in the *Durgāpradīpa*. However, in the *Gurukīlakapaṭala*, it is stated that one should first recite the middle chapter, then the first chapter, and then the third chapter.
Śiva said:

O sinless one, this was formerly given by me to Sanatkumāra; he gave it to Saṃvarta, and he in turn gave it to another. Throughout the entire earth, due to the great prevalence of the recitation of Caṇḍī, the Brahmakāṇḍa, Karmakāṇḍa, and Tantrakāṇḍa have in every way [become obscured].
By this, the [mantra] that bestows swift accomplishment has become frustrated.

172) Then, desiring to make them meaningful upon the surface of the earth, this mantra was fixed by me through the act of giving and receiving. That which is proclaimed as the "stake" (kīlaka) known as giving and receiving—

From that time on, this mantra has been pinned down by a stake; it will not lead to success for all those who are averse to the stake. Those men who recite this with supreme joy while performing the rite of pinning, the Goddess shall be pleased with them, and from that, all prosperities shall arise.
Born from you, commanded by you, your servant, and having you as my sole refuge.

I am intent on contemplating Your name; I have been employed for Your sake. O Supreme Goddess! All this that has been acquired by me—this kingdom, the army, the treasury, the forces, and whatever other means of action there may be—I shall place at Your disposal for whatever purpose You shall direct me. Therein, O Goddess, I shall always abide.
"Only by obeying your command," thus reflecting in his mind, [he gave away] the wealth he had acquired himself.
On the fourteenth or the eighth day of the dark fortnight, being composed in mind.

One should offer all wealth acquired by oneself to Mahādevī—the kingdom, the home, the treasury, the army, and whatever has been newly acquired—thinking: "O Goddess! All this has been offered by me to you in this month. Then, having accepted it through the grace of the Goddess, one should receive [the blessings].
Having divided everything into five parts, one should allocate three shares for one's own purpose.

One should designate one portion for the purpose of performing rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests; one should give one part to the Guru and the Vedas, by which the Goddess is pleased. His kingdom, his own army, and his wrath shall increase greatly. Thus is prescribed the great *utkīlana* (unbolting) called "Giving and Receiving. However, some [hold] that it applies only to *kīlana* (bolting).
They say these are the "Liberations from Curses."
The meaning of the nine-syllable mantra as taught in the Ḍāmara Tantra.
The extraordinary greatness of this mantra and its purpose, as taught in the *Ḍāmaratantra*, are now being examined.

"In the heart-lotus, we constantly meditate upon You—the supreme beyond the supreme, eternally liberated, with all darkness shaken away, whose nature is consciousness, existence, and bliss—for the sake of the unbroken knowledge of Brahman.
Thus does this auspicious nine-syllabled mantra clarify [the truth]. Even a mere fraction of its greatness is difficult to describe.
By whom can it be attained? It is obtained at the end of many births through the weight of one's good fortune.
p.

173) and so forth. Here, in the first verse, there are three vocative endings, then one ending in the dative case, and then again three vocative endings; thus, by means of these seven words, the mantra is [divided] into seven parts in sequence.
The word-segmentation (*padaccheda*) has been explained as consisting of the individual words in their respective case-endings and their respective meanings.
Following that, the supply (*adhyāhāra*) of words required by the sense is stated by means of the second half [of the verse]. The rest is clear.

Because Śakti also possesses the nature of Brahman—consisting of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss (saccidānanda)—she likewise has a threefold form; therein, Mahāsarasvatī, who is the aspect of Consciousness, is awakened by the Vāgbhava seed-syllable.

Since ignorance is destroyed by knowledge alone, it is indeed appropriate to describe [the Self] by the term "one from whom all darkness has been dispelled" (*nirghūta-nikhila-dhvānta*); eternality (*nityatva*) consists in being unsublated throughout the three periods of time. For this very reason, liberation (*muktatva*) consists in being the substratum for the sublation of the imagined phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of ether and so forth. By this, [it is established that] the nature of Mahālakṣmī, who is of the essence of Being (*sad-rūpa*), [is thus characterized].
The interpretation that the invocation is performed with the mantra of Bhuvaneśvarī is the most excellent.

Bliss alone is to be experienced through all experience, because that alone is the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*). According to the Śruti, "Everything becomes dear for the sake of the Self," bliss alone is supreme, as it is the remainder of everything else since all other things exist for its sake. And that [bliss]...

Beginning with human bliss, the Śruti describes it in many ways as increasing a hundredfold at each successive stage; among these, that single bliss of Brahmā, which is the supreme excellence, is indeed recorded as the ultimate limit as "higher than the highest. Therefore, Mahākālī is she whose primary nature is that bliss.

The invocation of the essential nature (svarūpa) is appropriately joined with the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja). Indeed, the word *Cāmuṇḍā* refers to a specific non-conceptual state (*nirvikalpa-vṛtti*) that brings about liberation. The dative case is used in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*). She "takes" (*ḍāti*)—the letters *ḍa* and *la* being interchangeable—meaning she seizes the army (*camūm*), which consists of the collection of the elements beginning with space (*viyat*).

Many say that all is well because of the etymology "she who fills by making [the world] one's own," and because of its inclusion in the *vṛṣodarādi* group [of irregular compounds]; however, they maintain that the meaning of the word *cāmuṇḍā* is simply "the unbroken knowledge of Brahman" (*akhaṇḍabrahmavidyā*). As for *vicce*, it consists of three words: *vit*, *ca*, and *i*.

The term ending in the vocative case "saṃbuddhi" is the designator (*vācaka*) for the three—consciousness (*cit*), existence (*sat*), and bliss (*ānanda*)—which have been described by means of the three seed-syllables (*bīja*);
it serves as a qualifier for the three seed-syllables in their respective order. When the feminine suffix *ī* of this [term] is shortened, the meaning is:
"O Consort (*mahiṣī*) of the Great Brahman, O Bliss! The word *vit* signifies knowledge (*jñāna*).

This very word *eva* is also well-known as neuter—[as in the rule] "when followed by *san*" (Pāṇini 8.3.109)—this is how it should be construed; the words "we consider" (*anusandhāmahe*) are to be supplied [as the verb]. And thus:

"O Caṇḍikā, who are in the form of Mahāsarasvatī and others, and who are in the form of Consciousness (cit) and others, we always meditate upon you for the sake of attaining the knowledge of Brahman. This is the realized meaning of the mantra; its summary is as follows:
"O Mahāsarasvatī, O Consciousness, O Mahālakṣmī, O Eternal Self, you are the form of the bliss of Makākālī."

"O Goddess! for the sake of attaining the knowledge of reality, we meditate upon you within the lotus of our hearts"—this meaning has indeed been described by the ancients, and it is here stated with full refinement. Thus ends the meaning of the nine-syllable mantra.
Now, the procedure for this as taught in the Merutantra is being described.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the great mantra of Cāmuṇḍā.
For whom this [mantra] consisting of nine syllables exists, from its service come both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 1 ||
By whose grace Suratha, having obtained a kingdom, became a Manu;
through whom he attained, by means of meditative absorption, that knowledge which destroys the bonds of worldly existence.
I shall now declare that mantra, the recitation and other practices of which bestow the fruit of the three-fold life-story of yours as told in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
At the end of the seed-syllables *vāṃ*, *lajjā*, and *kāma*, one should utter the word *cāmuṇḍāyai*.
"Vicce"—this is the nine-syllable mantra, the most excellent among all Śakti mantras. || 4 ||
"In this mantra of the lower line, Mahālakṣmī is established;

therefore, it is perfectly accomplished for all and is a lamp in every direction. By this much, the absence of any consideration regarding the categories of *siddha* (accomplished) and so forth is indicated here.
Now follows the rule regarding the use of young leaves and so forth.
"The *pallava* (appendix) of mantras is their clothing, and the *praṇava* is the head of mantras.

A mantra joined with the head and the *pallava*, along with 'Śam', becomes a cow of plenty. Because of this statement, the rule for the *pallava* and so forth is now stated. Among these, the *praṇava* is well known. As for the *pallava*: it ends with "Namaḥ" in rites for peace (*śāntika*).

For nourishment and prostration, it is proclaimed that the mantra ending in *svāhā* bestows success; for subjugation, attraction, and delusion, the mantra joined with the *vauṣaṭ* suffix accomplishes prosperity and other goals.

Accompanied by the sprout of the syllable *huṃ*, it is used for killing, except in the case of a Brahmin; in rites involving the breaking of yantras and for destroying most terrible fears, it should be fashioned with the word *vaṣaṭ* at its end, as it destroys the afflictions caused by planetary spirits.

175) For the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), however, the mantra is said to be provided with the *phaṭ*-sprout. These sprouts are to be joined at the end of each verse or at the end of the hymn during the recitation of Caṇḍī for each respective ritual. Now, here [is] only...

If it be argued: "Let there be the attainment of the desired goal through the mantra alone; what is the use of this elaborate expansion consisting of the conjunction of the Ṛṣi and the rest, ending with the *pallava*?"—it is not so. For: "That which is devoid of the deity, the Ṛṣi, and the meter is like a seven-hooded serpent; it is powerless, lacking efficacy, fruitless, and reduced to a mere seed-syllable. It is non-reality, not reality."

A mantra devoid of its application (viniyoga) is powerless; one who is without the ritual placement (nyāsa) becomes mute; and one without the head-mantra (śiras) is as if dead. One without the sprouts (pallava) is naked; one without the seat (āsana) is asleep. Without the Guru, a mantra is in vain; if recited without being heard [properly], it is empty. A mantra given by a wicked person is devoid of potency, as is one that possesses the seed-syllable of another.

"He is called Duṣṭadatta" (meaning "given to the wicked")—by such statements, [the name] reveals his lack of auspicious qualities from the beginning, starting with his divine seer (*devarṣi*) and ending with his lineage (*pallava*), and makes known that he is defiled by defects such as being a libertine (*bhujaṅgama*), which result in undesirable consequences. Others, however, [state]: "The Vedic seer (*ārṣa*) and the meter (*chandas*)."
"Likewise, the deity and the application (viniyoga) must be known with effort by a wise Brahmin"—

according to this statement of Yājñavalkya, they say that just as in a Vedic mantra there is no deliberation on other elements such as the "pallava" (supplementary details) beyond the fourfold set beginning with the seer (ṛṣi), so it is also in this case of the *avarṇa* (the letterless). Thus ends the section on the pallava and so forth.
Investigation.
In the Gandharva Tantra.
The deities, established in their own abodes, bestow the fruits of all desired objects.
Devas who have abandoned their own abodes bestow the fruit of sorrow, suffering, and fear.

Thus [composed] by Vidyābhūṣaṇa, son of Paṇḍita Bulākhīrāma, known as Gosvāmī, a preeminent scholar born of the Gauḍa caste in the lineage of Bhāradvāja residing in Argalapura, and teacher of the Karmakāṇḍa of the Yajurveda at the venerable Śrī Vidyādharmanvardhinī Pathashala.

The procedure for the worship of yantras and other rites as taught in the Tantras, within the ritual of the worship of Durgā, has been fully compiled by Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Gosvāmī, adorned with the title *Karmakāṇḍamaṇi*.
Oṃ, salutations to Caṇḍikā! To the high-souled great sage Mārkaṇḍeya, who was performing austerities...

(176) Jaimini, the disciple of Vyāsa and possessed of great splendor, asked: Jaimini said: "O Great Sage! Tell me in great detail the origin of Caṇḍikā, by whom these three worlds are entirely pervaded."
And he is both the moving and the unmoving.
Now begins the recitation of the Durgā [Stotra].

First, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana): Oṃ Aiṃ, I purify the principle of the self (ātmatattva); obeisance, svāhā! Oṃ Hrīṃ, I purify the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva); obeisance, svāhā! Oṃ Klīṃ, I purify the principle of Śiva (śivatattva); obeisance, svāhā! Then, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra (mūlamantra). Then...

Having bowed to Śrī Gaṇeśa, the Guru, and the others: *Oṃ tat sat*. Today, during the second half of the first watch of Brahmā’s day, in the illustrious Śvetavārāha Kalpa, on Jambūdvīpa, in the land of Bharata, within a specific region of Āryāvarta, in the Kali Yuga, during the first quarter of the Kali age, in a sacred field, in the year named [Name] of the Aṅgirasas, in the [Name] season...

In the month of [amuka], in the fortnight of [amuka], on the lunar day of [amuka], on the day of [amuka], under the asterism of [amuka], in the yoga of [amuka], in the karaṇa of [amuka], at the time when the planets beginning with the Sun are situated in the signs of [amuka] and [amuka], [the patron], born of the [amuka] lineage and named [amukaśarmā], [from his birth-ascendant]...

From the solar ascendant (varṣalagna) according to the planetary movements (gocara), when malefic planets such as the Sun and others are situated in the fourth, eighth, or twelfth houses, there may arise misfortune (ariṣṭa) caused thereby; [this results in] the removal of such misfortune, as well as the removal of misfortune arising from major periods (daśā), sub-periods (antaradaśā), minor sub-periods (upadaśā), and daily periods (dinadaśā), including the affliction of fever, the pain of burning sensations, afflictions of the eyes, ears, abdomen, and so forth, and the removal of a short lifespan.

And the former [is performed] preceded by the cessation of the flood of the threefold sins—physical, vocal, and mental—consisting of the afflictions born of the divine, the elemental, and the personal, for the sake of bodily health and the attainment of supreme sovereignty and so forth. Mārkaṇḍeya said: Om.
"Listen as I describe in detail the birth of that eighth Manu who is called Sāvarṇi, the son of the Sun"—
beginning with these words and extending to the end of the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, this section reveals the *Devīmāhātmya* concerning Mahākālī and Mahālakṣmī.
For the [rite] dedicated to the deity Mahāsarasvatī,
which consists of ten limbs, is for the warding off of untimely death, is joined at the beginning and end with the Tryambaka mantra and the Śāpotkīlana mantra,
and includes the Rātrisūkta at the beginning and the Devīsūkta at the end— [of this], O [Name]...
I shall perform the recitation of the mantra encapsulated by the [root] mantra, repeating it according to the prescribed number.
On the side of the patron, he should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), saying: "I shall have it performed through a Brāhmaṇa."
At the conclusion of the proclamation of the place and time.
In the sixth chapter of the Kulārṇava: "The purification of the self, the place, the mantra, the substance, and the deity is the fifth [requirement].
As long as the practitioner of mantra does not perform these, how can there be worship of the deity?"
p.
177) For the sake of the increase of welfare, stability, longevity, health, and sovereignty for all of us together with our families, and for the attainment of all auspiciousness—
I, [name], of the [gotra] lineage, for the sake of my patron [name], through the attainment of the grace and success of the venerable Jagadambā,
pray for the removal of all calamities and the acquisition of all desired fruits— dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
For the sake of accomplishing the fourfold aims of human life (*caturvidha-puruṣārtha*), for the purpose of gain through royal courts and business,
for the sake of victory, and for the propitiation of the deities Śrī Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī,
[this is] the recitation of the *kavaca*, *argala*, and *kīlaka*, preceded by the eleven-fold ritual placement (*ekādaśanyāsa*) of the nine-syllabled mantra (*navārṇa*).
After reciting the *Rātrisūkta* and performing one hundred and eight recitations (*japa*) of the mantra, followed by the recitation of the *Devīsūkta*,

one hundred and eight recitations of the nine-syllable mantra (*navārṇa-mantra*), and finally the recitation of the three secrets (*rahasya-traya*), [one should recite] from the words "Mārkaṇḍeya said" up to the end of the section beginning with "Sāvarṇi will be the Manu... (Amuka...).

I shall perform one hundred recitations (or nine recitations) of the Śrī Caṇḍī Saptaśatī, encapsulated by mantras (to be performed through a Brāhmaṇa). Daily Resolve: For the fulfillment of the desires previously resolved upon, [I shall perform] the Śata Caṇḍī.
(Navacaṇḍī) For the completion of the count, page 178):
"I shall perform the rite called the recitation according to the method previously resolved. [In the case of the patron (*yajamāna*):]
"I shall do so. Thus [he said].
The worship of the book.

Oṃ, obeisance to Piśācinī, Karaṅkiṇī, you who hold a trident and a sword in your hands, mounted upon a lion! Come, come! Approach, approach! Accept this worship, accept it! Svāhā! Obeisance to Hrīṃ Caṇḍikā, the embodiment of the Śrī Saptasatī. Having performed the worship of the book with the prescribed offerings, then—
The Removal of the Curse.
Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ krīṃ krīṃ, to the goddess Caṇḍikā: grant, grant the removal of curses; svāhā!
The Utkīlana (unbolting rite): Oṃ śrīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ, O Caṇḍikā of the Saptashatī, perform the unbolting, perform it twice! Svāhā!
The Science of Reviving the Dead: Oṃ hrīṃ hrāṃ vaṃ vaṃ aiṃ aiṃ, O Science of Reviving the Dead, raise up, cause to rise up the nectar of immortality!
Krīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ vaṃ svāhā!

Alternatively, here is the procedure for liberation from the curse according to the *Marīcikalpa* Saptashatī: First, having extracted the Praṇava (Oṃ), then the seed-syllable of Ramā (Śrīṃ); then Ramā, Kāma, and Krodha; then the Tāra (Oṃ) conjoined with Vāgbhava (Aiṃ); then Kṣobha and Moha; and after that, "Kīlaya" three times. 1. Oṃ Śrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ Hrīṃ Aiṃ Kṣobha Moha Kīlaya Kīlaya Kīlaya.
Dviṭham. Having performed the rite for liberation from curses, one should engage in the recitation of Caṇḍī: Oṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ hūṃ oṃ aiṃ, agitate, delude, uproot 3, ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ.
p.

179) Having first recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, and subsequently performing the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) before reciting the *Saptaśatī*, the accomplishment of one’s appropriate desires will come to pass; it will not be otherwise. Another method:
Now follows the liberation from the curse of Caṇḍikā.

Oṃ. Of this mantra for liberation from the curses of Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, and Viśvāmitra pertaining to the illustrious Caṇḍikā, the sage (ṛṣi) is Brahmā, the lord of the Sāmaveda, in the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Nārada;
the deity (devatā) is the illustrious Durgā, who bestows all sovereignty; the threefold conduct (caritatraya) is the seed-syllable (bīja); and Hrīṃ is the power (śakti).

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of liberation from the curse of Caṇḍikā and for the accomplishment of my intended task, [performed] while chanting this mantra whose essential nature consists of the three *guṇas*: Oṃ (Hrīṃ) Rīṃ!
O Thou whose form is semen, O Destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, be liberated from the curses of Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, and Viśvāmitra.
|| 1 || Oṃ! To her whose nature is the glorious intellect, who destroyed the army of the demon Mahiṣāsura; be liberated from the curses of Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, and Viśvāmitra. || 2 ||

Now follows the procedure for untying all mantras (*sarvamantrotkīlanavidhi*). In another tantra: the root mantra consists of nine syllables: *oṃ hrīṃ hyauṃ kṣmroṃ kṣmalavara pīḍaṃmalavara phrīṃ oṃ kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣaiṃ kṣauṃ kṣaḥ utkīlaya 2 svāhā*. Or [the root mantra]: *oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ cāmuṇḍāyai vicce* [repeated] seven times.

O Twelvefold Jayantī, Maṅgalā, Kālī, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī, Durgā, Kṣamā, Śivā, Dhātrī, Svāhā, Svadhā—salutations be to you! || 1 || Oṃ hrīṃ hyauṃ hrīṃ hyoḥ aiṃ kṣmalavara phrīṃ kṣamalavara phrīṃ oṃ hyauṃ utkīlaya 2 svāhā. (Mūla-mantra) 1 svāhā. Thus is the *utkīlana*. Oṃ.
"Salutation to the one whose body is pure knowledge, who possesses the divine eye of the three Vedas, who is the cause for attaining the highest good, and who bears the crescent moon.
Subjugate the three worlds! *kṣma-mala-vara-phrīṃ* Oṃ, [the root mantra] 1.
Thus one should conclude the first verse. This is the *Argalāmokṣa*. Now, the six-limbed armor (*ṣaḍaṅga-kavaca*) with the root mantra.
Lesson 11: *Nyāsa* as Unbolting (*Utkīlana*). Now, the Mantra for Liberation from Curses (*Śāpamocana*):

Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ krāṃ krīṃ, O Goddess Caṇḍikā, grant the grace of destroying curses! Grant it, grant it! Svāhā! One should recite this seven times at the beginning and at the end. Oṃ śrī klīṃ hrīṃ, O Caṇḍikā of the Seven Hundred Verses, perform the unbolting! Perform it, perform it! Svāhā!
One should recite it twenty-one times at the beginning and at the end.

Oṃ ra&! To her whose essential nature is red, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura; may you be liberated from the curses of Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, and Viśvāmitra. || 3 || Oṃ kṣu&! To her whose essential nature is hunger, who is saluted by the gods.

Be liberated from the curse of Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, and Viśvāmitra. (4) Oṃ Chāṃ! To her whose form is Shadow, who conversed with the messenger, [be liberated] from the curse of Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, and Viśvāmitra. (5) Oṃ Śaṃ! To her whose form is Power, the slayer of Dhūmralocana, [be liberated] from the curse of Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, and Viśvāmitra.

Śā0 || 6 || Oṃ Tṛṃ! To her whose nature is thirst, who performed the slaying of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa; [Salutation] to Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, Śā0 || 7 || Oṃ Kṣāṃ! To her whose nature is forbearance, who performed the slaying of Raktabīja; [Salutation] to Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, Śā0 || 8 || Oṃ Jāṃ...

Oṃ, salutations to her whose nature is *Jāti*, the slayer of Śumbha, [praised] by Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, and Viśvāmitra. || 9 || Oṃ, salutations to her whose nature is *Lajjā* (Modesty), the slayer of Śumbha, [praised] by Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, and Viśvāmitra. || 10 || Oṃ, salutations to her whose nature is *Śānti* (Peace), praised by the gods, [praised] by Brahmā and Vasiṣṭha... || 11 ||

Viśvāmitra Śākhā || 11 || Oṃ Śraṃ! To her whose nature is faith (śraddhā), the bestower of all fruits; [Salutation to] Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and the Śākhā || 12 || Oṃ Kāṃ! To her whose nature is beauty (kānti), the granter of boons to kings; [Salutation to] Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and the Śākhā || 13 || Oṃ Māṃ! To the Mother...

To her whose nature is the Supreme Sound, who possesses immeasurable majesty, [salutation] to Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra... || 14 || Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hraṃ Duṃ, [salutation] to Durgā, the bestower of all sovereignty, [who was liberated from] the curse of Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, and Viśvāmitra... || 15 || Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ, salutation to Śivā, the impenetrable armor.

To her whose nature is Svarūpā, to Brahmā and Vasiṣṭha... || 16 || Oṃ Krīṃ, to Kālī, to Kāli Hrīṃ Phaṭ Svāhā, to her whose nature is the Ṛgveda, to Brahmā and Vasiṣṭha... || 10 || Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ, obeisance to Goddess Durgā, who is the embodiment of Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī, and whose essence consists of the three qualities (triguṇātmikā).
In the eleventh chapter of the *Śāradā-tantra*, ten types of *puraścaraṇa* are described.

Japa, fire-offering (homa), libation (tarpaṇa), self-consecration (svābhiṣeka), the rite for wiping away sins (aghamarṣaṇa), water-offering to the Sun (sūryārghya), drinking [consecrated] water, giving gifts, prostration, worship of the deity, and feeding Brāhmaṇas— each preceding one should be performed with a tenth part of the quantity of the succeeding one. All of this is to be understood as pertaining to the preparatory observance (puraścaraṇa) of a mantra.
In the Bālakāṇḍa, the twelfth canto of the Vālmīkīya Rāmāyaṇa:
"The performer of a sacrifice devoid of the prescribed rules perishes immediately."
Just as prescribed by the rule, one should complete this rite;
thus it is stated in the fifteenth chapter of the Kulārṇava.

If one desires personal accomplishment regarding the ground of the suffering of saṃsāra, the reciter of the mantra shall proceed happily through the worship of the five limbs. Worship performed at the three times daily, constant recitation, libation (tarpaṇa), fire-offering (homa), and feeding Brahmins—this is called *puraścaraṇa*. If any limb is omitted, its [deficiency] must be compensated for by that same number [of repetitions].
The recitation should be doubled; O Dear One! everything done through knowledge or ignorance is destroyed by this recitation.
In that very same [text], it is stated: "From eating the food of others, there is a loss of accomplishment."

If one eats the food and drink of another and performs an accumulation of merit, half of the fruit belongs to the giver of the food and half to the doer; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, a wise person should avoid the food of others with every effort.

O Īśvarī! During the time of *puraścaraṇa* and even in rites performed for specific desires, the tongue is scorched by eating the food of others, the hands are scorched by accepting gifts, and the mind is scorched by other men's wives; how, then, can there be success in the task?

In the *Nīlatantra*: "The tongue is defiled by eating [impure things], and by speaking falsehoods; the tongue is defiled by quarrels and defiled by various faults. How then can a vulgar person recite the mantra with such a tongue?"

A common person should never perform purification or recitation without having sipped water (ācamana). O beautiful lady, one who desires supreme accomplishment should first recite Māyā, then Kūrca, and again Māyā; thus, O Goddess, he should purify his mouth.
The ritual placement (nyāsa), meditation (dhyāna), invocation (āvāhana), and likewise the hymns (sūkta) and names (nāma) follow in sequence.
The petals, the heart, as well as the armor, the bolt, and the pin.

(182) Having thus recited these great mantras, O Supreme Lord, one should indeed perform the recitation of Caṇḍī day and night; of this there is no doubt. (19) He who does not know the mantra in this way yet performs the recitation of Caṇḍī...
He who [destroys] both himself and the donor will undoubtedly bring about ruin. || 20 ||
Thus ends the "Liberation from Caṇḍikā’s Curse" within the Durgā-kalpa of the Śrī Rudrayāmala Mahātantra.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Now begins the Kavaca.

Oṃ. Of this *Śrī Caṇḍī-kavaca*, Brahmā is the *ṛṣi*. [What is the etymology? They are called *ṛṣis* because they "see" (*ṛṣanti*) or know everything; they are the seers of mantras, or those whose speech is truth. The root *ṛṣ* means "to go. The meter is *anuṣṭubh*, the deity is Cāmuṇḍā, the seed-syllable is that of the Mothers as prescribed for the *aṅga-nyāsa*, and the directional binding (*digbandha*).
