The deities are the principles of reality; for the sake of pleasing Śrī Jagadambā, this is the application (viniyoga) in the recitation as part of the seven-hundred-verse chant.
Oṃ, salutations to Caṇḍikā! Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Grandfather! Tell me that which is the supreme secret in the world, which provides protection for all men, and which has not been revealed to anyone else. (1)
Brahmā said:
O Brahmin! There exists a most secret [teaching], beneficial to all beings;
O great sage, listen to that meritorious armor (kavaca) of the Goddess. || 2 ||
First is Śailaputrī, second is Brahmacāriṇī;
third is Candraghaṇṭā, and fourth is Kūṣmāṇḍī. (3)
The fifth is called Skandamātā, the sixth is Kātyāyanī;
the seventh is Kālarātrī, and the eighth is Mahāgaurī.
The ninth is Siddhidātrī; thus the nine Durgās have been proclaimed.
These names were spoken by the Great-Souled Brahmā himself. (p. 184) 5.
Being consumed by fire in the midst of enemies on the battlefield,
and likewise in difficult and inaccessible places, those afflicted by fear have come to him for refuge.
Nothing inauspicious shall arise for them in the perils of battle;
nor do I see any calamity, grief, suffering, or fear for them.
But for those who remember you with devotion, their prosperity will surely arise;
O Goddess of gods! those who remember you, you shall protect them—of this there is no doubt.
Cāmuṇḍā has the form of a corpse; Vārāhī is seated upon a buffalo.
Aindrī is mounted on an elephant, and Vaiṣṇavī is seated upon Garuḍa. (9)
Māheśvarī is mounted upon a bull; Kaumārī has a peacock as her vehicle;
the goddess Lakṣmī, beloved of Hari, sits upon a lotus throne and holds a lotus in her hand.
The goddess Śvetarūpadharā is the sovereign whose vehicle is a bull;
Brāhmī is mounted upon a swan and adorned with all ornaments.
Thus, all these Mothers are endowed with every yoga;
they are richly adorned with various ornaments and beautified by diverse jewels.
The goddesses, mounted upon chariots and agitated with wrath,
were seen bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, the spear, the plow, and the club as weapons.
A shield, a javelin, an axe, and likewise a noose;
a spear-weapon, a trident, and the supreme weapon, the Śārṅga bow. (14)
Then, for the destruction of the bodies of the Daityas, for the granting of fearlessness to the devotees,
and indeed for the welfare of the gods, they took up their weapons.
Salutations to you, O most fierce one, whose prowess is most terrible;
O you of great strength and great energy, the destroyer of great fear! 16.
Protect me, O Goddess, you who are difficult for enemies to behold and the increaser of their fear!
May the goddess Indrāṇī protect me in the east, and the deity Agni in the southeast.
May Vārāhī protect in the south; may Khaḍgadhāriṇī protect in the southwest;
may Vāruṇī protect in the west; and may Mṛgavāhinī protect in the northwest.
May Kaumārī protect me in the north, and Śūladhāriṇī in the northeast;
may Brahmāṇī protect me above, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī below.
In this manner, Cāmuṇḍā, whose vehicle is a corpse, shall protect [the practitioner] in the ten directions.
May Jayā protect me from the front, and may Vijayā protect me from behind. || 20 ||
Ajitā is on the left side, while Aparājitā is on the right; Udyotinī should protect the topknot, and Umā is stationed upon the head. (21)
Mālādhārī shall protect the forehead, and Yaśasvinī the two eyebrows; Trinetrā shall protect the space between the eyebrows, and Yamaghaṇṭā the nose.
Śaṅkhinī protects the space between the two eyes; Dvāravāsinī protects the two ears; Kālikā protects the two cheeks; and Śāṅkarī protects the roots of the ears. (23)
Sugandhā is in the nose, Carcikā on the upper lip, Amṛtakalā on the lower lip, and Sarasvatī on the tongue. || 24 ||
May Kaumārī protect the teeth, and Caṇḍikā the region of the throat; may Citraghaṇṭā protect the uvula, and Mahāmāyā the palate.
May Kāmākṣī protect my chin, may Sarvamaṅgalā protect my speech,
Bhadrakālī my neck, and Dhanurdharī my backbone.
May Nīlagrīvā protect my neck externally; may Nalakūbarī protect the trachea;
may Khaḍginī protect my shoulders; and may Vajradhāriṇī protect my arms.
May Daṇḍinī protect the two hands, and Ambikā the fingers;
may Śūleśvarī protect the nails, and Kuleśvarī protect the belly.
The Great Goddess, who destroys mental grief, protects the breasts;
the goddess Lalitā is in the heart, and Śūladhāriṇī is in the belly. (29)
The goddess Guhyeśvarā, who is full of desire, should protect the secret organ at the navel;
Pūtanā, who is full of desire, protects the penis, and Mahiṣavāhinī protects the anus.
May the Goddess protect the hips; may Vindhyavāsinī protect the knees;
and may Mahābalā, the bestower of all desires, protect the shanks. 31.
Nārasiṃhā is in the two ankles, while Tejasī is in the backs of the feet;
Śrī protects the toes, and Stalavāsinī resides beneath the soles of the feet.
Nakhādaṃṣṭrākarālī is in the nails and teeth, and Keśāñcukā is in the hair standing on end; Ukāberī is in the pores of the skin, and likewise Vāgīśvarī is in the skin.
Blood, marrow, fat, flesh, bone, and fat are Pārvatī;
the entrails are Kālarātri, and the bile is Mukuṭeśvarī. (34)
Padmāvatī is at the tip of the lotus bud; likewise, Cūḍāmaṇi is there.
Jvālāmukhī is the net of splendor, which is impenetrable in all the joints. (35)
May Śukrā protect my semen and sacred knowledge, and likewise may Chatreśvarī protect my shadow;
may Dharmadhāriṇī protect my ego, mind, and intellect. (36)
May Vajrahastā, auspicious and beautiful, protect my prāṇa, as well as apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna. (37)
In taste, form, smell, sound, and touch, the Yoginī Nārāyaṇī always protects the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
May Vārāhī protect my life; may Vaiṣṇavī protect my Dharma;
and may Cakriṇī protect my fame, renown, fortune, wealth, and knowledge. (39)
May Indrāṇī protect my lineage; O Caṇḍikā, protect my cattle! May Mahālakṣmī protect my sons, and may Bhairavī protect my wife. (40)
May Supathā protect the path, and may Kṣemakarī likewise protect the way;
may Mahālakṣmī be at the king’s gate, and Vijayā be stationed everywhere. 41.
O Goddess Jayantī, destroyer of sins, protect all that place which is devoid of protection and abandoned by armor! 42.
If one desires one's own welfare,
one should not take even a single step without being constantly protected by the armor (kavaca), wherever one may go.

In every such place, there shall be the attainment of wealth and victory that fulfills all desires. Whatever object he contemplates, he will certainly obtain it; the man shall attain supreme and incomparable sovereignty upon the earth. (44)
A mortal becomes fearless and remains undefeated in battles; indeed, a man protected by this armor shall be honored throughout the three worlds. (45)
This armor of the Goddess, however, is difficult even for the gods to obtain;
he who, being self-restrained and endowed with faith, recites it daily at the three junctions of the day. (46)
A divine power shall belong to him, and he shall be unconquered throughout the three worlds;
he shall live for more than a hundred years, free from untimely death.
All diseases, such as spider-bites, boils, and the like, perish, as do all poisons—whether stationary, mobile, or even artificial. (48)

All the rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*), as well as all mantras and yantras on the surface of the earth— whether they belong to those who move on the ground, those who move in the sky, those born of the *kula*, or those who provide instruction— [are all overcome]. (49)
The Sahajas, the Kulajāmālās, the Ḍākinīs, and likewise the Śākinīs;
the Aghorās who move through the intermediate space, and the Ḍākinīs of great power. || 50 ||
Planets, spirits, and piśācas; yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas; brahmarākṣasas, vetālas, kūṣmāṇḍas, bhairavas, and so forth—|| 51 ||
When this armor is established upon the heart, [all enemies] perish at the mere sight of it;
it brings about the heightening of honor, and is supreme for increasing royal power and splendor.
He too shall increase in fame and be adorned with glory upon the earth;
provided he first recites the armor (kavaca) and then chants the Caṇḍī Saptaśatī.
As long as the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves,
remains supported, so long shall the lineage of sons and grandsons endure upon this earth.
At the end of the body, by the grace of Mahāmāyā, a person eternally attains that supreme state which is difficult even for the gods to reach. || 55 ||
He attains the supreme form and rejoices together with Śiva. Oṃ. 56.
Thus ends the *Devī-kavaca*, composed by Hari, Hara, and Brahmā, in the glorious *Vārāha-purāṇa*. (p.
195) Now begins the *Argalā-stotra*.

Oṃ. Of this mantra of the Śrī Argalā Stotra, Viṣṇu is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ), and Śrī Mahālakṣmī is the deity (devatā). Its application (viniyoga) is for the recitation of the Saptashatī as an ancillary rite for the propitiation of Śrī Jagadambā.
Oṃ, salutations to Caṇḍikā. Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Oṃ! Jayantī, Maṅgalā, Kālī, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī, Durgā, Kṣamā, Śivā, Dhātrī, Svāhā, Svadhā—homage be to you! || 1 ||
Victory to you, O Goddess Cāmuṇḍā; victory to you, O destroyer of enemies for the sake of the true reality!
Victory to you, O omnipresent Goddess; O Kālarātri, salutations be unto you!
Obeisance to the one who put Madhu and Kaiṭabha to flight, the granter of boons to Brahmā!
Grant me beauty, grant me victory, grant me fame, and slay my enemies. || 3 ||
O destroyer of the demon Mahiṣāsura, O bestower of happiness upon devotees, salutations to you!
Grant me beauty, grant me victory, grant me glory, and slay my enemies. (4)
O Goddess, slayer of Raktabīja, destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa!
Grant me form, grant me victory, grant me glory, and destroy my enemies. || 5 ||
O Goddess, whose pair of feet is worshipped, bestower of all prosperity!
Grant me beauty, grant me victory, grant me fame, and destroy my enemies.
O you of inconceivable form and conduct, who destroys all enemies!
Grant me form, grant me victory, grant me fame, and slay my foes. (7)
O Caṇḍikā, remover of misfortune, to those who always bow with devotion,
grant a beautiful form, grant victory, grant glory, and slay our enemies. (8)
O Caṇḍikā, destroyer of disease, to us who praise you with devotion, grant us beauty, grant us victory, grant us glory, and slay our enemies. (9)
O Caṇḍikā, those who here constantly worship you with devotion—
grant them beauty, grant them victory, grant them glory, and slay their enemies.
Grant me good fortune; grant me health; grant me supreme happiness. Grant me beauty; grant me victory; grant me glory; destroy my enemies.
Bring about the destruction of my enemies; bring about great strength!
Grant me beauty, grant me victory, grant me glory, and slay my foes.
O Goddess, ordain auspiciousness; ordain supreme prosperity.
Grant me beauty, grant me victory, grant me fame, and slay my enemies. (13)
O Ambikā, whose feet are rubbed by the crest-jewels of the gods and demons, grant me beauty, grant me victory, grant me glory, and slay my enemies! 14.
Make people possessed of knowledge, possessed of fame, and possessed of fortune.
Grant beauty, grant victory, grant glory, and slay the enemies. (15)
O Caṇḍikā, destroyer of the pride of the fierce Daityas, grant a form to me who am prostrate before you; grant victory, grant glory, and slay my enemies.
O Supreme Goddess, praised by the four-armed and the four-faced [Brahmā], grant me beauty, grant me victory, grant me glory, and slay my enemies. 17.
O Goddess, Mother Ambikā, who is eternally praised with constant devotion by Kṛṣṇa;
grant me form, grant me victory, grant me glory, and slay my enemies.
O Supreme Goddess, praised by the Lord of Himācala’s daughter,
grant me form, grant me victory, grant me glory, and slay my enemies. (19)
O Indrāṇī, O Supreme Goddess honored by the very existence of your husband, grant me beauty, grant me victory, grant me glory, and slay my enemies! 20.
O Goddess, destroyer of the pride of the Daityas with your fierce, staff-like arms!
Grant me beauty, grant me victory, grant me glory, and slay my enemies.
O Mother, who causes the arising of unrestrained bliss for those devoted to the Goddess,
grant me form, grant me victory, grant me fame, and destroy my enemies.
"Grant me a beautiful wife who follows the inclinations of my mind, who is born of a noble lineage, and who is a savior from the difficult ocean of worldly existence. (24)
Having recited this hymn, a person should then recite the Great Hymn;
he indeed obtains the excellence of the seven-hundred-verse count along with all prosperity. Om! 25.
Thus ends the Argalāstotra in the glorious Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.

Of this venerable Kīlaka-mantra, Śiva is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), the venerable Mahāsarasvatī is the deity (devatā); its application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of pleasing the venerable Jagadambā during the recitation of the Saptashatī as an ancillary part of the ritual chanting.
Oṃ, salutations to Caṇḍikā. Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Oṃ! Salutation to the one whose body is pure knowledge, who possesses the divine eye of the three Vedas, who is the cause for attaining the highest good, and who bears the crescent moon. || 1 ||
One should understand all this as the "pinning" (kīlaka) of the mantras;
he who is constantly intent upon recitation shall also attain perpetual well-being.
All matters, including rites such as eradication (uccāṭana), are accomplished;
for those who praise her, the Goddess is mastered by the mere recitation of this hymn. (3)
Neither mantra nor medicine is required there; not even the slightest thing is needed.
Everything, including rites such as eradication (uccāṭana), is accomplished without the need for recitation. || 4 ||
Even though all were present, Hara removed this suspicion of the world and invited everyone; thus, all this was auspicious.
He indeed composed that hymn to Caṇḍikā and kept it secret;
through great merit, he attained her proper and complete mastery.
He too attains all well-being, without a doubt,
if he remains composed on the fourteenth or the eighth day of the dark fortnight.
One gives and one receives; otherwise, this [process] is not established.
Thus, by means of this kind of *kīla*, it has been pinned down by Mahādeva. (p. 202) 8.
That man who, having rendered her free from obstacles, constantly recites this clearly, becomes a perfected one (siddha) along with his retinue; indeed, he becomes a Gandharva.
And as he wanders about, no fear whatsoever arises for him here;
he does not fall under the power of untimely death, and having died, he attains liberation.
Having understood [the situation], one should begin; by acting thus, one does not perish.
Therefore, this is undertaken by the wise only after having understood that it will be successful. 11.
Whatever good fortune and such is seen among women, all that is through your grace; therefore, let this auspicious recitation be performed. (12)
If this hymn is recited even slowly, complete prosperity indeed arises in abundance; therefore, it must certainly be commenced. (13)
Why is she not praised by people—she, by whose grace sovereignty, good fortune, health, and prosperity are attained, as well as the destruction of enemies and supreme liberation? Om. 14.
Thus ends the *Kīlaka-stotra* of the Bhagavatī; may there be auspiciousness. 3.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the nine-syllable mantra.
Victorious is Śrī Gaṇapati! Oṃ. Of this Śrī Navārṇa mantra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the ṛṣis;
Śrī Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī are the deities; Nandā, Śākambharī, and Durgā are the śaktis.

The application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of pleasing Śrī Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī through recitation (japa): the Bhīmas, the Śaktis, Raktadantikā, Durgā, the Bhrāmarīs, the seeds (bījas), the principles (tattvas) of fire, wind, and sun, and the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas as the meditations (dhyānas).
204) Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the sages and so forth.

Oṃ, salutations to the sages Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; [place this] on the head. Oṃ, salutations to the meters Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, and Anuṣṭubh; [place this] on the mouth. Oṃ, salutations to the deities Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī; [place this] on the heart. Oṃ, [salutations to] Nandā, Śākambharī, and Bhīmā.

"Oṃ, salutations to the Śaktis at the right breast. Oṃ, salutations to Raktadantikā, Durgā, Bhrāmarī, and the Bījas at the left breast. Oṃ, salutations to the principles of Fire, Wind, and Sun at the navel. Thus is the Nyāsa of the Seer and so forth. Alternatively, according to another Tantra: "Aiṃ is the Bīja, Hrīṃ is the Śakti, Klīṃ..."

The Kīlaka: *Oṃ aiṃ*, salutation to the Seed-syllable (*bīja*) at the secret place; *Oṃ hrīṃ*, salutation to the Power (*śakti*) at the feet; *Oṃ klīṃ*, salutation to the Kīlaka at the navel. (This is an alternative reading. Having purified both hands with the Root-mantra, [one should proceed] from verse 111 of the eighteenth wave in the *Mantramahodadhi* regarding the nine-syllabled [mantra].
There are eleven methods of ritual placement (nyāsa); among them, first is the pure Mātṛkā-nyāsa.
By performing this rite for the deity, a human attains a form identical to that of the god.
The Sarasvata Nyāsa. 2.
When this Sarasvatī-consecration has been performed, dullness is destroyed.
Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, salutation to the two little fingers. Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, salutation to the two ring fingers.
Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ namaḥ to the two middle fingers. Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ namaḥ to the two index fingers. Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ namaḥ to the two thumbs. Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ...
*Namaḥ* to the palms of the hands. *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ namaḥ* to the backs of the hands. *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ namaḥ* to the wrists. *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ namaḥ* to the elbows.

Oṃ e hrīṃ klīṃ namaḥ, salutation to the heart: namaḥ. Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ namaḥ, svāhā to the head. Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ namaḥ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhā). Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ namaḥ, huṃ to the armor (kavaca). Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ namaḥ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes. Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ... [and so forth].
*Klīṃ*, salutation to the weapon, *phaṭ*. Thus ends the second Sarasvatī-nyāsa.
Now follows the third: the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the groups of Mātṛkās.
When this third nyāsa has been performed, one becomes a conqueror of the three worlds.

Oṃ hrīṃ, may Brāhmī protect me in the east. Oṃ hrīṃ, may Māheśvarī protect me in the southeast. Oṃ hrīṃ, may Kaumārī protect me in the south. Oṃ hrīṃ, may Vaiṣṇavī protect me in the southwest. Oṃ hrīṃ, may Vārāhī protect me in the west. Oṃ...

Hrīṃ! May Indrāṇī protect me in the northwest. Oṃ Hrīṃ! May Cāmuṇḍā protect me in the north. Oṃ Hrīṃ! May Mahālakṣmī protect me in the northeast. Oṃ Hrīṃ! May Vyomeśvarī protect me above. Oṃ Hrīṃ! May Saptadvīpeśvarī protect me on the earth. Oṃ Hrīṃ...
May Kāmeśvarī protect me in the netherworld (pātāla). Thus ends the third assignment (nyāsa).
p. 206) Now follows the fourth [section]: the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six goddesses.

A person should perform the fourth placement (*nyāsa*); it dispels old age and death. Oṃ! May Tandrajā, adorned with a lotus and a goad, protect my eastern limb. Oṃ! May Raktadantikā, bearing a sword and a vessel, protect my southern limb. Oṃ! [May she who holds] flowers and sprouts...
May Śākambharī, joined [with her consort], protect my back;

Oṃ, may Durgā, who holds a bow and arrows in her hands and removes the distress of the difficult, protect my left side; Oṃ, may Bhīmā, who holds a skull-bowl in her hand, protect me from the head down to the feet; may Bhrāmarī, possessing variegated splendor, [protect me] with her two feet.
"May [he] protect me up to the head. Thus is the fourth placement (*nyāsa*).
Now begins the fifth placement (nyāsa), called Brahmā.
When this fifth placement has been performed, one shall obtain all desires.

Oṃ, may the eternal Brahmā protect me from the feet up to the navel. Oṃ, may Janārdana protect me eternally from the navel up to the Viśuddha [cakra]. Oṃ, may the three-eyed Rudra protect me from the Viśuddha up to the Brahma-randhra. Oṃ Haṃ Saḥ, may he protect my two feet.
May he protect! Oṃ, may Vainateya protect my two hands. Oṃ, may the Bull protect my eyes.
Oṃ, may Gajānana protect all my limbs. Oṃ, may Hari, who consists of universal bliss, protect both the higher and lower parts of my body. Thus ends the fifth Nyāsa, beginning with Brahmā.
(p. 207) Now follows the sixth nyāsa, beginning with Mahālakṣmī.

Oṃ, may Mahālakṣmī, endowed with eighteen arms, protect me from the center. Oṃ, may Mahāsarasvatī, endowed with eight arms, protect me from above. Oṃ, may Mahākālī, adorned with ten arms, protect me from below.
Oṃ, may the two lions protect my hands. Oṃ, may the pair of swans protect my eyes.
Oṃ, may Yama, mounted upon his divine buffalo, protect my two feet. Oṃ, may Maheśa, together with Caṇḍikā, protect all my limbs. Thus ends the sixth nyāsa.
Now follows the placement of the seventh seed-mantra.
When the placement is performed with the seventh [verse], the destruction of disease occurs.

Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to the crest-lock (śikhā). Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the right eye. Oṃ Klīṃ, salutation to the left eye. Oṃ Cāṃ, salutation to the right ear. Oṃ Muṃ, salutation to the left ear. Oṃ Ḍāṃ, salutation to the right nostril. Oṃ Yaiṃ, salutation to the left nostril. Oṃ Viṃ, salutation to the mouth.
Oṃ cceṃ, salutation to the anus. Thus ends the seventh [section], the seed-syllable placement (bījanyāsa).
Now follows the eighth [section]: the placement of the seed-syllables in reverse order (viloma-bīja-nyāsa).
When this eighth assignment has been performed, all suffering perishes.
Oṃ cceṃ, obeisance to the anus. Oṃ viṃ, obeisance to the mouth. Oṃ yaiṃ, obeisance to the left nostril.
Oṃ ḍāṃ, homage to the right nostril.

p. 208) Oṃ muṃ, salutation to the left ear. Oṃ cāṃ, salutation to the right ear. Oṃ klīṃ, salutation to the left eye. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the right eye. Oṃ aiṃ, salutation to the crest-lock. Thus is the eighth [section].
The ritual placement (nyāsa).
One should perform the ninth assignment (nyāsa), which consists of the nature of the pervasion of the mantra.

Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ cāmuṇḍāyai vicce namaḥ | [Recite] from the head to the feet on the eastern limb. Oṃ mūlaṃ (nine times) namaḥ | From the head to the feet on the southern limb. Oṃ mūlaṃ (nine times) namaḥ | From the head to the feet on the back. Oṃ mūlaṃ (nine times) namaḥ | [Recite]...
From the head down to the feet on the left side: *Oṃ mūlaṃ* (nine times) *namaḥ*, from the head to the end of the feet.
Oṃ, the root mantra nine times; "Salutation from the feet to the top of the head"—this is the ninth nyāsa.
Now follows the tenth, the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa);
when this tenth placement has been performed, the three worlds shall come under one's control.

Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ cāmuṇḍāyai vicce namaḥ | Namaḥ to the heart. Oṃ [mūla-mantra] 9 times | Namaḥ svāhā to the head. Oṃ [mūla-mantra] 9 times | Namaḥ vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhā). Oṃ [mūla-mantra] 9 times | Namaḥ huṃ to the armor (kavaca). Oṃ [mūla-mantra] 9 times | Namaḥ vauṣaṭ to the three eyes. Oṃ [mūla-mantra]...
9. *Namaḥ astrāya phaṭ*. The tenth: the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
(p. 209) Now begins the eleventh nyāsa.
Oṃ! Khaḍginī, Śūlinī, Ghorā, Gadinī, and likewise Cakriṇī;
Śaṅkhinī, Cāpinī, Bāṇā, Bhuśuṇḍī, and Parighāyudhā. || 1 ||
Gentle, more gentle than all others who are gentle, and exceedingly beautiful,
you alone are the Supreme Goddess, the highest among the high and the low.
Whatever object exists anywhere, whether real or unreal, you are the power inherent in all of them; O Universal Soul, why then are you being praised by me?
By you, the creator of the world, the protector of the world, and the devourer of the world have even been brought under the power of sleep; who here is capable of praising you?
Since Viṣṇu, I myself, and even Īśāna have been made to assume physical bodies by you,
who then would be capable of praising you?
Having meditated upon the first seed-syllable *aiṃ* as being intensely black, I perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon all my limbs.
Oṃ! Protect us with your trident, O Goddess; protect us with your sword, O Ambikā!
Protect us with the sound of your bell and with the twang of your bowstring. 1.
Protect me in the east and in the west, O Caṇḍikā; protect me in the south, and likewise in the north by the whirling of your own trident, O Īśvarī!
"Whatever gentle forms you traverse through the three worlds, and whatever extremely terrible ones there are—with those, protect us and this earth. (3)
O Tembhikā, with those weapons such as the sword, spear, mace,
and others that rest upon your sprout-like hands, protect us from all sides.
Having meditated on the second seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, which resembles the sun, one should place it upon the back of all [the limbs].
Oṃ! O Goddess who embodies all forms, sovereign of all, endowed with all powers; O Durgā, protect us from all fears! O Goddess, salutations be unto you! (1)
May this gentle face of yours, adorned with three eyes, protect us from all beings; O Kātyāyanī, salutations to you! || 2 ||
O Bhadrakālī, salutations to you! May the trident—fierce with its blazing flames, most terrible, and the destroyer of all asuras—protect me from fear. 3.
Filling the world with its sound, that bell destroys the splendor of the Daityas; O Goddess, may it protect us from sins as if protecting her own sons! 4.
Smeared with the mud of the blood and fat of the Asuras, this blazing sword shall be for your welfare; O Caṇḍikā, we bow down before you.
One should meditate upon the third seed-syllable, *klīṃ*, which has the luster of crystal, and place it upon all the limbs.
The Root Six-Limbed Nyāsa:
Oṃ Aiṃ, to the two thumbs (for the heart), *namaḥ*. Oṃ Hrīṃ, to the two index fingers (for the head), *svāhā*. Oṃ Klīṃ, to the two middle fingers...

Namaḥ (to the *śikhā*, vaṣaṭ). Oṃ Cāmuṇḍāyai, to the two ring fingers, namaḥ (to the *kavaca*, huṃ). Oṃ Vicce, to the two little fingers, namaḥ (to the two eyes, vauṣaṭ). Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Cāmuṇḍāyai Vicce.
"Salutation to the palms and backs of the hands" (Astrāya Phaṭ). Having thus performed the placement, one should perform the pervasive assignment (*vyāpaka*) eight times with the root mantra.
p.
211) Now, the placement of syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*) according to another tantra:
*Oṃ aiṃ namaḥ* on the head; *Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ* on the two eyes; *Oṃ klīṃ namaḥ* on the forehead.

Oṃ cāṃ, salutation to the two eyebrows. Oṃ muṃ, salutation to the two ears. Oṃ ḍāṃ, salutation to the two cheeks. Oṃ yaiṃ, salutation to the mouth (face). Oṃ viṃ, salutation to the rows of teeth. Oṃ cceṃ, salutation to the tongue. Oṃ aiṃ, salutation to the two shoulders.
Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the throat. Oṃ klīṃ, salutation to the two arms. Oṃ cāṃ, salutation to the heart.

Oṃ Muṃ, salutation to the two sides. Oṃ Ḍāṃ, salutation to the back. Oṃ Yaiṃ, salutation to the navel. Oṃ Viṃ, salutation to the *liṅga*. Oṃ Cceṃ, salutation to the two hips. Root mantra: Oṃ 9, salutation to the private parts. Root mantra: Oṃ 9, salutation to the hands. Root mantra: Oṃ 9, salutation to the feet. Root mantra: Oṃ.
Homage to all limbs.

Now, the ritual placement of the directions (*diṅnyāsa*): Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to the East. Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to the South-East. Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the South. Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the South-West. Oṃ Klīṃ, salutation to the West. Oṃ...

*klīṃ*, salutation to Vāyavyā. *Oṃ*, salutation to Cāmuṇḍā of the North. *Oṃ*, salutation to Vicce of the Northeast. *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*, salutation to Cāmuṇḍā Vicce of the Upper Direction. *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*, salutation to Cāmuṇḍā Vicce of the Earth. Having worshipped with mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*).
(p. 212) Now, meditation (dhyāna).
She holds a conch, a discus, a mace, arrows, a noose, an iron club, a trident, a *bhuśuṇḍī* weapon, a severed head, and a sword; she possesses ten faces.
I bow to Mahākālī, who bestows success through the path of darkness (tāmasī), who has ten arms, and who holds a garland,
an axe, arrows, a mace, and likewise a thunderbolt.
A lotus, a bow, a water-pot, a staff, a spear, a sword, as well as a shield, a conch, a bell, a vessel for liquor, and a trident.
I worship Mahālakṣmī, the slayer of Mahiṣa, who possesses a red luster, stands upon a lotus, and holds a noose and the Sudarśana discus.
I bow to the radiant Goddess born from Gaurī, who holds a bell, a trident, a plow, a conch, a mace, a sword, a bow, and arrows.
Having meditated thus and worshipped the rosary, one should offer this prayer:
Oṃ! O Mālā, O Great Illusion, whose very nature is all-pervading power!
The fourfold aims of human life have been entrusted to you; therefore, be the bestower of success upon me.
Thus, having made this request.

Having bowed to the rosary with the mantra "Hrīṃ Siddhyai Namaḥ," one should perform the recitation (japa) during the first watch of the night until the third watch; however, one should not recite during the remainder of the night. If the Śakti-mantra is recited openly, there will be a progressive decline in its efficacy. Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Cāmuṇḍāyai Vicce.
Having recited the nine-syllable mantra and performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), one should recite the *Rātrisūkta*.
The method for fashioning the rosary (*akṣamālā*) is as described in another Tantra.
The procedure for the rosary is now described in detail:
having diligently gathered the beads according to their availability and according to one's understanding.
They are all of equal form, neither too thick nor too thin;
they are not damaged by insects, nor are they decayed, but rather fresh.
Having washed those [vessels] separately with the five products of the cow,
one should arrange nine *aśvattha* leaves in the shape of a lotus.
One should place there the thread and the gems, having washed them with fragrant water;
likewise, one should project the Tāra, the Śakti, and the Mātṛkā upon the thread and the gems.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa), one should worship with clarified butter and offer oblations according to one's capacity;
then, taking a single jewel, one should join it to the thread there.
Having thus prepared the rosary, one should then perform the recitation with the mātṛkā;
then, having worshipped the guru, one should receive it from his hand for the sake of all spiritual accomplishments.
In the Śiva-āgama.
It should be made resembling a cow's tail, having a single prong or with Meru;
it is to be strung with white-colored threads and so forth for the successful accomplishment of various rites.
Having prepared the rosary, one should then begin the consecration ritual.
One should wash it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting: *Oṃ sadyojātaṃ prapadyāmi sadyojātāya vai namo namaḥ | bhave bhave nātibhave bhavasva māṃ bhavodbhavāya namaḥ*.
With water from that [vessel], and with scents such as sandalwood and agallochum, [one should worship] Vāma [with: *oṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ*,
*jyeṣṭhāya namaḥ*, *śreṣṭhāya namaḥ*, *rudrāya namaḥ*, *kālāya namaḥ*, *kalavikaraṇāya namaḥ*,
*balavikaraṇāya namaḥ*, *balāya namaḥ*, *balapramathanāya namaḥ*, *sarvabhūta*...].
Salutation to Damanāya; salutation to Manonmanāya. [With this] one should rub it with the deity.

One should fumigate it with the Aghora mantra: *Oṃ aghorebhyo 'tha ghorebhyo ghora-ghoratarebhyaḥ | sarvebhyaḥ sarvaśarvebhyo namas te astu rudrebhyaḥ*. One should smear it with the Tatpuruṣa mantra: *Oṃ tatpuruṣāya vidmahe mahādevāya dhīmahi | tanno rudraḥ pracodayāt*.
One should recite the mantra in the fifth [position]: Oṃ Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānām.
But one should not [use] a hundred for each individually; rather, one should consecrate Mount Meru with the fifth mantra in that same manner.

May the Lord of Brahmā, the Sovereign of Brahmā, the Auspicious Brahmā, be ever auspicious to me. Oṃ hrīṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ.

Having performed the ritual placement (*saṃvinyāsa*) of the nine syllables— *dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ*— upon a garland placed upon a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, one should perform the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) for the deity.
The Prayer of the Garland.
Oṃ! O Māla, O Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), whose very nature is all-pervasive power!
Since the fourfold aims of human life are entrusted to you, therefore, be the bestower of success upon me.
Oṃ! O rosary, bring about freedom from obstacles; I take you in my right hand.
Be gracious for the sake of my success during the time of recitation, so that my goal may be accomplished.
Oṃ, to the Lord of the Rosary, grant, grant excellent accomplishment; O you who fulfill the purpose of all mantras, accomplish, accomplish;
bring about all success for me, svāhā!
Having thus prayed.
With the mantra "Aiṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Akṣamālikā," one should worship the rosary.
The dismissal.
Oṃ! O Garland, be the giver of delight and the bestower of auspiciousness to all the gods.
O Blessed One, always bring about my welfare, as well as fame and valor.
Having thus placed the garland upon his head, performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), and made the ritual placement (nyāsa), he should perform the dismissal (visarjana).
The method of recitation with a rosary according to the Śaiva Āgama.
One should place the rosary on the middle finger and rotate it in sequence with the thumb;
this method of counting the *mātṛkā* syllables bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should perform the highest rites with the thumb and the ring finger;
indeed, for the purposes of inciting hatred and eradication, the recitation should be performed using the combination of the index finger and the thumb.
In the rite of killing (*māraṇa*), one should recite [the mantra] using the little finger and the thumb;
at times other than during recitation, one should worship that rosary and keep it concealed.
When the thread has worn out, one should tie on a new thread and recite the mantra a hundred times;
if it has been touched by something forbidden, one should wash it as appropriate and then recite.

In cases of coughing, spitting, yawning, or a single turn of the breath, one should abandon the *āvartaka*. If, through negligence, the touch of the forefinger occurs, one should abandon the *āvartaka*.
When the rosary is broken, one should then string it together as before;
once it has been consecrated, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind.
But when [the mantra] has been thus established, one should recite the mantra by means of another [method];
as it is also stated elsewhere:
The wise should never fasten the garland upon that very spot where it was previously fixed, whether it was made of muñja grass or produced by another mantra; it must never be pierced through.
One should not touch the thread with the index finger, nor shake it, nor wave it about;
one should not touch it with the left hand, nor allow it to fall from the hand.
When moving the beads, the wise practitioner should never let the thumb touch any other bead;
during the time of recitation, one should never cross over the *meru*.
And at the time of changing [the beads], one must not cause them to clash;
having understood all this, one should begin the recitation with the rosary.
One should always perform the daily recitation (japa) with the hand, but never the optional (kāmya) recitation;
however, O beautiful one, one may perform even the optional recitation with the hand in the absence of a rosary.
Now, regarding the rosary of power-fingers (*śaktikaramālā*) in the *Yāmala*:
The ring finger has three joints; the little finger has three joints;
and the middle finger has three joints, [the first of which is] at the base joint of the index finger.
One should recite [the mantra] in the sequence of circumambulation through the ten joints;
this is known as the Śaktimālā, the illuminator of all mantras.
Know, O Pārvatī, that the two joints of the index finger are Meru;
the person who performs japa there, at the tip and in the middle of the index finger, [attains success].
Four things perish for him: life, knowledge, fame, and strength.
One should not perform the counting of recitations (*japa-saṃkhyā*) by means of finger-joints, nor with grains, nor with flowers,
nor with sandalwood, nor with clay.

Having mixed lac, *kusīda* (red sandalwood), vermilion, cow dung, and dried cow manure, and having formed them into pills, one should perform the recitation and keep count of the number [of repetitions]. — From the ninth chapter (*ullāsa*) of the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*.
One should place the *nāgapāśa* and the *brahmagranthi* within the center of the jewel;
then, one should bind Mount Meru with the mantra *Hūṃ* and with the *praṇava* (*Oṃ*). Furthermore, this is the method for recitation (*japa*) elsewhere as well.
Whatever has been recited with the tip of a finger, or whatever has been recited while bypassing the *meru* bead, [is as if not done];
one should use a rosary obtained from the guru, or, in his absence, one self-made.
One should conceal all ritual activities if one desires the highest accomplishment;
one must not show one's own mantra or rosary even to the guru.
O Six-faced One! During the time of recitation, the rosary must be kept hidden;
if the rosary comes within the sight of others, it will be entirely fruitless in every respect.
Therefore, it should always be guarded with every effort by the wise;
that which is recited without [proper secrecy] becomes fruitless, as does that which has been recited [previously].
There is a distinction elsewhere, in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: recitation (*japa*) is said to be performed with the fingers and even with the finger-joints.
The fruit obtained by counting on the fingers is said to be single-fold;
one should know that it is eight-fold when using lines, and hundred-fold when using the knuckles.
Because Rākṣasas certainly seize that recitation from one who performs it by transgressing the rules of counting,
a wise person should count in every way.
In the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.
Having joined mouth to mouth and tail to tail,
one should place that single-eyed figure of its own kind at the front as the Meru.
By winding it two and a half times, one should make a firm knot below;
then one should apply either a *brahmagranthi* or a *nāgapāśa*.
One should fashion it resembling a cow's tail; otherwise, it would take the form of a serpent. It must not be made without a knot, for it is defiled by the "Meru-back" [flaw].
If a person recites the mantra with a rosary that is not fixed [to a base],
one should know that all of it is fruitless, and Caṇḍikā becomes enraged.
One should not hold the rosary in the hand, around the neck, or on the head.
[This is from] the Bhūtaśuddhi. Now follows the procedure for recitation (japa-vidhi).
Whichever mantra is prescribed and whichever deity is designated for it,
one should perform the recitation mentally while visualizing that deity's form with the mind.
One should pronounce the phonemes gradually and indistinctly, neither too fast nor too slow,
in their proper sequence according to the order of beginning and end.
An illness that is too short is a cause of disease, and one that is too long is a loss of wealth;
one should recite [the mantra] joined with both the syllable and the non-syllable, like a string of pearls.
In the Kulārṇava:

O Dear One! Being established in That, with one's life-force absorbed in That, contemplating That, and having That as one's supreme goal, one should mutter the mantra while performing an investigation into the meaning of the syllables.
(p. 216) Now follows the Rātrisūkta.

Oṃ. The Lord [worships] the Goddess Nidrā, the sovereign mistress of Viṣṇu, the peerless in splendor, the mistress of the universe, the sustainer of the world, and the cause of its preservation and destruction. || 1 ||
Brahmā said:
You are Svāhā, you are Svadhā, and you are indeed the Vaṣaṭkāra; you are the essence of the sacred sound (Svar).
You are pure, established eternally in the Imperishable, and abiding as the nature of the three abodes.
Abiding in the half-measure, you are eternal and especially beyond utterance;
you alone are she, you are Sāvitrī, O Goddess, the supreme progenitress.
By you this entire universe is sustained; by you this world is created;
by you it is protected, O Goddess; and you always consume it at the end.

O You who are identical with the universe, at the time of emission You take the form of creation, at the time of preservation You take the form of maintenance, and likewise at the end You take the form of withdrawal for this world.
Mahāvidyā, Mahāmāyā, Mahāmedhā, and Mahāsmṛti are the seats in the Tantra.
A seat may be made of silk, or cloth, or skin, or wool,
or of cane, or palm leaves, or of blankets, or of darbha grass.
The practitioner of mantra should avoid a seat made of bamboo, stone, wood, earth, grass, or leaves, for such a seat bestows poverty, disease, and suffering.

For the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, ascetics (yatins) should have a smooth seat made in the shape of a tortoise, with a cloth, an antelope skin, and kusha grass placed one above the other.
For others, however, one should have it made four-footed and square;
likewise, it may be made of cow-dung, clay, or [wood] from the Palāśa or Pippala trees, provided it is not broken.
A wise person should always avoid a seat made of iron;
rather, one should remain established in a single posture, such as Svastika, Padma, Vīra, or others.
One should perform recitation, worship, and so forth; otherwise, these acts would be fruitless.
[This includes] giving gifts, sipping water for purification, fire-offerings, eating, and the worship of deities.
One should not perform Vedic study or the libation of water (tarpaṇa) with the feet placed upon a seat.
[The definition of "having the feet placed upon a seat" (prauḍhapāda) follows:]
One who has placed his feet upon a seat, or upon the knees, or even the shanks, and has made a firm seat for himself, is called *prauḍhapāda*.
And Mahāmohā is the Great Goddess, the Great Surī. (6)
And you are the primordial nature (prakṛti) of all, manifesting the three qualities;
you are the night of time, the great night, and the terrible night of delusion.
You are Śrī, you are the Sovereign, you are Hrī; you are Intellect, characterized by awakening; you are Modesty, Nourishment, Contentment, Peace, and indeed Forbearance.
She holds a sword, a trident, and is formidable; likewise she holds a mace and a discus;
she possesses a conch, a bow, arrows, a bhuśuṇḍī weapon, and a bludgeon as her arms.
More gentle than all that is gentle, and more beautiful than the most beautiful;
you alone, O Supreme Goddess, are the highest among the high and the low.
Whatever object exists anywhere, whether real or unreal, within the universal self—whatever power belongs to all that, you are that; how then can you be praised? (11)
By you, the creator of the world, the protector of the world, and the devourer of the world have even been brought under the power of sleep; who then here is capable of praising you? (12)
Since Viṣṇu, I myself, and even Īśāna were caused by you to assume physical bodies, who would be capable of praising you? (13)
O Goddess, you who have been thus praised with your own noble powers,
delude these two unassailable Asuras, Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
"Let Acyuta, the Lord of the world, be quickly awakened;
let him be roused so that he may slay these two great asuras."
Thus ends the Rātrisūkta.
Oṃ. Of this [work] on the first, middle, and supreme images (p.
218), Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the seers; Śrī Mahākālī and Mahālakṣmī...

The deities are the Mahāsarasvatīs; the meters are Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, and Anuṣṭubh; the powers (śaktis) are Nandā, Śākambharī, and Bhīmā; the seed-syllables (bījas) are Raktadantikā, Durgā, and Bhrāmarī;
the principles (tattvas) are Fire, Wind, and Sun; and the meditations (dhyānas) are those of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas—these belong to me.

For the fulfillment of all the desires of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), this is the application (*viniyoga*) for recitation or oblation for the pleasure of the goddesses Śrī Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī. First, therein, is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).

Oṃ, Khaḍginī, Śūlinī, Ghorā, Gadinī, Cakriṇī, as well as Śaṅkhinī, Cāpinī, Bāṇā, Bhuśuṇḍī, and Parighāyudhā. Homage to the two thumbs. (Homage to the heart. Oṃ, protect us with your trident, O Goddess; protect us with your sword, O Ambikā!
Protect us with the sound of your bell and with the resonance of your bowstring. Homage to your two index fingers.

(To the head, Svāhā! || Oṃ! Protect me in the east, O Caṇḍikā, and protect me in the west; by the whirling of your own trident, protect me in the north, likewise, O Īśvarī! Salutations to the two middle fingers! (To the crest-lock, Vaṣaṭ! || Oṃ! Those gentle forms of yours which move about in the three worlds...
And with those which are exceedingly terrible, protect us likewise! Homage to the two ring fingers!
(Hūṃ for the armor! Oṃ, O Ambikā, [protect us] with the swords, tridents, maces, and whatever other weapons there are!
O you who cling to the sprout-like hands, protect us from all sides with those [fingers]. Homage to the two little fingers (kaniṣṭhikā).
(To the three eyes: Vauṣaṭ.)
Oṃ! O you who are the essence of all, the sovereign of all, endowed with all powers; O Goddess Durgā, protect us from fears—salutations be to you! Salutations to the palms and backs of your hands.
(Astrāya Phaṭ) The five-syllable Nyāsa of Caṇḍī:
Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the heart; Oṃ Caṃ, Svāhā to the head; Oṃ Ḍoṃ, [salutation] to the tuft of hair.
Vaṣaṭ! Oṃ kāṃ, for the armor, huṃ! Oṃ yaiṃ, for the three eyes, vauṣaṭ! Oṃ hrīṃ, for Caṇḍikā, for the weapon, phaṭ!
Now follows the placement of the wheels (cakranyāsa).

Oṃ śambhutejo jvala jvālāmālini pāvake hrāṃ, salutation to Nandā with the two thumbs (salutation to the heart). Oṃ śambhutejo jvala jvālāmālini pāvake hrīṃ, salutation to Raktadantikā with the two index fingers (svāhā to the head).
Oṃ śambhutejo jvala jvālāmālini pāvake hrūṃ śākambharyai madhyamābhyāṃ namaḥ (to the Śikhā, vaṣaṭ). Oṃ śambhutejo jvala jvālāmālinī pāvake hraiṃ durgāyai anāmikābhyāṃ namaḥ.
*(Kavacāya hūṃ)* || *Oṃ śambhutejo jvala jvālāmālini pāvake hrau*,

homage to Bhīmā with the two little fingers (*kaniṣṭhakābhyāṃ namaḥ*). *(Netratrayāya vauṣaṭ)* || *Oṃ śambhutejo jvalajvālāmālinī pāvake hraḥ*, [homage] to Bhrāmarī with the palms of the hands (*karatalakarābhyāṃ*).
Salutation to the two backs. (Astrāya phaṭ). In this same manner, [salute] the heart and the other limbs.
(p. 220) Now, meditation (dhyāna).
[An alternative reading in the Śāradā manuscript, Chapter 21, Verse 41]:
"One should contemplate a vast divine garden on the delightful slope of the Golden Mountain, adorned with wish-fulfilling trees and possessing a ground of gold."

One should contemplate a divine pavilion of variegated jewels, surrounded by a formidable mass of fire with a form like that of the sun, situated in the center of that [cavity]. Upon that lion-throne, in the pericarp of a lotus, one should meditate.

[He saw] a lion of black complexion, terrifying, with a gaping maw made formidable by its fangs, possessing an exceedingly fierce face resembling a blazing crest of fire. Above him was that Goddess, shining like ten million rising suns,
holding in her right arms a discus, a sword, arrows, and a trident, and [in her left] a conch, a discus, a bow, and arrows.

With her left arms making the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), she is endowed with crescent moons and possesses three most terrifying eyes. Her mass of hair blazes upward, and she is intent on the destruction of all things. She is joined by the enclosures of the limbs (*aṅga*) and so forth, surrounded by missiles and weapons, and is served by Indra and the other guardians of the world—the Goddess who dwells in the Vindhya mountains.

Madhusūdana resides in his neck; the illustrious Nīlakaṇṭha is stationed upon his head; the illustrious Goddess Girijā is on the surface of his forehead; Śāradā is in the region of his chest; the six-faced one (Kārttikeya) is at the joints of his wrists;
likewise, the serpents are situated at his sides; and his two ears are the Aśvins—that Lord is Siṃha.

May she who grants my desires be present. || 1 || She whose eyes are the moon and the sun, in whose teeth the Vasus reside, on whose tongue is the *huṃ* of Varuṇa—may this Śrī Carcikā Caṇḍikā [protect me]. Yakṣa and Yama are her two cheeks, the two twilights her pair of lips, and the thunderbolt shines upon her back.
May the Blessed One, who dwells in the assembly like a lion, be the granter of my desires. In the joints of his neck are the twenty-seven constellations;
the Sādhyas reside in his heart. His pride is cruelty, and his darkness is filled with great ferocity. The Mātṛs are his vital breaths, and his paternal lineage consists of Arati and Pāna.

In his form resides Śrī Kamalā; in his hair are the Vimalās; in his beard are the rays of light. His testicles are Mount Meru, while the oceans reside in the sweat of his birth. The rivers sport with their deities upon his tail, and the Vedas constitute his powerful semen. Indeed, all the gods abide in their respective places within this glorious Viṣṇu.

May Śrī Siṃha, whose body consists of all the deities and who is dear to the Goddess, protect me! He who is pleasing to the heart even when possessed by Bālagrahas, Pūtanās, and the like; he who bestows the fortune of sons; he who removes the fear of kings and diseases such as fever in dreams; he who is the auspiciousness within inauspiciousness; he who is the most excellent in all descriptions—[may he protect me].
May this lion-mantra, which removes the fear of diseases such as epilepsy, bestow all desired boons upon me— it is that for which poets draw their metaphors.
Thus ends the meditation on the lion, the vehicle of the Goddess, as described in the Devīpurāṇa:
[One should meditate upon her] possessing a luster like a mass of lightning, seated upon the shoulders of the Lord of Beasts, and terrifying.
[He saw it] attended by maidens whose hands were adorned with swords and shields.
In his hands [he holds] a discus, a mace, a sword, a shield, an arrow, a bow with its string, and a threatening forefinger.
I worship Durgā, who possesses the nature of fire, who bears the moon, and who has three eyes. || 1 ||
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should contemplate the identity of the Guru, the Deity, and the Self, and then perform the recitation (japa).
1. Now follows the arrangement of the *saṃpuṭa* (encasement), which is useful for the ritual applications (*prayoga*) intended for specific desires that will be described hereafter;
as, for example, the question regarding Pārvatī.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, I wish to know in truth how many kinds of *saṃpuṭas* there are;
tell me, O Lord of the Asuras, if I am dear to you! (1)
The Lord said:
O Dear One, the *saṃpuṭa* should be known as twofold, effecting both rising and setting; listen here to the rising first, and afterwards I shall tell you of the setting. (2)
One should recite the mantra first, then the verse, then the mantra again at the end;
this sequence is auspicious for the rising [of the breath]. || 3 ||
This *saṃpuṭa* (encasement) is taught for the sake of attaining excellence in spiritual progress;
here, throughout, the term "verse" (*śloka*) is indicative of the mantra.
In the medical treatises, the setting [of the sun] is said to be caused by two shallow bowls.
Therefore, with a one-pointed mind, I shall proclaim that here to you.
The mantra at the beginning and the verse at the end, with the mantra reversed—
this is declared to be the "encasement" (saṃpuṭa) for the rites of killing, driving away, and binding.
"Disregarding this method, those who act according to their own fabrications are cooked in the Raurava and other hells until the dissolution of all beings. Thus it is stated in the Marīci-kalpa.
First Chapter: Om. Here, in the present time, for the first narrative of the *Caṇḍīśaptaśatī*, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*).
Mahākālī is the deity, Gāyatrī is the meter,
and Medhā recounted the sixth dialogue of the Caṇḍīpāṭha to Suratha for the sake of his meditative concentration.
That story was later told by Mārkaṇḍeya to Bhārgava.
The birds spoke to Jaimini:
"By this very method, the six types of narratives are considered to be established."
The power Nandajā, the seed-syllable of Raktadantikā, the fire element, and the nature of the Ṛgveda—
by the grace of Śrī Mahākālī, for the sake of attaining one’s desired fruit, [may they grant] dharma, artha, and kāma.
The application (*viniyoga*) is for the recitation (or offering) of the first *caritra* for the sake of liberation.
p. 223) Now follows the deposition of greatness (*māhātmyanyāsa*).

Oṃ, salutations to the majesty of the slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha; at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). Oṃ, salutations to the majesty of the slaying of the army of Mahiṣāsura; at the hairline (sīmanta). Oṃ, salutations to the majesty of the slaying of Mahiṣāsura; between the eyebrows (bhrūmadhya). Oṃ, salutations to the majesty of Śakra and the others.

Oṃ, salutation to the greatness of the dialogue between the Goddess and Her messenger; [place this] on the eyes. Oṃ, salutation to the greatness of the slaying of Dhūmralocana; [place this] on the ears. Oṃ, salutation to the greatness of the slaying of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa; [place this] on the heart. Oṃ, salutation to the greatness of the slaying of Raktabīja; [place this] on the mouth.

At the navel: *Oṃ niśumbhabadhāmāhātmyāya namaḥ*. At the *liṅga*: *Oṃ śumbhabadhāmāhātmyāya namaḥ*. At the *mūlādhāra*: *Oṃ stutimāhātmyāya namaḥ*. At the knees: *Oṃ phalamāhātmyāya namaḥ*. At the ankles: *Oṃ varadāna...*
Salutation to the feet for the sake of greatness.
Immediately after, the pervasive assignment (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) is performed seven times with the seed-syllable of Māyā, *hrīṃ*.
Now follows the meditation on Mahākālī.

Oṃ! I bow to her who is Bhīmā, possessing terrifying and fierce fangs, with a luster equal to a shining mountain of collyrium; she has ten faces, thirty flickering eyes, ten quivering arms, and likewise ten feet; she holds a trident, an arrow, a mace, a bow, a conch, a discus, and a *bhuśuṇḍī* weapon. I pay homage to her.
Having meditated thus: "O Kālī, you hold a club joined with a noose in your hands and a skull in your head."
(p. 225) Now begins the first chapter.
Oṃ, salutations to Caṇḍikā. Oṃ Aiṃ. Mārkaṇḍeya said: [The definition of the Udaya-sampuṭa]. Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Cāmuṇḍāyai Vicce. Oṃ Aiṃ. Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Cāmuṇḍāyai Vicce Namaḥ. Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Cāmuṇḍāyai Vicce.

He who is called the eighth Manu, Sāvarṇi, the son of the Sun—listen to his origin as I describe it in detail. Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Cāmuṇḍāyai Vicce Amaḥ. *Asta-sampuṭa*: Huṃ Phaṭ Oṃ Aiṃ. Mārkaṇḍeya said: Phaṭ Huṃ. Huṃ Phaṭ. Sāvarṇi, the son of the Sun...
The eighth Manu who is spoken of—listen to his origin as I describe it to you in detail.
Listen as I describe in detail the birth of that Sāvarṇi, the son of the Sun, who is called the eighth Manu. (2)
By the power of Mahāmāyā, he became the illustrious Sāvarṇi, the son of the Sun and the sovereign of a Manvantara, just like [the previous] lords of the Manvantaras. (3)
Formerly, in the Svārociṣa Manvantara, there was a king named Suratha, born of the lineage of Caitra, who ruled over the entire circle of the earth.
While he was thus properly protecting his subjects like his own biological sons,
the kings known as the Kaulāvidhvaṃsins then became his enemies.
A battle took place between him and those [enemies], who possessed exceedingly powerful forces;
though they were fewer in number, he was defeated in battle by them, who were capable of destroying even a *kolā* tree.
Then, having returned to his own city, that illustrious one became the ruler of his own land;
yet he was then assailed by those powerful enemies.
Then, by wicked and evil-minded ministers who were powerful, the treasury and the army of that weak king were seized, even within his own city.
Then, under the pretext of hunting, that king, deprived of his sovereignty,
mounted a horse alone and went into the dense forest.
There he beheld the hermitage of Medhā, the best of the twice-born;
it was filled with peaceful wild beasts and graced by the disciples of the sage. (10)
Honored by that sage, he remained there for some time,
wandering here and there within that hermitage.
At that time, his mind drawn by a sense of possessiveness, he thought there:
"That city was formerly protected by my ancestors, but now it is indeed abandoned by me. (12)
I do not know whether my elephant Śūrasadāmada, along with his attendants, is being protected according to dharma by those wicked servants of mine or not. (13)
Having fallen under the power of my enemies, what enjoyments will he obtain?
Herein begins the *Saptashloki Durga*.
Śiva said:
O Goddess, who are easily accessible to your devotees and the accomplisher of all tasks,
please diligently tell us the means for the successful completion of our work in this Kali age.
The Goddess said:
Listen, O Lord! I shall proclaim that which accomplishes all desires in the Kali age—[that devotion] by which I am constantly followed through grace, wealth, and food. (14)
Today they constantly perform service to other kings;
for they, being of a proclivity toward improper expenditure, are perpetually making outlays. (15)
"That accumulated treasury will go to ruin through extreme suffering.
Thinking this and other such things constantly, the king brooded. (16)

"Why do you appear as if filled with grief, as if dejected in spirit?
Having heard these words spoken by the king out of affection, he bowed down. (18)
Out of affection for you, I shall also manifest this hymn of praise to the Mother.

Oṃ. Of this *Śrī Durgā-saptaślokī-stotra-mantra*, Nārāyaṇa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chanda*), and the goddesses Śrī Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī are the deities (*devatā*). [This is recited] for the purpose of pleasing Durgā; it consists of seven verses.
The application (viniyoga) is for the recitation of the Durgā [stotra].
Oṃ! Indeed, that Blessed Goddess, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), forcibly draws away even the minds of the wise and bestows them upon delusion. || 1 ||
When remembered in times of distress, you take away the fear of all living beings; when remembered by one who is at ease, you grant exceedingly auspicious wisdom.
O remover of the fear of poverty and suffering, who else besides you has a heart so constantly moist with compassion for the purpose of performing every kind of assistance?
(230) That Vaiśya, bowing with humility, replied to the king. || 19 ||
The Vaiśya said: || 20 ||
"I am indeed a Vaiśya named Samādhi, born into a family of wealthy men. (21)
Cast out by my sons and wife— who were wicked due to greed for wealth—
and deprived of both wealth and wife, I was abandoned by my kinsmen, wife, and sons after they had seized my property. (22)
Having come to the forest in misery, cast out by my trusted kinsmen, I do not know whether my sons are well or ill. (23)
Remaining here, [inform me] of the activities of my kinsmen and my wives. O Śivā, the most auspicious among all that is auspicious, the accomplisher of all goals,
the refuge, the three-eyed Gaurī, O Nārāyaṇī, salutations be to you!
O Goddess Nārāyaṇī, who are solely intent on protecting those who have come for refuge, the wretched, and the distressed; O Goddess who removes the suffering of all, salutations be to you! (4)
O Goddess who embodies all forms, sovereign of all, endowed with all powers; O Goddess Durgā, who protects us from fears, homage be to you! 5.
When pleased, she dispels all diseases without exception; when angry, however, she [destroys] all desired objects of pleasure.
Is there now security in their homes, or is there indeed insecurity? (24)
How is it that some of my sons are of good conduct, while others are of evil conduct? (25)
The king said: || 26 ||
By those greedy sons, wives, and other riches, you have been cast out.
Among them, what affection binds your mind? (28)
The Vaiśya said: || 29 ||
"It is exactly as you have said regarding the words directed toward us."
What can I do? My heart does not feel cruelty toward those by whom, greedy for wealth, he was cast out after they abandoned their affection for their father. (31)
For those who have taken refuge in you, there is no failure; indeed, those who have taken refuge in you attain the state of a true refuge.
O Sovereign of the entire three worlds, you who pacify all afflictions!
In this very manner, you must effect the destruction of our enemies.
This supreme secret, skilled in all forms of protection, is a hymn spoken by the Goddess that bestows eternal sovereignty. (8)
Whoever hears this, or even causes it to be recited with effort, surrounded by a retinue, shall become a conqueror of the three worlds. Thus ends the *Śrī Saptaślokī Durgā*.
Now begins the section on the petals of Caṇḍikā.
Oṃ, homage to Caṇḍikā!
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme *caṇḍikādala*:
my heart is drawn to my husband and kinsmen, and my mind is indeed fixed upon those who are dear to me.
O Mahāmati, even though I know this, I do not recognize what it is.
Because my mind is inclined toward love even for those kinsmen who are devoid of virtue, it is on their account that I experience sighing and dejection. (33)
What cruel thing shall I do toward those who are displeased with me? (34)

Then, O Brahmin, those two together approached that sage.

Oṃ, homage! O Blessed One, victory, victory! O Cāmuṇḍā, O Caṇḍī, O Mistress of the Fierce, O You who wield fierce weapons!

O you who assume a fierce form, O beloved of the *tāṇḍava* dance; O supreme one who causes the destruction of all the cosmic eggs (*jagadaṇḍa*), whose cheeks are adorned by the circle of world-serpents coiled like earrings, who possess infinite and endless forms; O Śivā, whose chest is decorated with a garland of human heads, and who wear a crown of blazing jewels upon a great skull-forehead.
O Goddess, you who possess a most terrifying crescent moon as a crest-ornament.
In her hand, which is radiant with a slender lotus and moistened by the blood of the great gods and asuras slain in battle, shines forth Mahāmāyā, made manifest by the sixteen digits (kalās).
O you who laugh with a face and great cheeks beautified by blood that fills [the mouth],

whose golden girdle is joined with a line of hair firmly bound, whose anklets have become red from the garments [they touch] and are blazing upon the flaming orb of the earth; O you who possess the form of Great Śambhu, wearing the skin of a great tiger and great serpents.
O you who wear the sacred thread; O you whose every limb is smeared with the ashes of the great cremation ground; O Kālī! O Kaṅkāli, Mahākālī, Kālāgnirudrakālī!
p. 233) This Vaiśya named Samādhi was the most excellent of kings;
having made an agreement with those two according to the rule and as was appropriate, he [acted]. (37)
Once seated, the Vaiśya and the king engaged in various conversations.

O Blessed One, I wish to ask you one thing; please speak it.
O you who bring suffering to me who lack self-mastery over my own mind;

O Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī! O destroyer of Time! O Kālarātri, salutations to you, devourer of the wicked! O you who move amidst thousands of hosts of various bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas! O pacifier of various diseases! O subduer of all the malevolent!

O destroyer of all poverty! O you who consume pieces of flesh with the sound "dhaga-dhaga"! O bearer of skeletons that jingle and clatter as your limbs move! O playful one, drenched in honey, meat, and blood!
O you whose deeds are praised by all the gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, vidyādharas, kinnaras, kimpuruṣas, and others!

O sovereign of all mantras! O preeminent one of all powers! O purifier of all worlds! O cleanser of all sins! O mother of all worlds! O Brāhmī! O Māheśvarī! O Kaumārī! O Vaiṣṇavī! O Śaṅkhinī! O Vārāhī! O Nārasiṃhī! O Indrāṇī! O Cāmuṇḍā! O you whose very nature is Mahālakṣmī!
O Great Knowledge! O Mistress of Yoga! O Yoginī! O Caṇḍikā! O Great Illusion! O You of Universal Form!

O you adorned with all ornaments; O sole sovereign of the fourteen worlds, beginning with Atala, Vitala, Sutala, Rasātala, Talātala, Mahātala, Pātāla, and those known as Bhūr, Bhuvar, Svar, Mahar, Jana, Tapa, and Satya; O you who are exceedingly fierce, yet assume a gracious form!

"O highly fortunate one, why is it that even for two people of knowledge, there is this delusion regarding an object whose faults have been perceived? Why is their mind drawn toward a sense of 'mine-ness'?

O you who are born as the sole source of all the worlds; O you who possess the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; O bearer of the staff and the water-pot; O Sāvitrī, Sarvamaṅgalā, Sarasvatī, Padmālayā; O Pārvatī, whose very nature is the entire universe; O bearer of the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus; O bearer of the axe, the trident, the Pināka bow, and the chisel; O Śarā...
With a bow, trident, sword, scimitar, drum, goad, mace, axe, lance,

Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, Īśāna.
The Sage said: "Food, sleep, fear, and sexual intercourse are common to all. (p. 235)
[The knowledge of men is superior to that of animals; those devoid of knowledge are equal to animals. || 46 ||
Knowledge exists for every living being within the range of sense objects.

some living beings are blind by day, while others are blind at night. (48)
Some wise men, viewing all living beings with equal vision day and night, perceive the truth; yet they are not merely [those who see] that alone. (49)

O Sovereign Mistress, who have become the cause through the power of Pradhāna; O Queen of the Earth, pervading the seven continents and oceans from above;

In the majesty of the forty-two syllables, [he is one] whose lotus feet are being worshipped by the hosts of great sages.

O Goddess Mātṛkā, the deity of script, who consists of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) and serves as the foundation for the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and many other scriptures— protect me, protect me for a long time!
And observe these human beings, who are equal to those two other species in every other respect;
even though they possess knowledge, look at them as they fall into the beaks of young hawks. (51)
O tiger among men, even when tormented by hunger, human beings— driven by attachment, fear, and delusion— remain full of longing for their sons.
Destroy, destroy my enemies with the syllable *huṃ*! Expel, expel the *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*!

Subjugate, subjugate all the planetary spirits (*grahas*)! Delude, delude! Paralyze, paralyze! Gladden, gladden! Intoxicate, intoxicate! Annihilate, annihilate! Put to flight, put to flight! Make them hear [my command]!
Make them hear! Praise them, praise them! Cause them to pass away, cause them to pass away! Burst the heads of all enemies, burst them! Quickly kill my enemies, kill them!
Whether we are in the states of waking, dreaming, or deep sleep, [protect us] from kings, thieves, fire, water, wind, poison, spirits, enemies, and death.

Protect me, protect me thoroughly from various diseases such as fever, from various malevolent spells (*abhicāra*), from various slanders, and from the actions of others—mantras, tantras, yantras, medicines, surgery, sorcery, and the base. Oṃ śroṃ hrīṃ kṣmauṃ! O you who cause the total destruction of the life-force of my enemies, huṃ phaṭ svāhā! Thus.
And in the Rudrayāmala Tantra, there is the Caṇḍikādala.
The Heart of Caṇḍikā.

Oṃ. Of this mantra of the *Śrī Caṇḍikā-hṛdaya-stotra*, Mārkaṇḍeya is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chanda*), the goddess Śrī Caṇḍikā is the deity (*devatā*), Hrāṃ is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), Hrīṃ is the power (*śakti*), and Hrūṃ is the pin (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is in recitation for the pleasure of Śrī Caṇḍikā. The six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) are performed with Hrāṃ and the other syllables.
Meditation. Obeisance to the most auspicious among all auspicious things.
Now, therefore, I shall proclaim in detail and exactly as it is the secret heart-mantra of Caṇḍikā; listen with a one-pointed mind.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Hrūṃ! Victory, victory, O Cāmuṇḍā, O Caṇḍikā, O jewel of the thirty gods!
Out of greed for a reciprocal favor, do you not indeed see these? (p. 237)
Nevertheless, they have been cast into the whirlpool of possessiveness and the pit of delusion. || 53 ||
"By the power of Mahāmāyā, he causes the persistence of cyclic existence;
therefore, no wonder should be felt here regarding the yogic sleep of the Lord of the World. (54)
O You whose lotus feet are pressed by the crowns and tiaras [of Your attendants], O Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī;
O You who wear great serpents as ornaments; O bearer of the form of Bhairava; O You whose fierce face has revealed fangs;
O Terrible One, O You of the horrific countenance; O You surrounded by thousands of blazing flames; O You who deafen the horizons with Your great laughter!

O Kālarātri, Great Illusion, eternal Śivā! You who hold a skull in hand filled with all weapons, draped in an elephant hide as an upper garment, surrounded by hosts of Bhūtas and Vetālas; you who cause the moving and unmoving world to tremble; you who have cleared away the thorns of the Daityas such as Madhu, Kaiṭabha, Mahiṣāsura, Dhūmralocana, Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, Raktabīja, Śumbha, and Niśumbha.

O you who are the primary power of Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna; O you praised by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; O support of the support of the three worlds; O Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Varadā, Raudrī, Ambikā, Brāhmī, Mahiśvarī, Kaumāri, Vaiṣṇavī, Śaṅkhinī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Śivadūtī!

O you who are the very embodiment of Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī; O you who abide in the center of the primordial sound (nāda); O you whose crown, bracelets, and other ornaments are formed by the hoods of fierce, venomous serpents; O you whose feet, arms, neck, and head consist of great flaming jewels; O you who are adorned with garlands; O you who are worshipped upon the great buffalo by Gandharvas and Vidyādharas.

In the treasury of the nine jewels, in the essential nature of reality, in that which consists of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals; in the nature of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; abiding in the skin, eyes, ears, tongue, nose, and the great intellect; Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ, [those] with the syllables Āṃ and Kroṃ in their hands.
O Āgneyanayanā, cause him to enter the vessel, cause him to dry up, cause him to become tender; by this Mahāmāyā of Hari, the world is utterly deluded.
For even the minds of the wise are indeed captivated by that divine Goddess.
Having forcibly drawn it forth, Mahāmāyā bestows it for the sake of delusion;
by her, this entire universe, including all moving and non-moving beings [the three worlds with all that moves and is stationary, according to the Pāṭhāntara], is emitted.
This very [knowledge], when serene, becomes the bestower of boons for the liberation of men;
it is that eternal Vidyā which serves as the cause of supreme liberation.
And she alone, the Sovereign of all sovereigns, is the cause of bondage in saṃsāra.

Śrīṃ! Cause everything to enter, enter! O you of excellent complexion of the three worlds, bring the entire mind under control, bring it under control! Quickly kill my enemies, kill them! Whether in the states of waking, dreaming, or deep sleep, [protect] us from kings, thieves, fire, water, wind, poison, spirits, enemies, death, fever, boils, and various other diseases.

Protect me perfectly, protect me from various malevolent rites, various slanders, the spells, tantras, yantras, medicinal poisons, and weapons of others, as well as from voids and trivialities! Oṃ aiṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ sphrāṃ sphrīṃ sphrūṃ sphreṃ sphrauṃ sphraḥ, [accomplish] all my undertakings!
Accomplish, accomplish! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
One should recite it twenty-one times.
At the king’s gate, in the cremation ground, in dispute, in danger from enemies, amidst spirits, fire, or thieves—accomplish my tasks while I am present; svāhā!
“O Blessed One, who indeed is that goddess Mahāmāyā, whom you [have spoken of]? (60)
"O twice-born one, how was she born, and what is her karma? Of what nature, what power, what form, and from what source does that goddess arise?
O best among the knowers of Brahman, I desire to hear all of this from you. (62)

for when Viṣṇu enters his yogic sleep, the world has been turned into a single ocean.
The man who recites this secret heart-mantra of Caṇḍikā at the three junctions of the day bestows all desires upon men and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

at that time, two terrible demons, the famous Madhu and Kaiṭabha, arose. (67)
Born from the wax of Viṣṇu’s ears and intent on killing Brahmā, [the two demons] approached;
meanwhile, Brahmā, the lord of progeny, remained situated in the navel-lotus of Viṣṇu.
Seeing those two fierce asuras and Janārdana fast asleep, he,
with his heart fixed in one-pointed concentration, praised that Yogic Sleep (Yoganidrā).
I bow to her who was made her abode by the eye of Hari for the purpose of awakening him,
the Sovereign of the Universe, the Sustainer of the World, and the Performer of its maintenance and destruction.
The Lord [created] Nidrā (Sleep), the incomparable power of Viṣṇu’s splendor.
Brahmā said: (72)
You are Svāhā, you are Svadhā, you are indeed the Vaṣaṭkāra, and you are the essence of the sacred sound (Svar).
You are the nectar, established in the imperishable and eternal, consisting of the three measures (mātrās) and abiding as the half-measure; you are the eternal one who is especially inexpressible.
You alone are Sāvitrī, the twilight (sandhyā); you, O Goddess, are the supreme mother, the progenitor of the Vedas.
By you this universe is sustained; by you this world is created. (75)
O Goddess, this is protected by you; you always consume it as well.
At the time of emission you are the form of creation, and at the time of preservation you are the form of maintenance.
Likewise, at the end of this world’s dissolution, she who consists of the universe is Mahāvidyā, Mahāmāyā, Mahāmedhā, and Mahāsmṛti. (77)
You are Mahāmohā, the Blessed One, the Great Goddess, the Great Goddess of the Asuras, and the Great Sovereign;
you are the primordial nature (prakṛti) of all, manifesting the three qualities (guṇas). || 78 ||
You are the Night of Time, the Great Night, and the terrible Night of Delusion;
you are Śrī, you are Āśvarī, you are Hrī, and you are Buddhi, characterized by awakening.
You are the nourishment of modesty, as well as contentment; you are peace and indeed forbearance.
You are the bearer of the sword, the bearer of the trident, the terrible one, and likewise the bearer of the mace and the discus.
Holding a conch, a bow, arrows, a *bhuśuṇḍī* weapon, and an iron club,
she is more gentle than all that is gentle and exceedingly beautiful. (81)
Among all things high and low, you alone are the supreme Supreme Goddess;
whatever object exists anywhere, whether real or unreal, O Soul of the All! 82.
Since you are the power of all that exists, why are you being praised?
For by you the creator of the world, the protector of the world, and the devourer of the world [are sustained].
He too has been brought under the power of sleep; who here is capable of praising you?
Even Viṣṇu, I myself, and Īśāna have taken on physical bodies.
Since they have been thus commissioned, who would be capable of praising you? O Goddess, you have been praised in this manner with your own noble powers. (85)
"Delude these two invincible Asuras, Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
and let Acyuta, the Lord of the World, be quickly awakened. (86)
"Let there be awakening and existence; let these two great asuras be slain. (77)
The sage said: || 88 ||
Thus was the goddess Tāmasī then praised there by the Creator.
For the purpose of awakening Viṣṇu and for the sake of slaying Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
[he emerged] from his eyes, mouth, nose, arms, heart, and likewise from his chest.
Having emerged, he stood within the sight of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest;
and Janārdana, the Lord of the World, rose up, released by her.
Then, while reclining upon the serpent-bed in the single vast ocean, he beheld those two evil-minded ones, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, possessed of exceeding heroism and prowess.
With eyes red with rage and having made an effort to devour Brahmā, they rose up;
then the Blessed Lord Hari fought with them. (93)
For five thousand years, the powerful lord used his arms as weapons;
yet even those two, intoxicated by their excessive strength, were utterly deluded by Mahāmāyā.
They both said to Keśava, "Choose a boon from us."
The Blessed One said: || 96 ||
If both of them were to be pleased with me today, they would both become subject to my execution.
What need is there for any other boon here? For this much alone has been my chosen vow.
The sage said: || 99 ||
"By those two who were deceived, at that time the entire world became made of māṣa beans. (100)
Having observed them, the lotus-eyed Lord was addressed by the two of them:
"Slay us where the earth is not submerged by water."
The sage said: (102)
Having said "So be it," the Blessed One, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace,
severed the hips and the heads of those two with his discus.
Thus has she arisen, praised by Brahmā himself;
hear further of the power of this Goddess as I speak it to you: Aiṃ Oṃ. 104.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha," in the *Devīmāhātmya* of the *Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, within the *Sāvarṇika Manvantara*. [Total: 14 verses spoken, 24 half-verses, 66 total verses.]
Thus [ends] 104.
The word "iti" takes away fortune; the word "vadha" (killing) causes the destruction of one's lineage; the word "adhyāya" (chapter) takes away one's life-force;
thus one should speak of Mārkaṇḍeya and others.

Oṃ, victory, victory! In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, in the Sāvarṇika Manvantara, in the Devīmāhātmya, may the desires of the sacrificer be realized; may there be the offering unto the Mother of the World.

The Tantric oblation: Oṃ, to Mahākālī, who is accompanied by her limbs, weapons, powers, retinue, and vehicles, and who is presided over by the seed-syllable Aiṃ; I offer this great oblation; obeisance!
