Oṃ. For the attainment of the desired fruits for oneself—namely, *dharma*, *artha*, and *kāma*—Viṣṇu is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of the *Madhyamacaritra*; Mahālakṣmī is the deity; the *uṣṇik* is the meter; Śākambharī is the power (*śakti*); Durgā is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); Vāyu is the essential principle (*tattva*); and the Yajurveda is the form (*mūrti*).
The application is for recitation (or oblation) for the sake of liberation. || 2 ||
The meditation on Mahālakṣmī.

Oṃ! I worship here Sairibhamardinī, who possesses the luster of coral and holds in her hands a rosary, an axe, a mace, an arrow, a thunderbolt, a lotus, a water-pot, a staff, a spear, a sword, a shield, a conch, a bell, a vessel of wine, a trident, a noose, and the Sudarśana discus.
Mahālakṣmī, born from the king of the gods.
Oṃ Hrīṃ. The Sage said: || 1 ||
In ancient times, there occurred a battle between the gods and the asuras lasting for a full hundred years,
while Mahiṣa was the lord of the asuras and Purandara was the lord of the gods.
There, the army of the gods was defeated by the asuras of great prowess;
having conquered all the gods, Mahiṣāsura became Indra.
Then the defeated gods, placing the lotus-born Prajāpati at their head, went to that place where the Lord and Garuḍadhvaja were. (4)
The gods related to them exactly as it had happened— the conduct of Mahiṣāsura and the full extent of his victory over the deities.
He himself presides over the offices of Indra, Agni, Anila, Indu, Yama, Varuṇa, and others as well.
Driven out from heaven by that evil-minded Mahiṣa, all the hosts of gods wander upon the earth like mortals.
All this activity of the enemies of the immortals has been told to you;
we have come to you for refuge—let his slaughter be considered.
Having thus heard the words of the gods, Madhusūdana and Śambhu both became enraged, their faces contorted with frowns. (9)
Then, from the mouth of the Discus-bearer (Viṣṇu), who was filled with intense wrath,
there issued forth the great splendor of Brahmā and Śaṅkara.
And from the bodies of other gods as well, such as Śakra and the rest,
a very great splendor emerged, and that [splendor] attained unity.
There the gods beheld a mass of extreme splendor, like a blazing mountain, with its flames pervading the quarters of space.
O Atula, the splendor born from the bodies of all the gods became concentrated in her;
she was a woman who pervaded the three worlds with her radiance.
That which was the splendor of Śambhu became his face;
by the splendor of Yama his hair was produced, and by the splendor of Viṣṇu his arms.
By the grace of Soma, the pair of breasts was formed; by that of Indra, the waist;
by that of Varuṇa, the shanks and thighs; and by the splendor of the Earth, the hips were produced. (15)
His two feet were formed by the splendor of Brahmā, the toes of those feet by the splendor of the Sun;
the fingers of his hands by the Vasus, and his nose by the splendor of Kubera.
Her teeth were produced by the splendor of Prajāpati,
and likewise her three eyes at the sacrifice by the splendor of the Fire-god.
Her eyebrows are the two twilights, her luster is that of the Sun, and her ears belong to the Wind;
moreover, Śivā is the source of the splendors of all other gods as well.

Then, beholding her who had arisen from the mass of the splendor of all the gods, the immortals, who had been oppressed by Mahiṣa, attained great joy. Then the gods gave her their respective weapons, and those seekers of victory cried out loudly, "Victory! Victory! to Jayantī. Thus it is said in the Śāradātilaka.
Having extracted the trident from the trident-bearer, the wielder of the Pināka bow,
Kṛṣṇa, produced a discus from his own discus and gave it to her. (20)
Varuṇa gave her a conch, and the Consumer of Oblations (Agni) gave her a spear;
Māruta gave her a bow and two quivers filled with arrows.
Having fashioned the thunderbolt from the adamantine peak, the thousand-eyed Indra, lord of the immortals, gave it to him and took a bell from his elephant Airāvata.
Yama gave him the staff of Time (Kāladaṇḍa), and Varuṇa, the lord of waters, gave him his noose; Prajāpati gave him a rosary of beads, and Brahmā gave him a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
The Sun-god bestowed his own rays upon all the pores of his skin,
and Time (Kāla) gave him a sword and a stainless shield.
Kṣīroda gave him a spotless necklace, as well as two unaging garments,
a divine crest-jewel, earrings, and bracelets. (25)
Likewise, he wore a bright, divine half-moon on his head, armlets on all his arms,
stainless anklets, and an unsurpassed neck-ornament.
Viśvakarman gave her all the jewel finger-rings for her own fingers, as well as an exceedingly stainless axe.
He [saw] weapons of many forms, as well as an impenetrable armor,
and a garland of unfading lotuses upon his head and another upon his chest.
The Ocean gave her an exceedingly beautiful lotus,
Himavat a lion as a vehicle, and various kinds of jewels.
The Lord of Wealth gave him a drinking vessel filled with divine liquor,
and Śeṣa, the lord of all nāgas, gave him one adorned with a great jewel. (30)
He gave her a necklace of serpents, he who supports this earth;
likewise, the Goddess was adorned by other gods with ornaments and weapons.
Being thus honored, she let out a loud cry with repeated bursts of boisterous laughter;
by that terrible sound, the entire sky was filled.
From that immense, guileless roar, a great sound arose;
all the worlds were agitated and the oceans trembled. (33)
The earth trembled and all the great oceans shook;
and with joy, the gods cried out "Victory! to her who was mounted upon a lion.
And seeing the entire three worlds agitated, the gods and the sages, their bodies bowed with devotion, praised her. (35)
With their entire armies arrayed and weapons raised, they rose up;
then Mahiṣāsura, out of anger, exclaimed, "Ah! What is this? (36)
Surrounded by all the asuras, he rushed toward that sound;
then he beheld the Goddess, whose splendor pervaded the three worlds.
She bent the earth with the tread of her feet, scraped the sky with her crown, and agitated the entire underworld with the twanging sound of her bowstring. (38)
Having pervaded all directions with her thousand arms, she remained there;
then a battle commenced between that goddess and the enemies of the gods.
The great asura named Cidkṣura, the commander-in-chief of the army of the demon Mahiṣāsura, set the horizons ablaze with various weapons and missiles discharged in many ways.
And Cāmara, accompanied by another fourfold army, fought;
likewise, the great asura named Udagra fought with sixty thousand chariots. (41)
Mahāhanu fought with ten thousand ayutas,
and the great asura Asiloman fought with fifty million (niyuta).
Vāṣkala fought in battle with six hundred times ten thousand [soldiers],
surrounded by many thousands of hosts of elephants and horses.
Surrounded by ten million chariots, the great Daitya named Biḍāla fought in that battle with five hundred thousand [ayutas] more. (44)
There, surrounded by chariots, he fought in the battle;
and others there, by the tens of thousands, were likewise encompassed by chariots, elephants, and horses. (45)
There, the great asuras fought in battle against the Goddess with thousands of millions upon millions of chariots and likewise elephants.
And in that battle where the horses were arrayed, Mahiṣāsura was present there with javelins, slings, spears, and likewise with clubs.
They fought in the encounter with the Goddess using swords, axes, and spears; some hurled javelins, while others likewise cast nooses.
Salutations to Śrī Sūryanārāyaṇa.

The Netropaniṣad. Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Now, therefore, we shall expound the Cākṣuṣmatī-vidyā, which is perfected through recitation and removes diseases of the eyes; by means of which all eye diseases are destroyed from every side, and [the health] of the eyes [is restored].

There shall be radiance for him from this *Cākṣuṣī* Vidyā. Ahi-Budhnya is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and the illustrious Sūrya is the deity (*devatā*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is in recitation for the removal of eye diseases: *Oṃ cakṣuṣe 2 cakṣuṣe tejaḥ sthiro bhava māyāhi 2 tvaritaṃ cakṣurogāñ śamaya 2 mama jātarūpaṃ tejo darśaya 2*.
As it is said in the *Mandhonasī*: "Thus perform the auspicious rite twice! Eradicate, eradicate all those misdeeds accumulated by me in previous births which obstructed my sight!
Oṃ, homage to you, the Eye, the Bestower of Light, the Divine Sun! Oṃ, homage to the Compassionate One, the Nectar! Oṃ, homage to Śrī!"
To Sūrya, Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Sūrya, whose splendor is the eye; obeisance, Oṃ, to Kechara;
obeisance, Oṃ, to Mahat; obeisance, Oṃ, to Tapas; obeisance to Rajas; from non-existence lead me to existence, from darkness lead me to light, from death lead me to immortality.
The Blessed One is warm, of pure form, the Swan.
(258) Those [demons] proceeded to strike that goddess with blows from their swords;
then the goddess Caṇḍikā [neutralized] those very weapons and missiles.
The Goddess, her face free from exertion and being praised by the gods and sages, effortlessly cut down [the weapons] as they rained down from her own arms. || 50 ||
The Sovereign Lady discharged weapons and missiles into the bodies of the Asuras.

The Blessed One, whose form is pure and delightful, has said: "The Brāhmaṇa who constantly studies this Cākṣuṣmatī Vidyā shall suffer no eye disease, nor shall there be blindness in his lineage. Having caused eight Brāhmaṇas to master it...

The accomplishment of knowledge occurs: Oṃ. He who is of universal form, compassionate, the knower of all beings, golden, the person whose nature is light—him, the thousand-rayed one, this Sun rises as the life-breath of living beings, circulating in a hundred ways. Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed Āditya.
Ahovāhinī ahovāhinī svāhā. Thus ends the Netra Upaniṣad as declared in the Śrī Atharvaveda.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, the goddess questioned Śaṅkara, the boon-granting Śiva, the omniscient Maheśvara, the God of gods.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, O God, Lord of Gods, O Lord who grants liberation to the gods!
O highly fortunate one, tell me, even if it be a secret, O Lord.
Tell me that which brings about the destruction of enemies, the protection of oneself, and through which one may obtain supreme and incomparable sovereignty— tell me what is beneficial.
Bhairava said:
O Great Goddess, for the benefit of all dharmas, I shall declare the wondrous armor of the Goddess, which provides protection for all human beings.
It pacifies all calamities, destroys all afflictions, bestows happiness and enjoyment, and is a marvelous means for subjugation and attraction. || 5 ||
It causes the destruction of enemies and wards off all diseases;
likewise, it brings about the fulfillment of the desired goals for those who are suffering, afflicted by fever, or otherwise distressed.
One should recite the *Kālikā-kavaca*, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
his enemies perish... Oṃ. Of this *Śrī-Kālikā-kavaca*, [the seer is] Śrī-Bhairava...
Oṃ. One should meditate upon Kālī, the Great Illusion (*Mahāmāyā*), three-eyed and multiformed.
Enraged, with his mane shaking, that lion, the mount of the Goddess, [roared]. (51)
She moved among the armies of the Asuras like fire in the forests;
and Ambikā, while fighting in the battle, released those very breaths she had previously held.
Those very hosts, having been produced instantly by the hundreds of thousands,
fought with axes, bhindipālas, swords, and paṭṭiśas.
Four-armed, with a protruding tongue and a face resembling the full moon,
she has the luster of blue lotus petals and is the destroyer of hosts of enemies.
She bears a human skull, a sword, a lotus, and likewise a boon-granting gesture;
she wears red garments, has prominent fangs, and possesses a terrifying form.
The Goddess is always intent on loud, boisterous laughter, naked,
seated upon a corpse, and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess, one should again recite the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Oṃ! Kālikā, endowed with a formidable form, the auspicious bestower of all desires. || 11 ||
May the Goddess praised by all the gods grant me the destruction of my enemies;
she whose very form is *hrīṃ hrīṃ*, and likewise she whose form is *hrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ*.
Hrīṃ hrīṃ kṣeṃ 2; she who is Svarūpā shall always tear asunder her enemies. Śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ; the Goddess Rūpiṇī is the liberator from the bonds of worldly existence. || 13 ||
Laughing, "hrīṃ hrīṃ," may the Goddess always destroy our enemies—she by whom the Daitya Śumbha and the great Asura Niśumbha were slain. (14)
For the destruction of enemies, I bow to that Kālikā, the beloved of Śaṅkara;
she who is Brāhmī, Śaivī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, and Nārasiṃhikā.
May Kaumārī, Aindrī, and Cāmuṇḍā devour my enemies—
Sureśvarī, who is of terrible form and the destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
With your body covered everywhere by a garland of severed heads, always protect me!
Hrīṃ hrīṃ! O Kālikā, you of terrible fangs, lover of blood, whose mouth is filled with blood! p. 260)
Strengthened by the power of the Goddess, the hosts destroyed the multitudes of Asuras;
some sounded kettledrums, while others blew conchs.
And others likewise played mṛdaṅga drums during that great festival of battle;
then the Goddess [assailed him] with a trident, a mace, and showers of javelins.
With his sword and other weapons, he struck down hundreds of great asuras,
and he caused others to fall, bewildered by the sound of his bell.
Having bound some asuras on the ground with a noose, he dragged others away;
some were split in two by sharp sword-strokes, while others were likewise treated.

Struck down by the fall of my mace, they lie upon the earth; with breasts drenched in blood, devour my enemies! Devour! Devour! Strike! Strike! Kill! Kill! Split! Split! Cut! Cut! Exterminate! Exterminate! Put to flight! Put to flight! Wither! Wither! Svāhā! Hrīṃ Hrīṃ! To Kālikā, [I offer] my enemies!

I offer, svāhā! Oṃ, victory! Victory! Kiri! Kiri! Kiṭi! Kiṭi! Kuṭa! Kuṭa! Kaṭṭa! Kaṭṭa! Crush! Crush! Delude! Delude! Seize! Seize! Destroy my enemies! Destroy! Devour! Devour! Tear asunder! Tear asunder! O Yātudhānī Cāmuṇḍā, bring all people—the king, the king’s men, women, and enemies—under my control! Subdue them! Subdue them!
"Grant us grain, wealth, horses, women, jewels, celestial damsels, sons, grandsons, and royal splendor!
(261) And some, struck violently with pestles, vomited blood. || 58 ||
Some did not fall to the ground, having been pierced in the chest by the spear;
others on the field of battle were rendered without intervals by the flood of arrows.
The harassers of the gods released life-breaths that resembled hawks;
some had their arms severed, while others had their necks cut off.
Bhakṣa 2 kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣaiṃ kṣauṃ kṣaḥ svāhā. This divine armor (kavaca) was narrated by Śambhu in ancient times. || 17 ||
For those who recite this constantly, their enemies are surely destroyed;
they become free from all diseases in this world—of this there is no doubt. (18)
His enemies shall always be devoid of wealth and devoid of sons;
likewise, success in the armor-mantra (kavaca) shall come from reciting it a thousand times.
Then all undertakings will succeed, just as Śaṅkara has declared:
having taken charcoal from a cremation ground and having carefully reduced it to powder... (20)
Having ground [the substances] with water from the feet, one should draw figures of the enemies on the ground with an iron stylus, making them deformed and with their heads facing north.

Placing his hand upon the enemy's heart, the knower of mantras should himself recite the armor mantra (kavaca) and perform the re-establishment of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) for the enemy with the mantra.
By the discharge of missiles, one may slay the enemy and cause him to go to his abode;
by the heat of blazing embers, enemies become afflicted with fever.
By sprinkling [the body] with water while standing on the left foot, one certainly becomes poor;
however, this armor-mantra (kavaca) is said to cause the destruction of enemies and to bring about subjugation.
It bestows supreme sovereignty and increases one's sons, grandsons, and progeny;
it should be recited with diligence at the time of dawn and during the period of worship. || 25 ||
By reciting it thus at evening time, all success will certainly be attained;
the enemy undergoes eradication and shall be driven away from the country. (26)
Afterwards, O auspicious Goddess, [the practitioner] undoubtedly attains the state of a servant (kiṅkara);
it destroys enemies, O Goddess, and bestows all prosperity. (27)
O Goddess praised by all the gods, O Kālikā, I bow down to you.
Thus ends the Kālī-kavaca from the Rudrayāmala.
The heads of some fell; others were torn asunder in the midst;
and other great asuras fell upon the earth with their shanks severed. (61)
Some, whose arms, eyes, and feet were severed by the Goddess into two parts, rose up again even after their heads had been cut off and fallen.

[The headless trunks fought with the Goddess, who had seized her supreme weapons. (This half-verse is not seen in the manuscript of the Gurjara tradition. (The headless trunks fought with the Goddess, who had seized her supreme weapons.)
And others there danced in that battle, following the rhythm of musical instruments.
Other great asuras, headless trunks with swords, spears, and double-edged blades in their hands, cried out "Stay! Stay! to the Goddess.
With chariots, elephants, horses, and asuras cast down, the earth there where that great battle took place became impassable.
Great rivers of blood flowed forth instantly there;
and in the midst of the asura army, the elephants and divine horses [were submerged]. (66)
In an instant, Ambikā brought that great army of the asuras to destruction,
just as fire consumes a vast heap of grass and wood.
And that lion, letting out a great roar with his mane bristling,
seemed to pluck the life-breaths from the bodies of the enemies of the gods, as it were.
A battle was waged there between the Goddess, her hosts, and those great asuras;
indeed, the gods praised them while releasing showers of flowers from the sky. Om. (69)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Army of the Asura Mahiṣa," in the Devī-māhātmya of the Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, within the Sāvarṇika Manvantara. [Chapter 2]. [Total verses spoken: 1; total verses:
68 + 69 = 137; thus from the beginning: 173].

Oṃ, victory, victory! In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, in the Devīmāhātmya of the Sāvarṇika Manvantara, may the desires of the sacrificer be fulfilled. May there be the offering unto the Mother of the World.
[This is] the Tantric oblation.

Hrīṃ! To the venerable Mahālakṣmī, who consists of twenty-eight syllables, who is the presiding deity of the Lakṣmī-bīja, together with her limbs, weapons, powers, retinue, and vehicles—I offer this great oblation; salutations, svāhā!
Now begins the third chapter: now, meditation.
Oṃ! She possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns, wears a saffron-colored silken garment and a garland upon her head;
her breasts are smeared with red pigment, and she holds a rosary, the Vidyā, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons.

I bow to the Goddess who stands with gentle grace, her lotus-like face graced by three eyes, holding the splendor of a lotus with her lotus-hands, and wearing a crown of jewels that resemble the cool-rayed moon.
Ṛṣi said: || 1 ||
Oṃ. Beholding that army being struck down, the great asura general Cikṣura then went forth in anger to fight Ambikā.
In that battle, the asura showered the goddess with a rain of arrows,
just as a cloud showers a peak of Mount Meru with a downpour of water. (3)
Then the goddess, having effortlessly severed his volleys of arrows,
struck down the horses with her shafts as well as the driver of those steeds.
And he immediately severed the bow and the exceedingly lofty banner;
he also pierced the limbs of him whose bow was broken with swift arrows.
With his bow severed, deprived of his chariot, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed, the asura,
wielding sword and shield, rushed toward that goddess.
Having struck the lion on the head with his sharp-edged sword, he,
possessing great speed, also struck the goddess on her left arm. (7)
O prince, having reached her arm, the sword shattered;
thereupon, his eyes red with rage, he seized a trident.
Then that great asura hurled it at Bhadrakālī;
it was blazing with splendors like the orb of the sun falling from the sky.
Seeing the spear falling, the goddess released her own trident;
that trident was brought down by him in a hundred pieces, along with that great asura.
When that exceedingly valiant general of Mahiṣa had been slain, Cāmara,
the tormentor of the gods, arrived mounted upon an elephant. (11)
He too then discharged his spear, but Ambikā quickly struck it down to the ground, rendered lusterless by her roar of "Hum."
Seeing his spear shattered and fallen, Cāmara, filled with rage, hurled a trident; but he [the opponent] cut that one down as well with his arrows.
Then the lion, springing up and standing between the frontal globes of the elephant,
fought intensely with that enemy of the gods in a hand-to-hand struggle.
Then, having fought from that elephant and descended to the earth, the two of them,
highly enraged, continued to battle with exceedingly terrible blows.
Then, leaping into the air with speed and descending again, the lion severed Cāmara’s head from his body with a blow of his paw.
Udagra was struck down in battle by the goddess with rocks, trees, and other weapons;
likewise, Karāla was felled by her teeth, fists, and palms. (17)
The enraged goddess crushed the arrogant Vāṣkala with blows from her mace,
and likewise struck Tāmra and Andhaka with her slings and arrows.
The Supreme Goddess struck Ugrāsya, Ugravīrya, and likewise Mahāhanu with her trident; she who has three eyes.
With his sword, he indeed struck off the head from the body of Biḍāla;
and with arrows, he sent both Durdhara and Durmukha to the abode of Yama.
While his own army was thus being decimated, Mahiṣāsura,
assuming his natural form as a buffalo, terrified those Gaṇas.
Some were struck by the blows of his snout, others by the thrusting of his hooves; some were beaten with his tail, and others were torn apart by his two horns. (22)
By his speed he struck some down, others by his roar, and still others by his whirling;
by the wind of his breath, he cast others to the ground.
Having struck down the army of the Pramathas, that Asura rushed forward;
then Ambikā became enraged at the one who was slaying the lion of the Great Goddess.
In his fury, that one of great prowess, stamping the surface of the earth with his hooves,
hurled high mountains with his two horns and let out a roar.
The earth, trampled by his forceful whirling, shattered;
and the ocean, struck by his tail, overflowed on all sides.
The clouds, shattered by the tips of his ascetic penance, went to pieces;
those mountain-like masses fell from the sky by the hundreds, driven by the wind of his breath. (27)
Seeing the great Asura approaching, swollen with rage, Caṇḍikā then manifested her wrath for his destruction. (28)
Having cast that noose, she bound the great asura;
being bound in that great battle, he abandoned his buffalo form.
Then he immediately became a lion; just as Ambikā was about to cut off his head, a man with a sword in hand appeared.
Then the goddess swiftly cut that man down with her arrows;
together with his sword and shield, he then became a great elephant.
With his trunk, he dragged that great lion and roared;
but as he was dragging it, the goddess cut off his trunk with her sword.
Then the great asura again assumed the form of a buffalo.
In that very manner, he agitated the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
Then the enraged Caṇḍikā, the Mother of the World, drank the excellent liquor again and again, and she laughed with her eyes reddened.
And that asura also, arrogant with the intoxication of his own strength and heroism,
bellowed and hurled mountains at Caṇḍikā with his two tusks.
And she, crushing those who were sent forth with her volleys of arrows, spoke to him—her words faltering due to the agitation of her flushed face, which was agitated by intoxication—with these words:
The Goddess said: (37)
Roar, roar for a moment, O fool, while I drink the honey!
Once you have been slain by me right here, the deities will quickly roar in response.
The sage said: || 39 ||
Having spoken thus, she sprang up and mounted that great asura;
pressing him down with her foot and seizing his throat, she struck him with her trident.
Then he too was trampled by her with her foot; yet, even while only half-emerged from his own mouth, he was sustained by the power of the Great Goddess.
While that great asura was still only half-emerged,
the Goddess struck off his head with her great sword and felled him.
Then that entire army of Daityas perished, crying out "Alas!
Alas!", while all the hosts of deities attained supreme joy.
The gods, together with the divine great seers, praised that goddess;
the lords of the Gandharvas sang, and the hosts of Apsaras danced. Om. 44.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Asura Mahiṣa," in the Devīmāhātmya of the Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, within the Sāvarṇika Manvantara. [Chapter 3; Verses spoken: 3; Total verses: 41;
Total from the beginning: 44; Grand total from the start: 217.]
The oblation as taught in the Tantras.
Oṃ, I offer this great oblation to Jayantī, together with her limbs, her weapons, her power, her retinue, and her vehicle, she who presides over the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī; salutations, svāhā!
The Fourth Chapter.
Now, meditation.
Oṃ! She has the luster of a dark cloud, strikes terror into the hosts of enemies with her sidelong glances, and bears upon her crown a crescent moon;
she holds in her hands a conch, a discus, a sword, and a trident, and possesses three eyes.

I meditate upon Durgā, known as Jayā, who is mounted upon the shoulders of a lion, filling the entire three worlds with her splendor, praised by the Lord of the Thirty-three gods, and served by those desiring spiritual perfection. (4)
The sage said: || 1 ||

Oṃ! When that evil-minded one of exceeding prowess had been slain by the Goddess, as did the host of the enemies of the gods, Śakra and the other hosts of deities—bending their necks and shoulders low in prostration, their bodies beautiful with the rising of horripilation from great joy—praised her with these words. (2)
By that Goddess, who is the power of the Self, this entire world is pervaded; she is the embodiment of the collective power of the multitude of all the gods without exception.
We bow with devotion to that Ambika, who is worshiped by all the gods, serpents, and sages;
may she bestow auspiciousness upon us. || 3 ||
May that Caṇḍikā, whose incomparable power and strength even the Blessed One Ananta, Brahmā, and Hara are not able to describe,
direct her mind toward the protection of the entire world and the destruction of the fear of inauspiciousness.
You who are Fortune herself in the dwellings of the virtuous, Misfortune among the wicked,
Intellect in the hearts of the wise,
Faith in the good, and Modesty in those born of noble lineage— to you, we bow; protect us!
O Goddess, the universe! || 5 ||
276) How can we describe this inconceivable form of yours, and how this vast, supreme vigor that brings about the destruction of the asuras?
Now follows the hymn of the hundred names of Durgā.
O lady of the household, listen to the hundred names of Durgā:
Durgā, Bhavānī, Deveśī, Viśvanāthapriyā, and Śivā. (1)
With a mouth made terrifying by fierce fangs, adorned with a garland of severed heads, she is Rudrāṇī, the Savior Tārā, the consort of Maheśvara, and the beloved of Bhava. || 2 ||
Nārāyaṇī, the sustainer of the world, the beloved of Mahādeva, Jayā, Vijayā, Jayārādhyā, Śarvāṇī, and Haravallabhā. || 3 ||
The goddess Asitā, Cāṇimā, Laghimā, and likewise Garimā; she is the power of Maheśa, the sovereign of the universe, Gaurī, the daughter of the mountain.
She is eternal, stainless, effortless, and ever-new;
she is the passionate Speech with a red face, endowed with wealth and the bestower of wealth.
The beloved of Rāma, devoted to Rāma, the bestower of boons upon the Lord of the Raghus;
the sovereign lady of the kingdom, delighting in the kingdom, the dark-complexioned one who grants boons to Kṛṣṇa.
Yaśodā, Rādhikā, Caṇḍī, Draupadī, and likewise Rukmiṇī;
she who is dear to Guha, who delights in Guha, and who sports in the lineage of Guha.
Gaṇeśa, Jananī, Mātā, Viśvarūpā, Jāhnavī, Gaṅgā, Kālī, Kāśī, Bhairavī, and Bhuvaneśvarī. (8)
She is stainless and sweet-smelling; she is Devakī, worshipped by the gods;
she is born of Dakṣa, the sacrificial fee (Dakṣiṇā), the clever one, and the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice. || 9 ||
Suśīlā, Sundarī, Saumyā, Mātaṅgī, Kamalā, Kalā, Niśumbhanāśinī, Śumbhanāśinī, and Caṇḍanāśinī. || 10 ||
The destroyer of Dhūmralocana, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura, Umā, Gaurī, Karālā, Kāminī, and the enchantress of the universe. || 11 ||
Thus, O lady of beautiful countenance, these hundred names have been told;
by the mere recollection of these names, a man becomes liberated while living.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites this while remembering the two feet of Durgā, is liberated from the bonds of birth; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (13)
By reciting the hundred names at the time of twilight, during the day, at night, or at the onset of night, one will certainly attain the perfection of mantras.
O Maheśvarī, even if one should worship the ten sciences without knowing this King of Hymns, there will nevertheless be no accomplishment; this is the truth, the absolute truth.
Thus ends the hymn of one hundred names of the venerable goddess Durgā in the second chapter of the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.
Moreover, O Goddess, your wondrous deeds in battles against all the hosts of gods, asuras, and others are exceedingly great. (6)
You are the cause of all the worlds, yet you are not known by Hari, Hara, and the others due to the defects arising from the three *guṇas*.
You are the boundless one, the support of all, and the primordial supreme *prakṛti*, from which this entire universe has emerged as a portion of yourself, before it was manifested.
O Goddess, since you attain satisfaction through the invocation of all the gods in every sacrifice, you are indeed Svāhā;
and since you are the cause of satisfaction for the host of ancestors, you are likewise called Svadhā by people.
Therefore, you who possess inconceivable great vows are the cause of liberation, and you are practiced [or meditated upon].

O Goddess, that Blessed One is indeed the supreme sword of knowledge for those sages seeking liberation— whose senses are well-restrained, who possess the essence of reality, and whose every defect has been destroyed.

The Goddess Trayī, the Blessed One, who consists of sound, is the repository of the most pure Ṛg and Yajus verses, and of the Sāman chants with their beautiful recitation of the *udgītha* phrases; she is the sovereign mistress of complete majesty, virtue, fame, and prosperity.
And because of [Your] knowledge and dispassion, as well as the six [perfections], You are called "Bhagavatī. The meaning is that You are eternally adorned with the six attributes of sovereignty.
Or rather, You are the discourse for the contemplation of existence; You are the supreme remover of the suffering of all the worlds.
O Goddess, You are Medhā, who has understood the essence of all the scriptures; You are Durgā, the unattached boat for the difficult ocean of worldly existence.
Śrī has made her sole dwelling in the heart of the enemy of Kaiṭabha; you alone, O Gaurī, have been established by the moon-crested Lord.
Seeing that face— slightly smiling, stainless, resembling the orb of the full moon, lovely with the luster of the finest gold,
and though struck with great fury, yet most wonderful— the Mahiṣa was suddenly struck with awe.
By means of the path. || 12 ||

O Goddess, it is truly marvelous that Mahiṣa did not immediately cast off his life upon seeing you, whose face was made terrible by a frown of anger and whose complexion resembled the rising moon; for who can survive the sight of the enraged Destroyer?
O Goddess, be most gracious for our welfare; you instantly destroy the families of those possessed by anger.
This has been understood this very moment, as the vast army of Mahiṣāsura has been brought to its end.
They are highly esteemed in the lands; they possess wealth and their respective reputations, and the category of Dharma does not decline.
Blessed indeed are those whose sons, servants, and wives are ever content, for whom you, being pleased, grant perpetual prosperity.
O Goddess, the virtuous man always performs all his righteous duties with great devotion every day;
through your grace, O Goddess, he then goes to heaven— indeed, you are the bestower of fruits throughout the three worlds.
O Durgā, when remembered, you take away the fear of all living beings; when remembered by those established in well-being, you grant them most excellent wisdom.
O remover of the fear and suffering of poverty, who else but you has a heart so tender toward performing every kind of assistance?
Thinking, "When these are slain, the world shall attain happiness; let them indeed commit sin for a long time in hell,
but by meeting death in battle, let them go to heaven," you surely destroy your enemies.
O Goddess! 18.

Why do you not reduce all the asuras to ashes at the mere sight of them? Since you discharge weapons against your enemies, let even those foes go to the higher worlds purified by the weapons; such a thought toward them would be most excellent for you.

That the eyes of the asuras did not meet their destruction while gazing upon Your face, which is worthy of being compared to the sun and a fragment of the moon, was due to the radiance of the multitude of sword-blades and the intense mass of light from the tips of the tridents.
O Goddess, your virtuous conduct pacifies the behavior of the wicked; likewise, this form of yours is inconceivable and incomparable to others.
And thus, by you, compassion has been manifested even toward enemies— those who have robbed the gods of their valor— even as you exerted your heroic prowess.

What comparison can there be for this prowess of yours? Your form, which captivates even the hearts of enemies with fear, and where have both compassion and martial ferocity ever been seen together in a single mind as they are in you, O Bestower of Boons?
By destroying the enemy at the head of the battle, you have protected this entire triple world; even they [the gods] were saved by you.
Having slain them, the hosts of enemies were led to heaven and even our fear of the intoxicated foes of the gods was cast away; salutations to you! 23.

"I am alone here in this world; who else could be my second?
Behold these wicked ones entering into me alone—they are but my own manifestations. (5)
Then all those goddesses, headed by Brahmāṇī, merged into the body of that Goddess;
at that time, Ambikā alone remained.
The Goddess said: || 7 ||
When I was present here with my manifold forms through my sovereign power, that has now been withdrawn by me; I remain as one alone. Be firm in battle!
The sage said: || 9 ||
Then a fierce battle commenced between the Goddess and Śumbha,
while all the gods and asuras looked on.
p.
340) With showers of sharp arrows, as well as weapons and terrible missiles—[the counteracting of missiles being as follows:
the *āgneya* by the *vāruṇa*, the *vāruṇa* by the *vāyavya*, the *vāyavya*...]

The Sārpa [weapon] was neutralized by the Gāruḍa; the Gāruḍa was neutralized by the Vaiṣṇava—these are well-known in the science of archery. Once again, a battle occurred between the two of them, causing terror to all the worlds.
The lord of the Daityas shattered by the means of counteracting them those hundreds of divine weapons which Ambikā had discharged.
O Supreme Goddess, she effortlessly shattered the divine weapons discharged by him through the utterance of fierce *huṃkāras* and other means. (13)
Then that asura covered the goddess with hundreds of arrows;
she, the goddess, being provoked, cut his bow apart with her own shafts.
When his bow was severed, the lord of the Daityas then took up a spear;
the Goddess, however, cut that too with her discus as it remained in his hand. (15)
Then, taking up his sword and his radiant shield marked with a hundred moons,
the lord of the Daityas rushed toward the Goddess.
As he was rushing forward, Caṇḍikā swiftly cut off his sword with sharp arrows released from her bow,
and likewise his shield, which was as bright as the rays of the sun.
Then that Daitya, his horses slain, his bow severed, and his charioteer lost,
seized a terrible mallet, intent on the destruction of Ambikā.
He cut down the mallet as it was falling with sharpened arrows;
nevertheless, that powerful one rushed forward, raising his fist.
That bull among the Daityas brought his fist down upon the heart [of the Goddess],
and the Goddess, in turn, struck him on the chest with her palm.
Struck by that blow of the palm, the king of the Daityas fell to the surface of the earth; yet he suddenly rose up once more in that same manner. (21)
Leaping up and seizing the goddess high aloft, he stationed himself in the sky;
even there, being without support, Caṇḍikā fought with him.
Then, in the sky, the Daitya and Caṇḍikā engaged in a wrestling match with one another;
it was their first [contest], which caused wonder even to the perfected sages.
Then, after engaging in wrestling for a very long time with Ambikā,
he lifted her up, whirled her around, and threw her down upon the surface of the earth.
Having been thrown down and reached the earth, that evil-minded one, rising up with his fist and acting with speed, rushed forward with the desire to slay Caṇḍikā.
Then,
as he approached, the goddess pierced that lord of all the Daityas in the chest with her trident and cast him down upon the earth. (26)
With his life departed, he fell upon the earth, pierced by the tip of the Goddess’s trident,
shaking the entire world along with its oceans, islands, and mountains.
Then, once that evil-minded one was slain, the entire world became serene;
it attained a state of supreme well-being, and the sky became stainless.
The portentous clouds accompanied by meteors that had previously appeared subsided;
likewise, the rivers that flowed out of their courses returned to their paths once he had been struck down.
Then all the hosts of gods, their minds overflowing with joy, became filled with delight; once he was slain, the Gandharvas sang merrily.
Likewise, other hosts of Apsarases played musical instruments and danced;
holy winds blew, and the sun became brilliantly radiant. || 31 ||
The fires that were previously extinguished blazed up again. Regarding the signs of the pacified directions, Varāha says:
"A direction is 'burning' when it is devoid of embers and the sun stands within it; it is 'smoky' when the smoke extends toward it."
The sun and the remaining planets, when pacified, become givers of auspicious results; likewise, sounds produced from the pacified directions [are auspicious]. Om. 32.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Śumbha," in the Devīmāhātmya of the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, within the Sāvarṇika Manvantara. [Total: 1 half-verse, 27 verses; thus, from the beginning, 575 units.]

Oṃ, victory, victory! In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, in the Devīmāhātmya of the Sāvarṇika Manvantara, may the desires of the sacrificer be fulfilled; may there be the offering unto the Mother of the World.
Chapter Eleven:
Now, on Meditation (dhyāna).

I worship Bhuvaneśī, who possesses the luster of the morning sun, who wears the moon as her crown, whose breasts are full, who is endowed with three eyes, whose face is smiling, and who holds in her hands the gestures of granting boons, the goad, the noose, and the gesture of fearlessness.
[Kṣīrikā] (Khīra). In the *Bhāvaprakāśa*, in the first section, within the chapter on prepared foods (*kṛtānnavarga*):

"Pāyasa is known as *paramānna*; it is also called *kṣīrikā*. When the milk is half-cooked, one should cook rice grains smeared with ghee; once they are cooked, they are called *kṣīrikā*, resembling [the original dish] when combined with sugar and clarified butter."
Kṣīrikā is difficult to digest, strengthening, heavy, and provides nourishment for the bodily tissues (dhātus).
It causes constipation and removes bile, hemorrhaging, digestive fire disorders, and wind.
The Sage said: 1.

Oṃ! When that great lord of the asuras had been slain by the Goddess, the gods, led by Indra and preceded by Agni, praised Kātyāyanī; having attained their desired object, they filled the quarters with the blossoming of their lotus-like faces. || 2 ||
O Goddess, remover of the distress of those who have sought refuge, be gracious, be gracious, O Mother of the entire world!
Be gracious, O Sovereign of the Universe; protect the universe, for you, O Goddess, are the Mistress of all that is moving and unmoving. (3)
Since you abide in the form of the earth, you alone are the sole support of the world;
O lady of invincible power, this entire universe is nourished by you as you exist in the form of the waters.

You are indeed the power of Viṣṇu, possessed of infinite valor, the seed of the universe, and the supreme Māyā. O Goddess, all this is deluded by you; when you are gracious, you are the cause of liberation on earth.
O Goddess, all branches of knowledge are your manifestations, and all women throughout the worlds are your forms;
since this entire universe has been filled by you alone, O Mother, what praise can there be for you, whose words of worship transcend both the praised and the praiser?
O Goddess, since you are the bestower of heaven and liberation upon all beings, what other supreme words could there be for your praise once you have been thus extolled? (7)
O Goddess Nārāyaṇī, who abides in the hearts of all people in the form of their intellect and who bestows both heaven and liberation— salutations be unto you!
O Nārāyaṇī, who bestows transformation in the form of moments, divisions of time, and so forth, and who brings the cessation of the universe—salutations be to you! || 9 ||
O most auspicious among all that is auspicious, O Śivā, who accomplishes all purposes,
O refuge, O Tryambakā, O Gaurī, O Nārāyaṇī, salutations be unto you!
O eternal one, who has become the power for creation, maintenance, and destruction;
O Narayani, the refuge of the qualities and composed of the qualities—salutations be to you! (11)
O Goddess Nārāyaṇī, who are solely intent on protecting those who have come for refuge and those who are miserable and distressed; O Goddess, who removes the suffering of all—salutations be unto you!
O Goddess who dwells in a celestial chariot yoked with swans, who assumes the form of Brahmāṇī;
O Goddess who flows with the waters of Kauśāmbī, O Nārāyaṇī, salutations be unto you! (13)
O bearer of the trident, moon, and serpent, who ride upon the great bull;
O Nārāyaṇī, in the form of Māheśvarī, salutations be unto you! 14.
O sinless one, surrounded by peacocks and cocks, wielder of the great spear, abiding in the form of Kaumārī—homage be to you, O Nārāyaṇī! 15.
O you who hold the supreme weapons—the conch, the discus, the mace, and the Śārṅga bow;
be gracious, O Vaiṣṇavī form; O Nārāyaṇī, salutations be unto you! 16.
O you who held up the great mountain with your tusk, O you who lifted the earth with your fang,
O auspicious one in the form of a boar, O Nārāyaṇī, salutations be to you!
O Nārāyaṇī, who are endowed with the protection of the three worlds and have exerted yourself to slay the Daityas with your fierce form as Nṛsiṃha, salutations be unto you! (18)
O wearer of the diadem, O wielder of the great thunderbolt, O you who shine with a thousand eyes, O destroyer of Vṛtra’s life, O son of Indrāṇī, O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you! 19.
O Nārāyaṇī, who possesses the form of Śivadūtī, who has slain the great strength of the Daityas, whose form is terrible and whose roar is mighty—salutations to you! || 20 ||
O Cāmuṇḍā, whose face is terrifying with fangs, who is adorned with a garland of heads,
who crushes the skulls [of enemies], O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you!
O Lakṣmī, O Lajjā, O Mahāvidyā, O Śraddhā, O Puṣṭi, O Svadhā, O Dhruvā;
O Mahārātri, O Mahāvidyā, O Nārāyaṇī, salutations be unto you! || 22 ||
O Medhā, O Sarasvatī, O Excellent One, O Bhūti, O Daughter of Vabhru, O Tamasī!
You who are restrained, be gracious, O Ruler; O Nārāyaṇī, salutations be unto you.
O Goddess who embodies all forms, sovereign of all, endowed with all powers; protect us from fears, O Goddess Durgā! Salutations be unto you. (24)
May this gentle face of yours, adorned with three eyes, protect us from all fears; O Kātyāyanī, salutations be unto you! (25)
O Bhadrakālī, salutations to you; may the trident—fierce with its blazing flames, most terrible, and the destroyer of all asuras—protect us from fear. 26.
May that bell, O Goddess, which fills the world with its sound and destroys the splendor of the Daityas, protect us from sins as it protects its children. (27)
Smeared with the mire of the blood and fat of the Asuras, may your radiant sword bring us auspiciousness; O Caṇḍikā, we bow before you.
When pleased, you destroy all diseases without exception; when angered, however, [you bestow] all desired objects.
For those who have taken refuge in you, there is no misfortune; indeed, those who take refuge in you attain their ultimate resort. (29)

O Goddess, O Mother, this slaughter of the great asuras who are the enemies of Dharma, which you have performed today by assuming many forms and dividing your own body into manifold shapes— what other being could accomplish such a deed?

Among the sciences, the scriptures, the lamps of discernment, and the primordial utterances—who other than you illumines this entire universe within the bottomless pit of possessiveness, which is shrouded in such profound darkness? (31)

Wherever there are *rakṣasas* and serpents with fierce venom, wherever there are enemies and the forces of bandits, wherever there is a forest fire, and likewise in the midst of the ocean— there you abide and protect the universe. (32)
O Sovereign of the Universe, you protect the universe; as the soul of the universe, you sustain the universe.
You are worshipped by the Lord of the Universe for those who take refuge in you and are bowed down in devotion to you. 33.

O Goddess, be gracious and protect us perpetually from the fear of enemies, just as You did immediately after the slaying of the Asuras; quickly bring to an end the sins of all the worlds, as well as the great calamities born from the ripening of portents.
Be gracious to those who bow before you, O Goddess, you who remove the suffering of the universe;
O you who are praised by the inhabitants of the three worlds, become the bestower of boons upon the worlds. (35)
The Goddess said: || 36 ||
"I am the granter of boons, O hosts of gods; choose whatever boon you desire in your hearts.
Choose that which shall be for the benefit of the worlds, and I shall grant it. (37)
The gods said: || 38 ||
O Sovereign of the entire triple world, you are the pacifier of all afflictions;
in this very manner, you must effect the destruction of our enemies.
The Goddess said: || 40 ||
When the Vaivasvata interval has arrived, in the twenty-eighth yuga,
two other great asuras, Śumbha and Niśumbha, will be born.
Born in the house on the banks of the Nandagā river, originating from the womb of Yaśodā—
I, dwelling on the Vindhya mountain, shall therefore destroy those two.
Furthermore, descending to the surface of the earth in an exceedingly fierce form,
I shall slay the Vaipracitta Dānavas. (43)
And as they devour those fierce great Asuras, the sons of Vipracitti,
their teeth will become red, resembling the blossoms of the pomegranate tree.
Then the deities in heaven and men in the mortal world, praising me, shall constantly address me as Raktadantikā.
Furthermore, during a hundred-year drought when there is no water,
I shall be born upon the earth from no womb, as praised by the sages.
Vipracitti is the name of a certain Dānava whose superior knowledge (*jñāna*) was "unopposed" (*viruddha-apraciti*).

He was the son of Kaśyapa’s third wife. Regarding him, the *Harivaṃśa* states: "Those Dānavas, headed by Vipracitti, were exceedingly powerful. The offspring of the famous Dānava Vipracitti are the Vaipracittas; they are the sons of Vipracitti.

This is well known in the *Harivaṃśa*: "Then, born of Siṃhikā, there were the sons of Vipracitti; through the union of Daityas and Dānavas, they were born with fierce prowess. These thirteen of great strength are known as the Saiṃhikeyas:
Vyaṅga, Śalya, the powerful Nabhas, and Mahābala."
Vātāpi, Namuci, Ilvala, Khasṛma, Āñjika, Naraka, and likewise Kālanābha; and among them, Rāhu was the eldest, the crusher of the moon and the sun.
In that regard, Rāhu remains for a long time; Vātāpi was consumed by Agastya; Namuci was slain by Indra;
and having killed Śumbha and Niśumbha, I shall slay the remaining sons of Vipracitti. Thus it is stated in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*.
Then, with a hundred eyes, I shall gaze upon these sages;
consequently, men will call me "Śatākṣī" (the Hundred-eyed One). (47)
Then, O gods, I shall sustain the entire world with vegetables produced from my own body, which will serve as the means of sustaining life until the rains return.
Furthermore, in that age, the gods, having become hopeless, beheld [Śacī] in the house of Mārīca while Śatakratu was away.

"O Amita, having united with the goddess Saptavāmā, I shall become the goddess Śākambharī," according to the permission granted by the Blessed One in the Vāmana Purāṇa: "At that time, I shall attain renown on earth as Śākambharī."

And right there I shall slay the great asura named Durga, who had obtained a boon from Brahmā, saying, "This son of Suru shall be my refuge; he shall be my food, and this shall be my immortality. It should be known that the incarnation of the goddess Śākambharī occurs here in the twenty-eighth Kali age. || 49 ||
"My name shall become renowned as the goddess Durgā;
furthermore, when I assume a formidable form on the Himālaya mountains," (50)
"I shall devour the rākṣasas for the sake of protecting the sages;
then all the sages, with bodies bowed in reverence, will offer praise to me. (51)
That shall become my daughter, renowned as Bhīmādevī,
when one named Aruṇa causes great affliction throughout the three worlds.
Then he said: "Having assumed the form of a bee with countless bees as its followers, I shall slay the great Asura for the sake of the welfare of the three worlds. (53)

"They will praise me by the name Bhrāmarī and worship me with speech. For it is stated in the Lakṣmī Tantra: 'Bhrāmarī is my descent in the four ages. And so: 'At that time, people everywhere shall praise me as Bhrāmarī; whenever there shall arise such affliction caused by the Dānavas. (54)
Then, descending at that very moment, I shall bring about the destruction of my enemies. Oṃ. 55.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Hymn to the Goddess," in the *Devīmāhātmya* of the *Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, within the *Sāvarṇika Manvantara*. [Total count: 4 *uvāca*s, 1 *ardha-śloka*, and 50 *ślokas*, making 55 in total.]
Thus from the beginning, [verse] 630.

Oṃ, victory, victory! May the desires of the sacrificer be fulfilled in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, in the Devīmāhātmya of the Sāvarṇika Manvantara; may all be true. May there be dedication to the Mother of the Universe.
The tantric oblation.

*Klīṃ*, I offer this great oblation (*mahāhuti*) with salutation and *svāhā* to Goddess Nārāyaṇī, who is accompanied by her limbs, weapons, powers, retinue, and vehicles; she who is the presiding deity of the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī and whose vehicle is Garuḍa.
*Namaḥ svāhā*.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Now, on meditation:
Oṃ, [I meditate upon her] who possesses a luster equal to a garland of lightning, and who is seated upon the shoulders of the king of beasts.
It was attended by terrifying young maidens whose hands gleamed with swords and shields.
I worship Durgā, who is three-eyed, who bears the moon, whose nature is fire, and who holds in her hands a discus, mace, sword, shield, arrow, bow, bowstring, and the raised index finger.
The Goddess said: (1)
Oṃ! For him who, with a concentrated mind, shall constantly praise me with these hymns, I shall undoubtedly pacify all his afflictions. (2)
Those who shall likewise proclaim the destruction of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, the slaying of the demon Mahiṣāsura, and the killing of Śumbha and Niśumbha— (3)
And those who, with single-minded devotion, shall hear this supreme majesty of mine on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the ninth [lunar days], [shall attain the highest state].
For them there shall be no misdeed whatsoever, nor any calamity arising from misdeeds;
there shall be neither poverty nor separation from what is beloved.
For him there shall never be fear from an enemy, nor from a bandit, nor from a king;
nor shall there ever be danger from weapons, fire, or floods of water.

Therefore, this majesty of mine should be recited with a concentrated mind and always listened to with devotion; it is the supreme and great means of securing well-being. (Thus in the ancient manuscript.)
The reading.

That which arises suddenly is called *utpāta* (calamity), and its suffering is threefold, distinguished as internal (*ādhyātmika*), celestial (*ādhidevika*), and elemental (*ādhibhautika*). Among these, the internal is twofold: physical and mental. Physical suffering is caused by the imbalance of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*). Mental suffering is [caused by] desire...

Anger, greed, delusion, envy, and despondency are bound to [wrong] views; all these are "internal" (ādhyātmika) because they are to be accomplished through internal means. Among these, that which is "pertaining to beings" (ādhibhautika) has its cause in humans, animals, birds, reptiles, and stationary objects. That which is "pertaining to the divine" (adhidaivika) has its cause in yakṣas, rākṣasas, vināyakas, planetary spirits (grahas), and so forth.
For that is indeed so. || 7 ||
May my majesty pacify all calamities arising from great pestilence, as well as the threefold portents.
Wherever this is recited properly and constantly in my temple, I shall never abandon that place; my presence remains there forever.
During the offering of oblations, in worship, in the fire-ritual, and at great festivals,
this entire account of mine should be recited and indeed heard. (10)
Whether performed knowingly or unknowingly, I shall accept with pleasure this offering of bali, as well as this fire-oblation thus performed. (11)
During the autumn season, the great annual festival is performed;
having heard this majesty of mine during that occasion, one should be endowed with devotion.
By my grace, human beings shall be completely freed from all afflictions and endowed with wealth, grain, and sons; of this there is no doubt. (13)
Having heard this majesty of mine, as well as my auspicious origins and my prowess in battles, a man becomes fearless.
Enemies go to destruction and prosperity arises;
the lineage of those men who hear of my greatness rejoices. (15)
In all rites for pacification, as well as upon seeing an evil dream,
and during fierce afflictions caused by planetary spirits, one should listen to my majesty. (16)
Adverse planetary influences are pacified, as are terrible afflictions by malevolent spirits;
and the bad dreams seen by men are transformed into auspicious dreams. (17)
It brings peace to children overcome by seizing spirits, and it is the supreme means for creating loving-kindness among men divided by factions. (18)
It is the supreme destroyer of the strength of all those of evil conduct;
it brings about the destruction of Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Piśācas merely by its recitation. (19)
All this majesty of mine brings about my presence;
[it is achieved] by means of animals, flowers, water-offerings, incense, as well as excellent perfumes and lamps. (20)

That [merit] which is obtained in a year by feeding Brahmins, by daily fire-offerings (homa), by sprinkling rites (prokṣaṇīya), and by various other enjoyments and gifts—[is attained through this]. 21.
(363) My joy is produced when this is performed or heard even once—[the reading is "sakṛtsucarite"].
It destroys sins when heard and likewise bestows health. || 22 ||
The recitation of my births provides protection from spirits;
likewise, the account of my deeds in battles, which consist of the destruction of wicked Daityas. (23)
Upon hearing that, fear caused by enemies does not arise for men;
so too [is dispelled] by the hymns composed by you and those composed by the Brahman-sages. (24)
And those [mantras] created by Brahmā bestow auspicious wisdom, even when one is surrounded by a forest fire in a wilderness or a remote region. (25)
Or if he is surrounded by bandits in a deserted place, or captured by enemies;
or if he is pursued by lions and tigers, or by wild elephants in the forest. (26)
Or he may be ordered by an enraged king to be executed, or even while in prison;
or he may be tossed about by a wind upon a ship on the great ocean.
Even when weapons are falling in a most fierce battle, or amidst all kinds of terrible afflictions, or even when oppressed by intense pain; || 28 ||
By remembering this conduct of mine, a person shall be released from distress;
by my power, lions and the like, as well as robbers and enemies [shall be overcome]. (29)
They flee from afar upon remembering my deeds.
The sage said: || 31 ||
Having spoken thus, that blessed goddess Caṇḍikā, possessed of fierce valor, [departed].
While all the gods were looking on, he vanished right there;
those gods, too, became free from fear and resumed their respective offices as before. (33)
When Śumbha, the enemy of the gods, had been slain in battle by the Goddess, all the Daityas who partook of sacrificial offerings and whose enemies had been destroyed [by her] were overcome.
When that most fierce Niśumbha of incomparable prowess and great heroism had destroyed the world, the survivors fled to the netherworld (Pātāla).
In this way, O King, that Blessed Goddess, though eternal, manifests again and again and brings about the protection of the world.
By her this entire universe is deluded; she alone gives birth to the universe.
When entreated, she bestows wisdom, and when pleased, she grants prosperity.
O lord of men, this entire universe is pervaded by that Mahākālī,
who, at the time of the Great Dissolution (Mahākāla), takes the form of the Great Pestilence (Mahāmārī).
At the proper time, she herself becomes the great pestilence; she herself is the unborn creation.
At the proper time, she alone, the eternal one, effects the maintenance of all beings. (39)
In times of prosperity, that very same [woman] bestows fortune and growth upon men in their home; likewise, in times of adversity, she arises for the destruction of fortune. (40)
When praised and fully honored with flowers, incense, perfumes, and the like, she bestows wealth, garments, and likewise auspicious wisdom regarding the Dharma. Oṃ. (41)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Praise of the Fruit," in the *Devīmāhātmya* within the *Sāvarṇika Manvantara* of the glorious *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*. [Total count: 2 verses spoken, 2 halves of verses, 37 verses;
thus 41 from the beginning. Total: 671.]

Oṃ, victory, victory! In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, in the Devīmāhātmya within the Sāvarṇika Manvantara, may the desires of the sacrificer be fulfilled; may there be the offering to the Mother of the Universe.
The Tantric oblation.
*klī*, to Jayantī, who is with her limbs, weapons, powers, retinue, and vehicles—
to the boon-granting Goddess Vaiṣṇavī [O Vālā Tripurasundarī], I offer this great oblation; salutations, *svāhā*.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter:
Next, meditation (dhyāna).

Oṃ, I worship the auspicious goddess who shines like the orb of the rising sun, who has four arms and three eyes, and who holds a noose, a goad, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness. 13.
The sage said: || 1 ||
Oṃ. Thus has been told to you, O King, the supreme majesty of the Goddess;
such is the power of that Goddess by whom this world is sustained.
In the same way, knowledge is produced by the illusory power (māyā) of Lord Viṣṇu;
by that [power], you, this Vaiśya, and likewise other discerning ones [are so constituted]. (3)
They are deluded, they have been deluded, and others will be deluded;
O Great King, go for refuge to that Supreme Goddess.
When propitiated, she alone bestows upon men worldly enjoyment, heaven, and liberation.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: || 6 ||
Having heard these words of his, that lord of men, Suratha, [acted accordingly]. || 7 ||
Having prostrated before that illustrious sage of celebrated vows,
he was despondent due to his excessive attachment and the seizure of his kingdom.

O great sage, that Vaiśya immediately departed for the sake of performing austerities to behold his mother. There, a river— characterized by a breeze carrying the fragrance of kumuda lilies— delighted the sandy bank with its shimmering waves, which possess the beauty of Lakṣmī.
Seated upon a sandbank. || 9 ||

And that Vaiśya performed austerities, muttering the supreme *devāsūkta* with his mind fixed on the deity: "One should move the tongue and lips slightly; that muttering which is somewhat audible to the ear is known as *upāṃśu*. Thus he muttered.
p.
369) Having fashioned a great image of the Goddess on that very sandbank, || 10 ||
They performed worship for her with offerings of flowers, incense, and fire-libations.

By the qualification "fasting" (*nirāhārau*), it is indicated that this is *haṭhayoga*, as in the thought: "I shall cast down my body" or "I shall accomplish the mantra. The meaning is that they were previously restrained in their intake of food, and subsequently remained entirely without food.
In a case of conflict, the sequence of meaning is more powerful than the sequence of recitation. Thus, they were eating, their minds fixed on that [object], and composed in concentration. (11)
The two of them gave what he had prescribed: an offering consisting of blood and flesh, whether from a bird or from a man.

Out of devotion, the great hero would cast off his garments for the sake of Mahāmāyā; he even offered as an oblation the blood flowing from his own limbs. Thus, as the two of them, self-restrained, propitiated her for three years, [the goddess appeared]. 12.
The world-mother Caṇḍikā, being thoroughly pleased, spoke directly to him.
The Goddess said: || 14 ||
"O King, O delighter of your lineage, whatever is requested by you from me—may all that be obtained; being well-pleased, I grant it. (15)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: || 16 ||
Then, in another birth, King Vavra regained his kingdom without falling from it;
and in this very life, he recovered his own realm by force, having destroyed the power of his enemies.
Then that Vaiśya, his mind filled with world-weariness, requested knowledge from him—
the wise one who brings about the cessation of attachment to the notions of "mine" and "I."
The Goddess said: || 19 ||
O King, you shall regain your own kingdom in a very few days.
Having slain your enemies there, it shall be unfailing for you. || 21 ||
And having died, he again obtained birth from the god Vivasvat.
"You shall become on earth the one named Manu, accompanied by the Sāvitrī. || 23 ||
O best of Vaiśyas, this boon which you have desired from us— [24]
I bestow that upon you for the sake of complete accomplishment; you shall possess knowledge. || 25 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said: || 26 ||
Having thus granted them both the boon as desired, the goddess,
praised by them with devotion, immediately vanished from sight.
Thus, having obtained the boon from the Goddess, Suratha, that bull among Kṣatriyas,
shall take birth from the Sun and become the Sāvarṇi Manu.
"One should recite the final verse in two ways, both in the hymn and in the *saṃhitā*," so it is said in the *Rudrayāmala*.
"Having drunk the nectar of the bliss of Brahman, those who are intoxicated with yoga—even Indra appears like a beggar; what then to say of a mere human insect?"
Praise of the Saptaśatī Stotra in the Lakṣmī Tantra.
This hymn of praise to the power of birth and deeds is correctly established in the heart;
a man who, having learned it from the mouth of a twice-born, studies it constantly.
Having shaken off all illusion, one attains perfect knowledge;
one obtains every prosperity and dispels all calamities.
"For all twice-born ones who have mastered the recitation of the *Saptashatī*, she is indeed the granter of desires. [May there be auspiciousness.
Thus, having obtained this boon from the Goddess, Suratha, that bull among Kṣatriyas, shall take birth from the Sun and become Sāvarṇi Manu. *Klīṃ Oṃ*. 29.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Bestowing of Boons upon the Merchant Suratha," in the *Devīmāhātmya* of the *Śrī Kārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, within the *Sāvarṇika Manvantara*. [The Goddess] said: 6. Now...
19 verses, 14 [verses], likewise 29, thus from the beginning [there are] 700. The Samasta said: 57 [verses], half [of that] 42, 535 verses; the Avadāna: 66.
Oṃ, victory, victory! O Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, in the Sāvarṇika Manvantara, in the Devīmāhātmya, may the desires of the sacrificer be fulfilled; may there be the offering unto the Mother of the World.
[This is the Tantric oblation.]

*klīṃ*, to the Victorious One (*jayantī*), together with her limbs, her weapons, her powers, her retinue, and her vehicle—to the venerable Mahātripurasundarī; to the Śrīvidyā, I offer this great oblation (*mahāhuti*); salutation, *svāhā*.
Now follow the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) for the subsequent [mantra].
Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the heart. Oṃ caṃ, svāhā to the head. Oṃ ḍiṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock. Oṃ kāṃ, huṃ to the armor. Oṃ ya, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes. Oṃ hrīṃ caṇḍikāyai, phaṭ to the weapon.
Oṃ, Khaḍginī, Śūlinī, Ghorā, Gādinī, and likewise Cakriṇī;
Śaṅkhinī, Cāpinī, Vāṇabhushuṇḍī, and Parighāyudhā—salutation to the heart.
Oṃ! Protect us with your trident, O Goddess; protect us with your sword, O Ambikā!
Protect us with the sound of your bell and with the twang of your bowstring! Svāhā to the head!
Oṃ! Protect me in the east, O Caṇḍikā, and protect me in the west;
protect me in the south by the whirling of your own trident, and likewise in the north, O Īśvarī. To the crest-lock, vaṣaṭ!
Oṃ! Whatever gentle forms wander through the three worlds, and whatever forms are exceedingly terrible—with those, protect us in that manner! For the armor: hūṃ!
O Ambikā, with those weapons such as the sword, trident, and mace that rest upon your sprout-like hands, protect us from all sides. *Vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes.
Oṃ! O you who are the essence of all, the sovereign of all, endowed with all powers;
protect us from all fears, O Goddess Durgā! Homage be to you, O Goddess! Phaṭ to the weapon!
Now, for the meditation:

Oṃ! [I meditate upon her] who possesses a radiance equal to a garland of lightning, who stands upon the shoulders of the king of beasts, who is terrifying, and who is attended by maidens whose hands shine with swords and shields.

I worship Durgā, who consists of fire, who bears the moon, and who has three eyes; she holds in her hands the discus, mace, sword, shield, arrow, bow with its string, and the gesture of threat (tarjanī).
(p. 374) Now follows the Devīsūkta as declared in the Ṛgveda.

For the eight-verse hymn beginning with "oṃ ahaṃ rudrebhiḥ," Vāgāmbhṛṇī is the seer (ṛṣi); the deity is the all-pervading Śrī Ādiśakti, whose nature consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss; Triṣṭubh is the meter for the verses, while the second verse is Jagatī and the remaining verses are Triṣṭubh; its application (viniyoga) is in the recitation at the conclusion of the Devīmāhātmya.
Now, meditation.

Oṃ! Seated upon a lion, crowned with the moon, and adorned with three eyes, Durgā—whose four arms, resembling emeralds, hold a conch, a discus, a bow, and arrows—is graced by armlets, necklaces, bracelets, jingling girdles, and tinkling anklets; she is the remover of all misfortune.
May you have earrings shining with jewels.
Oṃ. I move with the Rudras and the Vasus; I [move] with the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas.
I support both Mitra and Varuṇa; I [support] Indra and Agni, and I [support] both the Aśvins. 1.
I bear the abundant Soma; I [bear] Tvaṣṭṛ, as well as Pūṣan and Bhaga.
I bestow wealth upon the one who offers oblations, the skillful sacrificer, the one who presses the juice. 2.
I am the sovereign lady, the gatherer of treasures, the conscious one, the first among those worthy of sacrifice.
The gods have established me in many places, as one who has many abodes and causes many to dwell within her.
He who perceives, he who breathes, and he who hears what is spoken—by me has this food been eaten.
Those who do not understand shall perish before me; hear, O you who have heard! I speak to you with faith. 4.
I myself declare this, which is favored by both gods and men:
whomsoever I desire, him I make fierce; him I make a Brahman, him a seer, him a man of wise intellect. (5)
Now I bend the bow for Rudra, that his arrow may strike down the hater of sacred knowledge; now I stir up strife against the people, and now I have entered heaven and earth. 6.
Tomorrow I shall place my father upon his head; my source is in the waters, from there in the ocean.
From there I spread out over all worlds, and with my highest point I touch that very heaven. 7.
I alone blow forth like the wind, setting all worlds in motion; beyond the heavens and beyond this earth, I have come to be as vast as that in my majesty. || 8 ||
Oṃ tat sat.
The Devī Sūkta as declared in the Ṛgveda is complete.
Now follows the Devīsūkta.
Salutation to the Goddess, to Mahādevī; salutation always to Śivā.
Salutation to Prakṛti, to Bhadrā; we, being self-restrained, bow down to you. 1.
Salutations to Raudrī, to the Eternal One, and repeated salutations to Gaurī and Dhātrī;
constant salutations to Jyotsnā, to her who has the form of the moon, and to Sukhā. || 2 ||
To Kalyāṇī, to Vṛddhi, and to Siddhi, we offer salutations again and again;
to Nairṛtī, to the Fortune of the Mountains, and to Śarvāṇī, to you we offer salutations again and again. || 3 ||
Constant salutations to Durgā, to her who carries one across difficulties, to Sārā, to the accomplisher of all things;
likewise, constant salutations to Khyāti, to Kṛṣṇā, and to Dhūmrā. || 4 ||

Salutations again and again to her who is both exceedingly gentle and exceedingly fierce; salutations again and again to the Goddess who is the foundation of the universe and the sole performer of all actions.
To that Goddess who is designated as Viṣṇumāyā within all beings—salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation again and again! || 6 ||
To that Goddess who is designated as "consciousness" within all beings—homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again! (7)
To that Goddess who dwells in all beings in the form of the intellect—salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation again and again! || 8 ||
To that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of sleep—homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again! || 9 ||
Salutation to that Goddess who dwells in all beings in the form of hunger; salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation again and again. || 10 ||
Salutation to that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of a shadow; salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation again and again. || 11 ||
Salutation to her who abides in all beings in the form of power; salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation again and again. || 12 ||
To that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of craving—homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again! || 13 ||
Salutations to that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of patience; salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations again and again.
Salutations to that Goddess who is established in all beings in the form of birth; salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations again and again. || 15 ||
To that Goddess who dwells within all beings in the form of modesty—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again! (16)
To that Goddess who dwells within all beings in the form of peace—salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations again and again! || 17 ||
To that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of faith—homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again! || 18 ||
To that Goddess who dwells in all beings in the form of beauty, salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations again and again! || 19 ||
To that Goddess who is established in all beings in the form of Lakṣmī—homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again! || 20 ||
Salutations to that Goddess who is established in all beings in the form of their vital functions; salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations again and again.
Salutations to that Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of mindfulness; salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations again and again.
Salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her, repeated salutations to her—the Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of compassion. || 23 ||
Salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her, repeated salutations to her—the Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of contentment. 24.
Salutations to that Goddess who dwells within all beings in the form of a mother; salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations again and again. || 25 ||
Salutations to that Goddess who dwells within all beings in the form of delusion; salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations again and again. || 26 ||
Salutations again and again to that pervasive Goddess, who is the presiding deity of the senses and of all beings, and who is eternally present within every creature.
In the form of consciousness, she stands pervading this entire world.
Salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her; salutations again and again. || 28 ||

Praised by the gods in the past for providing refuge in their desires, and likewise served day after day by the Lord of the Gods—may that Sovereign, the source of auspiciousness, grant us blessings and destroy all calamities. (29)
"Who is now worshipped by us gods, who are tormented by the arrogant Daityas, and who,
when remembered by those whose bodies are bowed with devotion, instantly destroys all our calamities.
Having recited this *Devīsūkta*, one should perform the placements (*nyāsas*) as stated previously and meditate.
Meditation on Mahākālī and the others.
She who has ten faces, ten feet, and ten hands, praised by the Creator.
A sword with the luster of sapphire, a discus, a conch, a head, and arrows.
Holding a mace, a trident, and a bhuśuṇḍika weapon in her ten hands.
She bore an iron club, a bow, and two arrows, and was praised by Brahmā.
Then, for the sake of destroying Madhu and Kaiṭabha, she beheld the three-eyed Lord adorned with ornaments.
Then one should meditate upon Mahālakṣmī, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
Born from the splendor of all the deities, she is seated upon a lotus throne.
She has eighteen arms, holding a rosary and five arrows.
A sword, a vajra, a mace, and a discus in the right hands, and a water-pot [in the left].
Holding a conch in her left hand, as well as a spear, an axe, and a bow.
A leather strap, a staff, a vessel for liquor, a bell, a noose, and a trident. || 2 ||
Then one should meditate upon Sarasvatī, whose radiance is equal to the autumnal moon.
Holding a conch, a mace, a discus, and arrows in her right hands.
Holding a bell, a trident, a plow, and a bow in her left hands.
Born from a fair-complexioned body, she bestows bliss upon human beings.
She who is the foundation of the world and the crusher of Śumbha and the other demons.
Having meditated thus, one should perform worship with mental offerings and recite the nine-syllable mantra.

Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Cāmuṇḍāyai Vicce. Having recited the nine-syllable mantra 268 times as previously described, and having again performed the subsequent nyāsas, [one should pray]: "O Goddess, you who are the protector of the most secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us; may success be mine."
By your grace, O Maheśvarī. || 31 ||
The Request for Forgiveness.
Oṃ! Whatever may be deficient in syllables or words, or lacking in prosodic measures—forgive that, O Goddess; for whose mind has there not been a lapse? (1)
O Supreme Goddess, forgive all that which was deficient, excessive, omitted, or inverted, whether through ignorance, forgetfulness, or delusion. (2)
O Maheśvarī, by the remembrance, the name, or the utterance of which [mantra], whatever is deficient in penance, sacrifice, ritual acts, and the like, attains completeness through your grace. (3)

O Goddess of the gods, whatever praise has been offered to you by me, though deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, and deficient in devotion, therefore, O Goddess, be the bestower of boons.
O Kāmeśvarī, Mother of the World, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss! Accept this hymn of praise; be gracious, O Supreme Goddess. (5)

O Mother of the World, whatever has been uttered by me in this recitation that is deficient in visarga, bindu, or syllable, may that become perfectly complete through Your grace, and may the fulfillment of my intentions arise forever. (6)
That which is devoid of measure, bindu, the pair of bindus, the pair of feet, and the pair of syllables.
O Mother, through devotion after devotion, in succession, by the power of your manifest and unmanifest creative acts.
Whether recited or not recited out of delusion or ignorance, [it is now] yours in this hymn.
May all that be complete with its constituent parts, O Blessed One, Giver of Boons; through your grace, be gracious.
Be gracious, O Blessed Mother; be gracious, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees!
Grant me your favor, O Goddess Durgā; salutations unto you, O Goddess! (8)
O Śaṅkara’s beloved, may there always be peace for the body and the home of that person for whose sake this hymn has been recited by you. 9.
Whatever I do, O Goddess, whether good or evil, all that is entrusted to you; impelled by you, I act.
Thus one should offer everything.
Oṃ peace! Oṃ peace! Oṃ peace!
Now begins the secret section concerning Pradhāna.

Oṃ. Of this *Śrī-saptaśatī-rahasya-traya*, Nārāyaṇa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandas*), and Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī are the deities (*devatā*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is in recitation for the sake of attaining the aforementioned fruits.
The king said:
O Blessed One, you have described to me the incarnations of Caṇḍikā; O Brahman, you ought to tell me their primordial nature and the primary cause.
