O twice-born one, tell me in its entirety and exactly as it is, according to the prescribed rite, that form of the Goddess which is to be propitiated by me, since I am bowed before you.
The sage said:
"This is a supreme secret, which they declare should not be told;
yet, O lord of men, because you are my devotee, there is nothing that should not be spoken by me to you."

Mahālakṣmī is the primordial source of all, the Supreme Goddess of the three qualities (triguṇā). She is the fivefold aspect consisting of existence, luminosity, and loveliness, as well as form and name, which are beyond the reach of thought. Of these, the first three are the nature of Brahman, while the latter two are the nature of Māyā. Her essential being consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
They are established as pervading the whole.
[In the Sahyādrikhaṇḍa, in the Māhātmya of Reṇukā:
In his lower right hand he holds a vessel, and in his upper [right hand] the mace Kaumodakī.]
In her left hand she holds a shield, and below it, in her other hand, a bilva fruit;
bearing a linga upon her head, she should be worshipped for the sake of prosperity.
The meaning of these [verses] is according to the Bhuvaneśvarī Saṃhitā.
The multitude of actions is the mother’s characteristic; the mace consists of the power of action (kriyā-śakti);
the shield consists of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti); and the drinking vessel is the state of the Fourth (turya-vṛtti).
The *liṅga* is said to be the Puruṣa, while the *yoni* is traditionally known as Prakṛti;
Nāga is declared to be Time (*kāla*), and he is the connection between those two.
Likewise, by the taking of the mātuliṅga fruit, it is made known that "I am the bestower of the fruits of all actions."
By the wielding of the mace, it is made known that the power of projection (vikṣepa-śakti), whose very nature is activity, resides within me.
By the wearing of the staff (kheṭa) and by the manifestation of the presence of the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), the absence of obscuration (āvaraṇābhāva) is indicated.
It should be understood that with the drinking vessel of the mind, I continuously drink the essence of the experience of the bliss of my own Self.
For time is indeed of the nature of the relationship between the two, primordial matter (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa).
And thus, by their being upheld, the Goddess was awakened [to realize]: "I am the Supreme Brahman, the presiding principle over those—namely Prakṛti, Puruṣa, and Kāla.
Carrying a citron, a mace, a shield, and a drinking vessel, she appeared.
Bearing both the phallus of the Nāga and the womb upon the head of the king. || 5 ||
Having the luster of molten gold and adorned with ornaments of molten gold,
she filled that entire void with her own splendor.
Beholding that entire world as empty, the Supreme Goddess assumed a supreme form consisting solely of darkness.
Resembling crushed collyrium, with a beautiful face marked by fangs, large-eyed and slender-waisted, she became a woman of no small stature. (8)
Her four arms are adorned with a sword, a bowl, a severed head, and a shield;
she wears a necklace of headless trunks and a garland of heads upon her head. (9)
That most excellent woman, who was of the nature of Tamas, spoke to Mahālakṣmī:
"O Mother, give me a name and a deed; salutations, salutations unto you! (10)
Mahālakṣmī spoke to that most excellent woman, who was characterized by tamas:
"I shall give you names, and whatever actions you perform, those shall be your [deeds]. (11)
Mahāmāyā, Mahākālī, Mahāmārī, Hunger, Thirst, Sleep, Craving, Ekavīrā, and the insurmountable Kālarātri. (12)
These names of yours are to be established through your deeds;
he who studies them after having understood your deeds through these [names] attains happiness.
Having said "that," O King, Mahālakṣmī assumed another form,
possessing the quality known as *sattva*, which is exceedingly pure and radiant like the moon. (14)
Holding a rosary and a goad, and bearing a lute and a book, she became an excellent woman; and he gave her names.
She is the Great Vidyā, the Great Arrow, Bhāratī, Vāk, and Sarasvatī;
she is Āryā, Brāhmī, Kāmadhenu, the one whose womb is the Vedas, and Dhīśvarī. || 16 ||
Then Mahālakṣmī said to Mahākālī and Sarasvatī:
"O goddesses, may you two give birth to a pair of children who are mutually suitable to one another."
Having spoken thus, Mahālakṣmī herself created a pair,
a beautiful man and woman, both golden-hued and seated upon lotuses.
The mother Śrī addressed that man as "Brahman," "Vidhi," "Virinchi," and "Dhātṛ"; and she addressed that woman as "Padmā," "Kamalā," and "Lakṣmī."
Mahākālī and Bhāratī create together as a pair;
I shall also tell you their forms and names. (20)
Mahākālī gave birth to a person with a blue throat, red arms, white limbs, and the moon upon his crest, as well as a white woman.
He is Rudra, Śaṅkara, Sthāṇu, Kapardin, and the three-eyed one;
she is the triple Veda, the wish-fulfilling cow, that woman, speech, the syllables, and the vowels.
O King, Sarasvatī gave birth to a fair-complexioned woman and a dark-complexioned man;
I shall now tell you their names as well. (23)
Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, Vāsudeva, Janārdana;
Umā, Gaurī, Satī, Caṇḍī, Sundarī, Subhagā, Śivā. (24)
In this way, young women immediately attained manhood;
those with sight indeed see it, but not others who lack knowledge of that. (25)
Mahālakṣmī gave his wife, the triad of queens, to Brahmā;
Gaurī, the bestower of boons, to Rudra; and Śrī to Vāsudeva.
Having united with Svarā, Virañci produced the cosmic egg;
the powerful Lord Rudra, together with Gaurī, split it open.
O King, within the egg was produced the entire collection of effects, beginning with Pradhāna—the whole world consisting of the great elements, both stationary and moving. (28)
Keśava nourished and protected it along with Lakṣmī;
Maheśvara withdrew the entire universe along with Gaurī. || 29 ||
O Great King, Mahālakṣmī is the sovereign who consists of all sentient beings;
she is both formless and with form, bearing manifold names. (30)
She is to be defined by various names, but not by any other name—Oṃ. (31)
Thus ends the secret doctrine concerning the Pradhāna.
Now begins the Vaikṛtirahasya.
The sage said:
Oṃ! She who is the goddess of the three qualities, manifested in three ways as Tāmasī and Sāttvikī, is proclaimed as Śarvā, Caṇḍikā, Durgā, Bhadrā, and Bhagavatī. (1)
Yoganidrā is said to be the Mahākālī of Hari characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas),
whom the Lotus-seated One (Brahmā) praised for the sake of destroying Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
She has ten faces, ten arms, and ten feet with the luster of collyrium;
she shines brilliantly with a wide array of thirty eyes.
O King, with her quivering fangs and terrifying form,
she was the very embodiment of beauty, fortune, and splendor, the established seat of great majesty.
He bore a sword, arrows, a mace, a trident, a conch, a discus, and a bhushundi weapon;
he held an iron club, a bow, and a severed head from which blood was dripping.
This is that very Māyā of Viṣṇu, Mahākālī, who is difficult to overcome;
when propitiated, she can bring under her control the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings for the one who performs her worship.
She who has manifested from the bodies of all the gods with immeasurable radiance,
she is Mahālakṣmī, composed of the three qualities (guṇas), the manifest slayer of Mahiṣa.
She has a white face, blue arms, and very white breasts;
her waist and feet are red, while her shanks and thighs are blue and intoxicated with passion.
(391) She possessed a most variegated hip, was adorned with wonderful garlands, garments, and ornaments,
was anointed with exquisite unguents, and was endowed with loveliness, beauty, and good fortune. || 9 ||
She, who is truly thousand-armed, is to be worshipped as having eighteen arms;
her weapons shall be described here, starting from the lower right hand in sequence.
The rosary, the lotus, the arrow, the sword, the thunderbolt, the mace, the discus, the trident, the axe, the conch, the bell, and the noose. || 11 ||
With these weapons— a spear, a staff, a shield, a bow, a drinking vessel, and a water-pot—
her arms were adorned as she sat upon a lotus throne.
O King, one should worship this Mahālakṣmī, the sovereign who embodies all the gods; such a person shall become the lord of all worlds and of the gods.
She who has arisen from Gaurī and others, who rests solely upon the quality of *sattva*,
is declared to be Sarasvatī herself, the destroyer of the demon Śumbha. (14)
O Lord of the Earth, he held in his eight arms an arrow, a mace, a trident,
a discus, a conch, a bell, a plow, and a bow.
When worshipped with devotion, she bestows omniscience;
she is the Goddess who destroyed Niśumbha and the slayer of the demon Śumbha.
Thus have the essential forms of your manifestations been described, O King;
now listen to the separate modes of worship for each of these forms of the Mother of the World.
When Mahālakṣmī, Mahākālī, and Sarasvatī are to be worshipped,
the triad of couples is to be worshipped at the back, on the right and left sides.
Virinchi is in the middle with Svarā, Rudra is on the right with Gaurī, and Hṛṣīkeśa is on the left with Lakṣmī; these are the three deities at the front.
One should worship Mahālakṣmī as having eighteen arms, with ten faces on her left side and eight arms on her right side. (20)
The Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga, are to be worshipped starting from the eastern petal;
and when she is worshipped with eighteen arms, O lord of men, [the procedure is as follows].
When she has ten faces and eight arms,
then she is to be worshipped with ten faces on both the right and the left.
Kāla and Mṛtyu should also be worshipped for the pacification of all calamities;
and when she who destroys the demon Śumbha is to be worshipped with eight arms.
Then her nine powers, as well as Rudra and Vināyaka, should be worshipped; one should worship Mahālakṣmī with hymns beginning with "Namo Devyai. (24)
In the worship of the three incarnations, the hymns and mantras are based upon them;
this eighteen-armed Mahiṣamardinī is to be worshipped. (25)
She alone is declared to be Mahālakṣmī, Mahākālī, and Sarasvatī;
she is the sovereign of merits and sins, the Great Sovereign of all the worlds. (26)
He by whom she who puts an end to Mahiṣa has been worshipped is the Lord of the World;
he should worship Caṇḍikā, the Mother of the Worlds, who is affectionate toward her devotees. || 27 ||

With offerings of water for the hands (arghya) and other ornaments, with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), as well as with incense, lamps, and food offerings consisting of various kinds of edibles; || 28 ||

O King, this worship with offerings of meat, blood, liquor, and the like, which I have prescribed, is to be performed by a powerful person smeared with blood; it is to be excluded from the Brahmins. (29)
O King, it is said that for them, worship with liquor and meat is never prescribed;
rather, [they are worshipped] with prostrations, water for rinsing the mouth, and fragrant sandalwood.
Accompanied by betel leaves mixed with camphor and imbued with a spirit of devotion,
[he should place] the great demon Chinnashirsha on the left side in front of the Goddess.
One should worship Mahiṣa by whom union with the Lord was attained;
and to the right and in front, one should worship the Lion, the complete Lord Dharma.
One should worship the vehicle of the Goddess, by which the world of moving and non-moving beings is sustained.
Now, the Kuñjikā Stotra.
The Lord said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme Kuñjikā mantra (hymn),
by the power of which the recitation of Caṇḍī bestows perfect accomplishment.
There is no armor, no *argalā-stotra*, no *kīlaka*, nor the *nara-rahasya*;
there is neither hymn (*sūkta*), nor meditation (*dhyāna*), nor ritual placement (*nyāsa*), nor even worship (*arcana*). || 2 ||
By the mere recitation of the *Kuñjikā*, one obtains the fruit of reciting the *Durgā*.
O Goddess, this is most secret, difficult even for the gods to attain. (3)
O Pārvatī, one should guard this with great effort, like one's own private parts;
it includes the rites of killing, bewildering, subjugating, paralyzing, uprooting, and so forth.
This supreme *Kuñjikā-stotra* shall be perfected by mere recitation.
This is the mantra: Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ cāmuṇḍāyai vicce | Oṃ glauṃ huṃ klīṃ jūṃ saḥ jvālaya 2 jvala 2 prajvala 2 aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ cāmuṇḍāyai vicce jvala haṃ saṃ laṃ.
KṢAṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. Thus is the mantra.
Then, having joined his palms in reverence, he should offer praise with these deeds: || 33 ||
One should not recite even half of the practice with either one or the other of these two middling methods here; if one does so while reciting, one incurs a flaw.
One should praise this Mother of the World with hymns and mantras,
having performed circumambulations and prostrations, with palms joined above the head.
One should tirelessly seek forgiveness from the Mother of the World again and again;
and for every verse, one should offer oblations of milk-rice mixed with sesame and mustard seeds.
Or one should offer auspicious oblations to Caṇḍikā with the hymns and mantras:
"Salutations to you who possess the form of Rudra; salutations to you, O crusher of Madhu;
salutations to the destroyer of Kaiṭabha; salutations to you, O subduer of Mahiṣa. || 1 ||
Salutations to you, the slayer of Śumbha and the destroyer of the asura Niśumbha.
O Great Goddess, while I am awake, grant me the perfection of my recitation (japa);
Aiṃkārī is the form of emanation, and Hrīṃkārī is the protector.
Obeisance to you, the syllable *klīṃ*, who possesses a form at will and exists in the nature of seed-syllables;
you are Cāmuṇḍā, the slayer of the fierce, and the bestower of boons through the syllable *ya*.
O you who bestow fearlessness even here, salutations to you, O embodiment of the mantra! || 5 ||
Dhāṃ dhīṃ dhūṃ, O Consort of Dhūrjaṭi; vāṃ vīṃ vūṃ, likewise Vāgīśvarī; krāṃ krīṃ krūṃ kraiṃ, O Goddess Kālikā; śāṃ śīṃ śūṃ—grant me auspiciousness! || 6 ||
Furthermore, with great composure, one should worship the Goddess with names and words. (37)
Being self-restrained, with palms joined in reverence and bowing low, having fixed his vital breaths within himself,
he should meditate upon the goddess Caṇḍikā for a very long time and become absorbed in her essence.
Thus, he who worships the Supreme Goddess with devotion every day, having enjoyed pleasures according to his desire, shall attain union with the Goddess. || 39 ||
The Supreme Goddess, having reduced to ashes the merits of one who does not constantly worship Caṇḍikā, who is affectionate toward her devotees, shall utterly consume him.
Therefore, O protector of the earth, worship Caṇḍikā, the Great Sovereign of all the worlds, according to the prescribed rite; thus you shall attain happiness. Om. 41.
Thus ends the complete secret of the Vaikṛta.

Huṃ huṃ huṃ! O you whose form is the syllable *huṃkāra*, Jaṃ jaṃ jaṃ jaṃ! O you who cause the crushing [of foes], Bhrāṃ bhrīṃ bhrūṃ! O Bhairavī, O Auspicious One, salutations again and again to you, the consort of Bhava (Bhavānī)! Aṃ kaṃ caṃ ṭaṃ taṃ paṃ yaṃ śaṃ vīṃ duṃ aiṃ vīṃ haṃ kṣaṃ! O you who are at the tip of the twice-born’s [sacrificial] ladle, crush, crush! Make it blazing, make it blazing! Svāhā! Pāṃ!
Pīṃ, Pūṃ, O Pārvatī, Pūrṇā; Khāṃ, Khīṃ, Khūṃ, and likewise Khecarī. || 8 ||
Sāṃ sīṃ sūṃ! O Saptashati, grant success through one's own people alone.
This Kuñjikā-stotra mantra remains awake for the sake of [attaining] the cause.
O Pārvatī, it must be given by one who is devoted and guarded as a secret;
for he who recites the Saptashatī, O Goddess, without the key (kuñjikā), [attains no fruit].
Success does not arise for him; it is like weeping in the wilderness.
The Kuñjikā Stotra from the Rudrayāmala.
(p. 398) Now begins the Mūrtirahasya.
The sage said:
Oṃ! She who shall be known by the name of the Blessed One Nandā, born of Joy—when praised and worshipped with devotion, she shall bring the three worlds under her control. (1)
She is the stride of the most excellent gold, beautifully adorned with golden garments;
the goddess has the luster of the color of gold and wears ornaments of the finest gold.
Adorned with four arms holding a lotus, a goad, a noose,
and a water-lily, she is Indirā, Kamalā, Lakṣmī, Śrī, and Rukmiṇī, whose seat is a golden lotus.
O sinless one, I have already described the goddess named Yāraktadantikā;
I shall now describe her true form, which removes all fears—listen! (p. 399)
Having heard this, one is liberated from all sins; of this there is no doubt.
She is clad in red garments, red in complexion, and adorned with red ornaments on all her limbs.
With red weapons, red eyes, and red hair, she is exceedingly terrifying;
her sharp claws are red, her tongue is red, and her teeth are red.
Like a devoted wife toward her husband, that queen should worship the people who are devoted to her;
she is as vast as the earth, with the pair of Mount Sumerus for her breasts.
Long, hanging, and very thick, they were equally captivating; both were firm yet exceedingly beautiful, oceans of nectar for all delight. (8)
The Goddess nourishes her devotees with her two breasts that yield all desires;
she is adorned with four arms holding a sword, a vessel, a severed head, and a shield.
The goddess Raktacāmuṇḍā is called Yogeśvarī;
by her, the entire world, both stationary and moving, is pervaded. (10)
Whoever worships this [image] with devotion pervades the entire world of moving and unmoving beings;
having enjoyed pleasures according to his desire, he shall attain union (sāyujya) with the Goddess. || 11 ||
The goddess Raktadantī shall attend upon that man who constantly recites this hymn to her form, just as a loving woman attends upon her husband.
Śākambharī is blue in complexion, with eyes like blue lotuses;
she has a deep navel and a slender waist adorned with the three folds.
The Abode of Kamala possessed breasts that were very firm, symmetrical, high, rounded, full, and dense; she held a lotus filled with bees as if it were a fistful [of flowers]. 14.

It abounds in fruits such as flowers, sprouts, and roots, and consists of a collection of vegetables; it is endowed with desirable and endless virtues, and removes hunger, thirst, death, and old age. (15)
The Supreme Goddess bears a bow of shimmering luster;
she is Śākambharī, the hundred-eyed one, and she alone is celebrated as Durgā. (16)
Uma, Gauri, Sati, Chandī, Kālikā, and she who is Pārvatī—praising, meditating upon, chanting, fully worshipping, and bowing down to Śākambharī. (17)
One quickly attains inexhaustible food, drink, nectar, and water.
[She is] terrifying, blue-colored, and radiant with fangs and teeth. 18.
A woman with large eyes and rounded, full breasts, bearing a sword as bright as the moon, a hand-drum, and a skull-bowl. (19)
She alone is called the Solitary Heroine (Ekavīrā) and the Night of Time (Kālarātri), the bestower of desires;
she is difficult to overcome due to her circle of splendor and bears the variegated luster of a bee.
Resembling a variegated bee, she is celebrated as Mahāmārī;
thus, O lord of the earth, these forms of the Goddess have been described. (21)
(402) These wish-fulfilling cows of Caṇḍikā, the Mother of the World, have been proclaimed.
This supreme secret must not be spoken by you to anyone. 22.
Study yourself with focused attention the commentaries on the divine forms;
by her grace, you shall become honored by all. (23)
The gods consist of all forms, and the entire world consists of the Goddess;
therefore, I bow to you, the Supreme Sovereign, who are the embodiment of the universe. 24.
Thus ends the Mūrtirahasya in its entirety.

Out of grace, these verses [are spoken]: Oṃ! May that Sovereign Goddess—who is the Mistress of the Universe, the Sustainer of the World, and the cause of its preservation and destruction—be the source of our auspiciousness; may she grant us blessings and destroy all calamities. (1)

Oṃ! May that Goddess—who was formerly praised by the Asuras because they sought refuge in her desired [protection], and who is served day after day by the Lord of the Gods—be the cause of our welfare; may she bring auspiciousness and destroy all calamities. (2)
Oṃ! She who is now worshipped by us—the Daityas who have been shorn of their pride—and by the gods, including Īśa;
may that Sovereign Lady, the cause of our welfare, grant us auspicious things and drive away all calamities. (3)

Oṃ! May that Sovereign Goddess—who, when remembered, instantly destroys all our calamities for those whose forms are bowed in devotion—be the cause of our welfare; may she grant us auspiciousness and prosperity, and strike down our misfortunes. (4)
Oṃ, O Sovereign Lady of the entire three worlds, [the pacifier of all afflictions;
here, the phrase "destruction of enemies" is to be modified as "destruction of diseases," and likewise "tormented by the Daityas"].
May that Sovereign Lady, the cause of our auspiciousness, grant us blessings and destroy all calamities. || 5 ||
Oṃ! O auspicious one, most auspicious among all that is auspicious, O Śivā, accomplisher of all aims!
May that Sovereign Lady, the cause of well-being, grant us blessings and destroy our misfortunes. (6)

Oṃ! O eternal one, who has become the power of creation, maintenance, and destruction—may that Sovereign Lady, the cause of our welfare, grant us auspicious things, and may she strike down all calamities. (7)

Oṃ! May that Sovereign Lady, who is solely intent on protecting those who have come for refuge, the wretched, and the afflicted, be the cause of our welfare; may she grant us auspiciousness and prosperity, and destroy all calamities. (8)
Oṃ! O you who are the essence of all, the sovereign of all, endowed with all powers;
may that Sovereign Lady, the cause of our welfare, grant us auspicious things and destroy all calamities. (9)

These nine verses are for the rite of *anugraha* (favor/grace); however, for *vaśya* (subjugation), the remainder [is used]. *Oṃ hrīṃ raktacāmuṇḍe tūrṇam amukaṃ me vaśam ānaya svāhā.* With this mantra, worship is performed at the beginning and end of each chapter, and at the conclusion of all [chapters], there is a recitation (*japa*) of ten thousand (*ayuta*) mantras.

One should offer oblations of red *andana* and black mustard seeds with *kuṭu* oil; by merely performing a thousand oblations, one shall bring a king under control. By offering honey and *aśoka* flowers at night as previously described, one becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) and is brought under control through the power of the Caṇḍī mantra.
Now begins the Sarasvatī Kavaca.
Brahmā said:
Listen, my child, I shall proclaim the armor (kavaca) that grants all desires;
it is the essence of the Vedas, the mouth of the Vedas, declared by the Vedas, and honored by the Vedas.
This was spoken by Kṛṣṇa, the sovereign Lord of the Rāsa, in the forest of Vṛndāvana at Goloka,
during the Rāsa dance within the circle of the Rāsa.
It is exceedingly secret, supreme, and equal to the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa),
endowed with a collection of mantras never heard before and most wonderful.
O Brahman, by retaining and reciting which one becomes wise like Bṛhaspati;
by retaining which the venerable Śukra was honored among all the Daityas. (4)
From reciting or retaining it, one becomes eloquent; the sage Vālmīki became the lord of poets.
And Svāyambhuva Manu himself, having worn it, was honored by all;
as were Kaṇāda, Gautama, Kaṇva, Pāṇini, and Śākaṭāyana.
Having composed this work, Dakṣa Kātyāyana himself,
having taken up the division of the Vedas and all the Purāṇas, [attained success].
Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana himself performed this merely as a pastime,
as did Śātātapa, Saṃvarta, Vasiṣṭha, and Parāśara.
Having taken up this work, Yājñavalkya composed it;
as did Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Bharadvāja, Āstīka, and likewise Devala. (9)
O best of Brahmins, Jaigīṣavya and Jāvāli, who are honored by all because they have worn this armor— this Prajāpati is the seer (ṛṣi) of this kavaca.
He himself is Bṛhaspati, the deity of the Vedic meters, the Lord Rāseśvara,
the master in the full knowledge of all principles and in the accomplishment of all goals.
And its application is proclaimed for all poetic compositions:
"Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to Sarasvatī; may she protect my head on all sides. (12)
"Śrīṃ, svāhā to the goddess of speech; may she protect my forehead at all times.
Oṃ, svāhā to Sarasvatī; may she protect my hearing continuously. (13)
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to Bhāratī; may she always protect my pair of eyes. Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to Vāgvādinī; may she protect my nose from all sides. (14)
Hrīṃ! To the Goddess who presides over knowledge, Svāhā! May she always protect my lips.
Oṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ! To Brāhmī, Svāhā! May she always protect the rows of my teeth. (15)
May the single-syllable mantra *aim* always protect my throat;
may *oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ* protect my neck, and may *śrī* always protect my shoulders. (16)
Śrīṃ, svāhā to the Goddess who presides over the Vidyā; may she always protect my chest.
Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to her whose nature is the Vidyā; may she protect my navel. (17)
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ vāṇyai svāhā—may this protect my back forever. Oṃ sarvavarṇātmikāyai—may it protect the pair of feet forever. || 18 ||
Oṃ, may she who presides over passion always protect my entire body.
Oṃ, svāhā to her who dwells in all throats; may she always protect [me] in the east. 19.
Oṃ hrīṃ, may she who dwells on the tip of the tongue protect [me] in the southeast; svāhā!
Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, svāhā to Sarasvatī, the mother of the wise! || 20 ||
May this king of mantras always protect me in the south: Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ; may the three-syllabled mantra always protect me in the southwest. || 21 ||
To her who dwells on the tips of the tongues of poets, Svāhā! May she protect me in the northwest.
Oṃ, to the eternal Mother, Svāhā! May she always protect me in the northwestern direction.
Oṃ, svāhā to her who dwells in prose and verse; may she protect me from the north. Oṃ, svāhā to her who dwells in all the scriptures; may she always protect me from the northeast. || 23 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to her who is worshipped by all; may she always protect me from above. Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to her who dwells in the book; may she always protect me from below. || 24 ||
Oṃ, svāhā to her whose nature is the seed-syllable of the book; may she protect me from all sides.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have told you that which embodies the entire multitude of mantras. (25)
This armor, named Viśvajaya, is the very form of Brahman.
Formerly, this Dharma was heard from your own lips on Mount Gandhamādana;
out of affection for you, I have recounted it, but it must not be told to anyone else.
Having worshipped the Guru according to the rules with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste,
the wise man should prostrate himself like a staff upon the ground and wear the armor.
By reciting it five hundred thousand times, the armor-mantra (kavaca) becomes perfected;
if one possesses the perfected armor, he shall become equal to Bṛhaspati.
He shall become a great orator, a lord among poets, and a conqueror of the three worlds;
by the grace of this armor, he is able to conquer everything.
Thus, O Sage, I have related to you this armor (kavaca) spoken in the Kāṇva recension,
as well as the hymn, the ritual procedure for worship, the meditation, and likewise the salutation.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Armor of Sarasvatī," in the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
The nine-syllable variations are:
1. Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ ḷīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ namaḥ. 2. Aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ cāmuṇḍāyai vicce. 3. Hūṃ aiṃ aiṃ hrīṃ cāmuṇḍāyai svāhā.
As stated in the Ḍāmara: "Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ ḷṃ hrīṃ namaḥ"—thus say the southerners. 5.

"HŪṂ AIṂ AIṂ HRĪṂ CĀMUṆḌĀYAI SVĀHĀ"—this is the mantra of the Sārasvatas. Those who follow the *Devī-atharvaśiras* and those who follow the *Ḍāmara-tantra* are the learned ones (*śiṣṭas*). They establish the mantra as "OṂ AIṂ HRĪṂ KLĪṂ CĀMUṆḌĀYAI VICCE. By this stated authority, [the mantras for] Jīvana and others are also established.

"The greatness, the extraordinary purpose, and the ritual application of the mantra must be understood by the wise at every step by one desiring to know it"— this being the established position of the *Yajurvedabhāṣya* as recorded in traditional scripture (*smṛti*), it is precisely with reference to that [greatness] that the extraordinary greatness and purpose of this mantra are stated in the *Ḍāmaratantra*.
It is being examined.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the Sarvatobhadra mandala.
In the Skanda Purāṇa, within the Hemādri [section].
One should draw nineteen lines running from east to north.
A crescent moon is formed in a corner with three steps and five links. || 1 ||
The *padāvallī* is eleven [units] long and nine units wide;
the *vāpī* is twenty-four units long and twenty units wide. (2)
In the center, with sixteen squares, an eight-petaled lotus is prescribed;
one should fill the white moon, the black chain, and the creeper with blue.
The auspicious Aruṇa and Sita are the enclosure (paridhi) of yellow color;
with outer and inner petals, the pericarp (karṇikā) is white and yellow in color.
Outside the lotus encircled by the boundary-line, one should place the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas;
and in its center, one should establish the gods beginning with Brahmā, as well as the suras and asuras.

Thus ends the *sarvatobhadrapīṭha*. In all concluding rites (*udyāpana*) of vows, except for the *śivavrata*, one should have the *sarvatobhadra* mandala constructed. The preceptor, accompanied by the patron, should install the deities of the *sarvatobhadra* mandala as follows. Regarding this, there is a verse:
The wise should construct an altar out of pure clay, measuring either two cubits or one cubit in height.

Then, one should draw the Sarvatobhadra mandala upon that altar. Having sipped water (ācamana), restrained the breaths (prāṇāyāma), and recollected the place and time, [one should recite]: "Oṃ, today, in this rite called Homa, in this Sarvatobhadra mandala, by means of the Vedas (or by name) and mantras, [I shall install] Brahmā and the others..."
I shall perform the invocation, installation, and worship of the fifty-six deities.
Taking flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣatān*), one should invoke Brahmā in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*): Oṃ.

Brahmā, the first knower of sacrifice, has revealed from the front, from the firmament, the beautiful light of Vena. He, the foundation, has disclosed its supreme forms, the source of both the existent and the non-existent. Oṃ.
Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O Brahmā, come here; stay here! Salutation to Brahmā!

I invoke Brahmā; I establish him. Accept this worship; be present before me and be well-pleased. || 1 || Starting from the north and extending to the northwest corner, one should establish the eight world-protectors (lokapālas), beginning with Kubera and ending with Vāyu. In the northern pond: Oṃ vayaguṃ.
May we, possessing offspring, abide in the bodies that bear your mind through the Soma-vow. Bhūr!
O Soma, come here! One should invoke Īśāna in the northeast, upon the crescent moon: Oṃ!
Him, the Lord of the moving and the stationary world, the stimulator of intelligence, we invoke for protection with this great hymn—just as Pūṣan [protects] us.
The protector of the increase of the true Sāman, the undeceivable guardian who wards off misfortune—for our well-being! Īśāna... 3.
Oṃ, Indra the protector, Indra the savior, the one easy to invoke at every call— Indra the heroic!
I invoke Śakra, Indra, who is invoked by many; may the bountiful Indra grant us well-being.

*Bhūr*, O Indra, come here... 4. To Agni in the crescent moon in the southeast: *Oṃ*. O Agni, O God, protect our wealthy patrons and our bodies with your guardians, O worshipful one; be the savior of our lives, of our offspring, and of our cattle, never failing us.
Protecting the goat while observing your vow: *Oṃ bhūḥ*, O Agni, come here! (5) To Yama at the southern well:
*Oṃ sugannu panthāṃ pradiśanna ehi jyotiṣmadyehy ajaraṃ na āyuḥ | apaitu mṛtyur amṛtaṃ sa āgāt vaivasvato no abhayaṃ kṛṇotu*.

But for us [be] prosperity! O Bhūmi, Bhava, and Īśvara, come here! (6) To the southwest, [I invoke] Nirṛti, who has the crescent moon as her mark: "Oṃ, you seek one who does not press the Soma and does not sacrifice; you follow the path of the thief who steals the sacrificial fee."
"O Goddess Nirṛti, may you be pleased with us; let this [oblation] be for you, O Nirṛti.

*Bhūḥ*. O Bhavanirṛti, come here! 7. To Varuṇa in the western pond: "Oṃ, I approach you, worshipping you with a sacred prayer (*brahman*); the sacrificer desires that [favor] through oblations. Be not angry, O Varuṇa..."
O rogue, do not steal away the life of one who is equal to you! O Lord Varuṇa, come here! 8.

In the northwest, upon a crescent moon, [one should worship] Vāyu: *Oṃ ā noniyudbhiḥ śatinībhir adhvaragum sahasriṇībhir upayāhi yajñam | vāyo 'asmin savane mādayasva svayūyam pāta svastibhiḥ sadā naḥ |* Bhūr! O Vāyu, come here! (9) Between Vāyu and Soma, upon a *bhadra* [seat].

To the Eight Vasus: Oṃ! O divine Vasus, you who possess beautiful cattle, come to this libation which we have prepared; enjoying this libation, bringing and carrying the oblations, bestow upon us, O Vasus, excellent treasures. Svāhā! Bhūḥ! O Vasus, please come here! 10. [The offering] between Soma and Īśāna.

O auspicious lady, [worship] the eleven Rudras. Oṃ, the Rudras, together with Guṃ, having created the vast earth, kindled the great light; their unceasing radiance shines brightly among the gods. Bhūḥ! O Rudras, come here! 11. Between Īśāna and Indra, O auspicious lady, [worship] the twelve Ādityas. Oṃ.
The sacrifice goes forth toward the favor of the gods; O Ādityas, may you be gracious and bring us prosperity.
p.
408) May the benevolent thought of the Ādityas turn toward us; may they grant us wide space and be ever the best finders of wealth.
[I offer] you to the Ādityas. O Bhūḥ! O twelve Ādityas, come here! 12. Between Indra and Agni is the auspicious [spot].

To the Aśvins: Oṃ! O Aśvins, with that whip of yours which is honey-sweet and full of truth, seek a share for us at this sacrifice. You are taken with a support; for the two Aśvins you are; this is your womb; for the two Madhvis you are.
Obeisance! O Aśvins, come here! (13) Between Agni and Yama, O auspicious one, [invoke] the Viśvedevas:
"Om Om, O Viśvedevas, supporters of the people, come hither!"
[Drink] the pressed juice of the donor from the donor; you are taken with a support (upayāma). I take you for all the gods. This is your womb;
I take you for all the gods. *Bhūḥ*. O Viśvedevas, together with the ancestors, come here! 14. [I invoke] the seven Yakṣas in the auspicious space between Yama and Nirṛti. Om.

I praise with song this divine Savitar between the two worlds, the seer of inspired wisdom, the one whose ordinances are true, the bestower of jewels, the beloved, the sage of holy thought. His lofty splendor has shone forth;
he, the wise one, the golden-handed, has fashioned light with his skillful art. For the sake of all creatures, I turn to you.

May the subjects breathe after you; may I indeed breathe after the subjects. Oṃ, O seven Yakṣas, come here! [15] Between the directions of Nairṛti and Varuṇa, O auspicious one, [I invoke] the Bhūtas and Nāgas: "Oṃ, obeisance to the serpents, whoever they may be on earth, in the intermediate space, or in heaven; to them [be homage]."

Salutation to the serpents. O Bhūtas and Nāgas, come here! (16) Between Varuṇa and Vāyu, in the auspicious [quarter], are the Gandharva and Apsaras. Om, Ṛtāṣāṭ, whose abode is Truth, is Agni; his Gandharva is Vapu and his Apsaras is Mudā by name. May he protect this Brahman and Kṣatra; to him [be salutation].
Svāhā! Vāṭ! To the Tāmyas! Bhūḥ! O Gandharvas and Apsarases, come here! 18.

In the middle between the Brahmasoma and the pond, [one should worship] Skanda: "Oṃ, when you first cried out at birth, rising from the ocean, from the watery mass, with the wings of a hawk and the forelegs of a deer—O steed, your greatness is to be praised. Bhūḥ! O Skanda, come here! (19) [One should worship] Nandin with the *trava* mantra.
Oṃ! Let the prize-winning steed, neighing loudly like a braying donkey, go forth.
p.

409) "Maintaining the fire that nourishes the body, do not depart before the end of your life. *Bhūḥ*, O Nandin, come here, stay here. (20) There, to Īśvara: *Oṃ*, Īśāna of all sciences, Lord of all...

For embodied beings, may the Lord of Brahmā, the Overlord of Brahmā, the Brahmā who is Śiva, be ever auspicious to me—Śivom! Bhūḥ! O Īśvara, come here, stay here! 22. In that very place: Salutation to Mahākāla.

OṂ BHŪR BHO MAHĀKĀLA, COME HERE, STAY HERE! || 23 || [One should worship] the seven Yakṣas, Dakṣa and the others, upon the creepers between Brahmā and Īśāna. OṂ ADITIR DYAUḤ, ADITIR ANTARIKṢAM, ADITIR MĀTĀ SAPITĀ SAPUTRAḤ | VIŚVE DEVĀ ADITIḤ PAÑCA JANĀ ADITIR JĀTAM ADITIR JANITVAM || OṂ BHŪR BHO DAKṢĀDI... [and so forth].
"O seven yakṣas, come here! Stay! O Brahmā and Indra, [worship] Durgā in the pond. || 24 ||

Oṃ, O Ambā, O Ambikā, O Ambālikā, no one can lead you away. The little horse has mated with Subhadrikā, the dweller of Kāmpīla. Bhu00 Bho Durgā, come here, stay here! 25. In that very place: Oṃ, Viṣṇu strode across this; he established his foot in three places. His measured step is hidden in the cave. Sure.

Svāhā! Oṃ Bhūr! O Viṣṇu, come here, stay here! (26) [I offer] Svadhā among the creepers between Brahmā and Agni. Oṃ, svadhā and obeisance to the fathers who partake of the svadhā; svadhā and obeisance to the grandfathers who partake of the svadhā; svadhā and obeisance to the great-grandfathers who partake of the svadhā.
Svadhā namaḥ. The ancestors have eaten; the ancestors have rejoiced; the ancestors have been satisfied. O ancestors, be purified. Bhūḥ! O Svadhā, come here; stay here. 27.

In the middle between the Brahmayama [sections], at the pond, are Mṛtyu and Rogau: *Oṃ paraṃ mṛtyo 'anuparehi panthāṃ yaste 'anya itaro devayānāt | cakṣuṣmate śṛṇvate te bravīmi mā naḥ prajāṃ rīriṣo mota vīrān*. Bhūḥ! O Mṛtyu and Rogau, come here! 28.
Between the directions of Brahmā and Nirṛti, upon the creepers, [one should worship] Gaṇeśa:
"Oṃ, we invoke you, the leader of the hosts; we invoke you, the lord of beloved things, O Gaṇapati, for my well-being."
I have become the bearer of the embryo; you have become the impregnator of the embryo. O Bhūti, O Gaṇeśa, come here, come here;
stay, stay. 29.
p.
410) In the pond between Brahmā and Varuṇa: [Offering] water. *Oṃ śanno devīrabhiṣṭaye āpo bhavantu pītaye | śaṃ yor abhisravantu naḥ*. Bhūḥ! O Waters, come here!

"Come here, stay here. || 30 || [One should invoke] the Maruts in the center of the Brahmā and Vāyu [circles], upon the creepers: "Oṃ Maruts, you who indeed protect in whose abode, O you of great luster; may he, along with his guardians, protect us, O people. *Bhūḥ*. O Maruts, come here, stay here. || 31 || [One should place] the Earth at the base of the foot of Brahmā, beneath the pericarp.

Oṃ, O Earth, be pleasant to us, free from thorns, and providing a dwelling; grant us wide-spreading protection. O Earth, come here, be present! 32. In that very place, [invoke] the rivers such as the Gaṅgā:
Oṃ, the five rivers flow together with their currents into the Sarasvatī; the Sarasvatī indeed [surpasses] the five.
O rivers such as the Gaṅgā and others, who exist in the region of Dhāśā, come here and remain here!

33. Right there, [one should invoke] the seven oceans: *Oṃ, hear this my call, O Varuṇa, and be gracious to me today; seeking your favor, I pray to you.* *Bhūḥ! O Seven Oceans, come here, be present here!* 34.
Then, around the pericarp by name: *Oṃ, salutation to Meru.* [Invoke] Meru.
Outside, near the *parigha* and *soma* [gates]: Oṃ, obeisance to the mace (*gadā*). [I] invoke the mace. || 36 ||

In the northeast: *Oṃ* obeisance to the trident; invoke the trident. (37) In the east: *Oṃ* obeisance to the thunderbolt; invoke the thunderbolt. (38) In the southeast: obeisance to the spear; invoke the spear. (39) In the south: obeisance to the staff; invoke the staff and establish it. (40) In the southwest:

Salutation to Khaḍga; invoke Khaḍga. || 41 || In the west: salutation to Pāśa; invoke Pāśa. || 42 || In the northwest: salutation to Aṅkuśa; invoke Aṅkuśa. || 43 || Outside that, in the north: salutation to Gautama; [invoke] Gautama. || 44 || In the northeast: salutation to Bharadvāja; [invoke] Bharadvāja. || 45 ||
To Viśvāmitra in the east. [Invoke] Viśvāmitra. 46. To Kaśyapa in the south-east.

To Kaśyapa... || 47 || To Jamadagni in the south... [and] to Jamadagni... || 48 || In the southwest... || 49 || In the northwest, to Arundhatī... [and] to Arundhatī... || 50 || Outside of that, starting from the east: to Aindrī... [and] to Aindrī... || 51 ||
To Kaumārī... to Kaumārīḥ. || 53 || To Brāhmī... to Brāhmīṃ. || 54 || To Vārāhī... to Vārāhīṃ. || 55 || To Cāmuṇḍā... to Cāmuṇḍāmā. || 56 || To Vaiṣṇavī... to Vaiṣṇavīṃ.

57. To Koverī, [and] to the Kauverīs. 58. To Vaināyakī, [and] to the Vaināyakīs. 59. Thus, having invoked the deities beginning with Brahmā in the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala and worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings, one should place a water-pot (kalaśa) upon it according to the procedure stated previously for the twenty-five [deities], and worship Varuṇa along with his limbs (sāṅga).

Having performed the *agnyuttāraṇa* (ceremonial removal from the fire) and *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of life-force) for a golden image of Durgā, and having placed it upon a water-pot (*kalaśa*), one should cover it with silk cloths and worship it with the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Śrīsūkta*, or mantras mentioned in the Purāṇas; then one should pray [to the sword]. *Khaḍga*...
The wheel, the rosary, the bell, and the trident.
Now follows the installation of the fire preceded by the fivefold consecration (saṃskāra).

412) Then the teacher, having performed the five purificatory rites (*pañcabhūsaṃskāra*) on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) or in the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), should establish the worldly fire (*laukikāgni*). Now, the five purificatory rites: there, with three blades of *kuśa* grass, [he should draw] a line one cubit in length...
Having swept the ground into a square shape three times, having cast those *kuśa* grasses toward the northeast, and having smeared it with a mixture of cow dung and water three times,
one should draw three lines from west to east, each a span in length, with the base of the *sruva* ladle, following a sequence from south to north.
Having taken up earth with the ring finger and thumb according to the sequence of scraping,
and having sprinkled that spot with water, one should bring the common fire situated in a bronze vessel from the south-eastern corner and have a married woman establish it facing west.

One should expel the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters with this mantra: *Oṃ kravyādam agniṃ prahiṇomi dūraṃ yamarājyaṃ gacchatu ripravāhaḥ | ihaivāyam itaro jātavedā devebhyo havyaṃ vahatu prajānan* (I send the flesh-eating fire far away; let it go to the kingdom of Yama as a carrier of impurities. Let this other Jātavedas remain here and, knowing well, carry the oblation to the gods). Now, the invocation (*āvāhana*): *Oṃ agniṃ dūtaṃ puro dadhe* (I place Agni at the forefront as my messenger).
I invoke the carrier of oblations; bring the gods here to sit. One should pour water with unbroken grains (*akṣata*) into the vessel brought by Agni.
This is the ritual of facing [the deity] (*saṃmukhīkaraṇa*). "Roars the bull who has split himself threefold; Mahādeva... [and so on].
O Bhūmimātṛ, endowed with the three *pravaras*—Devale and others—O father Varuṇa, whose banner is the ram!
Facing east, be present before me. Having installed the fire named Varada.

"Salutation to Agni named Varada"—having thus performed the worship of the fire outside the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) located in the north-west corner with this name-mantra; then follows the meditation: "Oṃ [Lakṣmī, who was in her season there, by means of the householder’s rite with the Lord Nārāyaṇa...]"
One should contemplate the fire produced there, arisen from the splendor of Rudra, having two heads, two nostrils,
six eyes, four ears, three feet, and seven hands.

On the southern side, he has four hands, and on the left side, three hands; he holds a *śruva* ladle, a *śruci* spoon, and a spear in his right [hands], while in the left [hands] he holds a rosary, a lance, and a vessel of clarified butter. He bears these with seven hands, possesses two faces and seven tongues, and is situated on the south.

He has four tongues and three tongues, with his face turned toward the north; he is known by thirty-two crores of forms, endowed with fifty-two kalās, adorned with the utterances of Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭ, and has a ram as his vehicle.
I, whose name is auspicious, invoke you, Rudra, who are red with garlands and garments, seated upon a red lotus throne, and who are fire itself.
O you of immeasurable luster, seven-rayed one, who are the mouth of all the gods! Come, O Lord Agni, and grant your presence at this sacrifice. *Oṃ*, I bow to the blazing Agni, the Jātavedas.
The consumer of oblations, golden-hued, the fire, prosperous, with faces on all sides.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the *kuśuṇḍikā*.
There, first, the patron, having sat down to the west of the sacrificial pit (or the sacrificial mound), [should proceed].

Having proclaimed the place and time: I, [Name], of the [Gotra] lineage and [Name] Śarman, for the purpose of the Durgā-homa rite, offer this sacrificial substance to Gaṇeśa, the five Oṃkāras, the twelve Vināyakas, the sixteen Mātṛkās, Vāstupuruṣa, the Viśvedevas with the ancestors (Sapitṛka), the sixty-four Yoginīs, and the fifty Kṣetrapālas.

Salutations to the seven Vasus, the planets beginning with the Sun, the presiding deities (adhidevatās) beginning with Īśvara, the secondary deities (pratyadhidevatās) beginning with Agni, the five world-protectors (lokapālas), the ten guardians of the directions (digpālas), and the sixty-five deities situated within the Sarvatobhadra Maṇḍala, beginning with Brahmā. Then, the preceptor performs the strewing of grass (paristaraṇa) to the south of the fire.

Having vacated the ground and offered a seat to the Brahmin, having spread *kuśa* grass upon it with the tips pointing eastward and northward, and having led the Brahmin around the fire in a clockwise direction, one says: "In this rite of offering to Durgā, be my *brahmā*. Thus is the formal invitation (*varaṇa*).

One should seat upon a prepared seat, facing north, a Brahmin previously selected by means of [auspicious] action— or, in his absence, a [representation of] Brahmā fashioned from fifty blades of *kuśa* grass—
and worship him. Then, having placed the *praṇītā* vessel in front and filled it with water, [one should proceed].
Having covered it with the three types of *kuśa* grass and having looked at the face of Brahmā, he should place it upon *kuśa* grass to the north of the fire.
Then follows the strewing of the sacrificial grass.

Taking one-fourth of the sacrificial grass (*varhiṣ*), he [strews it] from the southeast to the northeast with four blades of *darbha* grass having their tips pointing eastward; and from the southeast to the northwest with [four blades] having their tips pointing eastward.

With the tips pointing eastward from the southwest to the northwest; with the tips pointing eastward from the southeast to the limit of the *praṇītā* vessel. Having performed the strewing (*paristaraṇa*), then, to the north of the fire in the western direction, three *kuśa* blades for the purpose of cutting [the grass], and [three] for the purpose of making the purifiers (*pavitra*).
A vessel with a wide interior and two kuśa-leaf corners; a sprinkling-vessel; and a vessel for clarified butter.

Five *kuśa* blades for wiping the *caru*-pot; seven *kuśa* blades for the supporting ladle (*upayamana*); three *kuśa* blades in the form of a braid; and three fuel sticks (*samidh*) made of *pālāśa* wood. (p.

Those that are shattered, split into two parts (possessing two halves), short, crooked, thick, split open from one side, bitten by insects, long, and stripped of their bark are proclaimed to be of inferior quality. A shattered leaf causes the destruction of life; a split leaf gives rise to disease; and in the case of a short leaf—

A curved [vagina] brings death, and likewise causes obstacles. One that is thick takes away fortune; when it is thin, there is the decay of the sacrificer. When it is bifurcated, eye diseases may arise; one bitten by insects destroys wealth. A long [vagina] produces hatred; those with no opening are known as killers of life. Those that have milk, nor are excessive or deficient— [Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment of a medical or astrological treatise concerning the characteristics of the female genitalia (*yonis*). The translation reflects the technical terminology used therein.]

"The fuel-sticks grant all desires. A wise man should offer as oblation such sticks that have moist bark, are cut evenly, and are as thick as the middle finger; he thereby attains great results. Their width at the tip should be known to be four finger-breadths. Thus it is stated in the *Guruproktavana-durgā-kalpa* for the sake of accomplishing all undertakings.
There, one should perform the fire-oblation upon the tongue; having recognized the eyes, ears, and so forth, the best of preceptors should perform the oblation.
If one performs a fire-oblation (homa) in the ear, it causes illness and fear; if performed in the nose, it results in great suffering;
and if in the eyes, it leads to their destruction. It is said that [an oblation] on the hair bestows poverty; therefore, one should offer the oblation upon the tongue.

"Where there is wood, there is the ear; where there is smoke, the two nostrils; where there is a small flame, the eyes; where there is ash, that is the head; and where the fire blazes intensely, that is declared to be the tongue. By the word "Vipaścit," this is what is meant: through offering oblations into these limbs during the *homa* for the destruction of enemies, those respective limbs [of the enemy] are destroyed.
It occurs as they say: "On the head of the fire, on the nose, on the ear, or likewise on the eye."

If one should offer oblations, then it will swiftly destroy his limbs. The sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) should be made of *khadira* wood, one cubit (*hasta*) in length and one span (*prādeśa*) in height. The clarified butter (*ājya*) should be from a cow. The rice grains should be purified. [The quantity is two hundred and fifty-six handfuls according to the teacher’s measure. As for the ten-ingredient incense (*daśāṅga-dhūpa*):

In the Vrata-khaṇḍa of Hemādri: Six parts of kuṣṭha, double that amount (twelve) of jaggery, three parts of lākṣā, five parts of nakha, equal portions (one part each) of harītakī and sarjarasa, one part of śilājatu with three lavas added, four parts of ghanasāra, and one part of pura— this is declared to be the ten-ingredient incense (daśāṅga-dhūpa).
[By the lords of sages: A full vessel; a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) or a bride;

the *kuśa* grass for cutting the *pavitra* should be placed in the eastern direction in due order. Then, the making of the *pavitra* with the *pavitrachedana* blades: having placed three *pavitra* blades upon two [other] *pavitra* blades, [one proceeds] from the front.
Having set aside a span's length, one should cut off three blades of kusha grass and two young shoots of kusha.

One should place two [blades] at the base and three towards the north. Then, taking the two strainers along with the *pavitra*, one performs the sprinkling three times. The vessel for the *prokṣaṇī* water is held in the left hand.

Having taken the two strainers with the ring finger and the thumb, one performs the sprinkling three times. Then, with water from the *praṇītā* vessel, one sprinkles the *prokṣaṇī* vessel. Having sprinkled each item individually in sequence, beginning with the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) and ending with the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*), by means of the *prokṣaṇī* water, one proceeds to the area free from movement (*asañcara*).

Having placed the *prokṣaṇī* vessel between the *praṇītā* and the fires, having poured the prepared clarified butter (*ājya*) into the *ājyasthālī* placed behind the fire, having poured the water from the *praṇītā* into the *caru* vessel,
and having thrown the prepared rice grains into it, [he places] the clarified butter therein.

He places the vessel for the *brahma* on the fire. To the north of that, having simultaneously placed the *caru* itself onto the fire, once the *caru* has become slightly cooked, he should brandish a flaming torch clockwise around both the clarified butter and the *caru*, causing them to be heated.
Having taken the *sruva* ladle with his right hand, having heated it in the fire with its opening facing downwards, and having placed it in his left hand;
p.
415) With the southern [hand], beginning from the tip with the tips of the brooms and ending at the base with the bases, [one should sweep] downwards as far as the root.

Having cleansed the *sruva* ladle and sprinkled it with water from the *praṇītā* vessel, and having heated it again, one should set it down to the south. Then, having lifted up the clarified butter (*ājya*),
having led it to the east of the cooked rice (*caru*) and placed it to the north of the fire, and having lifted up the cooked rice, [one should place it] to the west of the clarified butter.
Having led [the butter] and placed it to the north of the clarified butter, he brings the clarified butter from behind the fire and brings the *caru* as well.

He should place it to the north of the clarified butter (*ājya*). Then, having purified the clarified butter with the two strainers as before, and having inspected it, he should discard any impure substances from it and purify the *prokṣiṇī* water again. Then, taking the *upayamana* *kuśa* grass, he should rise while meditating upon Prajāpati in his mind.
Silently, he should cast three fuel sticks smeared with ghee into the fire; then, having sat down.
[The facing of the fire.]
Having generated the deity from the oblations, one should thereafter perform the ritual action;
O Bearer of Oblations, you face the east with your face downward and your feet upward.
"Since he remains with such power, to whom should an oblation be offered? This is the answer:
With water containing a *pavitra* in his hand, he should circumambulate the fire from left to right.
Seeing the fuel-wood and the water, he should stand facing it with trepidation.
Having sprinkled water around the fire with the *prokṣiṇī* vessel and the *pavitra*, starting from the northeast (Īśāna) and ending in the north, [he should proceed].
Having bent his right knee and being assisted by the Brahman priest— and also assisted by the sacrificer—
he should offer oblations of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle into the most brightly kindled fire.
(The characteristics of the "mouth" and other parts of the fire are described elsewhere.)
Fire with smoke should be known as the head; smokeless fire as the eyes;
a blazing and slender flame as the ears; and fire clinging to wood as the nose.
"Where the fire flickers, resembling pure crystal—that should be known as the mouth, measuring four finger-breadths. Thus it is said.
In the ritual manual for Vanadurgā as proclaimed by the Guru.
For the sake of accomplishing all undertakings, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) there upon the tongue;
having understood the eyes, ears, and so forth, the most excellent preceptor should perform the oblation.
If one performs an oblation in the ear, there will be danger from disease;
if in the nose, there will be great suffering; and if in the eyes, blindness shall occur.
It is said that [the smoke] causes loss of hair and poverty; therefore, one should offer oblations pleasing to the tongue.
Where there is wood, there is the ear; where there is smoke, however, there are the nostrils.
"Where there is a slight glow in the eyes, that is the head; where there is ash, that is the head;
and where the fire blazes intensely, that is proclaimed to be the tongue."

By the term "vipaścit" (the wise one), this is what is meant: through offering oblations into these specific limbs during the fire-sacrifice for the destruction of enemies, those limbs of the enemy are destroyed. As they say: "If one should offer oblations into the head, the nose, the ears, or likewise the eyes of the fire, then it will swiftly destroy those very limbs [of the enemy]."

Therein, having offered the two Ājyabhāga oblations into the supporting fires, one should immediately pour the remainder of the clarified butter remaining in the *sruva* ladle into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel.
(p. 416) Now, the fire-oblation (homa).
To the north of the fire: Oṃ (namaḥ) to Prajāpati, svāhā; this is for Prajāpati, [may it be] mine. To the south of the fire: Oṃ to Indra, svāhā; this is for Indra, [may it be] mine.

Thus are the two Āghāra oblations. In the center of the most intensely kindled fire: *Oṃ agnaye svāhā; to Agni, this food is mine.* *Oṃ somāya svāhā; to Soma, this food is mine.* Thus are the two Ājyabhāga portions. Then the preceptor, having worshipped the Fire, should perform the *havana* (oblation) for the deities established in the *maṇḍala* of Gaṇeśa and others, in the same manner on all sides.

One should also perform [the ritual] for the deities situated within the auspicious mandala. Again, having recited the *kavaca*, *argalā*, and *kīlaka*, and having performed the nine-syllable (*navārṇa*) placements (*nyāsa*), one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the nine-syllable mantra. Then, having performed the seven-hundred-verse (*saptaśatī*) placements, one begins again with "Mārkaṇḍeya said" and so forth, starting with *oṃ*.

Having offered oblations with the mantra ending in "sāvarṇirarbhitā manuḥ," and having again performed the subsequent ritual placements (*uttaranyāsa*), one should offer the nine-syllable mantra (*navārṇa*) one hundred and eight times. Then, taking the remaining sacrificial substance (*hutaśeṣa-havirdravya*), one should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation while being assisted by the Brahman priest, reciting: "Oṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte."
Svāhā! This is for Agni. Then, the oblations beginning with Bhūḥ: Oṃ Bhūḥ Svāhā! This is for Agni.
Oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā; this to Vāyu. Oṃ svaḥ svāhā; this to Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya.
Oṃ! O Agni, you who know, may you remove from us the wrath of the god Varuṇa.

O most excellent sacrificer, best bearer of oblations, shining brightly, release us from all hatreds—svāhā! This [is offered] to Agni and Varuṇa. Om! O Agni, be a protector for us; be near to us at the dawning of this very morning. O Varuṇa, being gracious, release us from our bonds; O you who are easily invoked, grant us well-being.

*edhi svāhā*—this [is offered] to Agni and Varuṇa. *oṃ ayāścāgne 'sy anabhiśastipāśca satyam it tvam ayā asi | ayā no yajñam vaha ayā no dhehi bheṣajaṃ svāhā*—this [is offered] to *ayās* Agni. *oṃ yete śataṃ varuṇa ye sahasram*...

The great sacrificial nooses are stretched out; by them may Savitṛ, Viṣṇu, and the Maruts, who are skilled in song, release us today. Svāhā! This [offering] is for Varuṇa, Savitṛ, Viṣṇu, the Viśvedevas, and the Maruts skilled in song. Oṃ! O Varuṇa, loosen the highest noose from us...
Having loosened the lowest bond, the middle one, and the highest, O Āditya, may we then be sinless before you and before Aditi.
Svāhā! This [is for] Varuṇa. Om, to Prajāpati, svāhā! This [is for] Prajāpati. Om, to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā! This [is for] Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
Now follows the offering of the sacrificial oblation (balidāna).

Today, for the sake of the complete accomplishment of the ritual performed, I shall offer oblations (*bali*) to the guardians of the directions and to the deities established in the mandala of the planets beginning with Āditya. [To the East: *Oṃ trātāram indram avitāram indraṃ have have suhavam śūraṃ indram*.
I invoke Śakra, Indra who is invoked by many; may the bountiful Indra grant us well-being.

"Obeisance to Indra. Having worshipped him with perfumes, unbroken rice, flowers, and so forth for the purpose of all ritual services (*sarvopacāra*), [one should do] thus everywhere. *Oṃ*, I offer this *bali* of sesame, black gram, and cooked rice along with a lamp to Indra, together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), his retinue (*saparivāra*), his weapons (*sāyudha*), and his powers (*saśaktika*). O Indra, protect the direction; accept the *bali*.

"Enjoy [this offering]; bring prosperity to me and my family; be the bestower of long life, the bestower of security, the bestower of peace, the bestower of nourishment, the bestower of contentment, and the remover of obstacles; grant your boon. By this offering of the *bali*, may Indra be pleased. [In the southeast: *Oṃ tvanno agne tavadeva...*

O worshipful one, protect us with your feet; O praiseworthy one, guard the descendants of Maghavan. You are the protector of Tuka’s son, guarding the cattle of Nimi within the span of an eyeblink according to your sacred law. Homage to Agni!

p. 418) To Agni, sā. O Agni, [protect] the eastern direction! This is the southern [direction], for Yama: *oṃ* svāhā to Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the Pitṛs. Svāhā to the Gharma; svāhā, the Gharma to the Father.

Salutation to Yama. O Yama! [Offering] in the southwest: *Oṃ asunvantam ayajamānam icchastenasyetyām anv ehi taskarasya | anyam asmād iccha sāta-ityānamo devinir-ṛte tubhyam astu*. Salutation to Nirṛti. [Offering] in the west.
Oṃ! I approach you, worshipping with a sacred prayer; the sacrificer, desiring that [favor], approaches you with oblations.
O Varuṇa, being unprovoked, grant us protection; do not steal away our common life-span.

Salutation to Varuṇa. [In the] north-western [direction]: Oṃ! Come to our sacrifice with your teams of horses, hundreds and thousands in number, O Vāyu, who go to the sacrifice. Rejoice in this libation, O Vāyu!
May you all protect us always with blessings. [Salutation] to Vāyu. [In the] northern [direction]: Oṃ! We have entered into your service, O Soma.
May we, possessing progeny, be united with those who bear the mind and the body. To Soma... [in the northeast] Om!
We invoke that Īśāna, the lord of the moving and the stationary world, the inspirer of wisdom, for our protection.
May Pūṣan, who knows our wealth, be present for our prosperity; may he be our protector and guardian, undeceived, for our well-being.
To Īśvara... [in the middle between the East and the North]... [above]: Oṃ.
Asme rudrā mehanā parvatāso vṛtrahatye bharahūtī sajoṣāḥ | yaḥ saṃgṛbhe tastuvate dhāyi pajra indro jyeṣṭhā asmān avantu devāḥ || To Brahmā...
In the lower space between the west and the southwest: Oṃ, O Earth, be soft for us, free from thorns, a dwelling place;
grant us wide-spreading shelter.

*Anantāya*... Then, near the sacrificial altar (*grahavedi*), the offering (*bali*) for the planets beginning with the Sun: *Oṃ ākṛṣṇena rajasā...* To the planets beginning with the Sun, together with their presiding deities (*adhidevatā*) and counter-deities (*pratyadhidevatā*), along with their limbs (*sāṅga*), [protective powers], and [attendants]—I offer this oblation (*bali*) consisting of a lamp, curd, black gram, and cooked rice.
O deities, Sūrya and the rest, protect the directions, consume the offering, and behold the lamps!

Grant prosperity to me, the sacrificer, together with my family. O makers of longevity, makers of security, makers of peace, makers of nourishment, makers of contentment, and makers of freedom from obstacles—be bestowers of boons! By this offering of oblations, may the planets beginning with the Sun [be satisfied].
[May they be] pleased. Then, one should offer a single bali-oblation to the Mothers:
*Oṃ samakhye devyādhiyāsaṃ dakṣiṇayorucakṣasā | māma' āyuḥ pramoṣīrmoṃa' ahaṃ tavavīraṃ videyata vadevisaṃdṛśi*. [This is for] Gaurī and the other Mothers; to them, this...
I offer this oblation of cooked rice with a lamp. O Bhogā and the other Mothers, accept this oblation! Grant prosperity to me, [Vajramāna], together with my family.
You who bestow long life, you who grant security, you who perform pacification, you who grant contentment, and you who remove obstacles—[act thus].
May they be granters of boons.
By this offering of the bali-oblation, may Gaurī and the sixteen Mothers be pleased.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the offering of the bali-oblation to the Kṣetrapāla.

Having spread *kuśa* grass upon a single bamboo vessel, and having placed upon it food—either fourfold or twofold—consisting of black-gram porridge (*māṣabhakta*), curd-rice (*dadhyodana*), and a water-vessel; and having provided it with turmeric, saffron, vermilion, collyrium, ritual substances, banners, and lamps; [one should recite]: *Oṃ adya* etc., [for the removal of] all misfortunes (*ariṣṭa*).

"I shall perform the worship of the Kṣetrapāla and the offering of the bali for the sake of achieving the successful completion of the rite I intend to begin, preceded by rites of pacification. This is the declaration. Taking unbroken rice grains (akṣata):
"Oṃ, they did not find any other touch than this Vaiśvānara Agni who goes before [all things]."

"The immortals, the gods, have increased the immortal Vaiśvānara for the sake of conquering sovereignty. With this mantra, "Oṃ Hrīṃ (Kṣaṃ) obeisance to Kṣetrapāla," one should worship him with the prescribed offerings and meditate upon him.
Oṃ! [I bow to him] who resembles a mountain of blue collyrium, whose hair is tawny and stands erect, whose round eyes are fierce, and who joyfully holds a mace and a skull-cup.
I bow to that God, the Lord of the Field, who is clothed in space, adorned with serpents, fierce with fangs, and possessed of a wondrous body. (From the *Śāradā*, a prayer.)
Oṃ, homage! You are the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla) together with the hosts of bhūtas and pretas;
accept this offering of worship and remain ever gracious.
Grant me long life and health; may you always ensure that I am free from obstacles.
Through this worship, may Kṣetrapāla be pleased.
Then follows the offering of the bali-oblation.
Oṃ! O Kṣetrapāla, you of mighty arms, great strength, and valor;
for the sake of protecting the fields, accept this offering; homage be to you!

KṢAṂ! To the Kṣetrapāla, together with his limbs (retinue), accompanied by his entourage of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, ḍākinīs, śākinīs, vetālas, and so forth, equipped with weapons, possessing power, and together with his vehicle— to him, this [offering] with a lamp.
I offer this oblation of curd and black gram; obeisance! O, O Kṣetrapāla, protect all directions;
consume the oblation, behold the lamp, and bring about the prosperity of me, the sacrificer, together with my family. You are the maker of long life, the maker of well-being, and the maker of peace.
Be the nourisher, the bringer of contentment, the remover of obstacles, the bestower of auspiciousness, and the granter of boons.

"May the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapa) be pleased by this offering. Having taken this offering, a base Brahmin who does not look back should cast it at a crossroads. The sacrificer, too, should follow behind him as far as the doorway and then scatter water. Thus ends the offering to the Guardian of the Field.
The procedure: Having washed one's hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should sit upon the seat.
After the offering of the bali, one should perform the subsequent worship of the deities beginning with Gaṇeśa.
Now follows the worship of the subsequent [deities].

On this day, during the Navarātra of the spring (or autumn), for the sake of accomplishing the completeness of the rite of offering oblations (*havana*) to Durgā, I shall perform the secondary worship (*uttara-pūjana*) of the deities established in the *maṇḍala*, beginning with Gaṇapati. *Oṃ gaṇānāṃ tvā...* *Oṃ grahā ūrjāhutayo vyanto viprāyamatim.*
From those wide-jawed ones, I have gathered together food, vigor, and strength. Oṃ, Amba, Ambika, Ambalika...
Salutations to all the deities established in the maṇḍala, beginning with Gaṇeśa.

Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, the recitation of the Veda follows: Oṃ iṣetvorjetvāvāyavastha devovaḥ savitāprārpayatu śreṣṭhatamāya karmaṇe | āpyāyadhvamaghnyā' indrāya bhāgaṃ prajāvatīranamīvā' ayakṣmā mā vastena' īśata māghaśaṃsaḥ || 1 ||
May you be firm with this lord of cattle; protect the many animals of the sacrificer. Om!

Agni, the domestic priest, the god, the officiating priest of the sacrifice, the invoker, the best bestower of jewels—Om! O Agni, come hither for the feast, being praised for the giving of the oblation; sit down as the invoker upon the sacred grass. Om! May the divine waters be auspicious to us...
May the waters be most propitious for our drinking; may they flow toward us for our well-being and happiness. Oṃ!
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, the destroyer of Tripura, the Sun, the Moon, Mars, and Mercury.
May Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu—all the planets—be bringers of peace.
I satiate Durgā; obeisance!
Having thus completed the fire-oblation (homa), one should perform the subsequent subsidiary rites (uttarāṅga).
Now follows the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
In the worship rites, there are the desired nine oblations, the bali offering, the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
the presentation of the āśrāvapada, the consecration (abhiṣeka), and the dismissal (visarjana).

Then, having summoned the sacrificer’s wife and tied a knot [in her garment], the officiant stands to her right and worships Gaṇeśa and the other deities with perfumes, unbroken rice, and so forth, reciting: "Obeisance to the deities beginning with Gaṇeśa."
Afterwards: Oṃ, Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, you who know all divine ways.
Drive away from us the crooked sin; with our most abundant speech, we offer this hymn of praise to you.

Having worshipped with scents and other offerings, saying "mṛḍāgnaye namaḥ," [one should say]: "Oṃ, today, etc., for the sake of accomplishing the completeness of the Durgā-homa rite already performed, I shall perform the Pūrṇāhuti oblation accompanied by the Vasordhārā. Then, in another vessel, [one should take] ghee four times with the *sruva* ladle.
Having taken [the vessel] twelve times, or having taken it once, one should hold a bilva fruit wrapped in cloth over the vessel;
having adorned it with fruits, betel, perfumes, garlands, and so forth, and having taken it, one should place the vessel upon the *śruci*.

Holding [the vessel] with both hands, the sacrificer should stand [and recite]: *oṃ samudrād ūrmir madhumān udārad upāṃśunā samamṛtatvam ānaṭ | ghṛtasya nāma guhyam yad asti jihvā devānām amṛtasya nābhiḥ || 1 || catvāri śṛṅgā trayo...*
Two of his feet are in the head, and seven are his hands. Moving in three ways, the bull bellows;
the great god has entered into mortals. O Vasunītha, may the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus kindle you again, and may the Brahmans do so again through sacrifices.
Increase our body with clarified butter; may the desires of the sacrificer come true. (3) Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues, seven your seers, and seven your beloved abodes.
The seven Hotṛ-priests worship you in seven ways; fill the seven wombs with clarified butter, Svāhā! 4.
O Full Ladle, fly away; O Well-Filled One, fly back again! Trade with us at any price;

bring hither food and strength, O Lord of a Hundred Powers! Svāhā! This [oblation] is for Agni Vaiśvānara, for the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, for the Lord of a Hundred Powers, for Agni Saptavān, and for Water. May it be well-pleasing.
The sacrifice to the Varuṇa-kalaśa [is performed]. Thereafter, one should offer the *avasordhārā* oblation with the verse: "Seven, O Agni, are your fuel-sticks..."

You are the purifier of wealth, with a hundred streams; you are the purifier of wealth, with a thousand streams. May the god Savitṛ purify you with the purifier of wealth, with a hundred streams—may he, the sweet-pressing one, yield sweetness for us. Svāhā!
p.
422) Thereupon, the prayer to Agni: "O Bearer of Oblations, grant me faith, intelligence, fame, wisdom, knowledge, nourishment, prosperity, strength, splendor, longevity, and health! O Agni!"
O Great Power, accomplisher of all actions! Even when another task has arisen, always grant your presence.

The rite for bestowing long life (*tryāyuṣakaraṇa*): *Oṃ tryāyuṣaṃ yamadagneḥ*, on the forehead; *Oṃ kaśyapasya tryāyuṣam*, on the neck; *Oṃ yad deveṣu tryāyuṣam*, on the right shoulder; *Oṃ tan no astu tryāyuṣam*, on the heart, and likewise on the left shoulder. Then follows the consumption of the residual drops (*saṃsrava*).

The sprinkling with the two purifiers (*pavitra*). The disposal of the purifiers into the fire. The offering of the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) to the Brahman priest. Thus, having recited "Today... and so forth: "In this rite called the oblation to Durgā performed today, for the sake of the firm establishment of the oblation-rite, this full vessel [is offered]."

"Along with the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), [this] dedicated to Prajāpati, I bestow upon you, O Brāhmaṇa, named Amukaśarman of such-and-such lineage, as the Brahmā priest. "Om, may there be well-being," is the reply. Then follows the untying of the knot of the Brahmā-thread. Then, with the water from the *praṇītā* vessel: "Om, may the waters and plants be friendly to us..."
"May they be so. [He recites: "Oṃ, may the waters be auspicious, most auspicious, peaceful, and most peaceful; may they provide healing for you. He sprinkles the head of the sacrificer.
Then, [he casts the water] toward the northeast with the words: "May those who are unfriendly be unfriendly to him who hates us and whom we hate."

One should place the *praṇītā* water-vessel upside down. Then, having placed the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) in the order of the surrounding strewn grass (*paristaraṇa*) and having sprinkled it with clarified butter (*ājya*), [one recites]: *oṃ devā gātuvido gātuṃ vittvā gātumita*.

With the mantra: "O Lord of the Mind, this divine sacrifice, svāhā! May it be placed in the wind, svāhā! he should offer oblations with his hand alone. Then, having placed the water from the pitcher into a single vessel, he sprinkles the head of the sacrificer with *dūrvā* grass using the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and others. Water...

May the mothers purify me with ghee; may they cleanse me with ghee. Carrying away all sin and impurity, O divine waters, I emerge from you pure and purified. O Waters, carry away this: whatever is blameworthy, whatever is foul, whatever malice I have committed, and whatever falsehood I have uttered.
O fearless one! O Pavamāna, son of Waters, release him from this sin. 5.

The glory is my head, fame my face, luster my hair and beard; the King is my vital breath, the Samrāṭ my eye, and the Virāṭ my ear. (6) The auspiciousness is my tongue, speech my greatness, thought my mind, anger my self-ruler, and passion my splendor; joy and delight are my fingers.
My colors are my companion; my two arms are my strength, my senses my wealth, and my two hands are my action and vigor.
The self is my invincible breast. || 8 ||
The spine is my kingdom, the belly is my domain; the neck and shoulders are my thighs, and the hips are my two knees.
The people are my limbs on all sides; my mind is my summit, my discernment is my tail, and my anus is my foundation.
Ānanda (bliss), Nanda (joy), Āṇḍau (the two testicles), Mebhaga (great fortune), Saubhāgya (good fortune), and Pasa (the penis).
I am Dharma, the King, established in the head, the thighs, and the feet. From whichever direction you seek [fear], from that very place grant us fearlessness. Grant auspiciousness to our progeny;
grant fearlessness to our cattle. Now, the mantras previously mentioned: "May the gods consecrate you; may Brahmā..."
Viṣṇu and Maheśvara; Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, remained there, as did the all-pervading Saṃkarṣaṇa. || 1 ||
May Pradyumna and Aniruddha bring you victory! May the Lord Ākhaṇḍala (Indra), Yama, Nairṛti, Varuṇa, Pavana, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), and Śiva likewise [grant you success].
May all the Brahmins together and the guardians of the quarters protect you always. || 3 ||
Fame, Fortune, Fortitude, Intelligence, Nourishment, Faith, Action, Intellect, Modesty, Body, Peace, Contentment, and Radiance are the Mothers. || 4 ||
"Let these wives of the gods, having assembled together, sprinkle you."
Āditya, Candra, Bhauma, Budha, Jīva, Śita, and Arkaja. || 5 ||
May the planets—Rāhu and Ketu being fully propitiated—consecrate you;
as well as the gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas; the sages, the Manus, the cows, and the divine mothers.

The wives of the gods, the trees, the nāgas, the daityas, and the hosts of apsarases; all weapons, all scriptures, kings, and vehicles; medicinal herbs, jewels, and whatever parts belong to Time (Kāla).
Rivers, oceans, mountains, sacred fords, clouds, and streams.
May these [deities] consecrate you for the accomplishment of all desires and purposes. May heaven be peaceful;
may the atmosphere be peaceful.
Circumambulation of the Maṇḍapa: Oṃ, those holy fords that wander about, with nooses in their hands and quivers at their sides.
We bow down to those whose extent is a thousand yojanas. Whatever sins have been committed throughout other births, they all perish at every step of the circumambulation.
"I am sinful, I am a doer of evil deeds, I am of a sinful nature, and born of sin. O Goddess Caṇḍikā, protect me;
be the remover of all sins. [This is] the *gocāriṇī-dakṣiṇā* (the cow-offering fee) in the rite called the oblation to Durgā, performed today, etc.

For the sake of fulfilling what is incomplete and perfecting what is complete, and to remove the defects of deficiency and excess, [I give] this sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), which moves with the speed of a cow (or for the purpose of drinking cow's milk), to [he of] such-and-such lineage (*gotra*) and such-and-such name (*śarman*).

I bestow [this] upon you, a well-honored Brāhmaṇa. For the sake of accomplishing the completeness of the performed rite of offering to Durgā, I relinquish this sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to you—the preceptor (*ācārya*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and others—according to their respective shares, for the sake of the various lineages (*gotra*). [The giving of further gifts. Of that which has been performed...
For the sake of accomplishing the completeness of the Durgā-homa rite and for the purpose of making what was incomplete complete,
I renounce this abundant sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be distributed as appropriate among Brāhmaṇas of various lineages, the poor, the helpless, the blind, and the lame.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the gift of a shadow-vessel.
Having gazed upon one's own reflection in the clarified butter placed within a bronze vessel,
he who gives it away along with gold shall ensure the pacification of all obstacles.
