The mantra: *Oṃ*. "He has become the form, the counterpart of form, for the sake of manifesting His form. Indra, through His powers of illusion (*māyā*), assumes many forms; yoked to Him are His bay steeds (*harayaḥ*), a hundred and ten.
These indeed are His bay steeds—ten, and thousands, and many, and infinite. This is that Brahman, the primordial, the unmanifest."
"Jama is the instruction for all. Having thus looked at the face [of the deity] over the clarified butter (ājya), the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) is made.
Today, etc., for the destruction of all my sins delimited by this body,
for the pacification of afflictions caused by all malevolent planets, for the destruction of bodily ailments, and for the attainment of all auspiciousness such as palaces,
desired longevity, health, and so forth, as well as for the attainment of all happiness— this [is offered].
This bell-metal vessel filled with clarified butter, containing its own reflection and gold,
dedicated to Lord Viṣṇu, together with the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), I give to you, O well-honored Brāhmaṇa of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name; may it be yours, not mine.
The two mantras.
Whatever misfortune and whatever wretchedness has arisen in all my limbs—destroy all that, O Agni, and increase my beloved lifespan. (1)
Clarified butter is the food of the gods; everything is established upon clarified butter.
By the gift of this vessel of clarified butter, may there be constant peace for me. (2)
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the gift of a shadow-vessel.
Blessing.
"Prajāpati, rich in offspring, on the right, under the sovereignty of Indra; may I be rich in offspring on the right.
There is nothing hidden here in this [formula]: "under the sovereignty of Indra"—he thus makes Indra her sovereign for the warding off of destructive spirits and demons; "may I be rich in offspring."
Thus, he bestows offspring and cattle upon himself; therefore, his son becomes possessed of cattle.

It consists of a hundred [verses]. Man indeed has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundred faculties; verily, he bestows upon himself life, faculties, and vigor. (1) "Thou art firm; may this sacrificer be firm in this non-falling [state] through offspring and cattle. (2) Then, having reached it, he causes it to be blown upon: "Thou art firm; may this [sacrificer] be firm..."

"The sacrificer has become possessed of progeny in this abode, and likewise of cattle"—in this way, whatever desire one may cherish, that desire is fulfilled. There are a hundred [bricks]; man indeed has a lifespan of a hundred years and possesses a hundredfold sensory power (*indriya*).
Verily, he places within himself life, sensory power, and vigor. Om! May Indra grant us well-being... [etc.]

May prosperity and splendor be yours. May the Rudras and Ādityas [protect you] once again. May the meanings of the mantras be fruitful; may all desires be fulfilled. May there be the destruction of the intellect of enemies, and likewise the rise of friends.
[May this be for one] desiring long life, desiring fame, and likewise desiring sons and grandsons.

"May health, wealth, and all my desires be fulfilled for me. [The donor] should thus accept the blessings. Then follows the dismissal of the deities and the fire: "May all the hosts of gods depart, having been worshipped by me according to my capacity."
For the sake of accomplishing desired wishes and for the purpose of returning again: Oṃ! Arise, O Brahmaṇaspati;
we, seeking the gods, call upon you. May the Maruts, the bounteous givers, come forward; O Indra, be swift and present with us.
Go, go, O best of gods, to your own abode, O Supreme Lord! Go, O Consumer of Oblations, to where the gods beginning with Brahmā reside. *Oṃ*, O Sacrifice, go to the sacrifice;
go to the Lord of Sacrifice; go to your own source, *svāhā*! This is your sacrifice, O Lord of Sacrifice, accompanied by the *sūktavāka*; all...

O Hero, may you accept this; Svāhā! In the supreme month of [Month Name], in the [Day Name] month, in the [Fortnight Name] fortnight, on the [Lunar Date Name] lunar day, whatever rite called the *Durgā-havana-śānti* was performed by me—whether deficient in timing, deficient in devotion, or deficient in faith—may that be [rendered perfect] through the word of the Brāhmaṇas and the deities invoked, beginning with the illustrious Sūrya.

"By your grace, may everything be completely fulfilled"—thus let the venerable ones say. "May it be completely fulfilled," the Brāhmaṇas should reply. "Whatever defect may occur in the sacrificial rites performed through negligence, by the mere remembrance of Durgā, it shall become complete; such is the Vedic revelation. And by whose death...

By uttering her name, austerity, sacrifice, ritual actions, and the like, though deficient, immediately attain completeness; therefore, one should salute Caṇḍikā. He who thus performs this propitiatory rite according to the authority of the Vedas and Śāstras—every undesirable thing for him perishes immediately.
O Śāṅkarī, I worship you, who are born from the four aims of life, who bestow the fruits of the four aims, who are the four castes, and who bring auspiciousness to the four castes.
Now follow other ritual applications (prayoga) as taught in the Kātyāyanī-tantra.
The accomplishment of the mantra (*mantra-siddhi*) occurs by reciting the mantra at the beginning and end of each verse;

here, the term "mantra" refers specifically to the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*). According to Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa, one should perform this by placing the three *vyāhṛtis* along with the *praṇava* in direct order at the beginning of each verse, and in reverse order at the end, repeating this for each verse one hundred times.

Success is attained very quickly. At the beginning of each verse, one should recite the Ṛgvedic mantra: "Oṃ jātavedase sunavāma somam arātīyato nidahāti vedaḥ | sa naḥ parṣad ati durgāṇi viśvā nāveva sindhūn duritāty agniḥ" (Oṃ, let us press the Soma for Jātavedas; may he burn away those who act with enmity; may he carry us across all difficulties as Agni carries us across rivers and over perils like a boat). By doing so, there is the fulfillment of all desires.
To ward off untimely death, one should first and last recite the Tryambaka mantra;
alternatively, one may perform the "encapsulation" (*saṃpuṭa*) by reciting that mantra at the beginning and end of each verse. Or, one may recite the verse "śaraṇāgatadīnārtā...
with every verse, whereby all undertakings will be successful. Others, however, say it is "śaraṇāgatarakṣa...".

It is stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa* that for the attainment of all auspiciousness, one should recite after each mantra: "O you who are the auspiciousness of all that is auspicious. For the attainment of every desire, one should recite the half-verse "May she grant us welfare" after each verse (*śloka*). Likewise, for the attainment of the boon desired by oneself...

One should recite the verse beginning with "devyā varam" at every subsequent verse. Others maintain that the mantra consisting of the half-verse beginning with "iti datvā," when chanted, grants all desired objects. To ward off all calamities and to drive away poverty, one should recite "durge smṛtā" at every verse; this [mantra] alone also [achieves these results].
The recitation of the verse should be performed one hundred thousand, ten thousand, one thousand, or one hundred times, according to the specific purpose.

By reciting "sarvābādha" one hundred thousand times, the fruit mentioned in the verse is attained. Regarding the phrase "nārāyaṇastu samanvitaḥ," since there is also a reading as "sutānvitaḥ," it is understood that the intention is that this mantra also bestows sons. By reciting the verse beginning with "itthaṃ yadāyadā" one hundred thousand times, the great pestilence (mahāmārī) is pacified.
Then, by reciting the mantra "tato bavre nṛporājyam" one hundred thousand times, there is the recovery of one's own kingdom once again.

Many [authorities] state that by reciting one hundred thousand times the mantra beginning with *svalpairahobhiḥ*, or by reciting each individual mantra, one attains sovereignty. By the mantra *hinasti daityatejāṃsi*, there is pacification of the *bālagrahas* (demons seizing children) through the offering of lamps and the ringing of a bell;
regarding this "ringing of the bell," Nāgeśabhaṭṭa and others [explain] the bell...

They call this "binding. Having tied a bell made of bronze, one should offer an oblation of black gram and cooked rice, according to the scriptural injunction. Having recited the mantra, the wise practitioner should cause the sound of that bell to resound.

"O Goddess, upon hearing that sound, the *piśācī*s flee"—thus, despite the difference between the preceding and following [statements], that binding is for the sole purpose of playing; therefore, these two are one and the same.
Alternatively, the unity of purpose should be understood as the statement of that [purpose] with respect to a capable person.

Having recited the thirteenth chapter in direct order for the first repetition, then performing the second in reverse order, and again the third in direct order— in this manner, when three repetitions have been performed according to these stated methods,
there is a swift accomplishment of the task for the purpose of warding off all calamities.

The half-verse beginning with "durgesmṛtā," followed by the verse ending with "yadanti yaccadūre bhayaṃ vindati māmiha pavamāna tadvi jahi," and finally the half-verse beginning with "dāridryaduḥkha"— thus, according to the requirements of the task, one should perform the recitation (japa) one hundred thousand, ten thousand, one thousand, or one hundred times.

One should recite the verse, "I invoke here Śrī, who has a golden smile, whose form is like gold, who is moist, blazing, satisfied, and satisfying; she who dwells in the lotus and is lotus-colored," with each verse of the *Pratiśloka*.
Through this, there is the attainment of Lakṣmī. With each verse of the *Pratiśloka*, one becomes free from debt in this world.

One should recite the verse: "May we be free from debt in the third world beyond; may we pass through all paths—those leading to the gods and those leading to the ancestors—free from debt. This constitutes the discharge of the debt.

If released for the purpose of killing, one should recite the verse beginning with "samutpatya"; by performing the recitation according to the methods prescribed for killing, the desired result is achieved. This mantra, beginning with "sarvābādhāpraśamanam," destroys enemies and rescues those in distress. By the mere recitation of the verse beginning with "jñānināmapi cetāṃsi," [the desired effect] occurs instantly.

That it is "deluding" (mohana) is established by experience; indeed, it is necessarily so when reciting that verse. By reciting the verse beginning with "rogānaśeṣān" at every single verse, all diseases are destroyed; the same result occurs even through the chanting of its mantra.

Thus addressed, the Goddess then [spoke]; by reciting a counter-verse (*pratiśloka*) to the verse beginning with "O Profound One" (*gambhīrā*), or by chanting it separately, there is the attainment of knowledge (*vidyā*) and the destruction of defects of speech. The verse beginning with "O Medha, O Sarasvatī, O Excellent One" (*medhe sarasvati vare*) is also understood to bestow knowledge. All this was performed by the Blessed Lady; thus ends the twelfth [chapter].

The hundred-syllable mantra bestows all desires and wards off all calamities; it has been stated previously that for the fire-oblation (homa), one should perform only half [of the recitation]. O Goddess, regarding the verse beginning with "O Destroyer of the distress of those who have sought refuge, be gracious," one should perform the recitation (japa) one hundred thousand times, ten thousand times, or one hundred times, whether by chanting the entire verse or by reciting it line by line.

"The cessation of all calamities and the attainment of all desires. Thus was that Blessed Lady described; this half-verse mantra bestows splendor through its recitation. By the recitation or chanting of the mantra "O Goddess, be gracious," there is the destruction of enemies, sins, and afflictions. The half-verse mantra beginning with "vañcitābhyām" is for the offering of water.

From the *Haragaurī Tantra*: "O Great One! Like Indra by his might, like Parjanya who brings rain, the sacrifice has increased through the son of Vatsa. You are taken with a vessel; for Mahendra you are! This is your womb; for Mahendra you are! O giver of water!"—thus say the followers of the Yajurveda. For the pacification of excessive rain: *Oṃ*.
Go to the ocean, svāhā! Go to the intermediate space, svāhā! Go to the divine Savitṛ, svāhā!
Go to Mitra and Varuṇa, svāhā! Go to Day and Night, svāhā! Go to the meters, svāhā!
Svāhā! Go to Heaven and Earth; Svāhā! Go to the sacrifice; Svāhā! Go to Soma; Svāhā!
Go to the celestial atmosphere; Svāhā! Go to Agni Vaiśvānara. Svāhā! May my mind enter into me; may your smoke go to heaven, and your light to the sun; [may] the earth [be covered] with ashes.
One should mutter the mantra "pṛṇasva āhā."

O King, that which you pray for is fulfilled by this single verse repeated many times, which brings satisfaction to the Goddess. Others maintain that the verse beginning with "śaṅkha-cakra-gadā-śārṅga-gṛhīta-paramāyudhe" also yields this same fruit. [This applies to] women as well.
Desiring good fortune and for the sake of obtaining a husband who is not separated from his wife, one should recite the mantra: "O Mother! O Ambika! O Ambalika!

Someone with well-fed horses is leading away Subhadrika, the dweller of Kampila. One should recite this verse along with its counter-mantra (*pratimantra*). In all cases, one may recite it either enclosing [the name] within the mantra (*saṃpuṭīkṛtya*) or by placing it at the beginning and end (*pallavīkṛtya*).

"One should mutter certain mantras; this is the sequence of the deities as declared by Śiva. In these applications, by performing a prostration before each verse or even just before the lamp, success is swiftly attained. Thus ends the procedure for the application as taught in the *Kātyāyanī-tantra*. [Endorsed by] one residing in Argaḷapura, of Gauḍa lineage.
By the eminent scholar born of the Bhāradvāja lineage, Gosvāmī Paṇḍita Bulākhirāma’s son,
the venerable Pūjya Śrī Vidyādharmavardhinī Pathashālā’s teacher of the Karmakāṇḍa of the Yajurveda, adorned with the title "Vidyābhūṣaṇa" and "Karmakāṇḍamaṇi."
The procedure for the worship of Durgā compiled by Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Gosvāmī is completed.
On the tenth day, there is the worship of the Vijayā and the Śamī tree.
Now, on the tenth day of Vijayā, for the sake of attaining the year-long journey without obstacles, there is the worship of the Śamī tree.

The time for the worship of the Śamī tree is as follows, according to the Jyotirnibandha: "When the twilight has slightly passed and the stars have just begun to appear, this period called Vijaya is the accomplisher of all desires and aims."
Having gone outside the city or village toward the northeast corner, near a *śamī* tree, one should sprinkle the ground,
spread a white cloth upon it, draw an eight-petalled lotus with rice grains on top of that,
and place a water-pot (*kalaśa*) in the center.

Having sipped water (ācamana), restrained the breaths (prāṇāyāma), and performed the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) preceded by the recitation of auspicious verses (svastivācana), one should worship Gaṇeśa, the five Oṃkāras, the sixteen Mothers (ṣoḍaśamātṛkā), the nine planets (navagraha), the ritual pitcher (kalaśa), and so forth. Then,
having dug up the earth from the root of a Śamī tree and placed white rice, betel nut, gold, or silver therein—
Having circumambulated, he then ties the *śamī* leaves together with the *golaka* and takes them at the conclusion of the worship for the sake of accomplishing all his undertakings.
p.

429) *Saṃkalpa*: Having recited the lunar day, weekday, and other details: "For the sake of attaining victory on this journey, [I shall perform] the worship of Vāstu, the worship of the Guardians of the Directions (*digpāla*), the worship of the deities of the path (*mārgadevatā*), the worship of the *śamī* tree, and the worship of the *aparājitā* plant."
I shall perform [this]. Oṃ, salutation to Aparājitā. To the south, Oṃ, salutation to Kriyā; to the left, Oṃ, salutation to Umā. Afterwards, one should meditate upon the Śamī tree.

"I take refuge in the auspicious Śamī tree, which pacifies inauspiciousness, pacifies evil deeds, destroys bad dreams, and is blessed. Obeisance to the deity of the Śamī. With this mantra, one should worship the Śamī tree with the prescribed offerings. Then follows the prayer:
In the future, O Śamī tree, may my sin be pacified; O red-thorned Śamī!

O upholder of Arjuna’s arrows, the beloved speaker of Rāma; may you, worshipped by Śrī Rāma, act as the remover of obstacles for me there during my upcoming journey at the proper time, so that it may proceed happily.

"O Śamī tree, pacify my sin; O Śamī, you are the destroyer of enemies! You are the wielder of Arjuna’s bow and the beloved speaker of Rāma. Thus is the prayer. The mantra for the stream of water is: "O Goddess, I have sprinkled [you] with water; grant me constant peace. With this, one should offer a stream of water at the root of the Śamī tree during the rite of worship.
May there be no obstacle to future undertakings. The consecration with the hymn beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā. Auspiciousness.
Benedictions. By this worship, may the deity Śamī be pleased.
Seeing the bow at the time of departure is auspicious.

Nīlakaṇṭha, Maṇigrīva, Svastika, Aparājita, Aśoka, Aviśoka, Nandana, and Puṣṭivardhana—these are the eight names of the blue jay (cāṣa). Whoever recites them upon seeing a blue jay shall achieve success in his undertakings and obtain delicious food and beautiful women. [The presiding deities of] the directions.
Worship: Homage to Śamī, the cow who milks out all desires. For the accomplishment of whatever tasks are to be done in the eastern direction, I undertake this journey. Oṃ!
That same journey which was Śaṅkara’s for the burning of Tripura, that which was Arjuna’s at Khāṇḍava, and that journey of Rāghava for crossing the ocean—[may it be mine].

May that sea voyage undertaken by the son of the Wind-god for the purpose of fetching the medicinal herbs— during which Lakṣmaṇa was pierced by a spear— be a bestower of success upon my journey and a grantor of all happiness within my home.
An image of the enemy should be fashioned with rice grains in all directions; having gone four or ten steps, one should recite:
"Oṃ, I invoke Indra, the protector, Indra, the helper;
at every call, I invoke the easily-invoked Śara-Indra; I invoke Śakra, the much-invoked Indra; may the bountiful Indra grant us well-being."

"Trātāram indra" (The Savior Indra)—thus, salutation to Indra. One should worship with milk, lamps, and so forth. Again, having placed one's foot upon an effigy of the enemy fashioned from rice grains.
Afterwards, having come to the foot of a *śamī* tree: "Homage to the *śamī*, the cow that milks one's desires."
For the sake of accomplishing the task desired by my noble kinsman, I shall commence my journey toward the southern direction.
Having recited "Oṃ yāyātra... and so forth, and having gone four steps or ten, [he says]: "Oṃ!
For the sake of going, for the sake of sacrifice, for the sake of the heat of the sun—may the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey;
touch the surface of the earth; protect us! You are flame, you are light, you are heat."
One should worship with a stream of milk, a lamp, and so forth, using either the mantra *oṃ yamāyātva* or the name-mantra *oṃ yamāya namaḥ*.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing one’s purpose, while remaining centered in the mind, one should worship with a stream of milk, a lamp, and so forth, [thinking]:
"I begin my journey toward the western direction. One should worship with a stream of milk, a lamp, and so forth.
Again, having fashioned an image of the enemy out of rice and holding it by the feet, one should go to the root of a *śamī* tree.
Furthermore, the mantra beginning with "To Abhilāṣā, the milch-cow; to Śamī, obeisance; to Yāyātrā... and so forth is recited.

Having gone four steps or ten, [recite]: "Oṃ, you are the support of Varuṇa; you are the pillar of Varuṇa; you are the two cords of Varuṇa; you are the seat of Varuṇa’s truth; you are the place where Varuṇa sits according to truth; sit upon the seat of Varuṇa’s truth. Oṃ.

One should worship Varuṇa with the mantra "varuṇasyottam" or with the mantra "varuṇāya namaḥ," using a stream of milk, lamps, and other offerings. Then, having placed one's feet upon a sacrificial seat (śrū) fashioned from rice grains and having approached the root of a Śamī tree, [one should worship] with the mantra: "abhilāṣa-dogdhryai śamyai namaḥ."

Then, in the northern direction, I shall commence my journey for the sake of accomplishing all goals. Having recited "Oṃ yāyātra... and so forth, and having gone four steps or ten, [the mantra]: *vayaguṃ somavrate tava manaḥ manūṣu bibhrataḥ prajāyantaḥ*.

We shall perform [the rite]. With the mantra "Oṃ Vayaguṃ Somavrata" or with the mantra "Oṃ Somāya Namaḥ," one should worship with a stream of milk, a lamp, and so forth. Then, having gone to the root of a Śamī tree and having collected earth and Śamī leaves—as it is stated in the Matsya Purāṇa:

At the conclusion of the worship, clay should be taken; it should be taken from the root of a *śamī* tree. From that, by the grace of the *śamī*, gold is obtained. The mantra for this is: Oṃ, O Agni, speak to us; be well-disposed toward us. Bestow upon us [wealth], O conqueror of thousands, for you are the giver of riches. Svāhā!
p.
431) The Prayer of the Khañjarīṭa Bird.
O blue-necked one, O auspicious-necked one, bestower of the fruits of all desires;
you have descended upon the earth—O Khañjarīṭa, salutations to you!
You are a son of a sage, disciplined in yoga; you have become invisible even with the rising of your crest-lock of fire.
You are seen when the rainy season has arrived; O wonder among the *khañjana* birds, salutations, salutations to you!
The fruit of seeing a wagtail varies according to each direction.
In lotuses, cows, elephants, horses, and great serpents, it bestows sovereignty; in pure green grassy meadows, it grants well-being.
O Khañjarīṭa bird, seen among ashes, bones, hair, nails, body hair, and husks, you surely cause much suffering.

Wealth is attained in the northeast (Īśāna); the incomparable accomplishment of one's purpose in the east (Brahman); fear in the southeast (Śakra) and the southwest (Hutāśa); fear of fire in the south (Yāmyā);
strife with the enemies of the gods in the west (Suradviṭ); gain in the northwest (Samudrālaya);
excellent garments, perfumes, water, and celestial women in the north (Vāyavyā); and death is declared to be certain in the northeast (Aiśānī).
The characteristic of direction is found in the crowing of a cock.
Some among them must be bears, while others must be monkeys;
some must have red faces, for the gratification of the Lord of Kosala.
The Rākṣasas and Daityas, the enemies upon the surface of the earth, have been utterly defeated;
"Rāma’s kingdom! Rāma’s kingdom! Rāma’s kingdom! they cried. (1)
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the worship of the Śamī tree.
p.
432) Materials for the oblation (*varaṇa*) in the *Rudrakalpa*.
Food, the vessel for food, the umbrella, sandals,
the water-pot, the seat, clothing, the mudrā, ear-ornaments, and the sacred thread.
These ten kinds of gifts should be given for the sake of attaining the supreme state;
in the absence of these, three things should be given: a vessel, a garment, and a finger-ring.
Now, an ancient verse found within the recitation of the Śrī Durgā Saptaśatī is presented.
The First Chapter.
While the king remained at the foot of a tree absorbed in such thoughts,
a certain merchant, likewise overcome by distress, arrived there.
Having sat down and become composed, that best of men spoke to him.
The Vaiśya said:
"O Vaiśya, I am indeed a Maitreya by caste, renowned by the name Samādhi. (20)
He was wealthy, skilled in righteousness, truthful in speech, and not a backbiter;
[he was devoted] to his sons and wife... || 21 ||
And deprived... [text missing] ... ||
Abandoned by my own kinsmen, I have indeed quickly reached this forest.
"O Koṣṭhika, you appear fortunate; tell me now about your beloved.
The king said:
"I am a king named Suratha, and I have been oppressed by bandits. (25)
"You have arrived here, deprived of your kingdom and deceived by your ministers; my family is left without support, bereft of me, and deeply distressed. (26)
And he will become distressed with anxiety, tormented by disease and grief; how is it for you? What indeed... [27]
O high-minded one, you have been abandoned by your sons and others who are of wicked conduct and utterly foolish; seeing them now, what happiness will there be for you today? (29)
An enemy who acts for one's benefit is superior, while friends who cause suffering are of no account;
therefore, having made your mind firm, sport with me.
The Vaiśya said:
"It is even as you have said... O King, my mind is not steady today; it is exceedingly distressed. (31)
"O wicked ones, why do you worry here about this family so difficult to abandon?
What shall I do... [etc. ...? (32)
The king said:
The sorrow born of my kingdom indeed torments my mind;
therefore, let us today question the peaceful Sage, who is the medicine that destroys grief.
Having formed this thought, both the king and the Vaiśya went to the sage;
endowed with humility, they questioned him regarding the cause of his grief. (38)
Having approached and prostrated before that unsurpassed seer as he sat there, the king, himself seated properly and having attained tranquility, spoke to the peaceful one.
He spoke to him that supreme knowledge which destroys sorrow and delusion.
Delusion does not depart; what is the cause of this wonder?
O Lord, you are omniscient, the destroyer of all doubt. (45)
The sage said:
Listen, O King, I shall explain the cause of bondage and liberation:
that which is renowned here as Mahāmāyā is the cause for all living beings. (46)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Īśāna, Turāṣāṭ (Indra), Varuṇa, and Anila—all the gods, humans, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas. || 47 ||
Various trees, creepers, beasts, wild animals, and birds—all these are subject to Māyā and are the vessel for both bondage and liberation. (48)
By her all this world, both stationary and moving, was created;
it certainly remains under her control, bound by the net of delusion. (49)
How insignificant you are among men, a single kṣatriya clouded by passion!
For she incessantly deludes even the minds of the wise.
Even Brahmā, Īśa, Vāsudeva, and the others, though possessing complete knowledge, wander deluded in the world under the influence of passion.
The king said:
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, what is this delusion that exists over the wise man, and which likewise exists for me and for him? ... 52 ...
He praised Hari, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, who was motionless in the sleep of yoga, with auspicious words of address for the purpose of awakening him.
Brahmā said:
O Hare, O Viṣṇu, O Vāmana, arise, O Mādhava!
O Hṛṣīkeśa, who removes the suffering of devotees, O Abode of All, O Lord of the Universe! 72.
O Inner Controller, O immeasurable Self, O Vāsudeva, Lord of the universe, O foremost destroyer of wicked enemies, O wielder of the discus and the mace! 73.
O Omniscient One, Lord of all worlds, endowed with all powers! Arise, arise, O Lord of gods; O destroyer of suffering, protect me! 74.
O Sustainer of the Universe, O Large-eyed One, whose hearing and chanting are meritorious;
O Source of the World, O Formless One, O Cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution! (75)
"O Great King, these two Daityas, arrogant with pride, desire to kill me;
O Support of All, how is it that you do not know that I have fallen into such peril? (76)
O Protector, O Mahāviṣṇu, if you disregard me who am afflicted by suffering and have come to you for refuge, then I shall be left without support.
When the Blessed One Hari, overcome by yogic sleep, did not wake even though praised in this manner, Brahmā then reflected: || 78 ||
Overcome by a deficiency of power, Viṣṇu fell under the sway of sleep;
the righteous-souled one did not wake, thinking, "What shall I do now, being so distressed? (79)
"Both these Dānavas, arrogant with pride, have arrived desiring to kill me.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? There is no refuge for me anywhere. (80)
Having reflected thus in his mind and reached a firm conclusion, he deliberated further in his mind: "Is my power sufficient for her protection? (81)
"Indeed, by her Viṣṇu was rendered insentient and devoid of movement";
having formed this thought, Brahmā then remained seated upon the lotus stalk.
O Goddess, you are indeed the cause of this world, as I have learned from the words of all the Vedas;

and even Viṣṇu, the supreme person and the discerning creator of all the worlds, has today been brought under the power of sleep. O Mother, who knows the playful sport of your delusive power? I am bewildered, and even this Hari is rendered helpless.
Thus, as the abode of the minds of all beings, he who is the most learned among millions of wise men lies down in such a state, for she is devoid of qualities.

The Sāṃkhyas speak of the Puruṣa and that Prakṛti which is devoid of the nature of consciousness, yet the creator of the world. Are you such a one? How is it that today, O Abode of the World, You have been fashioned by her as one devoid of consciousness?
You perform a drama of manifold kinds endowed with qualities, yet no one understands the application of the methods of Your deeds;
the hosts of sages meditate upon You, having designated You by the name "Sandhyā" (Twilight) due to Your attributes at the three fixed times of the day.
O Bhavānī! || 102 ||
For you are always the intellect that awakens all worlds; O Goddess, you are Śrī, the eternal bestower of happiness upon the gods.
Furthermore, O Mother, you are indeed fame, intelligence, fortitude, and beauty, as well as faith and passion among all people.
Since I have fallen into this miserable state, I have indeed obtained no proof through hundreds of further arguments;
and you here are truly the mother of all worlds, while Hari, who bestows even sleepiness upon this place, has [failed to protect me].
It has been seen. || 104 ||
O Goddess, you are difficult to be conceived even by those who know the Vedas; indeed, even the Veda does not know you in your entirety.
For this Śruti, having attained its origin from you, perceives all this activity of yours as if it were directly before its eyes.

The wise one alone on earth knows your entire conduct; neither I, nor Hari, nor Bhava, nor the other gods, nor even the sages, nor my own sons are capable of knowing it. Thus, your greatness is indeed beyond words.
In the entire world. || 106 ||
O Goddess, even when the learned ones perform oblations in sacrifices, if they do not utter "svāhā" to you,
the gods do not receive their constant share of the sacrificial offering; indeed, you alone are the recipient among the deities.
A female servant for wages. || 107 ||
O Blessed One, we were first protected by you from the fear of existence arising from the enemy of the gods; likewise,
O Goddess, granter of boons, I am now terrified and have come to you for refuge upon beholding the terrible Madhu.
And Kaiṭabha. || 108 ||
"Viṣṇu does not know this suffering of mine at present; I know that you have brought his slender body under your own control.
O high-minded one, either release the god or slay the two lords of the Dānavas; do as pleases you."
O Goddess, those who do not know your supreme power meditate even upon Hari and Hara with dull minds;
O Mother, it has been clearly proven by me today that even Viṣṇu is utterly surpassed [by you].
Then, rendered helpless, he lies down. || 110 ||
O Goddess, even Lakṣmī, born from the ocean, was not able to awaken Hari; yet today, by your power, she has brought your husband—who is now under your control—under her sway.
I believe that even Ramā was forcibly put to sleep by you and did not wake up.
As if rendered helpless. || 111 ||
Others on this earth, devoted solely to Your feet, having abandoned the worship of other deities and being absorbed in You,
perform all forms of worship with great zeal, O Goddess, knowing You indeed to be the Mother of all.
The realm of desire. || 112 ||

Where have your qualities— wisdom, beauty, fame, auspicious conduct, and virtue— now departed, leaving Viṣṇu behind? Indeed, Hari has been imprisoned here by Sleep, through the power of you alone, O Blessed One, who are so exceedingly proud!

You alone are the power of all worlds, possessing every majesty; indeed, everything composed by you is merely a manifestation of being. You sport within the web of delusion created by yourself, just as actors perform in a drama through their own creations.
At the beginning of the first age, Viṣṇu was manifested by you, and indeed the stainless power for protection was granted.
And everything has been entirely rescued and rendered submissive today; O Mother, you surely do exactly as pleases you. || 115 ||

O Blessed One, if you have no desire to destroy me after having created me here, why then, setting aside your silence out of compassion, have you manifested these two who are truly the very form of Death? Or rather, O Bhavānī, do you perhaps wish to laugh?
I have understood your wondrous activity: having created this entire universe, you sport as an independent one;
you indeed cause all to dissolve, and likewise, O Bhavānī, do you wish to destroy me—what is there in this?
The variegated. || 117 ||
O Mother, O Mother of the World, perform my execution this very day; let there be no grief for me born of death.
For you alone were appointed as the agent from the beginning, and thus the infamy will rest upon you: "He was slain by a demon and has died."
The most venerable. || 118 ||
Arise, O Goddess, and assume a wondrous form; either destroy me or these two as you wish, O playful child!
Otherwise, awaken Hari, for he would slay us both—he who must surely accomplish this entire task through you.
It has arisen. || 119 ||
The sage said:
Having emerged from the body of Hari, she then stood at his side,
having left behind all the limbs of Viṣṇu, who possesses incomparable splendor.
Then that yogic sleep departed for the destruction of those two;
when Janārdana became one whose body was moving again.
Then, seeing Hari, the Creator attained supreme joy when sleep had departed from the body of that Teacher of the World. (123)
And he rose up...
[omission] ...at that time, seeing Prajāpati standing there, terrified with fear. || 125 ||
And the one of great splendor spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Blessed One, O Lotus-born One, why have you come here, having abandoned your ascetic penance?"
"Why are you afflicted by illness, with your mind overwhelmed by fear?
Brahmā said:
O Lord, the two Daityas Madhu and Kaiṭabha were born from the wax of your ears.
"Those two of terrible form and great strength have approached to slay me.
Viṣṇu said:
"Stay today; you have become fearless, for I shall indeed slay those two. (128)
Confused and with their lives departed, the two warriors came to me from the battle;
for in the single ocean... || 129 ||
"The two terrible Dānavas are not tired, yet I am exhausted; this is a marvel.
Hari then reflected that there must be a cause for their death.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, request the boon desired by your heart;
we are satisfied with your battle and with your wonderful deeds, O Vāsudeva.
Having heard those words of theirs, Janārdana replied.
Viṣṇu said:
"May they become today... [and so forth]...
"Having seen them by those two... [and so forth]...
Having heard those words of Viṣṇu, those two Daityas were greatly astonished. (137)
Thinking, "We have been deceived," they stood there filled with grief;
having reflected thus in their minds, those two Dānavas spoke to Viṣṇu. (138)
"Having observed that everything is composed of water and devoid of land or ground, O Madhusūdana, slay him in a vast region where there is no water. (139)
"Kill us both... [omission] ...we two are to be slain by you; O Mādhava, be true to your word. (140)
Then, remembering that discus, Viṣṇu, the Lord Hari, smilingly said to them both: "O highly fortunate ones, today I shall slay you on a vast, waterless plain."
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods, having made his thighs exceedingly wide,
displayed them there above the water, even though they were without water. (142)
The Blessed One then doubled his loins; amazed, they both placed their heads upon those most wonderful loins.
When it was then split by the powerful Viṣṇu with the wheel of his chariot, [he] said, "So be it," and... || 144 ||
Then the two Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, became lifeless;
at that time, the entire ocean was indeed pervaded by their fat.
Thus has this [goddess] arisen... [omission] ...
May there be power for this goddess... [omission] ... || 146 ||

Now begins the second chapter.
The one of middling conduct. The gods said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction;
O great king, ocean of mercy, protect us who have come to you for refuge!
O Great King, they were oppressed by Mahiṣa, a man of evil deeds, incurable, exceedingly wicked, arrogant due to his boons, and sinful. || 5 ||
He enjoys the sacrificial portions offered by the Brāhmaṇas,
while the gods wander through mountain fastnesses, overcome with fear.
The sage said:
Having heard those words, Viṣṇu spoke to them as if smiling:
"War was fought by us in the past, yet even so, he did not die."
If this woman of excellent hips were born today from the combined splendor and the perfection of form of all the gods, she would surely overcome him by force in battle.
"A woman fashioned from a portion of Śakti would indeed be capable of slaying this enemy of horses, who is exceedingly proud and skilled in the employment of illusion. (13)
And let them again request portions of our splendor so that,
born from those portions of splendor, he may become a mass of radiance.
We all, led by Rudra, give her all our divine weapons, including the trident and whatever others there may be. (15)
A woman bearing all weapons and endowed with all splendor shall slay that wicked-souled, sinful man who is arrogant on account of me. (16)
Having heard this thus... [he] became enraged... || 17 ||
Red in color, of auspicious form, with the luster of a ruby;
somewhat cool and likewise warm, adorned with a network of rays. || 21 ||
It was seen by Hari and by the high-souled Hara;
O great king, those two of wide stride were filled with wonder.
From the body of Śaṅkara, however, there issued forth a great marvel:
a fierce, silver-colored, formidable, and vast being that was difficult to behold. || 23 ||
It was terrifying to the Daityas and a source of wonder to the gods;
it was of a terrible form, resembling a mountain, like another manifestation of the quality of darkness (tamas).
Then, from the body of Viṣṇu, there appeared another mass of splendor,
blue in color and endowed with the quality of sattva, possessing great radiance.
Then, from the body of Indra, there emerged a radiant form of variegated appearance, difficult to approach, perfectly formed, and consisting of all excellent qualities.
From the bodies of Kuvera, Yama,
and Vahni, as well as from that of Varuṇa, a great splendor issued forth on all sides.
And from the bodies of other gods as well, that exceedingly radiant and most brilliant mass of great splendor emerged. || 28 ||
Seeing him, all the gods, led by Viṣṇu, were struck with wonder;
he was a mass of splendor, most divine, like another Himalaya mountain.
While the gods were watching there, from the emergence of a mass of splendor,
there arose an exceedingly excellent woman, beautiful and inspiring wonder.
She is Mahālakṣmī, composed of the three guṇas, born from the bodies of all the gods;
she has eighteen beautiful arms, possesses three colors, and is the enchantress of the universe.
With a white face and black eyes, her sprout-like lower lip was reddened;
she had copper-colored palms, was lovely, and adorned with divine ornaments.
The goddess has eighteen arms and is adorned with a thousand arms;
whatever was of Śambhu became... || 34 ||
Beholding her, they experienced great joy;
then, those beings endowed with vigor extracted the splendor from their own weapons. (40)
Then the gods gave her their own various weapons and cried out loudly, "Victory! Victory! desiring her triumph as she was victorious. (41)
Seeing her equipped with weapons and adorned with ornaments, those sages were filled with wonder and praised her. || 56 ||
Salutations to Śivā, the auspicious one; salutations again and again to Peace and Nourishment.
O Blessed One, salutations to the Goddess; constant salutations to Rudrāṇī.
Salutations again and again to you, Kālarātri, and likewise to Ambā, Indrāṇī;
salutations again and again to you, Siddhi, Buddhi, Vṛddhi, and Vaiṣṇavī. || 58 ||
I bow to that supreme Goddess who, though situated within the earth, is not known as "earth" by the earth itself, yet from within it impels all things. 59.
"O Mother, do what is auspicious; protect us who are tormented by enemies!
O Enemy of Māra, destroy with your own splendor this evil one who has been deluded. (60)
Wicked, deceitful, and terrible, he was to be slain by a woman; arrogant due to his boon, a giver of misery to all the gods, and a rogue who assumed various forms.
O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, you alone are the refuge of all the gods; O Goddess, protect us today from the oppressed by the Dānava; salutations to you!
The sage said:
Thus praised then by all the gods, the Goddess who bestows all happiness spoke these auspicious words with a smile to them: || 63 ||
The Goddess said:
"O gods, cast away your fear of the dull-witted Mahiṣa;
today itself in battle, I shall slay him who is arrogant due to his boons and utterly deluded."
Having thought thus, the goddess let out a smile accompanied by a loud, most terrible laugh, which struck fear into the Dānavas. (65)
Upon hearing that wondrous sound, the earth trembled there;
all the mountains shook, and the powerful ocean was agitated.
All the directions were filled with the sound of Meruścapāla;
hearing that great noise, the Dānavas then fell into terror.
"Victory! Protect us! the gods said to her, filled with supreme joy;
and Mahiṣa, too, hearing that sound, became enraged, intoxicated by his pride.
Suspecting it to be his own voice, he asked those Daityas, "What is this?
and commanded, "Let messengers go quickly to discover the source of this sound."
(445) Whence and who is this most fierce sound that causes pain to the ears? Is it a god or perhaps a dānava who is the maker of this noise? (70)
"Let them seize that evil-minded one and bring him here to me;
I shall go and slay that sinner whose efforts have been in vain."
Thus addressed by him, those messengers [approached] the Goddess, who was beautiful in all her limbs,
possessing eighteen divine arms, and adorned with every ornament.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, bearing excellent weapons, and beautiful, she held a goblet in her hand and drank from it again and again. || 73 ||
Having observed this, terrified of worldly existence, they fled in fear and great alarm;
they quickly went into the presence of Mahiṣa and told him the cause of their own terror.
The messengers said:
"O Lord of the Daityas, a certain mature woman is seen;
she is an ornament to every limb, a lady adorned with all kinds of jewels. (75)
She is neither human nor asura; she is divine in form and captivating.
Mounted upon a lion, bearing weapons, and possessing eighteen hands, she is most excellent.
That woman utters a cry and appears intoxicated with passion; she is clearly devoted to drinking liquor. We know her to be a wanton woman who is not faithful to her husband.
Standing in the sky, the gods, accompanied by me, praised her:
"For what purpose have you come here, and what does this beautiful woman intend to do? (78)
"Overwhelmed by his splendor, we are not at all able to look upon him.
Mahiṣa said:
"Go, O hero, commanded by me, O best of ministers, accompanied by an army. (79)
"Bring together that lady of beautiful countenance by means of conciliation and other such methods.
The sage said:
Having heard the eloquent words of Mahisha, the best of ministers [spoke].
He went swiftly, accompanied by elephants, horses, and chariots;
having gone a great distance and come to a halt, he spoke to that high-minded woman.
The minister said:
"Who are you, O sweet-spoken one? What is the purpose of your coming here?
O illustrious lady, my lord asks after you through my mouth. (82)
"Indeed, he is the creator of all gods and is invulnerable to men;
the king named Mahiṣa, a ruler of the earth, desires to see me. (83)
(446) He is utterly under your sway because of the fame of your beauty;
O lady with thighs like a young elephant’s trunk, tell me quickly how I should act. 84.
The seer said:
Having heard these words of his, that most excellent of women laughed and,
O Great King, spoke to him with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The Goddess said:
"O best of ministers, know me indeed to be the mother of the gods;
I am renowned as Mahālakṣmī, the destroyer of all the Daityas. (86)
"I was requested by all the gods for the sake of slaying Mahiṣa;
therefore, I have come here today, having made an effort for his destruction. (87)
"Go to the netherworld with honey, if you have any desire for life;
otherwise, I shall slay you, O wicked evildoer, upon the field of battle. (88)
"Let Mādhava attain heaven; let the gods be consumers of the oblation.
Go to the netherworld as pus, if you wish to live! (89)
The sage said:
Having heard what the goddess said, the Dānava reflected:
"Let him do as the goddess has commanded today, according to her pleasure. (90)
Having reflected thus, the wise son of the minister went into the presence of the king;
having prostrated before him, he spoke these words with palms joined in reverence. (91)
The minister said:
O King, the goddess of beautiful form is seated upon a lion;
she has eighteen arms, is enchanting, and is supreme, bearing excellent weapons.
I said to her, "O great king, O beautiful woman, choose Mahiṣa;
become the queen of the king, the beloved of the sovereign of the three worlds. (93)
Having heard these words of mine, that large-eyed woman, deluded by the onset of a smile, spoke these words to me with a preceding smile: 94.
"I shall wage war against you in battle and slay you, O beloved of the gods;
or go, O wicked one, to the netherworld (pātāla), if you have any desire for life. (95)
Mahiṣa said:
"Go, O illustrious Tāmra, resolved for battle;
having conquered that proud woman of noble form by righteous means, bring her back. (96)
The seer said:
Having heard those words spoken by him, Tāmra, overcome by the power of time, departed after bowing down to King Mahiṣa. || 97 ||
Having gone there and beheld her seated upon a lion,
being praised by all the gods and adorned with every kind of weapon, he [the god] approached.
Vinīti spoke these words to her with a sweet voice:
"O Queen, Śṛṅgin, the lord of the Daityas, is infatuated by the beauty and virtues of your form. (99)
The buffalo king indeed desires to take your hand in marriage;
enjoy the full happiness of sovereignty for tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of years.
The Goddess said:
"Go and speak to Tāmrapati, who is on the verge of death and whose mind is obsessed with me—to Mahiṣa, who is excessively lustful, deluded, and devoid of wisdom. (101)
I am not a woman choosing her own husband; rather, my husband is the Lord.
He is the creator of all, the witness of all, indeed the non-doer, free from desire, and eternal.
Devoid of qualities, free from the sense of "mine," infinite, without support, and without refuge;
omniscient, omnipresent, the witness, perfect, with a perfect intention—He is Śiva. || 103 ||
He is the abode of all, patient, peaceful, all-seeing, and the creator of all;
having abandoned that bull [of a man], how could I venture to serve this dull-witted one? 104.
"O wicked one, if you have a desire for life, go quickly to the netherworld along with all the dānavas; otherwise, I shall slay you in battle."
The sage said:
Having spoken thus, that goddess always roared most wonderfully;
she let out a sound like the end of a kalpa, bringing fear to the Daityas.
Having heard that sound, Tāmra, his mind then terrified with fear,
fled from there and went into the presence of Mahiṣa.
And those Daityas who were in Ayodhyā also fell into anxiety;
seeing that Tāmra had arrived, even Hayāri was deluded.
"Stay! Stay! ... [and so on] ...
Having cried out "Stay! Stay!", other Daityas fought in the battle. (139)
In that hair-raising battle, their limbs were drenched in streams of blood, as chariots and elephants were struck down. (140)
(448) By the Goddess and by the Gaṇas... ... ... | As they were satisfied... ... ... ... || 144 ||

A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose in the army of that evil-minded one;
they wailed and shrieked loudly with cries of "Save us! Save us! (20).
"O King, those other soldiers who were devoured by the lion—
" having heard those words of theirs, the buffalo then became dejected in mind.
Having heard those words of theirs, the lord of men, filled with wrath, quickly said to Dāruka: "Bring me that wonderful chariot!"
Yoked with a thousand donkeys, adorned with banners and flags,
equipped with weapons, white, with excellent wheels and a beautiful pole.
Knowing that the chariot had been brought, the exceedingly powerful lord of the Dānavas, equipped with all weapons and furnished with excellent coverings, [prepared to depart]. || 24 ||
Having assumed a human body and being prepared to go into battle,
he abandoned that buffalo form and became an auspicious man.
Wearing divine garments, he was as lovely as another God of the Flower-arrows;
then, they beheld him approaching as the sovereign of the Daityas.
While he was surrounded by many heroes, the goddess sounded her conch shell;
approaching the goddess, he spoke to her as if smiling.
O Goddess, while revolving in this wheel of saṃsāra, a person—whether man or woman—indeed desires happiness in every way. (28)
The union that is always described as occurring between a woman and a man who are equally beloved and of equal age is considered the most excellent. (29)
If you enter into union with me, a hero, there will undoubtedly be for you the attainment of the most supreme happiness. (30)
All the gods, beginning with Indra, have been conquered by me in battle;
whatever divine jewels there are in this palace of mine now [are mine]. (31)
Enjoy all of these as you wish, or give them away as you please;
become the chief queen today, O beautiful one, for I am your slave.
(449) By the Goddess and by the Gaṇas... ... ... | Just as they were satisfied... ... ... || 144 ||

A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose in the army of that evil-minded one;

"O King, those other soldiers who were devoured by the lion—
" having heard those words, the buffalo then became dejected in mind.
Having heard those words of theirs, the lord of men, filled with wrath, quickly said to Dāruka: "Bring me that wonderful chariot!"
It was yoked to a thousand donkeys, adorned with banners and flags,
equipped with weapons, brilliant, with excellent wheels and a beautiful pole.
Knowing that the chariot had been brought, the mighty lord of the Dānavas, equipped with all weapons and furnished with excellent coverings, [prepared to depart]. || 24 ||
Having assumed a human body and being prepared to go into battle,
he abandoned that buffalo form and became an auspicious man.
Wearing divine garments, the lovely one was like another god of the flower-arrows;
seeing him, the lord of the Daityas, approaching at that time—
While the hero was surrounded by many, the goddess sounded her conch shell;
approaching the goddess, he spoke to her as if smiling.
O Goddess, while remaining in this wheel of saṃsāra, a person—whether man or woman—indeed desires happiness in every way. (28)
The union that is always described as occurring between a woman and a man who are equally beloved and of equal age is considered the most excellent of all. || 29 ||
If you enter into union with me, a hero, there will undoubtedly be for you the attainment of the most supreme bliss. (30)
All the gods, beginning with Indra, have been conquered by me in battle;
whatever divine jewels there are in this palace of mine now—[all these belong to me]. (31)
Enjoy all of these as you wish, or give them away as you please;
become the chief queen today, O beautiful one, for I am your slave.
The sage said:
To that Daitya who was speaking thus, the goddess, the blessed one,
that woman of excellent complexion, laughed with a smile and spoke these words.
The Goddess said:
"I do not desire any man other than the Supreme Puruṣa;
O Daitya, it is for his sake that I desire him, and I create this entire world."
He, the Soul of the Universe, beholds me; I am his auspicious Prakṛti.
You are a fool, for you desire union with another woman while I am your very self.
A woman is proclaimed to be a chain for the purpose of binding a man;
knowing that great suffering arises from association with women, why do you remain deluded? (36)
Abandon your enmity with the gods and roam the earth as you please;
or go to the netherworld (pātāla) at your will, if there is any desire for life remaining in you.
Or else, engage in battle; I am powerful at this moment.
O Dānava, I have been sent by all the gods for your destruction.
"O mighty-armed one, I shall slay you; of this there is no doubt.
The sage said:
Thus addressed by the virtuous goddess, the Dānava took up his bow.
She swiftly released arrows, whetted on stone and drawn back to her ear;
the goddess cut them down with iron-tipped shafts discharged in fury.
A terrifying battle took place between the two;
the army, along with its foot-soldiers and chariots, was destroyed by the Goddess and her lion. || 41 ||
The Goddess said:
"Do not be arrogant, O dull-witted one! Stay, stay on the field of battle!
Having slain you, I shall make the best of the gods free from fear. (58)
The sage said:
Having spoken thus, she took a golden goblet filled with wine and drank from it again and again out of anger, desiring to kill the great asura.
Thus that one named Mahiṣa, together with his army and his circle of friends, having deluded the three worlds, was struck down by that goddess. (65)
The gods praised her... [the Gandharva lords sang... || 66 ||
Thus ends the third chapter. || 3 ||

Then, all the gods, led by Indra, being filled with joy upon the slaying of the demon Mahiṣāsura, began to offer hymns of praise.
The hosts of gods, headed by Śakra... [and so forth]...
that entire triple world... [and so forth]... ||

Brahmā creates this world, Viṣṇu sustains it, and Maheśa indeed withdraws it at the time of its end through Your very power.
Even Īśāna becomes destitute when separated from you; therefore, you alone are the cause of the preservation and destruction of the world.
You are fame, intelligence, mindfulness, compassion, mercy, faith, fortitude, the earth, and Lakṣmī, whose abode is the lotus.
You are nourishment (puṣṭi), the digit (kalā), dissolution (vilayā), and Girijā; you are absorption (layā), contentment (tuṣṭi), radiance (prabhā), intellect (buddhi), Umā, and Ramā. || 25 ||
Knowledge, forbearance, fame, and even intelligence—all these are known to reside in you alone within these three worlds.
O Abode of all the worlds, who else is capable of acting swiftly without these powers of yours? (26)
If you are indeed not the power of retention (dhāraṇā), how could even those two— the tortoise and the serpent— be capable of supporting the earth?
If you were not the Earth, how could this entire world, burdened with such great weight, remain suspended in the sky? (27)

O Mother, those deluded men who praise the immortals— the four-faced Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra— along with the Moon, Fire, Yama, Vāyu, Gaṇeśa, and others as being your illusory manifestations, [do so] only because they do not know you. What else could it be?
They prevail in their respective functions. || 28 ||
Those who, having resolved upon the gods, offer abundant oblations into the fire that carries their fame— the fire which has been kindled by those of expanded intellect—
if you are not "Svāhā" for them, how indeed did they attain [their goal]? For do not the deluded ones sacrifice to you alone?
O Goddess, you become the provider of enjoyments for all things moving and unmoving in this world; indeed, by your own portions, you grant life itself eternally.
O Mother, because you nourish your own sons just as you protect others, [you are called Ambā]. || 30 ||

It is a marvel that these demons, though possessing great renown for their power, have not perished even while deprived of life by You; O Mother, for whose sake You have assumed this bodily form, Your delight lies in the sport of battle, and neither of these two is the cause here.
O Mother, you alone are knowledge that bestows happiness, and you are ignorance that brings misery; you alone are the remover of the pain of birth for men.
Yet, though sought after by those seeking liberation, O Mother, you were not truly worshipped by those of dull intellect.
Likewise, by those intent on enjoyments and by those who are distressed.
And for the protection of the worlds... [omitted] ...||
Listen to that which has been told by me... || 42 ||
